Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Majjhimanikāye

The Middle-Length Discourses

Majjhimapaṇṇāsaṭīkā

The Subcommentary to the Middle Fifty Discourses

1. Gahapativaggo

1. The Householder Chapter

1. Kandarakasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Kandaraka Sutta

1. Ārāmapokkharaṇīādīsūti [V 2.0001][M 2.0001] ārāmapokkharaṇīuyyānacetiyaṭṭhānādīsu. Ussannāti bahulā. Asokakaṇikārakoviḷārakumbhīrājarukkhehi sammissatāya taṃ campakavanaṃ nīlādipañcavaṇṇakusumapaṭimaṇḍitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, na campakarukkhānaṃyeva nīlādipañcavaṇṇakusumatāyāti vadanti. Bhagavā kusumagandhasugandhe campakavane viharatīti iminā na māpanakāle eva tasmiṃ nagare campakarukkhā ussannā, atha kho aparabhāgepīti dasseti. “Pañcasatamattehi aḍḍhateḷasehī”ti evaṃ adassitaparicchedena. Hatthino cāreti sikkhāpetīti hatthācariyo hatthīnaṃ sikkhāpako, tassa puttoti āha “hatthācariyassa putto”ti. Tadā bhagavā tesaṃ pasādajananatthaṃ attano buddhānubhāvaṃ aniguhitvāva nisinnoti dassento “chabbaṇṇānaṃ ghanabuddharasmīna”ntiādimāha. Bhagavato ceva gāravenāti bhagavato garubhāvena, bhagavati gāravenāti vā pāṭho.

1. "In the garden ponds, etc." means in the garden ponds, parks, shrines, and other such places. "Abundant" means plentiful. That Campaka grove should be seen as adorned with flowers of five colors, including blue, due to the mingling of Asoka, Kanikara, Kovilara, and Kumbhiraja trees; it is said that this should not be understood as the Campaka trees themselves bearing flowers of five colors. The statement "The Blessed One dwells in the Campaka grove, fragrant with the scent of flowers" indicates that the Campaka trees were abundant in that city not only at the time of measurement but also at a later time. "With about five hundred and twelve and a half" is stated without a specified limit. A `hatthācariyo` is one who guides and trains elephants, an instructor of elephants; `tassa putto` means 'his son', hence it is said, "the son of the elephant trainer." To show that at that time the Blessed One was sitting without concealing his Buddha-power in order to inspire faith in them, he said, beginning with, "of the dense Buddha-rays of six colors..." "Out of reverence for the Blessed One" means due to the venerable state of the Blessed One; or, the reading is "out of reverence toward the Blessed One."

Niccaṃ [V 2.0002] na hotīti abhiṇhaṃ na hoti, kadācideva hotīti attho. Abhiṇhaniccatā hi idha adhippetā, na kūṭaṭṭhaniccatā. Loke kiñci vimhayāvahaṃ disvā hatthavikārampi karonti, aṅguliṃ vā phoṭayanti, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ [M 2.0002] “accharaṃ paharituṃ yutta”nti. Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtanti ayaṃ niruttinayo yebhuyyena upādāya ruḷhīvasena vuttoti veditabbo. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ “yepi te, bho gotama, ahesuṃ atītamaddhāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ, kiñci akattabbampi kariyamānaṃ dukkarabhāvena vimhayāvahaṃ hoti, tathā kiñci kattabbaṃ, purimaṃ garahacchariyaṃ, pacchimaṃ pasaṃsacchariyaṃ, tadubhayaṃ suttapadaso dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

"It is not constant" means it does not occur frequently; the meaning is that it happens only occasionally. For here frequent constancy is intended, not static constancy. When people in the world see something astonishing, they make gestures with their hands or snap their fingers. With reference to this, it is said, "it is fitting to snap the fingers in wonder." The expression 'what has not been before has come to be' is a linguistic principle that should be understood as stated generally by way of established convention. For thus it is said in the Pāli, "Those, Master Gotama, who were in the past..." and so on. Something that should not be done, being done, is astonishing because of its difficulty; likewise something that should be done. The former is blameworthy astonishment, the latter is praiseworthy astonishment. To show both of these by way of sutta passages, it is said, "There..." and so on.

Sammā paṭipāditoti sammāpaṭipadāyaṃ ṭhapito. Esā paṭipadā paramāti etaparamaṃ, bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesoyaṃ yathā “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”ti (a. ni. 4.70). Ayañhettha attho – bhagavā bhikkhusaṅgho paṭipadāya tumhehi paṭipādito, atītepi kāle buddhā etaparamaṃyeva bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sammā paṭipādesuṃ, anāgatepi kāle etaparamaṃyeva bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sammā paṭipādessantīti paribbājako nayaggāhena diṭṭhena adiṭṭhaṃ anuminanto sabbesampi buddhānaṃ sāsane saṅghasuppaṭipattiṃ majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya samasamaṃ katvā dasseti, evaṃ dassento ca tesaṃ sudhammatañca tathā dasseti evāti veditabbo, buddhasubuddhatā pana nesaṃ sarūpeneva dassitāti. Na ito bhiyyoti iminā pāḷiyaṃ etaparamaṃyevāti avadhāraṇena nivattitaṃ dasseti sīlapadaṭṭhānattā samādhissa, samādhipadaṭṭhānattā ca paññāya sīlepi ca abhisamācārikapubbakattā ādibrahmacariyakassa vuttaṃ “ābhisamācārikavattaṃ ādiṃ katvā”ti.

"Rightly conducted" means established in the right practice. "This practice is supreme"—this is the ultimate. This is a statement in the neuter indicating a state, similar to the phrasing, "The sun and moon revolve unevenly." Here the meaning is this: "The Blessed One, the Sangha of monks, has been rightly conducted by you in the practice." In the past, too, the Buddhas rightly conducted the Sangha of monks to this ultimate state. In the future, they will also rightly conduct the Sangha of monks to this ultimate state. Thus, the wanderer, inferring the unseen from the seen by grasping the method, shows that in the dispensation of all Buddhas, the good practice of the Sangha is perfectly equal, like gold broken in the middle. In showing this, he also reveals their excellent Dhamma in the same way; it should be understood thus. Moreover, the well-enlightened state of the Buddhas is shown by its very nature. "Nothing beyond this"—by this, what is excluded by the emphasis in the Pāli phrase "this is the ultimate" is shown. Because virtue is the foundation for concentration, and concentration is the foundation for wisdom, and because proper conduct is preliminary to virtue, it is said of the beginning of the holy life, "having made the practice of proper conduct the beginning."

2. Pucchānusandhiādīsu anantogadhattā “pāṭiekko anusandhī”ti vatvā tamevatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ “bhagavā kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Upasantakāraṇanti upasantabhāvakāraṇaṃ. Tañhi ariyānaṃyeva visayo, tatthāpi ca buddhānaṃ eva anavasesato visayoti imamatthaṃ byatirekato anvayato ca dassetuṃ na hi tvantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ñātatthacariyā kākajātakādivasena veditabbā, lokatthacariyā taṃtaṃpāramipūraṇavasena, buddhatthacariyā mahābodhijātakādivasena. Acchariyaṃ bho gotamātiādinā kandarakena kataṃ pasādapavedanaṃ dasseti.

2. In the connections of questions and so forth, owing to their endless depth, it is said, "Each connection is individual." To make that very meaning clear, it is said, "The Blessed One, it is said..." and so on. "The cause of peace" means the cause of the state of peace. For that is indeed the domain of the noble ones, and even among them, it is the domain of the Buddhas alone without remainder; to show this meaning by way of contrast and agreement, it is said, "For not you..." and so on. Therein, conduct for the welfare of relatives is to be understood by way of the Kāka Jātaka and so on; conduct for the welfare of the world by way of the fulfillment of the various perfections; conduct for the welfare of Buddhahood by way of the Mahābodhi Jātaka and so on. The declaration of faith made by Kandaraka with the words, "Wonderful, Master Gotama!" and so on, is shown.

Yepi tetiādinā tena vuttamatthaṃ paccanubhāsantena bhagavatā sampaṭicchitanti caritattā āha – “santi hi kandarakāti ayampi pāṭiyekko anusandhī”ti[M 2.0003]. Yo hi kandarakena bhikkhusaṅghassa upasantabhāvo kittito, taṃ vibhajitvā dassentopi tena apucchitoyeva attano ajjhāsayena bhagavā “santi hī”tiādinā desanaṃ ārabhi. Tenāha “bhagavato kira etadahosī” [V 2.0003] tiādi. Kappetvāti aññathā santameva attānaṃ aññathā vidhāya. Pakappetvāti sanidassanavasena gahetvā. Tenāha “kuhakabhāvenā”tiādi. Paṭipadaṃ pūrayamānāti kāmaṃ avisesena sekkhā vuccanti, te pana adhigatamaggavasena “pūrayamānā”ti na vattabbā kiccassa niṭṭhitattā. Maggo hi ekacittakkhaṇikoti āha “uparimaggassa vipassanāya upasantā”ti. Ito muttāti maggenāgatūpasamato muttā. Kalyāṇaputhujjane sandhāya vadati. Tenāha “catūhi satipaṭṭhānehi upasantā”ti.

The meaning spoken by him, who was repeating "Those who were..." and so on, was accepted by the Blessed One. Thus, because of his conduct, he said: "For there are, Kandaraka..."—this too is an individual connection. For the Blessed One, though unasked by him, began the teaching with "For there are..." out of his own inclination, while analyzing and showing the peaceful state of the Sangha of monks that had been praised by Kandaraka. Therefore, it is said: "It is said that this occurred to the Blessed One..." and so on. "Having fashioned" means having arranged oneself, who is one way, in another way. "Having conceived" means having grasped it by way of showing off. Therefore, it is said, "through deceitfulness," and so on. "Fulfilling the practice": although trainees are spoken of without distinction, they should not be called "fulfilling" by way of having attained the path, because their task is finished. For the path is of a single mind-moment; thus, it is said, "peaceful through insight for the higher path." "Released from this" means released from the peace that comes with the path. This is said with reference to a virtuous worldling. Therefore, it is said, "peaceful through the four establishments of mindfulness."

Satatasīlāti avicchinnasīlā. Sātisayo hi etesaṃ sīlassa akhaṇḍādibhāvo. Suparisuddhasīlatāvasena santatā vutti etesanti santatavuttinoti āha “tasseva vevacana”nti. Evaṃ sīlavuttivasena “santatavuttino”ti padassa atthaṃ vatvā idāni jīvitavuttivasena dassento “santatajīvikāvāti attho”ti āha. Sāsanassa jīvitavutti sīlasannissitā evāti āha “tasmi”ntiādi.

"Those of continuous virtue" means those of unbroken virtue. For the excellence of their virtue lies in its being unbroken and so forth. Because of their perfectly pure virtue, their conduct is continuous, thus they are called 'those of continuous conduct'; it is said that this is a synonym for the former. Having thus explained the meaning of the term 'those of continuous conduct' in terms of virtuous conduct, now showing it in terms of livelihood, he says, "the meaning is 'those of continuous livelihood'." The livelihood in the Dispensation is based on virtue; hence it is said, "in that..." and so on.

Nipayati visoseti rāgādisaṃkilesaṃ, tato vā attānaṃ nipātīti nipako, paññavā. Tenāha “paññavanto”ti. Paññāya ṭhatvā jīvikākappanaṃ nāma buddhapaṭikuṭṭhamicchājīvaṃ pahāya sammājīvena jīvananti taṃ dassento “yathā ekacco”tiādimāha. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.14) taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāyañca (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.14) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Rathavinītapaṭipadādayo tesu tesu suttesu vuttanayena veditabbā. Ito aññattha mahāgopālakasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 1.346 ādayo) lokuttarasatipaṭṭhānā kathitāti āha – “idha pana lokiyalokuttaramissakā satipaṭṭhānā kathitā”ti, satipaṭṭhānasuttepi (dī. ni. 2.373-374; ma. ni. 1.106 ādayo) vomissakāva kathitāti. Ettakenāti ettakāya desanāya.

One who dries up, who desiccates, defilements such as lust, or who protects oneself from them, is `nipako`, wise. Therefore, it is said, "wise ones." Arranging one's livelihood while established in wisdom means living by right livelihood, having abandoned wrong livelihood, which is censured by the Buddhas. To show this, he said, "Just as a certain one..." and so on. Whatever should be said there is to be understood in the way it is stated in the Visuddhimagga and its subcommentary. The practices of the Rathavinīta and so on are to be understood in the way stated in their respective suttas. Elsewhere, in the Mahāgopālaka Sutta and others, the supramundane establishments of mindfulness are spoken of; thus he says: "Here, however, the establishments of mindfulness are spoken of as mixed, mundane and supramundane," for in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta too they are spoken of as mixed. "By this much" means by this much of the teaching.

3. Kārakabhāvanti [M 2.0004] paṭipattiyaṃ paṭipajjanakabhāvaṃ. Mayampi nāma gihī bahukiccā samānā kālena kālaṃ satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittā viharāma, kimaṅgaṃ pana vivekavāsinoti attano kārakabhāvaṃ pavedento evaṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca ukkhipati. Tenāha “ayañhettha adhippāyo”tiādi. Nānārammaṇesu aparāparaṃ uppajjamānānaṃ rāgādikilesānaṃ ghanajaṭitasaṅkhātākārena pavatti kilesagahanena gahanatā, tenāha “anto jaṭā bahi jaṭā, jaṭāya jaṭitā pajā”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192). Manussānaṃ ajjhāsayagahaṇena sāṭheyyampīti dassento āha “kasaṭasāṭheyyesupi eseva nayo”ti. Yathā sappimadhuphāṇitādīsu kacavarabhāvo, [V 2.0004] so kasaṭoti vuccati, evaṃ santāne aparisuddho saṃkilesabhāvo kasaṭanti āha “aparisuddhaṭṭhena kasaṭatā”ti. Attani asantaguṇasambhāvanaṃ kerāṭiyaṭṭho. Jānātīti “idaṃ ahitaṃ na sevitabbaṃ, idaṃ hitaṃ sevitabba”nti vicāreti deseti. Vicāraṇatthopi hi hoti jānāti-saddo yathā “āyasmā jānātī”ti. Sabbāpi…pe… adhippetā “pasupālakā”tiādīsu viya. Idha antara-saddo “vijjantarikāyā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.149) viya khaṇatthoti āha “yattakena khaṇenā”ti. Tenāti hatthinā. Tānīti sāṭheyyādīni.

3. “The state of being an agent” means the state of one who undertakes the practice. “Even we, as householders with many duties, from time to time dwell with minds well-established in the foundations of mindfulness—how much more so those who live in seclusion?” Thus, by declaring his own state as an agent, he also extols the community of monks. Therefore, it is said: “This is the intention here,” and so on. The occurrence of defilements such as lust, arising again and again in diverse objects in a form characterized as a dense tangle, is an entanglement by the thicket of defilements. Therefore, it is said: “The tangle within, the tangle without, the people are entangled in the tangle” (SN 1.23). To show that deceitfulness is also to be understood through grasping the inclinations of people, he says: “This same method applies to crude deceitfulness.” Just as there is the state of being refuse in ghee, honey, molasses, and so on, which is called “crudeness,” so too the impure, defiled state in the mental continuum is “crudeness.” Thus, he says: “crudeness in the sense of being impure.” The meaning of hypocrisy is the assumption of non-existent virtues in oneself. “He knows” means he investigates and teaches: “This is unbeneficial and should not be cultivated; this is beneficial and should be cultivated.” For the word “knows” also has the meaning of investigation, as in: “The venerable one investigates.” All are intended, as in “cowherds,” and so on. Here, the word “antara” has the sense of a moment, as in “in the interval of knowledge” (MN 2.149); hence, he says: “by however short a moment.” “By that” means by the elephant. “Those” refers to deceitfulness and so on.

Atthato kāyacittujukatāpaṭipakkhabhūtāva lobhasahagatacittuppādassa pavattiākāravisesāti tāni pavattiākārena dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yassāti pāṇabhūtassa assassa vā hatthino vā. Ṭhassāmīti tattheva sappaṭibhaye ṭhāne gantvā ṭhassāmīti na hoti. Imassa sāṭheyyatāya pākaṭakaraṇaṃ vañcanādhippāyabhāvato. Tathā hi catūsu ṭhānesu “vañcetvā” icceva vuttaṃ, niguhanto pana tattheva gantvā tiṭṭheyya. Esa nayo sesesupi. Paṭimaggaṃ ārohitukāmassāti āgatamaggameva nivattitvā gantukāmassa. Leṇḍavissajjanādīsu kālantarāpekkhābhāvaṃ “tathā”ti iminā upasaṃharati.

In essence, they are particular modes of occurrence of a consciousness accompanied by greed, which are the very antithesis of bodily and mental rectitude. To show these modes of occurrence, “Therein,” etc., was stated. Therein, “of whom” refers to a living being, whether a horse or an elephant. “I will stand” does not mean that, having gone to that very place fraught with danger, one thinks, “I will stand.” The manifestation of this as deceitfulness is due to the intention to deceive. Thus, indeed, in the four instances, it is simply stated as “having deceived,” but one who conceals would go to that very place and stand there. This is the method in the remaining cases as well. “Of one wishing to ascend the return path” means of one who wishes to turn back on the very path one came and go. By “thus,” he summarizes the absence of need for another moment of time in acts such as throwing a clod.

Antojātakāti attano dāsiyā kucchimhi jātā. Dhanakkītāti dhanaṃ datvā dāsabhāvena gahitā. Karamarānītāti dāsabhāvena karamaraggāhagahitā. Dāsabyanti dāsabhāvaṃ. Pessāti adāsā eva hutvā veyyāvaccakarā. Imaṃ vissajjetvāti imaṃ attano hatthagataṃ vissajjetvā. Imaṃ [M 2.0005] gaṇhantāti imaṃ tassa hatthagataṃ gaṇhantā. Sammukhato aññathā parammukhakāle kāyavācāsamudācāradassaneneva cittassa nesaṃ aññathā ṭhitabhāvo niddiṭṭhoti veditabbo.

“Born inside” means born in the womb of one's own female slave. “Bought with wealth” means taken into slavery by giving wealth. “Brought as a captive” means taken into slavery by being seized as a captive. “To slavery” means to the state of being a slave. “Servants” are those who, though not slaves, perform services. “Having dismissed this” means having dismissed this which has come into one's own hands. “Taking this” means taking this which has come into his hands. It should be understood that the state of their minds being otherwise is indicated merely by observing their bodily and verbal conduct when face-to-face and otherwise when out of sight.

4. Ayampi pāṭiyekko anusandhīti etthāpi anantare vuttanayeneva anusandhiyojanā veditabbā. Tenevāha “ayañhī”tiādi. Catuttho hitapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannoti yojanā. Puggalasīsena puggalapaṭipattiṃ dassento “puggale pahāyā”ti āha. Paṭipatti hi idha pahātabbā, na puggalā. Yathā assaddhādipuggalaparivajjanena saddhindriyādibhāvanā ijjhanti, evaṃ micchāpaṭipannapuggalaparivajjanena micchāpaṭipadā vajjitabbāti āha – “purime tayo puggale pahāyā”ti. Catutthapuggalassāti imasmiṃ catukke vuttacatutthapuggalassa hitapaṭipattiyaṃyeva paṭipādemi pavattemīti dassento. Santāti samaṃ vināsaṃ nirodhaṃ pattāti ayamettha atthoti āha “niruddhā santāti vuttā”ti. Puna santāti bhāvanāvasena kilesapariḷāhavigamato santāti [V 2.0005] ayamettha atthoti āha “nibbutā”ti. Santāti ānetvā yojanā. Santo haveti ettha samabhāvakarena sādhubhāvassa visesapaccayabhūtena paṇḍiccena samannāgatā ariyā “santo”ti vuttāti āha – “santo have…pe… paṇḍitā”ti.

4. This too is a separate connection—here also, the connection should be understood in the same way as stated immediately before. For this reason, he says, “For this…,” and so on. The construction is: “The fourth is one who has entered upon the beneficial path.” Explaining the practice of individuals under the heading of individuals, he says, “having abandoned the individuals.” For here, it is the practice that is to be abandoned, not the individuals. Just as the cultivation of the spiritual faculty of faith and so on succeeds by avoiding individuals who lack faith, so too the wrong practice should be avoided by avoiding individuals who have entered upon the wrong practice. Thus, he says: “having abandoned the first three individuals.” Explaining the phrase “of the fourth individual”: this indicates, “I establish and maintain myself only in the beneficial practice of the fourth individual mentioned in this tetrad.” “At peace” means having reached complete destruction and cessation—this is the meaning here. Thus, he says: “ceased, they are said to be at peace.” Again, “at peace” means at peace due to the departure of the torment of defilements by means of cultivation—this is the meaning here. Thus, he says: “extinguished.” The word “at peace” should be supplied and construed. In the phrase “The peaceful, indeed,” the noble ones, endowed with the wisdom that is the special condition for the state of excellence that acts with impartiality, are called “peaceful.” Thus, he says: “The peaceful, indeed… the wise.”

Āhito ahaṃmāno etthāti attā (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.198) attabhāvo, idha pana yo paro na hoti, so attā, taṃ attānaṃ. Paranti attato aññaṃ. Chātaṃ vuccati taṇhā jighacchāhetutāya. Anto tāpanakilesānanti attano santāne attapariḷāhajananasantappanakilesānaṃ. Cittaṃ ārādhetīti cittaṃ pasādeti, sampahaṃsetīti attho. Yasmā pana tathābhūto cittaṃ sampādento ajjhāsayaṃ gaṇhanto nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “cittaṃ sampādetī”tiādi.

“Self” (attā) is so called because the conceit “I am” is placed (āhito) in it; it means self-being (attabhāvo) (A.N. Ṭī. 2.4.198). Here, however, that which is not other is the self; that is “oneself.” “Other” means different from oneself. Craving is called “hunger” because it is the cause of famine. “The defilements that burn within” means the defilements in one's own mental continuum that generate and afflict with personal torment. “He gratifies the mind” means he pleases the mind, he delights it. And since one who is like that, in accomplishing this for the mind, is one who grasps the other's inclination, it is therefore said, “he accomplishes this for the mind,” and so on.

5. Dukkhaṃ paṭikkūlaṃ jegucchaṃ etassāti dukkhapaṭikkūlo taṃ dukkhapaṭikkūlaṃ. Visesanavisesitabbatā hi kāmacārā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana dukkhassa visesitabbataṃ sandhāya bāhiratthasamāsaṃ anādiyitvā “dukkhassa paṭikkūla”nti attho vutto. Yena hi bhāgena purisassa dukkhaṃ paṭikkūlaṃ, tena dukkhassa purisopīti. Tenāha – “paccanīkasaṇṭhita”nti.

5. Suffering is disagreeable and repulsive to him; hence, he is “one to whom suffering is repulsive.” That is “repulsive to suffering.” For the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified is flexible. In the commentary, however, not adopting an exocentric compound, the meaning is given as “repulsive of suffering,” with reference to suffering being the thing qualified. For in whatever way suffering is repulsive to a person, in that way the person is also repulsive to suffering. Therefore, he says: “established in opposition.”

6. Catūhi [M 2.0006] kāraṇehīti dhātukusalatādīhi catūhi kāraṇehi. Kammaṃ karotīti yogakammaṃ karoti. Yasmā sambuddhā paresaṃ maggaphalādhigamāya ussāhajātā, tattha nirantaraṃ yuttappayuttā eva honti, te paṭicca tesaṃ antarāyo na hotiyevāti āha “na pana buddhe paṭiccā”ti. Kiriyaparihāniyā desakassa tasseva vā puggalassa tajjapayogābhāvato. “Desakassa vā”ti idaṃ sāvakānaṃ vasena daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahatā atthenāti ettha attha-saddo ānisaṃsapariyāyoti āha “dvīhi ānisaṃsehī”ti. Pasādaṃ paṭilabhati “arahanto”tiādinā saṅghasuppaṭipattiyā sutattā. Abhinavo nayo udapādi santatasīlatādivasena anattantapatādivasena, sopi taṃ sutvā dāsādīsu savisesaṃ lajjī dayāpanno hitānukampī hutvā sekkhapaṭipadaṃ sīlaṃ sādhento anukkamena satipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ paribrūheti. Tenāha bhagavā “mahatā atthena saṃyutto”ti.

6. “By four reasons” means by the four reasons beginning with skill in the elements. “Performs a task” means performs the task of striving. Because the Fully Enlightened Ones, filled with enthusiasm for others' attainment of the path and fruit, are continuously and appropriately engaged therein, an obstacle does not arise for those disciples on account of them. Hence, it is said: “But not on account of the Buddhas.” This is due to a decline in action because of the teacher’s, or that same person’s, lack of appropriate effort. “Or of the teacher”—this should be understood in relation to the disciples. “With great benefit”—here, the word “benefit” is a synonym for advantage; therefore it is said: “with two advantages.” He gains confidence, having heard of the Sangha’s good practice, beginning with “they are worthy ones,” etc. A new method arose—by way of continuous virtue, by way of not tormenting oneself, etc.—and having heard that, he becomes especially conscientious in relation to slaves and others, compassionate, and concerned for their welfare. Fulfilling the trainee's path of virtue, he gradually develops the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “endowed with great benefit.”

8. Paresaṃ hananaghātanādinā rodāpanato luddo, tathā vighātakabhāvena kāyacittānaṃ vidāraṇato dāruṇo, viruddhavādatāya kakkhaḷo, bandhanāgāre niyutto bandhanāgāriko.

8. He is fierce because he makes others weep through killing, slaughtering, and so on; likewise, he is cruel because he tears apart the body and mind by way of affliction; he is harsh because of his contentious speech; a jailer is one appointed to a prison.

9. Khattiyābhisekenāti [V 2.0006] khattiyānaṃ kattabbaabhisekena. Santhāgāranti santhāravasena kataṃ agāraṃ yaññāvāṭaṃ. Sappitelenāti sappimayena telena, yamakasnehena hi tadā kāyaṃ abbhañjati. Vacchabhāvaṃ taritvā ṭhito vacchataro. Parikkhepakaraṇatthāyāti vanamālāhi saddhiṃ dabbhehi vediyā parikkhepanatthāya. Yaññabhūmiyanti avasesayaññaṭṭhāne. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ taṃ suviññeyyameva.

9. By the consecration of a noble means by the consecration to be performed for nobles. The assembly hall means a house made for assembly in the manner of a meeting place, the sacrificial enclosure. With ghee-oil means with oil made from ghee, for at that time, they anoint the body with a double unguent. Having passed beyond the state of a calf, a young bull stands. For the purpose of enclosing means for enclosing the altar with garlands and darbha grass. On the sacrificial ground means in the remaining place of sacrifice. Whatever here is not clearly divided in meaning is easily understood.

Kandarakasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Obscure Meaning in the commentary on the Kandarakasutta is completed.

2. Aṭṭhakanāgarasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta.

17. Avidūreti [M 2.0007][V 2.0007] iminā pāḷiyaṃ “vesāliya”nti idaṃ samīpe bhummavacananti dasseti. Sārappattakulagaṇanāyāti (a. ni. ṭī. 3.11.16) mahāsāramahappattakulagaṇanāya. Dasame ṭhāneti aññe aññeti dasagaṇanaṭṭhāne. Aṭṭhakanagare jāto bhavo aṭṭhakanāgaro. Kukkuṭārāmoti pāṭaliputte kukkuṭārāmo, na kosambiyaṃ.

17. By 'not far,' it shows that 'in Vesālī' in the Pāli text is a locative of proximity. 'By the counting of families that have attained essence' means by the counting of families that have attained great essence and great prosperity. 'In the tenth place' means in the place of the tenth count, which is 'each other.' One born or existing in the city of Aṭṭhaka is an Aṭṭhakanāgara. 'Kukkuṭārāma' means the Kukkuṭārāma in Pāṭaliputta, not the one in Kosambī.

18. Pakatatthaniddeso ta-saddoti tassa “bhagavatā”tiādīhi padehi samānādhikaraṇabhāvena vuttassa yena abhisambuddhabhāvena bhagavā pakato adhigato supākaṭo ca, taṃ abhisambuddhabhāvaṃ saddhiṃ āgamanīyapaṭipadāya atthabhāvena dassento “yo so…pe… abhisambuddho”ti āha. Satipi ñāṇadassana-saddānaṃ idha paññāvevacanabhāve tena tena visesena tesaṃ visayavisese pavattidassanatthaṃ asādhāraṇañāṇavisesavasena vijjāttayavasena vijjāabhiññānāvaraṇañāṇavasena sabbaññutañāṇamaṃsacakkhuvasena paṭivedhadesanāñāṇavasena ca tadatthaṃ yojetvā dassento “tesaṃ tesa”ntiādimāha. Tattha āsayānusayaṃ jānatā āsayānusayañāṇena sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ passatā sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇehi. Pubbenivāsādīhīti pubbenivāsāsavakkhayañāṇehi. Paṭivedhapaññāyāti ariyamaggapaññāya. Desanāpaññāya passatāti desetabbadhammānaṃ desetabbappakāraṃ bodhaneyyapuggalānañca āsayānusayacaritādhimuttiādibhedaṃ dhammadesanāpaññāya yāthāvato passatā. Arīnanti kilesārīnaṃ, pañcavidhamārānaṃ vā, sāsanassa vā paccatthikānaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ tesaṃ pana hananaṃ pāṭihāriyehi abhibhavanaṃ appaṭibhānatākaraṇaṃ ajjhupekkhanameva vā, kesivinayasuttañcettha nidassanaṃ.

18. The exposition of the meaning of 'pakata' is as follows: The word 'that' refers to him who is spoken of in apposition with terms such as 'the Blessed One,' and by which state of perfect enlightenment the Blessed One is manifested, attained, and clearly revealed. Showing that state of perfect enlightenment, along with the meaning of the path to be followed, he says, 'He who... is perfectly enlightened.' Although the terms 'knowledge' and 'vision' are here synonyms for wisdom, to demonstrate their application to specific objects through particular distinctions, he shows their meaning by combining them with unique aspects of knowledge, such as by way of the threefold knowledge, by way of knowledge, supernormal knowledge, and unobstructed knowledge, by way of omniscient knowledge and the fleshly eye, and by way of the knowledge of penetration and teaching, saying 'of these, of these,' etc. Herein, 'knowing inclinations and latent tendencies' is by the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies; and 'seeing all knowable phenomena' is by the knowledges of omniscience and non-obstruction. 'By knowledge of past lives, etc.' means by the knowledges of past lives and the destruction of the taints. 'By penetrating wisdom' means by the wisdom of the Noble Path. 'Seeing with the wisdom of teaching' means accurately perceiving the nature of what should be taught, the manner of teaching, and the various inclinations, latent tendencies, character, and dispositions of those to be taught, through the wisdom of teaching the Dhamma. 'Of enemies' means of the enemies who are the defilements, or the five kinds of Māra, or the opponents of the Dispensation, the adherents of other sects. Their destruction, however, is overpowering through miracles, rendering them speechless, or simply overlooking them—the Kesivinaya Sutta serves as an illustration here.

Tathā ṭhānāṭṭhānādivibhāgaṃ jānatā yathākammūpagasatte passatā, savāsanānaṃ āsavānaṃ khīṇattā arahatā, abhiññeyyādibhede dhamme abhiññeyyādito aviparītāvabodhato sammāsambuddhena. Atha vā tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇatāya jānatā, kāyakammādivasena tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ ñāṇānuparivattito nisammakāritāya passatā, davādīnaṃ abhāvasādhikāya [M 2.0008] pahānasampadāya arahatā, chandādīnaṃ ahānihetubhūtāya akkhayapaṭibhānasādhikāya sabbaññutāya sammāsambuddhenāti evaṃ dasabalaaṭṭhārasaāveṇikabuddhadhammavasenapi yojanā kātabbā.

Similarly, by one who knows the distinction between what is possible and impossible, by one who sees beings according to their karmic destinations, by one who is an Arahant due to the destruction of the taints along with their residues, and by one who is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One due to the unerring comprehension of phenomena such as the knowable, etc. Or alternatively, by one who knows without obstruction in the three times; by one who sees by discerning the three types of actions through bodily action, etc., with knowledge following them, acting considerately; by one who is an Arahant due to the perfection of abandoning defilements like passion, which brings about their non-existence; and by one who is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One due to omniscience, which brings about inexhaustible insight, being the cause of the non-diminishment of zeal, etc. In this way, the application should be made also by way of the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddha.

19. Abhisaṅkhatanti [V 2.0008] attano paccayehi abhisammukhabhāvena samecca sambhūyya kataṃ, svassa katabhāvo uppādanena veditabbo, na uppannassa paṭisaṅkharaṇenāti āha “uppādita”nti. Te cassa paccayā cetanāpadhānāti dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “abhisaṅkhataṃ abhisañcetayita”nti vuttanti “cetayitaṃ pakappita”nti atthamāha. Abhisaṅkhataṃ abhisañcetayitanti ca jhānassa pātubhāvadassanamukhena viddhaṃsanabhāvaṃ ulliṅgeti yañhi ahutvā sambhavati, taṃ hutvā paṭiveti. Tenāha pāḷiyaṃ ‘abhisaṅkhata’ntiādi. Samathavipassanādhamme ṭhitoti samathadhamme ṭhitattā samāhito vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā aniccānupassanādīhi niccasaññādayo pajahanto anukkamena taṃ anulomañāṇaṃ pāpetā hutvā vipassanādhamme ṭhito. Samathavipassanāsaṅkhātesu dhammesu rañjanaṭṭhena rāgo, nandanaṭṭhena nandīti. Tattha sukhumā apekkhā vuttā, yā “nikantī”ti vuccati.

19. 'Conditioned' means made by its own conditions coming together directly and arising together. Its made nature is to be understood as being caused by its arising, not by reforming what has already arisen—hence it is said 'produced.' And to show that its conditions are primarily intention, the Pāli text states 'conditioned and intended,' the meaning of which is given as 'intended and planned.' The terms 'conditioned' and 'intended' also indicate the nature of destruction by way of the appearance of jhāna, for what comes into being after not having been, ceases after having been. Therefore, the Pāli text says 'conditioned,' etc. 'Established in the qualities of serenity and insight' means that, being established in the quality of serenity, one becomes composed; and having established insight, by abandoning perceptions of permanence and so on through the contemplations of impermanence and so on, one gradually attains conformity knowledge and becomes established in the quality of insight. In the phenomena designated as serenity and insight, 'lust' is in the sense of colouring, and 'delight' is in the sense of delighting. Therein, a subtle expectation is mentioned, which is called 'hankering'.

Evaṃ santeti evaṃ yathārutavasena ca imassa suttapadassa atthe gahetabbe sati. Samathavipassanāsu chandarāgo kattabboti anāgāmiphalaṃ nibbattetvā tadatthāya samathavipassanāpi anibbattetvā kevalaṃ tattha chandarāgo kattabbo bhavissati. Kasmā? Tesu samathavipassanāsaṅkhātesu dhammesu chandarāgamattena anāgāminā laddhabbassa aladdhānāgāmiphalena laddhabbattā tathā sati tena anāgāmiphalampi laddhabbameva nāma hoti. Tenāha – “anāgāmiphalaṃ paṭividdhaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Sabhāvato rasitabbattā aviparīto attho eva attharaso. Aññāpi kāci sugatiyoti vinipātike sandhāyāha. Aññāpi kāci duggatiyoti asurakāyamāha.

'This being so' means: when the meaning of this Sutta passage is to be taken literally. If 'desire and lust should be applied to serenity and insight,' it would mean that without having produced the non-returner's fruit, and without having produced serenity and insight for that purpose, one would merely have to apply desire and lust there. Why? Because what is to be attained by a non-returner would have to be attained by one who has not attained the non-returner's fruit, merely through desire and lust for those phenomena called serenity and insight. That being so, the non-returner's fruit would indeed have to be attained by him. Therefore, it is said, 'The non-returner's fruit will be realized.' The unperverted meaning, which is to be savored for its intrinsic nature, is the true essence of the meaning. 'Any other good destination'—this is said referring to the `vinipātika` asuras. 'Any other bad destination'—this refers to the asura realm.

Samathadhurameva dhuraṃ samathayānikassa vasena desanāya āgatattā. Mahāmālukyovāde “vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāra”nti pādakajjhānaṃ katvā “so yadeva tattha hoti rūpagataṃ vedanāgata”ntiādinā vipassanaṃ vitthāretvā “so tattha ṭhito āsavānaṃ khayaṃ [M 2.0009] pāpuṇātī”ti (ma. ni. 2.133) āgatattā “mahāmālukyovāde vipassanāva dhura”nti āha. Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutte (dī. ni. 2.373 ādayo; ma. ni. 1.106 ādayo) sabbatthakameva tikkhatarāya vipassanāya āgatattā vuttaṃ “vipassanuttaraṃ kathita”nti. Kāyagatāsatisutte (ma. ni. 3.153-154) ānāpānajjhānādivasena savisesaṃ samathavipassanāya āgatattā vuttaṃ “samathuttaraṃ kathita”nti.

The burden of serenity is indeed the primary burden, as the teaching is presented in terms of one who follows the vehicle of serenity. In the Mahāmālukyovāda, having established the foundational jhāna with 'secluded from unwholesome states, with initial and sustained thought,' and then elaborating on insight with 'whatever there is therein of form, feeling,' etc., because it is stated, 'standing there, he attains the destruction of the taints' (MN 2.133), it is said, 'In the Mahāmālukyovāda, insight is indeed the burden.' In the Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta (DN 2.373 ff.; MN 1.106 ff.), because it is presented entirely through keener insight, it is said to be 'supreme in insight.' In the Kāyagatāsatisutta (MN 3.153-154), because it is presented with specialized serenity and insight by way of the jhānas on mindfulness of breathing, etc., it is said to be 'supreme in serenity'.

Appaṃ yācitena bahuṃ dentena uḷārapurisena viya ekaṃ dhammaṃ pucchitena “ayampi ekadhammo”ti [V 2.0009] kathitattā ekādasapi dhammā pucchāvasena ekadhammo nāma jāto paccekaṃ vākyaparisamāpanañāyena. Ekavīsati pabbāni tehi bodhiyamānāya paṭipadāya ekarūpattā paṭipadāvasena ekadhammo nāma jātoti. Idha imasmiṃ aṭṭhakanāgarasutte. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanadhammānaṃ saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattatāya tattha sāvakānaṃ dukkaranti na catutthāruppavasenettha desanā āgatāti catunnaṃ brahmavihārānaṃ, heṭṭhimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ āruppānañca vasena ekādasa. Pucchāvasenāti “atthi nu kho, bhante ānanda, tena…pe… sammāsambuddhena ekadhammo akkhāto”ti (ma. ni. 2.18) evaṃ pavattapucchāvasena. Amatuppattiyatthenāti amatabhāvassa uppattihetutāya, sabbānipi kammaṭṭhānāni ekarasampi amatādhigamapaṭipattiyāti attho, evamettha aggaphalabhūmi anāgāmiphalabhūmīti dveva bhūmiyo sarūpato āgatā, nānantariyatāya pana heṭṭhimāpi dve bhūmiyo atthato āgatā evāti daṭṭhabbā.

Just as a noble person gives much when asked for little, so too, when one asks about a single Dhamma, because it is said, 'ayampi ekadhammo' (this too is one Dhamma), the eleven Dhammas become one Dhamma by way of questioning, by the principle of concluding each statement. The twenty-one sections, being unified in the path that leads to awakening, become one Dhamma by way of the path. This is in this Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta. Because the states of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have reached the subtlety of residual formations, it is difficult for disciples there; therefore, the teaching does not come here by way of the fourth immaterial attainment. Thus, by way of the four divine abodes and the three lower immaterial states, there are eleven. 'Pucchāvasena' (by way of questioning) means by way of the question that proceeds thus: 'Is there, Venerable Ānanda, one Dhamma declared by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One...?' (MN 2.18). 'Amatuppattiyatthenāti' (in the sense of producing the deathless) means being the cause for the arising of the deathless state; the meaning is that all meditation subjects, even of a single savor, are the path to realizing the deathless. Thus, here, the stage of the highest fruit and the stage of the non-returner's fruit are the two stages that come in their own form. But because of their immediacy, the two lower stages also come by way of meaning and should be seen as such.

21. Pañca satāni aggho etassāti pañcasataṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

21. 'Pañca satāni aggho etassa' (its value is five hundred), therefore 'pañcasataṃ' (five hundred). The rest is indeed clear.

Aṭṭhakanāgarasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The elucidation of hidden meanings in the Commentary on the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta is complete.

3. Sekhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sekha Sutta

22. Santhāgāranti [V 2.0010] atthānusāsanāgāraṃ. Tenāha – “uyyogakālādīsū”tiādi. Ādi-saddena maṅgalamahādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Santhambhantīti vissamanti, parissamaṃ vinodentīti attho. Sahāti sannivesavasena [M 2.0010] ekajjhaṃ. Saha atthānusāsanaṃ agāranti etasmiṃ atthe ttha-kārassa ntha-kāraṃ katvā santhāgāranti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Santharantīti sammantanavasena tiṭṭhanti.

22. The Santhāgāra is a hall for instruction in the meaning. Therefore, it is said: 'at times of exertion, etc.' By the word 'etc.' are included great auspicious occasions and so forth. 'Santhambhanti' means they rest, they dispel fatigue—this is the meaning. 'Saha' means together, in one place, by way of arrangement. It should be understood that in the sense of 'a hall for instruction in the meaning together,' the 'ttha' sound has been changed to 'ntha' to form 'santhāgāra'. 'Santharanti' means they remain by way of consultation.

Tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ āgatameva bhavissatīti buddhavacanassa āgamanasīsena ariyaphaladhammānampi āgamanaṃ vuttameva, tiyāmarattiṃ tattha vasantānaṃ phalasamāpattivaḷañjanaṃ hotīti. Tasmiñca bhikkhusaṅghe kalyāṇaputhujjanā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpentā hontīti ce? Ariyamaggadhammānaṃ tattha āgamanaṃ hotiyeva.

The Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, will indeed have come; thus, by the coming of the Buddha's word as the chief, the coming of the noble fruition-states is also stated. For those dwelling there during the three watches of the night, there is the enjoyment of fruition attainment. And if in that community of monks, virtuous worldlings are keen on developing insight? Then the noble path-states do indeed arise there.

Allagomayenāti acchena allagomayarasena. Opuñchāpetvāti vilimpitvā. Catujjātiyagandhehīti tagarakuṅkumayavanapupphatamālapattāni pisitvā katagandhehi nānāvaṇṇeti nīlādivasena nānāvaṇṇe, na bhittivisesavasena. Bhittivisesavasena pana nānāsaṇṭhānarūpameva. Mahāpiṭṭhikakojavaketi hatthipiṭṭhīsu attharitabbatāya mahāpiṭṭhikāti laddhasamaññe kojaveti vadanti. Kuttake pana sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ hatthattharaṇā hatthirūpavicittā. Assattharakasīhattharakādayopi assasīharūpādivicittā eva attharakā, cittattharakaṃ nānārūpehi ceva nānāvidhamālākammādīhi ca vicittaṃ attharakaṃ.

'Allagomayena' means with clear fresh cow dung juice. 'Opuñchāpetvā' means having smeared. 'Catujjātiyagandhehi' means with perfumes made by grinding tagara, saffron, yavanapuppha flowers, and tamāla leaves; 'nānāvaṇṇe' means of various colors, such as blue, etc., not by way of differences in walls. By way of differences in walls, however, it is merely of various shapes. 'Mahāpiṭṭhikakojavake' means they call a 'kojavaka' that which is known as 'mahāpiṭṭhikā' because it is to be spread on elephants' backs. But this is said with reference to artificial ones: elephant covers adorned with elephant figures. Horse covers, lion covers, etc., are indeed covers adorned with horse, lion, etc., figures. A 'cittattharaka' is a cover adorned with various figures and various kinds of garland work, etc.

Upadhānanti apassayanaṃ upadahitvāti apassayayoggabhāvena ṭhapetvā gandhehi katamālā gandhadāmaṃ, tamālapattādīhi kataṃ pattadāmaṃ. Ādi-saddena hiṅgulatakkolajātiphalajātipupphādīhi katadāmaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Pallaṅkākārena katapīṭhaṃ pallaṅkapīṭhaṃ, tīsu passesu, ekapasse eva vā saupassayaṃ apassayapīṭhaṃ, anapassayaṃ muṇḍapīṭhaṃ yojanāvaṭṭeti yojanaparikkhepe.

'Upadhāna' means a support; 'upadahitvā' means having placed it in a condition suitable for reclining. Garlands made of scents are 'gandhadāmaṃ'; garlands made of tamāla leaves, etc., are 'pattadāmaṃ'. By the word 'etc.' are included garlands made of asafoetida, cardamom, nutmeg, nutmeg flowers, etc. A seat made in the form of a couch is a 'pallaṅkapīṭhaṃ'; a 'saupassayaṃ apassayapīṭhaṃ' is a support-seat with a support on three sides or on just one side; a 'muṇḍapīṭhaṃ' is one without a support. 'Yojanāvaṭṭa' means a league in perimeter.

Saṃvidhāyāti antaravāsakassa koṇapadesañca itarapadesañca samaṃ katvā vidhāya. Tenāha – “kattariyā padumaṃ kantanto viyā”ti timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādentoti ettha ca yasmā buddhānaṃ rūpasampadā viya ākappasampadāpi paramukkaṃsagatā, tasmā tadā bhagavā evaṃ sobhatīti [V 2.0011] dassento “suvaṇṇapāmaṅgenā”tiādimāha, tattha asamena buddhavesenātiādinā [M 2.0011] tadā bhagavā buddhānubhāvassa niguhaṇe kāraṇābhāvato tattha sannipatitadevamanussanāgayakkhagandhabbādīnaṃ pasādajananatthaṃ attano sabhāvapakatikiriyāyeva kapilavatthuṃ pāvisīti dasseti. Buddhānaṃ kāyappabhā nāma pakatiyā asītihatthamattameva padesaṃ pharatīti āha – “asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesī”ti nīlapītalohitodātamañjiṭṭhapabhassarānaṃ vasena chabbaṇṇā buddharasmiyo.

'Saṃvidhāya' means having made the corner part and the other part of the inner robe even, having arranged it. Therefore, it is said: 'as if cutting a lotus with a knife,' concealing the three mandalas. Here, because the perfection of the Buddhas' bearing, like the beauty of their form, is of the highest excellence, therefore, showing how the Blessed One shone at that time, he said: 'with a golden girdle,' etc. In that context, by 'with the unequaled Buddha's dress,' etc., he shows that because there was no reason for the Blessed One to conceal the Buddha's majesty at that time, he entered Kapilavatthu merely by his natural innate action, in order to generate faith in the devas, humans, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and others assembled there. He says that the Buddhas' bodily aura naturally pervades a space of only eighty cubits: 'He occupied a space of eighty cubits.' The Buddha's rays are of six colors: blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and luminous.

Sabbapāliphulloti mūlato paṭṭhāya yāva aggā phullo vikasito. Paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitānantiādi parikappūpamā. Yathā taṃ…pe… alaṅkataṃ añño virocati, evaṃ virocittha, samatiṃsāya pāramitāhi abhisaṅkhatattā evaṃ virocitthāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pañcavīsatiyā nadīnanti gaṅgādīnaṃ candabhāgāpariyosānānaṃ pañcavīsatiyā mahānadīnaṃ. Sambhijjāti sambhedaṃ missībhāvaṃ patvā mukhadvāreti samuddaṃ paviṭṭhaṭṭhāne.

'Sabbapāliphulla' means fully blossomed and open from the roots up to the very top. 'Arranged in sequence,' etc., is an illustrative comparison. Just as…adorned, another shines, so it shone; it is said that it shone thus because it was fashioned by the thirty perfections. 'Pañcavīsatiyā nadīnaṃ' means of the twenty-five great rivers, from the Ganges up to the Candabhāgā. 'Sambhijjā' means having reached a state of combination and mingling; 'mukhadvāre' means at the place where they enter the ocean.

Devamanussanāgasupaṇṇagandhabbayakkhādīnaṃ akkhīnīti cetaṃ parikappanavasena vuttaṃ. Sahassenāti padasahassena, bhāṇavārappamāṇena ganthenāti attho.

The eyes of devas, humans, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, yakkhas, and so forth—this is said by way of conventional designation. 'Sahassena' means by a thousand padas, meaning by a text of the measure of a recitation section.

Kampayanto vasundharanti attano guṇavisesehi pathavīkampaṃ uppādento, evaṃbhūtopi aheṭhayanto pāṇāni. Sabbadakkhiṇattā buddhānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ uddharanto. Samaṃ samphusate bhūmiṃ suppatiṭṭhitapādatāya. Yadipi bhūmiṃ samaṃ phusati, rajasānupalippati sukhumattā chaviyā. Ninnaṭṭhānaṃ unnamatītiādi buddhānaṃ suppatiṭṭhitapādasaṅkhātassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇapaṭilābhassa nissandaphalaṃ. Nātidūre uddharatīti atidūre ṭhapetuṃ na uddharati. Naccāsanne ca nikkhipanti accāsanne ca ṭhāne anikkhipanto niyyāti. Hāsayanto sadevake loke tosayanto. Catūhi pādehi caratīti catucārī.

'Kampayanto vasundharaṃ' means causing the earth to tremble by his own excellent qualities; yet, being such, he harms no living beings. Because of the Buddhas' supreme worthiness, he lifts the right foot first. He touches the ground evenly, due to his well-established feet. Even when he touches the ground evenly, he is not soiled by dust, because of the fineness of his skin. 'Ninnaṭṭhānaṃ unnamati,' etc., are the unfailing results of the Great Man’s characteristic called 'well-established feet,' which the Buddhas have attained. 'Nātidūre uddharati' means he does not lift it to place it at too great a distance. 'Naccāsanne ca nikkhipati' means he proceeds without placing it in a place too close. Delighting the world with its devas, he pleases them. 'Catūhi pādehi carati' means he walks with four feet; thus, he is 'catucārī'.

Buddhānubhāvassa pakāsanavasena gatattā vaṇṇakālo nāma kiresa. Sarīravaṇṇe vā guṇavaṇṇe vā kathiyamāne dukkathitanti na vattabbaṃ. Kasmā? Aparimāṇavaṇṇā hi buddhā bhagavanto, buddhaguṇasaṃvaṇṇanā jānantassa yathādhammasaṃvaṇṇanaṃyeva anupavisatīti.

This is indeed called the time of praise, because it proceeds by way of manifesting the Buddha's majesty. When speaking of the color of the body or the qualities, it should not be said that it is poorly spoken. Why? Because the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have immeasurable virtues, and the praise of the Buddha's virtues for one who knows enters into a proper praise of the Dhamma itself.

Dukūlacumbaṭakenāti [M 2.0012] ganthitvā gahitadukūlavatthena, nāgavikkantacaraṇoti hatthināgasadisapadanikkhepo. Satapuññalakkhaṇoti anekasatapuññanimmitamahāpurisalakkhaṇo maṇiverocano yathāti ativiya virocamāno maṇi viya verocano nāma eko maṇivisesoti keci mahāsālovāti [V 2.0012] mahanto sālarukkho viya, koviḷārādimahārukkho viya vā padumo kokanado yathāti kokanadasaṅkhātaṃ mahāpadumaṃ viya, vikasamānapadumaṃ viya vā.

'Dukūlacumbaṭakena' means with a roll of dukūla cloth, gathered and tied. 'Nāgavikkantacaraṇa' means with a foot-placement like that of a noble elephant. 'Satapuññalakkhaṇa' means possessing the marks of a great man, produced by hundreds of meritorious deeds; 'maṇiverocano yathā' means like a gem shining exceedingly. Some say 'verocana' is a particular kind of gem. 'Mahāsālo' means like a great Sal tree, or like a great tree such as a Koviḷāra, etc. 'Padumo kokanado yathā' means like a great lotus called 'kokanada,' or like a blossoming lotus.

Ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viyātiādi tassā pakiṇṇakakathāya aññesaṃ dukkarabhāvadassanañceva suṇantānaṃ accantasukhāvahabhāvadassanañca pathavījaṃ ākaḍḍhento viyāti nāḷiyantaṃ yojetvā mahāpathaviyā heṭṭhimatale pappaṭakojaṃ uddhaṃmukhaṃ katvā ākaḍḍhento viya yojanikanti yojanappamāṇaṃ madhubhaṇḍanti madhupaṭalaṃ.

'Ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viya,' etc.—this miscellaneous talk shows both the difficulty for others and the bringing of supreme happiness to those who listen. 'Pathavījaṃ ākaḍḍhento viya' means like attaching a pipe and, on the lower level of the great earth, making the earth's crust-essence face upwards and drawing it up. 'Yojanika' means of the measure of a yojana. 'Madhubhaṇḍa' means a layer of honey.

Mahantanti uḷāraṃ. Sabbadānaṃ dinnameva hotīti sabbameva paccayajātaṃ āvāsadāyakena dinnameva hoti. Tathāhi dve tayo gāme piṇḍāya caritvā kiñci aladdhā āgatassapi chāyūdakasampannaṃ ārāmaṃ pavisitvā nhāyitvā paṭissaye muhuttaṃ nipajjitvā uṭṭhāya nisinnassa kāye balaṃ āharitvā pakkhittaṃ viya hoti. Bahi vicarantassa ca kāye vaṇṇadhātu vātātapehi kilamati, paṭissayaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya muhuttaṃ nisinnassa visabhāgasantati vūpasammati, sabhāgasantati patiṭṭhāti, vaṇṇadhātu āharitvā pakkhittā viya hoti, bahi vicarantassa ca pāde kaṇṭako vijjhati, khāṇu paharati, sarīsapādiparissayo ceva corabhayañca uppajjati, paṭissayaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya nipannassa pana sabbe parissayā na honti, ajjhayantassa dhammapītisukhaṃ, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontassa upasamasukhaṃ uppajjati bahiddhā vikkhepābhāvato, bahi vicarantassa ca kāye sedā muccanti, akkhīni phandanti, senāsanaṃ pavisanakkhaṇe mañcapīṭhādīni na paññāyanti, muhuttaṃ nisinnassa pana akkhipasādo āharitvā pakkhitto viya hoti, dvāravātapānamañcapīṭhādīni paññāyanti, etasmimpi ca āvāse vasantaṃ disvā manussā catūhi paccayehi sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “āvāsadānasmiṃ dinne sabbaṃ dānaṃ dinnameva hotī”ti. Bhūmaṭṭhaka…pe… na sakkāti ayamattho mahāsudassanavatthunā (dī. ni. 2.241 ādayo) dīpetabbo.

'Mahanta' means magnificent. 'Sabbadānaṃ dinnameva hoti' means all gifts are indeed given; for all kinds of requisites are given by the donor of a dwelling. For example, even for one who, having wandered for alms in two or three villages and obtained nothing, comes to a monastery endowed with shade and water, bathes, rests for a moment in his lodging, and rises to sit, it is as if strength has been brought and placed in his body. Moreover, for one wandering outside, the complexion of the body is wearied by wind and sun; having entered his lodging and closed the door, the disharmonious continuity subsides, harmonious continuity is established, and it is as if the complexion has been brought and placed there. Furthermore, for one wandering outside, a thorn pierces his foot, a stump strikes him, and dangers from reptiles and fear of thieves arise; but for one who has entered his lodging, closed the door, and lies down, all those perils do not exist. For one studying, the joy and happiness of the Dhamma arise; for one attending to his meditation subject, the happiness of tranquility arises, because of the absence of external distractions. Moreover, for one wandering outside, sweat pours forth from his body, his eyes flicker, and at the moment of entering his dwelling, couches, chairs, etc., are not apparent; but for one who has sat for a moment, it is as if clarity of the eye has been brought and placed there, and doors, windows, couches, chairs, etc., become apparent. And seeing one living in such a dwelling, people respectfully attend to him with the four requisites. Therefore it was said: 'When a dwelling is given, all gifts are indeed given.' The meaning of 'Bhūmaṭṭhaka…etc… na sakkā' should be elucidated by the story of Mahāsudassana (Dī. Ni. 2.241 ff.).

Sītanti [M 2.0013] (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.295; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.4.243) ajjhattadhātukkhobhavasena vā bahiddhautuvipariṇāmavasena vā uppajjanakasītaṃ. Uṇhanti aggisantāpaṃ. Tassa pana davadāhādīsu sambhavo daṭṭhabbo. Paṭihantīti paṭibāhati. Yathā tadubhayavasena kāyacittānaṃ bādhanāni na honti, evaṃ karoti. Sītuṇhabbhāhate hi sarīre vikkhittacitto bhikkhu yoniso padahituṃ na sakkoti. Vāḷamigānīti sīhabyagghādivāḷamige. Guttasenāsanañhi pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya nisinnassa te parissayā na honti[V 2.0013]. Sarīsapeti ye keci sarantā gacchante dīghajātike. Makaseti nidassanametaṃ, ḍaṃsādīnaṃ eteneva saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Sisireti sītakālavasena sattāhavaddalikādivasena ca uppanne sisirasamphasse. Vuṭṭhiyoti yadā tadā uppannā vassavuṭṭhiyo paṭihanatīti yojanā.

Cold (sīta): The cold that arises due to internal disturbance of the elements or external changes in the weather. Heat (uṇha): The burning heat of fire. Its occurrence should be understood in instances such as forest fires and so on. It wards off (paṭihanti): It repels. It acts in such a way that afflictions of body and mind do not arise due to both those factors. For when the body is afflicted by cold and heat, a bhikkhu with a distracted mind cannot strive wisely. Wild beasts (vāḷamiga): Wild beasts such as lions, tigers, and the like. For one who enters a guarded dwelling and sits with the door closed, these dangers do not occur. Creeping creatures (sarīsapa): Any long-bodied creatures that move by creeping. Mosquitoes (makasa): This is an example; gadflies and the like should be understood as included by this. In the cold season (sisira): The cold touch that arises due to the cold season, or due to a week of bad weather, and so on. Rain (vuṭṭhi): The connection is that it wards off rain showers that arise from time to time.

Vātātapo ghoroti rukkhagacchādīnaṃ ummūlabhañjanavasena pavattiyā ghoro sarajaarajādibhedo vāto ceva gimhapariḷāhasamayesu uppattiyā ghoro sūriyātapo ca. Paṭihaññatīti paṭibāhīyati. Leṇatthanti nānārammaṇato cittaṃ nivattetvā paṭisallānārāmatthaṃ. Sukhatthanti vuttaparissayābhāvena phāsuvihāratthaṃ. Jhāyitunti aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesu yattha katthaci cittaṃ upanijjhāyituṃ. Vipassitunti aniccādito sabbasaṅkhāre sammasituṃ.

The fierce wind and heat (vātātapo ghoro): The fierce wind, of the dusty and dustless kind, which causes the uprooting and breaking of trees and shrubs; and the fierce heat of the sun that arises in the hot season. It is warded off (paṭihaññati): It is repelled. For the sake of a dwelling (leṇatthaṃ): For the purpose of delighting in seclusion, by turning the mind away from various objects. For the sake of happiness (sukhatthaṃ): For the sake of comfortable living, free from the aforementioned troubles. To meditate (jhāyituṃ): To contemplate closely any of the thirty-eight objects. To practice insight (vipassituṃ): To thoroughly examine all conditioned things as impermanent and so forth.

Vihāreti paṭissaye. Kārayeti kārāpeyya. Rammeti manorame nivāsasukhe. Vāsayettha bahussuteti kāretvā pana ettha vihāresu bahussute sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme nivāseyya. Te nivāsento pana tesaṃ bahussutānaṃ yathā paccayehi kilamatho na hoti, evaṃ annañca pānañca vatthasenāsanāni ca dadeyya ujubhūtesu ajjhāsayasampannesu kammaphalānaṃ ratanattayaguṇānañca saddahanena vippasannena cetasā.

He dwells (vihāreti): In a dwelling place. He causes to build (kārayeti): He should cause to be built. He delights (rammeti): In the comfort of a delightful dwelling. Vāsayettha bahussute: Having caused monasteries to be built, he should settle therein the learned, the virtuous, and those of good qualities. And while settling them, he should give food, drink, clothing, and lodgings to those learned ones—who are upright and endowed with good intentions—so that they do not suffer hardship regarding requisites, doing so with a serene mind and with faith in the fruit of actions and the qualities of the Triple Gem.

Idāni gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ aññamaññūpakārataṃ dassetuṃ “te tassā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha teti bahussutā tassāti upāsakassa. Dhammaṃ desentīti sakalavaṭṭadukkhapanudanaṃ dhammaṃ desenti. Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāyāti so puggalo yaṃ saddhammaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane sammāpaṭipajjanena jānitvā aggamaggādhigamena anāsavo hutvā parinibbāyati.

Now, to show the mutual assistance between householders and renunciants, he speaks the verse 'te tassa.' Here, 'te' refers to the learned ones, and 'tassa' to the lay follower, the upāsaka. Dhammaṃ desenti: They teach the Dhamma, which dispels all the suffering of the cycle of existence. Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāya: That Dhamma, which that person understands here—having rightly practiced the true Dhamma in this dispensation, having attained the supreme path, becomes free from defilements, and attains final nibbāna.

Pūjāsakkāravaseneva [M 2.0014] paṭhamayāmo khepito, bhagavato desanāya appāvaseso majjhimayāmo gatoti pāḷiyaṃ “bahudeva ratti”nti vuttanti āha “atirekataraṃ diyaḍḍhayāma”nti. Sandassesīti ānisaṃsaṃ dassesi, āvāsadānapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ sutvā tato paraṃ, “mahārāja, itipi sīlaṃ, itipi samādhi, itipi paññā”ti sīlādiguṇe tesaṃ sammā dassesi, hatthena gahetvā viya paccakkhato pakāsesi. Samādapesīti “evaṃ sīlaṃ samādātabbaṃ, sīle patiṭṭhitena evaṃ samādhi, evaṃ paññā bhāvetabbā”ti yathā te sīlādiguṇe ādiyanti, tathā gaṇhāpesi. Samuttejesīti yathā samādinnaṃ sīlaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hoti, samathavipassanā ca bhāviyamānā yathā suṭṭhu visodhitā uparivisesāvahā honti, evaṃ cittaṃ samuttejesi nisāmanavasena vodāpesi. Sampahaṃsesīti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ ṭhitasīlādiguṇehi sampati laddhaguṇānisaṃsehi [V 2.0014] ceva upari laddhabbaphalavisesehi ca uparicittaṃ sammā pahaṃsesi, laddhassāsavasena suṭṭhu tosesi. Evametesaṃ padānaṃ attho veditabbo.

The first watch of the night was spent in offerings and honors, and the middle watch had mostly passed with the Blessed One’s teaching, thus it is said in the Pāli, 'Much of the night had gone,' which means, 'More than one and a half watches had passed.' Sandassesīti: He showed the benefits; after they heard the Dhamma talk connected with the gift of a dwelling, he then rightly showed them the qualities of virtue and so on, saying, 'Great king, such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom,' making them evident as if holding them in his hand. Samādapesīti: He encouraged them, saying, 'Thus should virtue be undertaken; established in virtue, thus should concentration and thus should wisdom be developed,' causing them to grasp these qualities of virtue and so on in such a way that they adopted them. Samuttejesīti: He roused them, so that the virtue they undertook became thoroughly purified, and serenity and insight, when developed, became well purified and conducive to higher distinctions; thus he roused their minds, purifying them through reflection. Sampahaṃsesīti: He gladdened them; with the qualities of virtue and so on established as instructed, with the benefits of the qualities already attained, and with the higher fruits yet to be gained, he rightly gladdened their minds, thoroughly satisfying them with the assurance of what they had attained. Evametesaṃ padānaṃ attho veditabbo: Thus should the meaning of these words be understood.

Samudāyavacanopi asītimahāthera-saddo tadekadesepi niruḷhoti āha “asītimahātheresu vijjamānesū”ti. Ānandattheropi hi antogadho evāti. Sākiyamaṇḍaleti sākiyarājasamūhe.

The term 'asītimahāthera' (eighty great elders), although a collective term, is also established as conventional usage even when referring to a portion of them, as he said, 'when the eighty great elders are present.' Indeed, the Elder Ānanda is included among them. Sākiyamaṇḍaleti: In the assembly of Sākiya rulers.

Paṭipadāya niyuttattā pāṭipado. Tenāha – “paṭipannako”ti. Sikkhanasīlatādinā sekho, odhiso samitapāpatāya samaṇo. Sekho pāṭipado paṭipajjanapuggalādhiṭṭhānena paṭipadādesanaṃ niyamento paṭipadāya puggalaṃ niyameti nāmāti “paṭipadāya puggalaṃ niyametvā dassetī”ti. Sekhappaṭipadā sāsane maṅgalapaṭipadā sammadeva asevitabbaparivajjanena sevitabbasamādānena ukkaṃsavatthūsu ca bhāvato asekhadhammapāripūriyā āvahattā ca vaḍḍhamānakapaṭipadā. Akilamantāva sallakkhessantīti idaṃ tadā tesaṃ asekhabhūmiadhigamāya ayogyatāya vuttaṃ. Akilamantāvāti iminā paṭisambhidāppattassapi anadhigatamaggasaññāpanā bhāriyāti dasseti. Osaṭāti anuppaviṭṭhā. Sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ kathitameva hoti tassa sīlakathābāhullato sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Tīhi piṭakehīti karaṇatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Tena taṃtaṃpiṭakānaṃ tassā tassā sikkhāya sādhakatamabhāvaṃ dasseti.

Because he is engaged in the path, he is one on the path (pāṭipado). Hence it is said, 'one who has entered upon the path' (paṭipannako). A trainee (sekha) is one by reason of his nature of training and so on; a recluse (samaṇa) is one who has quelled evil. The trainee on the path (Sekho pāṭipado), through the person practicing as the foundation, while directing the teaching of the path, regulates the person by means of the path—thus it is said, 'having regulated the person by the path, he shows it.' The path of a trainee in the Dispensation is an auspicious path, rightly followed by avoiding what should be avoided and undertaking what should be undertaken; and, due to growth in elevating qualities and bringing about the complete fulfillment of the qualities of the non-trainee, it is a path of growth. 'They will discern it without weariness' (akilamantāva sallakkhessanti): This was said then regarding their unfitness to attain the stage of the non-trainee. 'Without weariness' (akilamantāva): By this, it is shown that even for one who has attained the analytical knowledges, making known the path not yet attained is a heavy burden. Osaṭa: Entered, penetrated. The entire Vinaya Piṭaka is thus spoken of due to its abundance of discussion on virtue. The same principle applies to the remaining two. By the three Piṭakas (tīhi piṭakehi): The instrumental case is used in the sense of instrument. By this, it is shown that each Piṭaka is most effective for its respective training.

Piṭṭhivāto [M 2.0015] uppajjati upādinnakasarīrassa tathārūpattā saṅkhārānañca aniccatāya dukkhānubandhattā. Akāraṇaṃ vā etanti yenādhippāyena vuttaṃ, tameva adhippāyaṃ vivarituṃ “pahotī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Catūhi iriyāpathehi paribhuñjitukāmo ahosi sakyarājūnaṃ ajjhāsayavasena. Tathā hi vakkhati “satthāpi tadeva sandhāya tattha saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā nipajjītī”ti. Yadi evaṃ “piṭṭhi me āgilāyatī”ti idaṃ kathanti āha “upādinnakasarīrañca nāmā”tiādi.

Back pain (piṭṭhivāto) arises due to the nature of the body produced by clinging and because formations are impermanent and followed by suffering. To explain the very intention with which the phrase 'This is without cause' was spoken, the words 'it is capable,' and so on, were said. He wished to make use of the four postures due to the disposition of the Sakyan kings. For it will be said: 'The Teacher also, with that very thing in mind, having spread out his outer robe there, lay down.' If that is so, then how is it that he said, 'My back aches' (piṭṭhi me āgilāyati)? To this, it is said: 'And what is called a body produced by clinging' (upādinnakasarīrañca nāmā) and so on.

23. “Iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena…pe… sampanno”tiādīsu (vibha. 511) samannāgatattho sampanna-saddo, idha pana pāripūriatthoti dassetuṃ “paripuṇṇasīloti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Yo pana sampannasīloyeva, so paripuṇṇasīlo. Parisuddhañhi sīlaṃ “paripuṇṇa”nti vuccati, na sabalaṃ kammāsaṃ vā. Sundaradhammehīti sobhanadhammehi. Yasmiṃ santāne uppannā tassa sobhanabhāvato. Tehi sappurisabhāvasādhanato sappurisānaṃ dhammehi.

23. In such phrases as 'endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha... perfected' (iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena...pe... sampanno), the word 'perfected' (sampanna) has the meaning of 'endowed with'. Here, however, to show that the meaning is 'fulfillment', it is said, 'the meaning is "one of complete virtue" (paripuṇṇasīlo).' For one who is perfected in virtue is one of complete virtue. Indeed, pure virtue is called 'complete' (paripuṇṇa), not mottled or stained. With beautiful qualities (sundaradhammehi): With excellent qualities, because they make excellent the mental continuity in which they arise. Because they accomplish the state of a good person, they are the qualities of good people.

24. Iminā [V 2.0015] ettakena ṭhānenāti “idha, mahānāma, ariyasāvako”ti ārabhitvā yāva “akasiralābhī”ti padaṃ iminā ettakena uddesapadena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā. Paṭipāṭiyāti uddesapaṭipāṭiyā. Evamāhāti “evaṃ kathañca, mahānāmā”tiādinā idāni vuccamānena dassitākārena āha.

24. Iminā ettakena ṭhānenāti: By this much of a passage, that is, having established the matrix by this much of a recitation heading, beginning with 'Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple' and ending with the phrase 'one who obtains without difficulty' (akasiralābhī). Paṭipāṭiyāti: In sequence, meaning in the sequence of the recitation heading. Evamāhāti: He spoke thus, that is, he spoke in the manner now being explained, beginning with 'And how, Mahānāma...'

25. Hirīyatīti lajjīyati pīḷīyati. Yasmā hirī pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇā, tasmā “jigucchatīti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Ottappatīti uttappati. Pāputrāsalakkhaṇañhi ottappaṃ. Paggahitavīriyoti saṅkocaṃ anāpannavīriyo. Tenāha “anosakkitamānaso”ti. Pahānatthāyāti samucchindanatthāya. Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadā nāma adhigamo evāti āha “paṭilābhatthāyā”ti. Satinepakkenāti satiyā nepakkena tikkhavisadasūrabhāvena. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana nepakkaṃ nāma paññāti adhippāyena “satiyā ca nipakabhāvena cā”ti attho vutto, evaṃ sati añño niddiṭṭho nāma hoti. Satimāti ca imināva visesā sati gahitā, parato “cirakatampi [M 2.0016] cirabhāsitampi saritā anussaritā”ti satikiccameva niddiṭṭhaṃ, na paññākiccaṃ, tasmā satinepakkenāti satiyā nepakkabhāvenāti sakkā viññātuṃ. Teneva hi paccayavisesavasena aññadhammanirapekkho satiyā balavabhāvo. Tathā hi ñāṇavippayuttacittenapi ajjhayanasammasanāni sambhavanti.

25. Hirīyati: To be ashamed, to be distressed. Because moral shame (hirī) has the characteristic of disgust towards evil, it is therefore said, 'the meaning is "to be disgusted."' Ottappati: To be apprehensive. For moral dread (ottappa) has the characteristic of fear of evil. Paggahitavīriya: One whose energy is not slack. Therefore, it is said, 'with a mind not shrinking back' (anosakkitamānaso). Pahānatthāya: For the sake of abandoning, meaning for the sake of cutting off. The attainment of wholesome states is indeed acquisition; thus, it is said 'for the sake of gaining' (paṭilābhatthāya). Satinepakkena: With the prudence of mindfulness, meaning with the sharp, clear, and courageous nature of mindfulness. In the commentary, however, with the intention that 'prudence' (nepakka) means wisdom, the meaning is given as 'with mindfulness and with the state of prudence.' If that were so, another thing would have been specified. Moreover, by 'mindful' (satimā) itself, a special mindfulness is understood. Further on, 'remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago' is specified, which is the function of mindfulness, not the function of wisdom. Therefore, 'satinepakkena' can be understood as 'with the prudent nature of mindfulness' (satiyā nepakkabhāvena). For it is precisely due to a special condition that mindfulness becomes strong, independent of other states. Indeed, even with a mind dissociated from knowledge, study and reflection can occur.

Cetiyaṅgaṇavattādīti ādi-saddena bodhiyaṅgaṇavattādīni saṅgaṇhāti. Asītimahāvattapaṭipattipūraṇanti ettha asītivattapaṭipattipūraṇaṃ mahāvattapaṭipattipūraṇanti vattapaṭipattipūraṇa-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo. Tattha mahāvattāni (vibha. mūlaṭī. 406) nāma vattakhandhake (cūḷava. 356 ādayo) vuttāni āgantukavattaṃ āvāsikaṃ gamikaṃ anumodanaṃ bhattaggaṃ piṇḍacārikaṃ āraññikaṃ senāsanaṃ jantāgharaṃ vaccakuṭi upajjhāyaṃ saddhivihārikaṃ ācariyaṃ antevāsikavattanti cuddasa. Tato aññāni pana kadāci tajjanīyakammakatādikāle pārivāsikādikāle ca caritabbāni asīti khuddakavattāni sabbāsu avatthāsu na caritabbāni, tasmā mahāvattesu, aggahitāni. Tattha “pārivāsikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vattaṃ paññapessāmī”ti ārabhitvā “na upasampādetabbaṃ…pe… na chamāyaṃ caṅkamante caṅkame caṅkamitabba”nti (cūḷava. 81) vuttāni pakabhatte caritabbavattāvasānāni chasaṭṭhi, tato paraṃ “na, bhikkhave, pārivāsikena bhikkhunā pārivāsikavuḍḍhatarena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ mūlāyapaṭikassanārahena mānattārahena mānattacārikena abbhānārahena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ ekacchanne āvāse vattabba”ntiādīni (cūḷava. 82) pakatatte caritabbehi anaññattā visuṃ visuṃ agaṇetvā pārivāsikavuḍḍhatarādīsu puggalantaresu [V 2.0016] caritabbattā tesaṃ vasena sampiṇḍetvā ekekaṃ katvā gaṇitabbāni pañcāti ekasattativattāni, ukkhepaniyakammakatavattesu vattapaññāpanavasena vuttaṃ – “na pakatattassa bhikkhuno abhivādanaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ…pe… nhāne piṭṭhiparikammaṃ sāditabba”nti (cūḷava. 51) idaṃ abhivādanādīnaṃ asādiyanaṃ ekaṃ, “na pakatatto bhikkhu sīlavipattiyā anuddhaṃsitabbo”tiādīni ca dasāti evametāni dvāsīti. Etesveva pana kānici tajjanīyakammādivattāni kānici pārivāsikādivattānīti aggahitaggahaṇena dvāsīti, evaṃ appakaṃ pana ūnamadhikaṃ vā gaṇanupagaṃ na hotīti idha “asīti”cceva vuttaṃ. Aññattha pana aṭṭhakathāpadese “dvāsīti khandhakavattānī”ti vuccati.

Cetiyaṅgaṇavattādīti: By the word 'etc.' in 'duties concerning the shrine grounds, etc.', duties concerning the Bodhi tree grounds, etc., are included. Asītimahāvattapaṭipattipūraṇanti: Here, in 'the fulfillment of the practice of the eighty great duties', the phrase 'fulfillment of the practice of duties' should be connected to each term, as 'the fulfillment of the practice of the eighty duties' and 'the fulfillment of the practice of the great duties'. Among these, the great duties are the fourteen stated in the chapter on duties (Cv. 356ff.): the duty for incoming monks, for resident monks, for traveling monks, for expressing appreciation, for the meal hall, for the alms-round, for forest-dwelling, for lodging, for the steam-bath house, for the latrine, for the preceptor, for the co-resident, for the teacher, and for the pupil. Other than these, there are eighty minor duties to be practiced only on certain occasions, such as when one has undergone the act of censure, or during a period of probation, etc. They are not to be practiced in all circumstances and are therefore not included among the great duties. Here, beginning with 'I shall prescribe the duties for monks undergoing probation,' up to 'He should not give ordination... he should not walk on the ground when walking on the cloister path' (Cv. 81), sixty-six duties are stated, ending with those to be practiced at the time of the appointed meal. After that, from 'Monks, a monk undergoing probation should not dwell in the same covered residence with a senior monk undergoing probation, one eligible for reinstatement to the original position, one eligible for mānatta, one practicing mānatta, or one eligible for absolution' etc. (Cv. 82), since these are not different from the duties to be practiced by a normal monk, they are not counted separately. But because they are to be practiced with respect to different individuals, such as senior monks undergoing probation, etc., by combining them accordingly, they are counted as one each, making five. Thus, there are seventy-one duties. Regarding the duties for those subject to an act of suspension, it is stated concerning the laying down of duties: 'A normal monk should not accept a greeting, rising up... nor should he have his back massaged during bathing' (Cv. 51). This non-acceptance of greeting, etc., is one duty. And there are ten others beginning with 'A normal monk should not be reproved for a failure in morality.' Thus, these make eighty-two. Among these, some are duties for those subject to an act of censure, etc., and some are duties for those undergoing probation, etc. By including those not previously included, the total becomes eighty-two. However, a slight deficiency or excess does not invalidate the count. Hence, here it is simply called 'eighty.' Elsewhere, in a passage of the commentary, it is said: 'eighty-two duties of the Khandhakas.'

Sakkaccaṃ [M 2.0017] uddisanaṃ sakkaccaṃ uddisāpananti paccekaṃ sakkaccaṃ-saddo yojetabbo. Uddisanaṃ uddesaggahaṇaṃ. Dhammosāraṇaṃ dhammassa uccāraṇaṃ. Dhammadesanā –

In 'carefully reciting, carefully causing to recite,' the word 'carefully' should be connected to each. Reciting means grasping the recitation. Rehearsing the Dhamma means uttering the Dhamma. Teaching the Dhamma—

“Ādimhi sīlaṃ deseyya, majjhe jhānaṃ vipassanaṃ;

Pariyosāne ca nibbānaṃ, esā kathikasaṇṭhitī”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.190; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.4.246) –

"At the beginning, one should teach virtue; in the middle, jhāna and insight; and at the end, Nibbāna. This is the established method of the preacher."

Evaṃ kathitalakkhaṇā dhammakathā. Upagantvā nisinnassa yassa kassaci gahaṭṭhassa pabbajitassa vā taṅkhaṇānurūpā dhammī kathā upanisinnakathā. Bhattānumodanakathā anumodaniyā. Saritāti ettha na kevalaṃ cirakatacirabhāsitānaṃ saraṇamanussaraṇamattaṃ adhippetaṃ, atha kho tathāpavattarūpārūpadhammānaṃ pariggahamukhena pavattavipassanācāre satisambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpananti dassetuṃ “tasmiṃ kāyena cirakate”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sakimpi saraṇenāti ekavāraṃ saraṇena. Punappunaṃ saraṇenāti anu anu saraṇena. Satisambojjhaṅgampi vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vosaggapariṇāmiñca katvā saranto tattha tattha javanavāre saraṇajavanavāre parittajavanavasena anussaritāti veditabbā.

Such is a Dhamma talk, whose characteristics have been explained. A Dhamma talk suitable for the moment, given to any layperson or monastic who has come and sat down, is an 'upanisinnakathā'. A talk of appreciation after a meal is an 'anumodaniyakathā'. Here, by 'remembered' (saritā), it is not merely intended to mean the recollection of things done or spoken long ago. Rather, to show that it is the arousal of the awakening-factor of mindfulness through the practice of insight, which proceeds by way of comprehending material and immaterial phenomena as they occur, it is said, 'in that body, of things done long ago,' etc. By 'even a single act of remembering' (sakimpi saraṇena) is meant remembering once. By 'repeated remembering' (punappunaṃ saraṇena) is meant remembering again and again. The awakening-factor of mindfulness, too, should be understood as having been recollected by making it based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and culminating in relinquishment, and by recollecting in each and every moment of impulsion, in the moment of recollection-impulsion, by way of limited impulsion.

Gatiatthā dhātusaddā buddhiatthā hontīti āha – “udayañca vayañca paṭivijjhituṃ samatthāyā”ti. Missakanayenāyaṃ desanā āgatāti āha – “vikkhambhanavasena ca samucchedavasena cā”ti. Tenāha “vipassanāpaññāya cevā”tiādi. Vipassanāpaññāya nibbedhikapariyāyato. Sā ca kho padesikāti nippadesikaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “maggapaññāya paṭilābhasaṃvattanato cā”ti vuttaṃ. Dukkhakkhayagāminibhāvepi eseva nayo. Sammāti yāthāvato. Akuppadhammatāya [V 2.0017] hi maggapaññā khepitakhepanāya na puna kiccaṃ atthīti upāyena ñāyena yā pavatti sā evāti āha – “hetunā nayenā”ti.

He says that the root words signifying 'going' have the meaning of 'understanding,' as in 'capable of penetrating both arising and passing away.' He says that this teaching has come by a mixed method, as in 'by way of suppression and by way of eradication.' Therefore, he says, 'and by insight wisdom,' etc. Insight wisdom is by way of penetration. And yet, that is partial. To show it as comprehensive, it is said: 'and through being conducive to the attainment of path wisdom.' The same method applies even in the aspect of leading to the cessation of suffering. 'Rightly' means according to reality. For path wisdom, being of an unshakeable nature, having eliminated what is to be eliminated, there is no further task. Thus, he says, 'by cause and by method,' meaning that is precisely the way it proceeds, by means of skill and method.

26. Adhikaṃ ceto abhiceto, mahaggatacittaṃ, tassa pana adhikatā kāmacchandādipaṭipakkhavigamena visiṭṭhabhāvappatti, tannissitāni ābhicetasikāni. Tenāha “abhicittaṃ seṭṭhacittaṃ sitāna”nti. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānanti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve phāsuvihārabhūtānaṃ. Tehi [M 2.0018] pana samaṅgitakkhaṇe yasmā vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ apītijaṃ satipārisuddhiñāṇasukhañca paṭilabhati vindati, tasmā āha – “appitappitakkhaṇe sukhapaṭilābhahetūna”nti. Icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjitāti iminā tesu jhānesu samāpajjanavasībhāvamāha, “nikāmalābhī”ti pana vacanato āvajjanādhiṭṭhānā paccavekkhaṇavasiyo ca vuttā evāti veditabbā. Nidukkhalābhīti iminā tesaṃ jhānānaṃ sukhapaṭipadākhippābhiññataṃ dasseti, vipulalābhīti iminā paguṇataṃ tappamāṇadassitabhāvadīpanato. Tenāha “paguṇabhāvenā”tiādi. Samāpajjituṃ sakkoti samāpajjanavasībhāvatāya sādhitattā. Samādhipāripanthikadhammeti vasībhāvassa paccanīkadhamme. Jhānādhigamassa pana paccanīkadhammā pageva vikkhambhitā, aññathā jhānādhigamo eva na siyā. Akilamanto vikkhambhetuṃ na sakkotīti kicchena vikkhambheti visodheti, kāmādīnavapaccavekkhaṇādīhi kāmacchandādīnaṃ aññesaṃ samādhipāripanthikānaṃ dūrasamussāraṇaṃ idha vikkhambhanaṃ visodhananti veditabbaṃ.

26. The mind is 'superior' (abhiceto) because it is a lofty mind. Its superiority, however, is the attainment of a distinguished state through the removal of opposing states such as sensual desire; the mental factors dependent on it are called 'supreme mental states' (ābhicetasikāni). Hence he says, 'the supreme mind is the best mind, the peaceful mind.' The 'blissful abidings in this very life' (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ) refers to pleasant dwellings in this very existence. At the moment of being endowed with these, one gains and experiences the joy and happiness born of seclusion, the joy and happiness born of concentration, and the happiness of knowledge and purity of mindfulness which is without joy. Therefore, he says, 'the causes for gaining happiness at the very moment of absorption.' By 'one attains at will' (icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjitā), he states the mastery in entering these jhānas. And by the phrase 'one who gains at will' (nikāmalābhī), the masteries of adverting, resolving, and reviewing are also stated, so it should be understood. By 'one who gains without difficulty' (nidukkhalābhī), he shows that these jhānas are characterized by pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge. By 'one who gains abundantly' (vipulalābhī), he indicates their proficiency, as it illustrates their immeasurable nature. Hence he says, 'by the nature of proficiency,' etc. 'One is capable of attaining' means one has achieved mastery in entering. 'Obstacles to concentration' refers to factors opposed to mastery. Indeed, the obstacles to attaining jhāna are already suppressed; otherwise, the attainment of jhāna would not be possible. One who does not exert himself is unable to suppress them, and so one suppresses and purifies them with difficulty. Here, suppression and purification should be understood as the complete removal of sensual desire and other obstacles to concentration by reflecting on the danger of sensual pleasures and so on.

27. Vipassanāhitāya uparūparivisesāvahattā vaḍḍhamānāya pubbabhāgasīlādipaṭipadāya. Sā eva pubbabhāgapaṭipadā yathābhāvitatāya avassaṃ bhāvinaṃ visesaṃ pariggahitattā aṇḍaṃ viyāti aṇḍaṃ, kilesehi adūsitatāya apūti aṇḍaṃ etassāti apuccaṇḍo, vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ṭhitapuggalo, tassa bhāvo apuccaṇḍatā.
