Sampattīnaṃ mūlanti yā imā loke padesarajjasirissariyasattaratanasamujjalacakkavattisampadāti evaṃpabhedā mānusikā sampattiyo, yā ca cātumahārājādigatā dibbā sampattiyo, yā vā panaññāpi sampattiyo, tāsaṃ sabbāsaṃ idaṃ mūlakāraṇaṃ. Bhogānanti bhuñjitabbaṭṭhena “bhogo”nti laddhanāmānaṃ manāpiyarūpādīnaṃ, tannissayānaṃ vā upabhogasukhānaṃ, patiṭṭhā niccalādhiṭṭhānatāya. Visamagatassāti byasanappattassa. Tāṇanti rakkhā tato paripālanato. Leṇanti byasanehi paripātiyamānassa olīyanapadeso. Gatīti gantabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Parāyaṇanti paṭisaraṇaṃ. Avassayoti vinipatituṃ adento nissayo. Ārammaṇanti olubbhārammaṇaṃ.

A source of happiness means a cause of all kinds of happiness: those in the present life, in future lives, and those connected with Nibbāna. For whatever happiness from wealth there is in the world, all of it has giving as its source—this meaning is clear. Moreover, for the happiness connected with jhāna, insight, path, fruition, and Nibbāna, giving is also indeed a decisive support condition. The root of attainments means this is the root cause of all of them: human attainments of such kinds as regional kingship, glorious sovereignty, the attainment of a wheel-turning monarch resplendent with the seven treasures, and so on; and divine attainments such as those of the Four Great Kings and so on; and whatever other attainments there may be. 'Of wealth' means of pleasing forms and so on, which have obtained the name "wealth" (bhoga) in the sense that they are to be enjoyed, or of the pleasures of enjoyment dependent on them. A foundation: because it is an unshakable basis. For one in a difficult situation: for one who has met with misfortune. Shelter: protection, because it guards from that. A cave: a place of shelter for one being pursued by misfortunes. A destination: a place to go. A final resort: a refuge. A support: a basis that does not allow one to fall. An object: an object to hold on to.

Ratanamayasīhāsanasadisanti [M 2.0037] sabbaratanamayasattaṅgamahāsīhāsanasadisaṃ, mahagghaṃ hutvā sabbaso vinipatituṃ appadānato. Mahāpathavisadisaṃ gatagataṭṭhāne patiṭṭhāsambhavato. Yathā dubbalassa purisassa ālambanarajju uttiṭṭhato tiṭṭhato ca upatthambho, evaṃ dānaṃ sattānaṃ sampattibhave upapattiyā ṭhitiyā ca paccayo hotīti āha “ālambanaṭṭhena ālambanarajjusadisa”nti. Dukkhanittharaṇaṭṭhenāti duggatidukkhanittharaṇaṭṭhena. Samassāsanaṭṭhenāti lobhamacchariyādipaṭisattupaddavato sammadeva assāsanaṭṭhena. Bhayaparittāṇaṭṭhenāti dāliddiyabhayato paripālanaṭṭhena. Maccheramalādīhīti maccheralobhadosaissāmicchādiṭṭhivicikicchādi cittamalehi. Anupalittaṭṭhenāti anupakkiliṭṭhatāya. Tesanti maccheramalādīnaṃ. Etesaṃ eva durāsadaṭṭhena. Asantāsanaṭṭhenāti asantāsahetubhāvena. Yo hi dāyako dānapati, so sampatipi na kutoci santasati, pageva āyatiṃ. Balavantaṭṭhenāti mahābalavatāya. Dāyako hi dānapati sampati pakkhabalena balavā hoti, āyatiṃ pana kāyabalādīhi. Abhimaṅgalasammataṭṭhenāti “vuḍḍhikāraṇa”nti abhisammatabhāvena. Vipattito sampattiyā nayanaṃ khemantabhūmisampāpanaṃ.

"Similar to a jeweled lion-throne" means similar to the great seven-limbed lion-throne made of all kinds of jewels, because, being of great value, it does not allow one to fall completely. "Similar to the great earth" because it makes a footing possible in every place one goes. Just as a support-rope is a help for a weak person in getting up and standing, so giving is a condition for beings' arising and stability in a good existence; thus it says, "similar to a support-rope in the sense of being a support." "In the sense of crossing over suffering" means in the sense of crossing over the suffering of a bad destination. "In the sense of giving relief" means in the sense of giving proper relief from the trouble from such adversaries as greed and stinginess. "In the sense of protection from fear" means in the sense of protecting from the fear of poverty. "By the stains of stinginess, etc." means by such mental stains as stinginess, greed, hatred, envy, wrong view, and doubt. "In the sense of being unsmeared" means because of being undefiled. "Of them" means of the stains of stinginess, etc. Because of being hard to assail by them. "In the sense of not trembling" means by being a cause of fearlessness. For a donor, a master of giving, does not tremble at anything even in the present, let alone in the future. "In the sense of being powerful" means because of great power. For a donor, a master of giving, is powerful in the present through the power of his faction, and in the future through physical strength, etc. "In the sense of being deemed a high blessing" means because of being considered a "cause of growth." Leading from misfortune to success is the attainment of the state of security.

Idāni [V 2.0035] mahābodhicariyabhāvenapi dānaguṇaṃ dassetuṃ dānaṃ nāmetantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha attānaṃ niyyādentenāti etena dānaphalaṃ sammadeva passantā mahāpurisā attano jīvitampi pariccajanti, tasmā ko nāma viññujātiko bāhire vatthumhi saṅgaṃ kareyyāti ovādaṃ deti. Idāni yā lokiyā lokuttarā ca ukkaṃsagatā sampattiyo, tā sabbā dānatoyeva pavattantīti dassento “dānañhī”tiādimāha. Tattha sakkamārabrahmasampattiyo attahitāya eva, cakkavattisampatti pana attahitāya ca parahitāya cāti dassetuṃ sā tāsaṃ parato vuttā. Etā lokiyā, imā pana lokuttarāti dassetuṃ “sāvakapāramīñāṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tāsupi ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭhatarukkaṭṭhatamameva dassetuṃ kamena ñāṇattayaṃ vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ pana dānassa paccayabhāvo heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Eteneva tassa brahmasampattiyāpi paccayabhāvo dīpitoti veditabbo.

Now, to demonstrate the virtue of generosity even in the mode of the great bodhisatta's conduct, it is said, “Generosity is called…,” and so on. Herein, by the words “by one who offers himself,” he gives the admonition that great beings, rightly seeing the fruit of giving, renounce even their own lives; therefore, what person of understanding would form an attachment to external things? Now, to show that all worldly and supramundane excellent attainments proceed from giving alone, he said, “For giving…,” and so on. Herein, the attainments of Sakka, Māra, and Brahmā are for one’s own welfare only, while the attainment of a wheel-turning monarch is for both one’s own welfare and the welfare of others. To indicate this, it is mentioned after them. These are worldly; but to show that the others are supramundane, it is said, “the knowledge of the disciples’ perfections,” and so on. Among these too, to show what is excellent, more excellent, and most excellent, the threefold knowledge is stated in sequence. But the status of giving as a condition for these has already been stated below. By this itself, it should be understood that its status as a condition for the Brahmā attainment is also explained.

Dānañca nāma hitajjhāsayena, pūjāvasena vā attano santakassa paresaṃ pariccajanaṃ, tasmā dāyako purisapuggalo paresaṃ santakaṃ harissatīti [M 2.0038] aṭṭhānametanti āha – “dānaṃ dadanto sīlaṃ samādātuṃ sakkotī”ti. Sīlālaṅkārasadiso alaṅkāro natthi sobhāvisesāvahattā sīlassa. Sīlapupphasadisaṃ pupphaṃ natthīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sīlagandhasadiso gandho natthīti ettha “candanaṃ tagaraṃ vāpī”tiādikā (dha. pa. 55; mi. pa. 4.1.1) gāthā – “gandho isīnaṃ ciradikkhitānaṃ, kāyā cuto gacchati mālutenā”tiādikā (jā. 2.17.55) jātakagāthāyo ca āharitvā vattabbā, sīlañhi sattānaṃ ābharaṇañceva alaṅkāro ca gandhavilepanañca dassanīyabhāvāvahañca. Tenāha “sīlālaṅkārena hī”tiādi.

Giving is the relinquishing of one’s own possessions to others out of a benevolent disposition or by way of veneration. Therefore, he says it is impossible that a person who is a giver would take what belongs to others: “While giving, one is able to undertake moral virtue.” There is no ornament like the ornament of moral virtue, for moral virtue brings a special splendor. The same principle applies here to the words, “There is no flower like the flower of moral virtue.” Regarding the words, “There is no fragrance like the fragrance of moral virtue,” the verse beginning “Sandalwood, tagara…” (Dhp 55; Mil 4.1.1) and the Jātaka verse beginning “The fragrance of the long-ordained seers, issuing from their bodies, travels on the wind…” (Ja 2.17.55) should be cited. For moral virtue is for beings an adornment, an ornament, a fragrant ointment, and it brings a pleasing appearance. Hence it is said, “For by the ornament of moral virtue…,” and so on.

Ayaṃ saggo labbhatīti idaṃ majjhimehi chandādīhi samādānasīlaṃ sandhāyāha. Tenāha sakko devarājā –

The words, “This heaven is attainable,” are said in reference to the moral virtue undertaken with middling intention and so on. Therefore Sakka, the king of the devas, said:

“Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati;

Majjhimena ca devattaṃ, uttamena visujjhatī”ti. (jā. 1.8.75; 2.22.429; dī. ni. ṭī. 2.75-76);

“By an inferior holy life, one is reborn among the khattiyas; by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; by a superior one, one is purified.”

Iṭṭhoti sukho. Kantoti kamanīyo. Manāpoti manavaḍḍhanako. Taṃ pana tassa iṭṭhādibhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “niccamettha kīḷā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Pleasant means agreeable. Lovely means desirable. Agreeable means gladdening the mind. But to show its nature of being pleasant and so on, it is said, “Here there is constant sport…,” and so on.

Dosoti aniccatādinā appassādādinā ca dūsitabhāvo, yato te viññūnaṃ cittaṃ nārādhenti[V 2.0036]. Atha vā ādīnaṃ vāti pavattetīti ādīnavo, paramakapaṇatā. Tathā ca kāmā yathābhūtaṃ paccavekkhantānaṃ paccupatiṭṭhanti. Lāmakabhāvoti aseṭṭhehi sevitabbo, seṭṭhehi na sevitabbo nihīnabhāvo. Saṃkilissananti vibādhakatā upatāpatā ca.

Fault means the state of being corrupted by impermanence and so on, and by little gratification and so on, since they do not please the minds of the wise. Or, it is a drawback (ādīnava) because it emits (vāti) misery (ādīnaṃ); it is extreme wretchedness. And sensual pleasures appear in such a way to those who review them as they really are. The state of being inferior means a base condition to be resorted to by the ignoble, not to be resorted to by the noble. ‘They are defiling’ means oppressiveness and torment.

Nekkhamme ānisaṃsanti ettha yattakā kāmesu ādīnavā, tappaṭipakkhato tattakā nekkhamme ānisaṃsā. Apica – “nekkhammaṃ nāmetaṃ asambādhaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ nikkhantaṃ kāmehi, nikkhantaṃ kāmasaññāya, nikkhantaṃ kāmavitakkehi, nikkhantaṃ kāmapariḷāhehi, nikkhantaṃ byāpādasaññāyā”tiādinā (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.26; dī. ni. ṭī. 2.75-76) nayena nekkhamme ānisaṃse pakāsesi, pabbajjāya jhānādīsu ca guṇe vibhāvesi vaṇṇesi. Kallacittanti heṭṭhā pavattitadesanāya assaddhiyādīnaṃ cittadosānaṃ vigatattā uparidesanāya bhājanabhāvūpagamanena kammakkhamacittaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana yasmā assaddhiyādayo cittassa rogabhūtā[M 2.0039], tadā te vigatā, tasmā āha “arogacitta”nti. Diṭṭhimānādikilesavigamena muducittaṃ. Kāmacchandādivigamena vinīvaraṇacittaṃ. Sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ uḷārapītipāmojjayogena udaggacittaṃ. Tattha saddhāsampattiyā pasannacittaṃ. Yadā bhagavā aññāsīti sambandho. Atha vā kallacittanti kāmacchandavigamena arogacittaṃ. Muducittanti byāpādavigamena mettāvasena akathinacittaṃ. Vinīvaraṇacittanti uddhaccakukkuccavigamena vikkhepassa vigatattā tena apihitacittaṃ. Udaggacittanti thinamiddhavigamena sampaggahitavasena alīnacittaṃ. Pasannacittanti vicikicchāvigamena sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ adhimuttacittanti evamettha sesapadānaṃ attho veditabbo.

The benefits in renunciation: Here, however many drawbacks there are in sensual pleasures, there are just as many benefits in renunciation, as their opposite. Further, by the method beginning: “Renunciation is unconfined, undefiled, departed from sensual pleasures, departed from perceptions of sensuality, departed from thoughts of sensuality, departed from the fever of sensuality, departed from perceptions of ill will…,” he proclaimed the benefits in renunciation, and he explained and extolled the qualities in the going forth, in the jhānas, and so on. A ready mind means a mind fit for the task, since the mental faults of lack of faith, etc., have departed on account of the preceding discourse, and it has become a vessel for the subsequent discourse. In the commentary, however, it is said: “Since lack of faith and so on are diseases of the mind, when they have departed, it is called ‘a healthy mind.’” A malleable mind is one so called because of the departure of the defilements of views, conceit, etc. A mind without hindrances is one so called because of the departure of sensual desire, etc. An uplifted mind is one so called because of its connection with sublime rapture and joy in right practice. Therein, a confident mind is one so called because of its endowment with faith. The connection is with “When the Blessed One knew….” Or, a ready mind means a healthy mind through the departure of sensual desire. A malleable mind means a mind that is not stiff, through the departure of ill will, by way of loving-kindness. A mind without hindrances means a mind that is not covered by them, since distraction has departed through the departure of restlessness and remorse. An uplifted mind means a mind that is not sluggish, by way of being well exerted, through the departure of sloth and torpor. A confident mind means a mind resolved upon right practice through the departure of doubt. In this way the meaning of the remaining terms should be understood here.

Seyyathāpītiādinā upamāvasena upālissa saṃkilesappahānaṃ ariyamagganipphādanañca dasseti. Apagatakāḷakanti vigatakāḷakaṃ. Sammadevāti suṭṭhu eva. Rajananti nīlapītādiraṅgajātaṃ. Paṭiggaṇheyyāti gaṇheyya pabhassaraṃ bhaveyya. Tasmiṃyeva āsaneti tissaṃ eva nisajjāyaṃ. Etenassa lahuvipassakatā tikkhapaññatā sukhapaṭipadākhippābhiññatā ca dassitā hoti. Virajanti apāyagamanīyarāgarajādīnaṃ vigamena virajaṃ. Anavasesadiṭṭhivicikicchāmalāpagamena vītamalaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ maggānanti heṭṭhimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ. Tassa uppattiākāradassananti kasmā vuttaṃ? Nanu maggañāṇaṃ asaṅkhatadhammārammaṇanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “taṃ hī”tiādi. Tattha paṭivijjhantanti asammohapaṭivedhavasena paṭivijjhantaṃ. Tenāha “kiccavasenā”ti.

By the passage beginning “Just as…,” he shows by way of a simile the abandoning of the defilements and the accomplishment of the noble path in Upāli. Free from dark stain means with its dark stain departed. Properly means quite well. Dye means a kind of color such as blue or yellow. Would take means it would accept it, it would become bright. On that very seat means in that very sitting. By this is shown his swift insight, sharp wisdom, and pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge. Stainless means stainless through the departure of the dust of lust, etc., which leads to the plane of misery. Unblemished means with its blemishes removed through the complete removal of the stain of views and doubt. Of the three paths means of the three lower paths. Why was it said, “seeing the mode of its arising”? Anticipating the objection, “But doesn’t path knowledge have the unconditioned Dhamma as its object?” he says, “For that…,” and so on. Therein, penetrating means penetrating by way of undeluded penetration. Hence he says, “by way of function.”

Tatridaṃ [V 2.0037] upamāsaṃsandanaṃ – vatthaṃ viya cittaṃ, vatthassa āgantukamalehi kiliṭṭhabhāvo viya cittassa rāgādimalehi saṃkiliṭṭhabhāvo, dhovanasilā viya anupubbīkathā, udakaṃ viya saddhā, udake temetvā ūsagomayachārikābharehi kāḷakapadese sammadditvā vatthassa dhovanapayogo viya saddhāsinehena temetvā satisamādhipaññāhi dose sithile katvā sutādividhinā cittassa sodhane vīriyārambho. Tena payogena vatthe kāḷakāpagamo viya vīriyārambhena kilesavikkhambhanaṃ, raṅgajātaṃ viya ariyamaggo, tena suddhassa vatthassa pabhassarabhāvo viya vikkhambhitakilesassa cittassa maggena pariyodapananti.

Here is the application of the simile: The mind is like the cloth. The mind's state of being defiled by the stains of lust, etc., is like the cloth's state of being defiled by adventitious stains. The graduated discourse is like the washing stone. Faith is like the water. The application of effort to wash the cloth by wetting it with water and rubbing the dark spots with a load of lye, cow dung, and ash is like the arousal of energy to purify the mind by the method of hearing, etc., after having moistened it with the moisture of faith and loosened the faults with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The removal of the dark stains from the cloth by that application of effort is like the suppression of the defilements by the arousal of energy. The noble path is like the dye. The brightness of the clean cloth from that dye is like the purification by the path of the mind whose defilements have been suppressed.

Diṭṭhadhammoti vatvā dassanaṃ nāma ñāṇadassanato aññampi atthīti tannivattanatthaṃ “pattadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Patti ca ñāṇasampattito aññāpi vijjatīti [M 2.0040] tato visesanatthaṃ “viditadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Sā panesā viditadhammatā dhammesu ekadesanāpi hotīti nippadesato viditabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “pariyogāḷhadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Tenassa saccābhisambodhaṃyeva dīpeti. Maggañāṇañhi ekābhisamayavasena pariññādikiccaṃ sādhentaṃ nippadesena catusaccadhammaṃ samantato ogāhantaṃ nāma hoti. Tenāha – “diṭṭho ariyasaccadhammo etenāti diṭṭhadhammo”ti. Tiṇṇā vicikicchāti sappaṭibhayakantārasadisā soḷasavatthukā aṭṭhavatthukā ca tiṇṇā vicikicchā tiṇṇavicikicchā. Vigatakathaṃkathoti pavattiādīsu “evaṃ nu kho, kiṃ nu kho”ti evaṃ pavattikā vigatā samucchinnā kathaṃkathā. Sārajjakarānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ pahīnattā tappaṭipakkhesu sīlādiguṇesu suppatiṭṭhitattā vesārajjaṃ visāradabhāvaṃ veyyattiyaṃ patto. Attanā eva paccakkhato diṭṭhattā na tassa paro paccetabbo atthīti aparappaccayo.

Having said ‘one who has seen the Dhamma,’ to prevent the idea that there is some seeing other than knowledge-and-vision, the words ‘one who has attained the Dhamma’ were stated. And since there is also attainment apart from the attainment of knowledge, to distinguish it from that, the words ‘one who has understood the Dhamma’ were stated. And since that understanding of the Dhamma can be of only one part of the teachings, to show that it was understood without remainder, the words ‘one who has penetrated the Dhamma’ were stated. By this he indicates the very awakening to the truths. For path knowledge, while accomplishing the functions of full understanding, etc., by way of a single penetration, is said to plunge into the Dhamma of the four truths all-round, without remainder. Hence it is said: “The Dhamma of the noble truths has been seen by him, thus he is one who has seen the Dhamma.” ‘One who has crossed over doubt’ means that the sixteen-based and eight-based doubt, which is like a perilous wilderness with its dangers, has been crossed over. ‘One who is without perplexity’ means that the perplexity that proceeds as “How is it? What is it?” in regard to continuity, etc., has departed, has been cut off. Because the evil things that cause diffidence have been abandoned, and because he is well established in the qualities of moral virtue, etc., which are their opposite, he has attained fearlessness, confidence, and expertise. Since he has seen it directly for himself, there is no other who is his authority; thus he is not reliant on another.

71. Paṇḍitoti paññavā.

71. A wise person (paṇḍito) means one possessing wisdom (paññavā).

72. Tena hi sammāti dovārikena saddhiṃ sallapatiyeva, “etthevā”ti tena vuttavacanaṃ sutvāpi tassa atthaṃ asallakkhento. Kasmā? Paridevatāya. Tenāha “balavasokena abhibhūto”ti.

72. Then, “Friend,” he was conversing with the gatekeeper, but though he heard the words spoken by him, “Right here,” he did not notice their meaning. Why? Because of lamentation. Hence it is said, “overcome by powerful sorrow.”

73. Tenevāti yena uttarāsaṅgena āsanaṃ sammajjati, teneva udare parikkhipanto “māhaṃ satthāraṃ mama sarīrena phusi”nti antaraṃ karonto uttarāsaṅgena taṃ udare parikkhipanto pariggahetvā. “Dattapaññatta”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.171) viya datta-saddo ettha bālapariyāyoti [V 2.0038] āha “jaḷosi jāto”ti. Upaṭṭhākassa aññathābhāvenāti pubbe attano upaṭṭhākassa idāni anupaṭṭhākabhāvena.

73. “With that very upper robe”: this means with the very upper robe with which he sweeps the seat, wrapping it around his belly. Thinking, “May I not touch the Teacher with my body,” he thus creates a barrier, wrapping and grasping it around his belly with the upper robe. Just as in such cases as “Dattapaññatta,” etc., the word “datta” here is a synonym for a fool; thus he said, “You are born a dullard.” “Due to the attendant's change of state” means: because one who was formerly his attendant is now no longer an attendant.

75. Aviññāṇakaṃ dārusākhādimayaṃ. Bahalabahalaṃ pītāvalepanaṃ raṅgajātanti ativiya bahalaṃ pītavaṇṇamañjiṭṭhaādiavalepanarajanaṃ. Ghaṭṭetvā uppāditacchaviṃ, yā raṅgaṃ pivati. Nillomatanti punappunaṃ anulimpanena. Khaṇḍakhaṇḍitanti khaṇḍakhaṇḍitabhāvaṃ. Raṅgakkhamo rajaniyo. Tenāha “rāgamattaṃ janetī”ti. Anuyoganti codanaṃ. Vīmaṃsanti vicāraṇaṃ. Thuse koṭṭetvā taṇḍulapariyesanaṃ [M 2.0041] viya kadaliyaṃ sārapariyesanaṃ viya ca nigaṇṭhavāde sāravīmaṃsanaṃ. Tato eva ca taṃ vīmaṃsanto rittako tucchakova hotīti. Sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ catusaccavinimuttaṃ natthi, tañca vīmaṃsiyamānaṃ viññūnaṃ pītisomanassameva janeti, atappakañca asecanābhāvenāti āha “catusaccakathā hī”tiādi. Yathā yathāti yadi khandhamukhena yadi dhātāyatanādīsu aññataramukhena buddhavacanaṃ ogāhissati, tathā tathā gambhīrañāṇānaṃyeva gocarabhāvato gambhīrameva hoti. Yo cettha paṇḍito nipuṇo kataparappavādo paṇidhāya sabbathāmena codanaṃ ārambhati tassa codanā kesaggamattampi cāletuṃ na sakkoti. Puna sucirampi kālaṃ vicārentesupi vimaddakkhamato, evaṃ tathāgatavādo svākhyātabhāvatoti āha “anuyogakkhamo vimajjanakkhamo cā”ti.

75. Without consciousness, made of wood, branches, and the like. 'A very thick coating of yellow paint, a type of coloring' means a very thick dyeing with a yellow-colored coating such as madder and other substances. Having been rubbed, a surface is produced that absorbs the color. 'Smooth' means by repeated smearing. 'Broken into pieces' means the state of being broken into pieces. It is suitable for color, dyeable. Hence it is said: 'it generates passion.' 'Investigation' means a charge. 'Examination' means scrutiny. Scrutinizing the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas for its essence is like pounding husks to seek rice or seeking heartwood in a banana tree. And in examining it, one becomes empty and void. There is no word of the Buddha that is devoid of the Four Noble Truths; and when examined, it generates only joy and gladness for the wise. And because it is not fatiguing and is satisfying, it is said: 'For the discourse on the Four Noble Truths…,' and so on. 'In whatever way': whether one delves into the Buddha's word by way of the aggregates, or by way of one of the elements, sense bases, etc., in that very way it is profound, because it is the domain only of those with profound knowledge. If a wise, skilled person here, who has refuted the doctrines of others, having made a resolve, initiates a charge with all his might, his charge cannot shake it even by a hair's breadth. Again, even when people examine it for a very long time, it is able to withstand scrutiny; thus, because the Tathāgata's teaching is well-proclaimed, it is said: 'It is able to withstand investigation and able to withstand examination.'

76. Visayapariññāṇena dahati paṭipakkhe sodhetīti dhīro, svāyamassa dhīrabhāvo sabbaso sammohaviddhaṃsanatāyāti āha – “yā paññā…pe… tena samannāgatassā”ti. Pabhinnakhīlassāti samucchinnasabbacetokhīlassa, kilesamaccumāravijayeneva abhisaṅkhārakhandhamārā jitāva hontīti tesaṃ dvinnaṃ idha aggahaṇaṃ. Īgha-saddo dukkhapariyāyoti āha “niddukkhassā”ti. Tattha saupādisesanibbānappattiyā kilesena niddukkhatā, anupādisesanibbānappattiyā vipākadukkhena niddukkhatā. Rajjanadussanamuyhanādivasena vividhaṃ īsanato vīsaṃ, vīsameva vesaṃ, rāgādīti āha – “vesantarassāti rāgādivīsaṃ taritvā vitaritvā ṭhitassā”ti.

76. He is wise (dhīro) because with the full understanding of the object-domains, he burns up and purifies opposing factors. This wisdom of his consists in the complete demolition of delusion; thus it is said: 'that wisdom...pe... of one endowed with that.' 'Of one with broken stakes' means of one whose every mental stake has been eradicated. By the very conquest of the Māras of defilements and death, the Māras of formations and the aggregates are also conquered; hence these two are not mentioned here. The word 'īgha' is a synonym for suffering; thus it is said: 'of one without suffering.' Herein, freedom from suffering through the attainment of Nibbāna with residue is freedom from the suffering of defilements; freedom from suffering through the attainment of Nibbāna without residue is freedom from the suffering of resultants. Because it lords it over in various ways—by way of lusting, hating, and being deluded—it is poison (vīsaṃ). Poison itself is vesaṃ. This refers to lust, etc. Thus it is said: 'of one who has crossed beyond' means of one who stands having crossed over and gone beyond the poison of lust and so on.

Tusitassāti karuṇāyanavasena tusiyā itassa saṃvattassa. Evaṃ sati “muditassā”ti idaṃ punaruttameva hoti. Manujassāti paṭhamāya jātiyā bhagavā manussajātiyo hutvā vuttānaṃ vakkhamānānañca vasena sadevakaṃ abhibhavitvā ṭhito acchariyo bhagavāti dasseti. Sadevakaṃ lokaṃ saṃsārato nibbānasukhaṃ narati neti pāpetīti naro, nāyakoti attho, tassa narassa, tenāha [V 2.0039] “punarutta”nti. “Manujassā”ti vatvā “narassā”ti punaruttaṃ padaṃ. Atthavasena aññathā vuccamāne ekekagāthāya dasaguṇā nappahonti, na pūrentīti attho.

'Of the satisfied one' (tusitassa): of one who has gone to satisfaction by way of compassion. This being so, the word 'of the gladdened one' (muditassa) is just a repetition. 'Of the human' (manujassa): this shows that in his first birth, the Blessed One, having been of human birth, stands as the marvelous Blessed One, having overcome the world with its gods by means of what has been said and what will be said. He is a man (naro) because he leads (narati, neti), he makes attain (pāpeti), the world with its gods from saṃsāra to the bliss of Nibbāna; the meaning is 'leader' (nāyako). Of that man (narassa). Hence it is said, 'repetition.' Having said 'of the human,' the word 'of the man' is a repeated word. When expressed differently in terms of meaning, the ten qualities for each single verse are not sufficient, they are not fulfilled; this is the meaning.

Vinetīti vinayo, vinayo eva veneyikoti āha “sattānaṃ vināyakassā”ti. Viññūnaṃ ruciṃ rāti, īretīti vā ruciro, svāyamassa rucirabhāvo [M 2.0042] kusalatāyāti āha “sucidhammassā”ti. Pabhāsakassāti ñāṇālokena pabhassarabhāvakarassa. Nissaṅgassāti aṭṭhasupi parisāsu, sadeve vā sabbasmiṃ loke aggaṇhāpanapariccāgena nissaṭassa. Gambhīraguṇassāti paresaṃ ñāṇena appatiṭṭhabhāvā gambhīraguṇassa. Tenāha bhagavā – “atthi, bhikkhave, aññeva dhammā gambhīrā”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.28). Ariyāya vā tuṇhībhāvena monappattassa. Dhamme ṭhitassāti dhammakāye suppatiṭṭhitassa. Saṃvutattassāti arakkhiyakāyasamācārāditāya saṃvutasabhāvassa.

'It trains,' thus it is discipline (vinayo). Discipline itself is the training (veneyiko); thus it is said: 'of the trainer of beings.' He gives or inspires delight in the wise, thus he is delightful (ruciro). This delightful quality of his is due to his skillfulness; thus it is said: 'of one with pure Dhamma.' 'Of the illuminator' means of one who causes a state of radiance with the light of knowledge. 'Of one without attachments' means of one who is detached in the eight assemblies, or in the entire world with its gods, through relinquishing the causing of grasping. 'Of one with profound qualities' means of one whose qualities are profound because they cannot be fathomed by the knowledge of others. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'There are, bhikkhus, other things that are profound...' (DN 1:28), and so on. Or, of one who has attained sagehood through noble silence. 'Of one standing in the Dhamma' means of one well established in the Dhamma-body. 'Of one with a restrained self' means of one whose nature is restrained because of guarded bodily conduct and so on.

Āguṃ na karotītiādīhi catūhi kāraṇehi, pantasenāsanassāti vivittasenāsanassa. Paṭimantanapaññāyāti sabbaparappavādānaṃ viparāvattamantanapaññāya. Monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ sabbato kilesānaṃ nidhunanato.

For the four reasons beginning with 'He commits no fault…' 'Of a remote lodging' means of a secluded lodging. 'With confuting wisdom' means with the wisdom that counsels the reversal of all the doctrines of others. Sagehood (monaṃ) is called knowledge (ñāṇaṃ) because it shakes off all defilements from every side.

Isisattamassāti sabbaisīsu jeṭṭhassa sādhutamassa. Seṭṭhappattassāti seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ pattassa. Akkharādīnīti akkharapadabyañjanākāra-niruttiniddesa-saṃkāsanapakāsana-vivaraṇa-vibhajanuttānīkaraṇānīti byañjanatthapadāni. Samodhānetvā vineyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ pakāsanato kathanato padakassa. Puri-saddo “pubbe”ti iminā samānatthoti āha – “purindadassāti sabbapaṭhamaṃ dhammadānadāyakassā”ti. Bhagavā asayhaṃ sahituṃ samatthoti āha “samatthassā”ti. Tenāha – “tathāgataṃ buddhamasayhasāhina”nti (itivu. 38). Te pattassāti te guṇe anavasesato pattassa. Vitthāretvā saṃkilesavodānadhammaṃ byākarotīti byākaraṇo, byākaraṇo eva veyyākaraṇo. Tantipadanti tantiṃ āropetvā ṭhapitaṃ padaṃ.

'Of the seventh of the seers' means of the chief and best among all seers. 'Of one who has attained the best' means of one who has attained the best, the supreme, perfect self-enlightenment. 'Letters, etc.' are terms for the literal meaning: letter, word, phrase, form, expression, designation, indication, clarification, exposition, analysis, and making plain. Of the speaker, because he speaks and explains in a way that is suitable to the disposition of those to be trained, having brought the terms together. The word 'puri' has the same meaning as 'before'; thus it is said: 'of Purindada' means 'of the one who first of all gave the gift of the Dhamma.' The Blessed One is able to endure the unendurable; thus it is said: 'of the able one.' Therefore it is said: 'The Tathāgata, the Buddha, who endures the unendurable' (Iti 38). 'Of one who has attained them' means of one who has attained those qualities without remainder. He is a declarer (byākaraṇo) because he declares the phenomena of defilement and purification in detail; a declarer is an expounder (veyyākaraṇo). 'A canonical word' (tantipada) means a word established by placing it on the canon.

Taṇhābandhanena sabbena vā kilesabandhanena abaddhassa. Mahāpaññāyāti mahānubhāvāya paññāya, mahāvisayāya vā paññāya. Sabbā hi bhagavato paññā mahānubhāvā, yathāsakaṃ visaye mahāvisayā ca ekādivasena anavasesato mahāvisayā nāma sabbaññutāva. Ānubhāvadassanaṭṭhenāti acchariyācinteyyāparimeyyassa attano ānubhāvassa lokassa dassanaṭṭhena[V 2.0040]. Yakkhassāti vā lokena pūjanīyassa[M 2.0043]. Ayaṃ upāsako khujjuttarā viya upāsikā sekhapaṭisambhidāppattoti āha “sotāpattimaggeneva paṭisambhidā āgatā”ti. Kilesappahānavaṇṇaṃ kathentoti kilesappahānaṃ visayaṃ nimittaṃ katvā vaṇṇaṃ kathento.

Of one unbound by the bondage of craving or by any bondage of defilements. 'By great wisdom' means by wisdom of great power, or by wisdom of great scope. For all the Blessed One's wisdom is of great power, and of great scope in its respective domain; but omniscience is called 'of great scope' because it is all-encompassing without remainder by way of one thing, and so on. 'For the purpose of showing his power' means for the purpose of showing to the world his own marvelous, inconceivable, immeasurable power. Or, 'of the yakkha' means of one worthy of veneration by the world. This lay follower, like the laywoman Khujjuttarā, has attained the discriminations of a trainee; thus it is said: 'The discriminations came with the very path of stream-entry.' 'Speaking in praise of the abandoning of defilements' means speaking in praise by making the abandoning of defilements the object and basis.

77. Sampiṇḍitāti sannicitā, ganthitāti attho. Ime sattāti yaṃ yadeva paribbhamantā sattā. Attanova cintayantīti avītataṇhatāya sakaṃyeva payojanaṃ cintenti. Tathā hi mate ñātake anusocantāpi tehi sādhetabbassa attano payojanasseva vasena anusocanti. Uṇhaṃ ahosīti balavatā cittassa santāpena santattaṃ abbhantaraṃ hadayaṭṭhānaṃ khadiraṅgārasantāpitaṃ viya uṇhaṃ ahosi. Tenāha “lohitaṃ vilīyitthā”ti. Pattamattanti ekapattapūramattaṃ. Abhisamayasādhikāya catusaccadesanāya saṅkhepeneva desitattā āha – ‘ugghaṭitaññupuggalassa vasena dhammadesanā pariniṭṭhitā”ti.

77. 'Amassed' means accumulated; the meaning is 'strung together.' 'These beings' means whatever beings are wandering about. 'They think only of themselves' means that because their craving is not overcome, they think only of their own purpose. For even when lamenting for dead relatives, they lament only on account of their own purpose that was to be accomplished by them. 'It became hot' means the inner heart-base, scorched by the powerful torment of the mind, became hot as if heated by glowing acacia-wood embers. Therefore it is said: 'The blood melted.' 'The measure of a bowl' means the amount that fills a single bowl. Because the discourse on the Four Noble Truths, which leads to breakthrough, was taught only in brief, it is said: 'The Dhamma discourse was concluded for the sake of a person of quick understanding.'

Upālisuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Upāli Sutta is completed.

7. Kukkuravatikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Kukkuravatika Sutta.

78. Koliyesūti [V 2.0041] bahuvacanavasenāyaṃ pāḷi āgatā. Evaṃnāmake janapadeti atthavacanaṃ kasmā vuttanti āha “so hī”tiādi. Na niyamitoti “asukamhi nāma vihāre”ti na niyametvā vutto. Senāsaneyevāti āvāseyeva, na rukkhamūlādike. Vesakiriyā ghāsaggahaṇādinā samādātabbaṭṭhena govataṃ, tasmiṃ niyutto govatiko. Tenāha “samādinnagovato”ti. Yaṃ sandhāyāhu vedavedino – “gacchaṃ bhakkheti, tiṭṭhaṃ mutteti, upāhā udakaṃ dhūpeti, tiṇāni chindatī”tiādi. Ayaṃ aceloti acelakapabbajjāvasena acelo, purimo pana govatiko kukkuravatikoti ettha vuttanayānusārena attho vattabbo. Palikuṇṭhitvāti ubho hatthe ubho pāde ca samiñjitvā. “Ukkuṭiko hutvā”tipi vadanti. Gamanaṃ nipphajjanaṃ gatīti āha – “kā [M 2.0044] gatīti kā nipphattī”ti. Nipphattipariyosānā hi vipākadhammappavatti. Katūpacitakammavasena abhisampareti etthāti abhisamparāyo, paraloko. Tatthassa ca nipphattiṃ pucchatīti āha – “abhisamparāyamhi kattha nibbattī”ti. Kukkuravatasamādānanti kukkurabhāvasamādānaṃ, “ajja paṭṭhāya ahaṃ kukkuro”ti kukkurabhāvādhiṭṭhānaṃ.

78. The Pāḷi has 'among the Koliyans' (Koliyesu), in the plural. Why is the meaning given as 'in the country of that name'? It is explained: 'For that…,' etc. It is not restricted: it is stated without specifying, 'in such and such a monastery.' 'In dwellings only' means in residences, not at the foot of trees, etc. The cow-observance (govataṃ) is to be undertaken by means of taking up grass, etc. One devoted to this is a cow-practitioner (govatiko). Hence it is said, 'one who has undertaken the cow-observance.' In reference to this, those who know the Vedas say: 'He eats while walking, urinates while standing, sniffs water, and cuts grass,' etc. This one is naked (acelo) in the sense of the going forth of a naked ascetic. As for the former, the cow-practitioner, the meaning should be understood according to the method stated here for the dog-practitioner. 'Having curled up' (palikuṇṭhitvā) means having drawn in both hands and both feet. Some also say, 'having squatted.' Regarding movement, accomplishment, destination (gati), it is said: 'What is the destination? What is the outcome?' The outcome is the culmination of the process of resultant dhammas. 'Future existence' (abhisamparāyo) is where one fares on by means of kamma that has been done and accumulated; it is the next world. He asks about his outcome there, thus it is said: 'In the future existence, where will he be reborn?' 'Undertaking the dog-observance' means undertaking the state of being a dog, the determination of the state of being a dog by thinking, 'From today onwards, I am a dog.'

79. Paripuṇṇanti yattakā kukkuravikārā, tehi paripuṇṇaṃ. Tenāha “anūna”nti. Abbokiṇṇanti tehi avomissaṃ. Kukkurācāranti kukkurānaṃ gamanākārotiādiācārena kukkurabhāvādhiṭṭhānacittamāha. Tathā tathā ākappetabbato ākappo, pavattiākāro. So panettha gamanādikoti āha “kukkurānaṃ gamanākāro”tiādi. Ācārenāti kukkurasīlācārena. Vatasamādānenāti kukkuravatādhiṭṭhānena. Kukkuracariyādiyeva dukkaratapacaraṇaṃ. Tena gativipariyesākārena pavattā laddhi. Assa kukkuravatikassa aññā gati natthīti itaragatiṃ paṭikkhipati, itarāsaṃ pana sambhavo eva natthīti. Nipajjamānanti vatasīlādīnaṃ saṃgopanavasena sijjhamānaṃ. Yathā sakammakadhātusaddā atthavisesavasena akammakā honti “vibuddho puriso vibuddho kamalasaṇḍo”ti, evaṃ atthavisesavasena akammakāpi sakammakā hontīti dassento “na paridevāmi na anutthunāmī”tiādimāha. Anutthunasaddo ca sakammakavasena payujjati “purāṇāni anutthuna”ntiādīsu. Ayañcettha payogoti iminā gāthāyañca anutthunanarodanaṃ adhippetanti dasseti.

79. 'Complete' means complete with all the various dog-like behaviors. Hence it is said, 'not deficient.' 'Uninterrupted' means unmixed with them. 'A dog's conduct' refers to the mind determined on the state of being a dog through conduct such as a dog's manner of movement. 'Appearance' (ākappo) is the mode of conduct, so called because it is to be arranged in such and such a way. Here it refers to movement and so on, thus it is said: 'a dog's manner of movement,' etc. 'By conduct' means by the virtue and conduct of a dog. 'By undertaking the observance' means by the determination of the dog-observance. The practice of a dog's behavior itself is a difficult ascetic practice. Through this, a view arises in the form of a perverted destiny. For this dog-practitioner there is no other destination; thus he rejects any other destination, for there is indeed no possibility of others. 'Being accomplished' means being accomplished by way of safeguarding one's observance, virtue, and so on. Just as words from the same root have different meanings, as in 'an awakened man' (vibuddho puriso) and 'a blossomed lotus cluster' (vibuddho kamalasaṇḍo), so too, showing that words with different meanings can have the same function, he says: 'I do not lament, I do not groan,' etc. The word 'groan' (anutthuna) is also used with the same function, as in 'recounting old things' (purāṇāni anutthuna). And this is the usage here; by this he shows that in the verse, groaning and weeping are intended.

80. Vuttanayenevāti [V 2.0042] iminā govatanti govatasamādānaṃ. Gosīlanti gavācāraṃ. Gocittanti “ajja paṭṭhāya gohi kātabbaṃ karissāmī”ti uppannacittanti imamatthaṃ atidisati. Gvākappe pana vattabbaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ “kukkurākappe vuttasadisamevā”ti imināva atidiṭṭhaṃ, visiṭṭhañca yathā pana tatthātiādinā vuttameva. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ kukkuravatādīsu vuttanayameva.

80. By 'in the way already stated,' he applies the following meaning: 'cow-observance' is the undertaking of the cow-observance; 'cow-virtue' is the conduct of a cow; 'cow-mind' is the mind that has arisen with the thought, 'From today onwards, I will do what should be done by cows.' But as for the 'cow-appearance,' what remains to be said is applied by the phrase 'it is just like what was said about the dog-appearance.' And the specific details have already been stated by 'but just as there,' etc. Whatever should be said here follows the same method as stated for the dog-observance and so on.

81. Ekaccakammakiriyāvasenāti ekaccassa akusalakammassa kusalakammassa karaṇappasaṅgena. Imesanti govatikakukkuravatikānaṃ. Kiriyāti govatabhāvanādivasena pavattā kiriyā. Pākaṭā bhavissatīti “imasmiṃ kammacatukke idaṃ nāma kammaṃ bhajatī”ti pākaṭā bhavissati.

81. 'By way of performing some kamma' means on the occasion of performing some unwholesome kamma or wholesome kamma. 'Of these' means of the cow-practitioners and dog-practitioners. 'Action' means the action that proceeds by way of developing the cow-observance and so on. 'It will become manifest' means it will become manifest thus: 'In this tetrad of kammas, he resorts to such and such a kamma.'

Kāḷakanti [M 2.0045] (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.232) malīnaṃ, cittassa apabhassarabhāvakaraṇanti attho. Taṃ panettha kammapathasampattameva adhippetanti āha “dasaakusalakammapatha”nti. Kaṇhanti kaṇhābhijātihetuto vā kaṇhaṃ. Tenāha “kaṇhavipāka”nti. Apāyūpapatti manussesu ca dobhaggiyaṃ kaṇhavipāko, yathā tamabhāvo vutto, ekattaniddesena pana “apāye nibbattanato”ti vuttaṃ, nibbattāpanatoti attho. Sukkanti odātaṃ, cittassa pabhassarabhāvakaraṇanti attho, sukkābhijātihetuto vā sukkaṃ. Tenāha “sukkavipāka”nti. Saggūpapatti manussaloke sobhaggiyañca sukkavipāko, yathā ca jotibhāvo vutto, ekattaniddesena pana “sagge nibbattanato”ti vuttaṃ, nibbattāpanatoti attho, vomissakakammanti kālena kaṇhaṃ, kālena sukkanti evaṃ missakavasena katakammaṃ. “Sukhadukkhavipāka”nti vatvā sukhadukkhānaṃ pavattiākāraṃ dassetuṃ “missakakammañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kammassa kaṇhasukkasamaññā kaṇhasukkābhijātihetutāyāti, apaccayagāmitāya tadubhayavinimuttassa kammakkhayakarakammassa idha sukkapariyāyopi na icchitoti āha – “ubhaya…pe… asukkanti vutta”nti. Tattha ubhayavipākassāti yathādhigatassa vipākassa. Sampattibhavapariyāpanno hi vipāko idha “sukkavipāko”ti adhippeto, na accantaparisuddho.

'Dark' (kāḷakaṃ) means stained; the meaning is that it makes the mind lose its luminosity. Here it is intended to mean only the attainment of the courses of kamma, thus he says, 'the ten unwholesome courses of kamma.' 'Dark' (kaṇhaṃ) is so called because it is a cause for a dark birth, or because it is dark. Hence it is said, 'with a dark result.' Rebirth in the plane of misery and misfortune among humans is the dark result. Just as its dark nature has been stated, so by a unitary explanation it is said, 'because it brings rebirth in the plane of misery'; the meaning is that it causes rebirth there. 'Bright' (sukkaṃ) means pure; the meaning is that it makes the mind luminous. Or it is bright because it is a cause for a bright birth. Hence it is said, 'with a bright result.' Rebirth in heaven and good fortune in the human world is the bright result. Just as its luminous nature has been stated, so by a unitary explanation it is said, 'because it brings rebirth in heaven'; the meaning is that it causes rebirth there. 'Mixed kamma' is kamma done in a mixed way, being dark at one time and bright at another. Having said 'with a result of pleasure and pain,' in order to show the mode of occurrence of pleasure and pain, it is said, 'for mixed kamma...,' etc. The designation of kamma as 'dark' and 'bright' is due to its being a cause for dark and bright births. Since the kamma that leads to the destruction of kamma—which is free from both extremes and does not lead to a future state—is not intended here even as a type of bright kamma, it is said: '...neither... nor... not bright is it said to be.' Therein, 'of the result of both' means of the result as it has been obtained. For here 'bright result' is intended to mean a result included in a fortunate state of existence, not one that is utterly pure.

Sadukkhanti attanā uppādetabbena dukkhena sadukkhaṃ, dukkhasaṃvattanikanti attho. “Imasmiṃ sutte cetanā dhuraṃ, upālisutte (ma. ni. 2.56) kamma”nti heṭṭhā vuttampi atthaṃ idha sādhayati vijānanatthaṃ. Abhisaṅkharitvāti āyūhitvā. Taṃ pana paccayasamavāyasiddhito saṃkaḍḍhanaṃ piṇḍanaṃ viya hotīti āha – “saṅkaḍḍhitvā, piṇḍaṃ katvāti attho”ti, sadukkhaṃ lokanti [V 2.0043] apāyalokamāha. Vipākaphassāti phassasīsena tattha vipākapavattamāha. Bhūtakammatoti nibbattakammato attanā katūpacitakammato. Yathābhūtanti yādisaṃ. Kammasabhāgavasenāti kammasarikkhakavasena. Upapatti hotīti apadādibhedā upapatti. Kammena viya vuttāti yaṃ karoti, tena upapajjatīti ekakammeneva jāyamānā viya vuttā apadādibhedā. Upapatti ca nāma vipākena hoti vipāke sambhavante ekaṃsena te upapattivisesā sambhavanti. Yadi evaṃ kasmā “tena upapajjatī”ti upapattikammahetukā vuttāti āha “yasmā panā”tiādi. Yena kammavipākena nibbattoti [M 2.0046] yena kammavipākena vipaccamānena ayaṃ satto nibbattoti vuccati. Taṃkammavipākaphassāti tassa tassa kammassa vipākabhūtā phassā. Kammena dātabbaṃ dāyaṃ tabbipākaṃ ādiyantīti kammadāyādā, phassā. Kammassa dāyajjatā kammaphalassa dāyajjaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “kammadāyajjā”ti. Tenāha “kammameva nesaṃ dāyajjaṃ santaka”nti.

'Painful' (sadukkhaṃ) means with pain that is to be produced by oneself; the meaning is that it leads to pain. For the sake of understanding, he here establishes the meaning stated below: 'In this sutta, volition is primary; in the Upāli Sutta (MN 56), kamma is primary.' 'Having formed' (abhisaṅkharitvā) means having striven. But since that is accomplished through a combination of conditions, it is like a drawing together and compressing, thus he says: 'having drawn together, having made into a lump, that is the meaning.' 'A painful world' refers to the world of misery. 'Resultant contacts': with contact as the heading, he speaks of the process of result there. 'From the kamma that has come to be' means from the kamma that has been produced, from the kamma done and accumulated by oneself. 'As it really is' means of such a kind. 'In accordance with the kamma' means in a way similar to the kamma. 'Rebirth occurs' means rebirth of different kinds, such as footless, etc. 'As if said to be by kamma': 'One is reborn according to what one does'—thus the different kinds of rebirth are spoken of as if they are born from a single kamma. But rebirth is by way of result; when the result occurs, those specific kinds of rebirth definitely occur. If so, why is it said, 'by that one is reborn,' as if rebirth were caused by kamma? He says, 'But because...,' etc. 'By which kamma-result one is reborn' means this being is said to be reborn by that kamma-result as it ripens. 'Those kamma-resultant contacts' means the contacts that are the results of that particular kamma. They are 'heirs of kamma' because they receive the inheritance (dāyaṃ) to be given by kamma, that is, its result; these are the contacts. The state of being an inheritance of kamma is the inheritance of the fruit of kamma; therefore it is said, 'heirs of kamma.' Hence he says: 'Kamma is their inheritance, their own property.'

Tisso ca heṭṭhimajjhānacetanāti idaṃ abyābajjhavedanaṃ vediyanaekantasukhuppattiyā hetubhāvasādhanaṃ. Yadi evaṃ yathāvuttā jhānacetanā tāva hotu ekantasukhuppattihetubhāvato. Kāmāvacarā kintīti kāmāvacarā pana kusalacetanā taṃsabhāvābhāvato kinti kena pakārena abyābajjhamanosaṅkhāro nāma jātoti codeti, itaro pana na sabbā kāmāvacarakusalacetanā tathā gahitā, atha kho ekaccā jhānacetanānukūlāti dassento “kasiṇasajjanakāle kasiṇāsevanakāle labbhantī”ti āha. Tattha kasiṇāsevanacetanā gahetabbā, sā upacārajjhānassa sādhikā. Tena kāmāvacaracetanā paṭhamajjhānacetanāya ghaṭitāti kasiṇasajjanacetanāpi kadāci tādisā hotīti gahitā. Parikammādivasena hi pavattā bhāvanāmayā kāmāvacarakusalacetanā paṭhamajjhānassa āsannatāya vuttā. Catutthajjhānacetanā tatiyajjhānacetanāya ghaṭitāti idaṃ ekattakāyaekattasaññīsattāvāsavatāya taṃsarikkhakā upekkhāpi īdisesu ṭhānesu sukhasarikkhatā, evaṃ santasabhāvatā ñāṇasahitatā ca. Keci pana catutthajjhānacetanānuguṇāti nidassentā kasiṇasajjanakāle kasiṇajjhānakāle kasiṇāsevanakāle labbhatīti tatiyajjhānacetanāya āsannaghaṭitatā vuttāti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ, vuttanayeneva tāsaṃ ghaṭitatā veditabbā. Ubhayamissakavasenāti ubhayesaṃ kusalākusalasaṅkhārānaṃ sukhadukkhānañca missakabhāvavasena. Vemānikapetānanti idaṃ bāhullato vuttaṃ, itaresampi vinipātikānaṃ kālena dukkhaṃ hotiyeva.

The three intentions of the lower and middle jhānas—this is the basis for experiencing non-afflictive feeling, serving as the cause for the arising of exclusively pleasant feeling. If so, as stated, then the jhāna intention itself should be the cause for the arising of exclusively pleasant feeling. But what about sense-sphere intentions? Since sense-sphere wholesome intentions lack that nature, one objects: 'In what way can a mental formation free from ill will arise?' The other replies: Not all sense-sphere wholesome intentions are taken thus. Rather, some are favorable to the jhāna intentions. To show this, it is said: 'They are obtainable at the time of preparing the kasiṇa and at the time of developing the kasiṇa.' Here, the intention associated with developing the kasiṇa should be taken, for it is conducive to access concentration. Thus, the sense-sphere intention is connected to the first jhāna intention. Even the intention of preparing the kasiṇa is sometimes of such a nature, so it is included. For the sense-sphere wholesome intentions consisting in mental development, which arise by way of preliminary practice and so on, are said to be near to the first jhāna. The fourth jhāna intention is connected to the third jhāna intention. This is because, as in the abode of beings with a single body and a single perception, the equanimity in such states resembles happiness; thus their nature is peaceful and accompanied by knowledge. Some, however, indicating that it is favorable to the fourth jhāna intention, say that since it is obtainable at the time of preparing the kasiṇa, at the time of the kasiṇa-jhāna, and at the time of developing the kasiṇa, its close connection with the third jhāna intention is stated. That is merely their opinion; their connection should be understood according to the method stated. 'By way of the mixture of both' means by way of the mixed state of both wholesome and unwholesome formations, and of pleasure and pain. 'Celestial mansions-dwelling pretas'—this is said by way of preponderance, for suffering also occurs from time to time for other fallen beings.

Tassa [V 2.0044] pahānāyāti tassa yathāvuttassa kammassa anuppattidhammatāpādanāya. Yā cetanāti yā apacayagāminicetanā. Kammaṃ patvāti sukhakammanti vuccamāne maggacetanāya añño paṇḍarataro dhammo nāma natthi [M 2.0047] accantapārisuddhibhāvato. Akaṇhā asukkāti āgatāti ettha sukkabhāvapaṭikkhepakāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Tenāha “idaṃ pana kammacatukkaṃ patvā”tiādi.

‘For its abandonment’ means for bringing about the state of non-arising for that action as described. ‘The intention’ is the intention that leads to diminution. ‘With reference to action’: when ‘bright action’ is mentioned, there is no other phenomenon purer than the intention of the path, because of its state of utter purity. ‘Having come to be neither dark nor bright’: here, the reason for rejecting the quality of brightness is just as explained above. Therefore he said: ‘But with reference to this tetrad of action,’ and so on.

82. Aniyyānikapakkheti aceḷakapabbajjāya kukkuravate ca. Yogeti ñāyadhammapaṭipattiyanti attho. Yonenāti yo titthiyaparivāso tena bhagavatā paññatto. Yaṃ titthiyaparivāsaṃ samādiyitvāti ayamettha yojanā. Ghaṃsitvā suvaṇṇaṃ viya nighaṃsoppale. Koṭṭetvā hatthena viya kulālabhājanaṃ.

82. ‘In the party not leading to release’: in the naked ascetic’s going forth and in the dog-duty asceticism. ‘In the application’: the meaning is, in the practice of the true Dhamma. ‘By the means’: by the probation for adherents of other sects laid down by the Blessed One. The construction here is: ‘Having undertaken the probation for adherents of other sects.’ Like gold that has been rubbed on a touchstone. Like a potter’s vessel that has been struck by the hand.

Vūpakaṭṭhoti vivitto ekībhūto. Pesitattoti nibbānaṃ pati pesitatto. Kāmaṃ tadanuttaraṃ brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ…pe… vihāsīti imināva arahattanikūṭena desanā niṭṭhāpitā hoti, āyasmato pana seniyassa paṭipattikittanaparametaṃ ujukaṃ āpannaarahattabhāvadīpanaṃ, yadidaṃ “aññataro kho panā”tiādivacananti āha “arahattanikūṭenevā”ti. Arahattādhigamoyeva tassa tesaṃ abbhantaratā. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ suviññeyyameva.

‘Withdrawn’ means secluded, solitary. ‘With mind dispatched’ means with his mind dispatched towards Nibbāna. With this very pinnacle of arahantship—‘…that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life…he dwelt’—the discourse is concluded. But for the Venerable Seniya, this is the supreme praise of his practice, a direct declaration of his having attained the state of an arahant, that is, the statement beginning: ‘Now one of them….’ Thus it is said: ‘by the pinnacle of arahantship alone.’ The attainment of arahantship itself is what is internal to them. The rest is all easily understood.

Kukkuravatikasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

Here ends the Elucidation of the Obscure Meaning in the Commentary on the Sutta on the Dog-Duty Ascetic.

8. Abhayarājakumārasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse to Prince Abhaya

83. Jātiyā [V 2.0045] asamāno nihīnācariyo paradattūpajīvikāya mātuyā kucchiyaṃ jāto pādasikaputto. Nindāvasena vadati etenāti vādo aguṇoti āha – “vādaṃ āropehīti dosaṃ āropehī”ti. Nibbattavasena nirayaṃ arahati, nirayasaṃvattaniyena vā kammena niraye niyutto nerayiko. Āpāyikoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Avīcimhi uppajjitvā tattha āyukappasaññitaṃ antarakappaṃ tiṭṭhatīti kappaṭṭho. Nirayūpapattipariharaṇavasena tikicchituṃ sakkuṇeyyoti tekiccho, na tekiccho atekiccho. Dve ante mocetvāti pharusaṃ vā appiyaṃ vā kappeyyāti dve koṭṭhāse muñcitvā [M 2.0048] te anāmasitvā pucchitaṃ atthaṃ tato bahi karonto uggilati nāma. Taṃ pana evaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotīti āha – “uggilituṃ bahi nīharituṃ na sakkhitī”ti. Evamevāyaṃ pucchā na gahetabbā, ayamettha dosoti taṃ apucchaṃ karonto apanayanto ogilati nāma, tathā pana asakkonto patiṭṭhāpento na ogilati nāma, bhagavā pana tamatthaṃ okāsampi akaronto ubhayathāpi asakkhīti veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Bhagavā hi “na khvettha rājakumāra ekaṃsenā”ti vadanto nigaṇṭhassa adhippāyaṃ viparivatteti, ubho ante mocetvā pañhaṃ vissajjesi, evaṃ tāva uggilituṃ asakkhi. “Na tatra rājakumāra ekaṃsenā”ti vadanto eva ca “nāyaṃ pucchā evaṃ avibhāgena pucchitabbā, vibhajitvā pana pucchitabbā”ti pucchāya dosaṃ dīpento taṃ hārento ogilitumpi sakkhatīti.

83. Unequal by birth, of inferior conduct, born in the womb of a mother who subsisted on what was given by others, a son of a commoner. ‘He speaks by way of censure’: this is a contention, a fault. Thus he says: ‘“Impute a contention” means “impute a fault.”’ ‘He deserves hell’: by way of rebirth, or, being assigned to hell by kamma that leads to hell, he is a hell-being. ‘Bound for a plane of misery’: here too the same method applies. ‘Remaining for an eon’: having arisen in Avīci, he remains there for an intermediate eon, which is reckoned as a life-span. ‘Curable’: he could be cured by way of avoiding rebirth in hell. One who cannot is ‘incurable.’ ‘Having released the two ends’: this means he might utter what is harsh or unpleasing. Releasing the two portions, not touching upon them, one who makes the meaning of the question something external to that is said to ‘vomit’ it. But he is unable to do so. Thus it is said: ‘He will be unable to vomit it, to bring it out.’ In the same way, this question should not be taken up; this is the fault here. One who makes it a non-question, who removes it, is said to ‘swallow’ it. But one who is unable to do so, who establishes it, does not swallow it. However, the Blessed One, by not giving that matter an opportunity, should be understood as having been able in both ways. How? For the Blessed One, by saying, ‘In this case, prince, it is not a one-sided matter,’ overturns the intention of the Nigaṇṭha. Having released both ends, he answered the question. Thus he was able to ‘vomit.’ And by saying, ‘In that case, prince, it is not a one-sided matter,’ and, ‘This question should not be asked in this undifferentiated way, but should be asked analytically,’ he points out the fault in the question and dismisses it, thus he is also able to ‘swallow.’

Uṭṭhātuṃ na sakkhissati cittassa aññathā pavattiyā. Abhayo dve magge kataparicayo cheko nipuṇo vādasīlo ca hutvā vicarati. Tenāha – “so vādajjhāsayatāya tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchanto ‘evaṃ, bhante’ti āhā”ti.

He will not be able to get up because his mind will be proceeding otherwise. Prince Abhaya, being experienced in two paths, clever, astute, and fond of debate, went about. Therefore it is said: ‘Because of his inclination for debate, accepting his words, he said, “So be it, venerable sir.”’

85. Evarūpanti yā paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā duruttavācā, evarūpā vācā, na pana pharusavācā. Pharusavācāya hi setughāto tathāgatānaṃ. Cetanāpharusatāya hi pharusavācā icchitā, na paresaṃ appiyatāmattena. Naṭṭhā nigaṇṭhā ogilikādisammatassa pañhassa ekavacanena viddhaṃsitattā.

85. ‘Such speech’: speech that is unpleasing and disagreeable to others, ill-spoken words. This is such speech, but it is not harsh speech. For the Tathāgatas, harsh speech is a ‘bridge-breaker.’ Harsh speech is defined by the harshness of the intention, not merely by its being disagreeable to others. The Nigaṇṭhas were lost because the question, which was based on the idea of swallowing and so on, was demolished by a single statement.

86. Dārakassa aṅke nisīdanassa kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “lesavādino”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha lesavādinoti [V 2.0046] chalavādino, vādamagge vā aparipuṇṇatāya lesamatteneva vādasīlā. Osaṭasaṅgāmoti anekavāraṃ paravādamaddanavasena otiṇṇavādasaṅgāmo. Vijjhitvāti nakhena vijjhitvā. Imamevāti yvāyaṃ dārako attano vādabhaṅgapariharaṇatthaṃ iminā aṅke nisīdāpito, imameva assa dārakaṃ upamaṃ nissayaṃ katvā vādaṃ bhindissāmi. “Assa vādaṃ appaṭitatāya upamāya bhañjissāmī”ti cintetvā.

86. To show the reason for the child sitting on his lap, the words ‘speakers of trifles,’ etc., were said. Here, ‘speakers of trifles’ means speakers of pretext, or those who are fond of debate with a mere trifle because of their incompleteness in the path of debate. ‘One who has entered the fray’: one who has entered the battle of debate on numerous occasions by way of crushing the arguments of others. ‘Having pierced’: having pierced with a fingernail. ‘This very one’: ‘Just as this child has been made to sit on my lap by me to avoid the defeat of my own argument, so I will break his argument by relying on this very child as a simile.’ Thinking, ‘I will shatter his argument with an unassailable simile.’

Apaneyyaṃ [M 2.0049] assa ahanti assa dārakassa mukhato ahaṃ taṃ apaneyyaṃ. Abhūtatthova abhūtaṃ uttarapadalopenāti āha “abhūtanti abhūtattha”nti. Atacchanti tasseva vevacananti āha “atacchanti na taccha”nti. Abhūtanti vā asantaṃ avijjamānaṃ. Atacchanti atathākāraṃ. Anatthasaṃhitanti diṭṭhadhammikena, samparāyikena vā anatthena saṃhitaṃ, anatthe vā saṃhitaṃ, na atthoti vā anattho, atthassa paṭipakkho sabhāvo, tena saṃhitanti anatthasaṃhitaṃ, pisuṇavācaṃ samphappalāpañcāti attho. Evamettha catubbidhassapi vacīduccaritassa gahitatā daṭṭhabbā.

‘I would remove it from him’: I would remove that from this child’s mouth. ‘False’: this is ‘what has a false meaning’ (abhūtattha), with the elision of the final member of the compound. Thus it is said: ‘“False” means having a false meaning.’ ‘Untrue’: this is a synonym for that. Thus it is said: ‘“Untrue” means not true.’ Or, ‘false’ means non-existent, not present. ‘Untrue’ means not so. ‘Unbeneficial’: connected with what is unbeneficial in the present life or in a future life; or connected with what is unbeneficial; or what is not the benefit is the ‘un-benefit,’ the nature opposite to the benefit, and it is connected with that. The meaning is slanderous speech and idle chatter. Thus it should be seen that here all four kinds of verbal misconduct are included.

Duppayuttoti duppaṭipanno. Na taṃ tathāgato bhāsati abhūtatādidosaduṭṭhattā. Tampi tathāgato na bhāsati bhūtatthepi anatthasaṃhitatādidosaduṭṭhattā.

‘Wrongly applied’: wrongly practiced. The Tathāgata does not speak that because it is corrupted by the faults of falseness and so on. The Tathāgata does not speak that either, even though it is true, because it is corrupted by the faults of being unbeneficial and so on.

Ṭhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ etissā atthīti ṭhāniyā ka-kārassa ya-kāraṃ katvā, na ṭhāniyāti aṭṭhāniyā, nikkāraṇā ayuttiyuttā, sā eva kathāti aṭṭhāniyakathā. Attapaccakkhakathaṃ kathemāti attanā eva paccakkhaṃ katvā pavattiyamānaṃ chalakathaṃ kathema.

‘Grounded’ (ṭhāniyā) is because it has a ground (ṭhānaṃ), a reason (kāraṇaṃ); the ‘k’ has been changed to ‘y.’ ‘Not grounded’ is ‘ungrounded’ (aṭṭhāniyā), which means without reason, illogical. Such talk is ‘ungrounded talk.’ ‘Let us have a talk that is personally verified’: let us have the six kinds of deceptive talk that are conducted after being personally verified.

Gāmikamahallako “ime maṃ vañcetukāmā, ahameva dāni ime vañcessāmī”ti cintetvā “evaṃ bhavissatī”tiādimāha. “Na mayaṃ dāsā”tipi vattuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu pubbe tathākatikāya katattā.

The village elder thought, ‘These men want to deceive me, but now I will deceive them,’ and he said, ‘So it will be,’ and so on. They were unable to say, ‘We are not your slaves,’ because of the agreement they had made previously.

Tatiyaṃ tatiyamevāti dvīsupi pakkhesu tatiyaṃ tatiyameva vācaṃ. Bhāsitabbakālaṃ anatikkamitvāti yassa yadā yathā bhāsitabbaṃ, tassa tadā tatheva ca bhāsanato bhāsitabbaṃ kāraṇaṃ bhāsitabbakālañca anatikkamitvāva bhāsati.

‘The third, only the third’: the third kind of speech in both sets. ‘Without transgressing the time for speaking’: because he speaks to a person at the time and in the way it should be spoken, he speaks without transgressing the reason for speaking and the time for speaking.

87. Ṭhānuppattikañāṇenāti [V 2.0047] ṭhāne eva uppajjanakañāṇena. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāraṇe tassa taṃ taṃ avatthāya uppajjanakañāṇena, dhammānaṃ yathāsabhāvato avabujjhanasabhāvoti dhammasabhāvo. Dhamme sabhāvadhamme anavasese vā yāthāvato upadhāretīti dhammadhātu, sabbaññutā. Tenāha “sabbaññutaññāṇassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Suppaṭividdhanti sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ suṭṭhu paṭivijjhanavasena, suṭṭhu paṭividdhanti attho. Tenāha “hatthagataṃ bhagavato”ti. Neyyapuggalavasena pariniṭṭhitāti kathāparivibhāgena ayameva [M 2.0050] desanā cattāri ariyasaccāni dassento arahattaṃ paccakkhāsīti.

87. With knowledge arising on the spot: with knowledge arising right in that place. In each and every case, with knowledge arising for that particular state; the nature of phenomena is the nature of understanding phenomena according to their true nature. The element of phenomena, omniscience, is to comprehend phenomena—things in their own nature—without remainder, just as they are. Hence it is said: 'This is a designation for the knowledge of omniscience.' Well-penetrated: by way of thoroughly penetrating every knowable phenomenon, the meaning is 'well penetrated.' Hence it is said: 'It is in the Blessed One’s grasp.' ‘Established as complete by way of the persons to be guided’ means that through the analysis of the discourse, this very teaching, by showing the four noble truths, brought about the realization of arahantship.

Abhayarājakumārasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Abhayarājakumāra Sutta is completed.

9. Bahuvedaniyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Bahuvedanīya Sutta

88. Pañcakaṅgoti [V 2.0048] vaḍḍhakīkiccasādhane vāsiādipañcakaṃ aṅgaṃ saṃdhanaṃ etasminti pañcakaṅgo. Thambhādivatthūnaṃ thapanaṭṭhena thapati. Paṇḍitaudāyitthero, na kāḷudāyī thero.

88. Pañcakaṅga: He is called 'Five-limbed' (Pañcakaṅga) because the fivefold set of tools beginning with the adze is the equipment for accomplishing a carpenter's work. A carpenter (thapati) is so called in the sense of setting up pillars and other structures. This was the elder Paṇḍita Udāyī, not the elder Kāḷudāyī.

89. Pariyāyati attano phalaṃ vattetīti pariyāyo, kāraṇaṃ. Vedanāsannissito ca kāyikacetasikabhāvo kāraṇaṃ. Tenāha – “kāyikacetasikavasena dve veditabbā”ti. Tattha pasādakāyasannissitā kāyikā, cetosannissitā cetasikā. Sukhādivasena tissoti ettha sukhanadukkhanupekkhanāni sukhādivedanāya kāraṇaṃ. Tāni hi pavattinimittāni katvā tattha sukhādisaddappavatti, iminā nayena sesesupi yathārahaṃ kāraṇaṃ niddhāretvā vattabbaṃ. Upavicāravasenāti ārammaṇaṃ upecca savisesapavattivasena. Yasmiñhi ārammaṇe somanassavedanā pavattati, ārammaṇatāya taṃ upagantvā itaravedanāhi visiṭṭhatāya savisesaṃ tattha pavatti. Tenāha “somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ rūpaṃ upavicaratī”ti. Esa nayo sesavedanāsu gehassitānīti gehanissitāni.

89. A way of exposition (pariyāyo): because it brings about its own result, it is a reason. And a bodily or mental state dependent on feeling is a reason. Hence it is said: 'Two are to be understood by way of the bodily and the mental.' Herein, what is dependent on the sensitive body is bodily; what is dependent on the mind is mental. Threefold by way of pleasure, etc.: here, pleasure, pain, and equanimity are the reason for feelings of pleasure, etc. For it is by taking these as the signs of their occurrence that the terms 'pleasant,' etc., are used. By this method, the reason should be determined as is fitting in the remaining cases and stated. By way of close investigation: by way of a distinct occurrence on approaching the object. For when a feeling of joy arises in regard to an object, having approached it as an object, it occurs there distinctly, being distinguished from other feelings. Hence it is said: 'One closely investigates a form that is a basis for joy.' This is the method for the remaining feelings. Based on the household life means dependent on the household life.

90. Pariyāyenāti “idamettha dukkhasminti vadāmī”ti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Taṃ dassentoti kāmañcettha sutte – “dvepānanda, vedanā vuttā”ti dve ādiṃ katvā vedanā dassitā, ekāpi pana dassitā evāti dassento. Upatthambhetunti ekāpi vedanā vuttā mayā pariyāyena, evaṃ sati dvepi vattabbāti evaṃ tassa vādaṃ upatthambhetuṃ. Kathaṃ pana ekā vedanā vuttāti? Yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā, idamettha dukkhasminti vadāmīti. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ itivuttakavaṇṇanāyaṃ (itivu. aṭṭha. 52 ādayo) paramatthadīpaniyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

90. ‘By way of exposition’: this is said with reference to the passage, ‘This, I say, is included in suffering.’ To show this: Although in this sutta feelings are shown beginning with two—‘Ānanda, two feelings have been taught’—he shows that even one has also been shown. To support: this is said in order to support his own thesis, thus: ‘Even one feeling has been taught by me by way of exposition; this being so, two can also be stated.’ But how has one feeling been taught? ‘Whatever is felt—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—this, I say, is included in suffering.’ Whatever should be said on this should be understood according to the method stated in the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Itivuttaka (Itiv-a 52ff.).

Kathaṃ [M 2.0051] panettha rūpāvacaracatutthe arūpesu saññāvedayitanirodhe sukhaṃ uddhatanti āha “ettha cā”tiādi. Santaṭṭhenāti paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ vūpasantabhāvena. Paṇītaṭṭhenāti bhāvanāvisesavisiṭṭhena atappakabhāveneva seṭṭhabhāvena ca, paccayavisesena padhānabhāvaṃ nītantipi paṇītaṃ. Vedayitasukhaṃ nāma vedanābhūtaṃ sukhanti katvā. Avedayitasukhaṃ nāma yāvatā niddukkhatā, tāvatā sukhanti vuccatīti.Atha vā nirodho suṭṭhu khādati khanati kāyikacetasikābādhanti [V 2.0049] vattabbataṃ arahati sattāhampi tattha dukkhassa nirujjhanato. Tenāha “niddukkhabhāvasaṅkhātena sukhaṭṭhenā”ti.

How, then, is happiness specified here in the fourth form-realm jhāna, in the formless attainments, and in the cessation of perception and feeling? He says, 'Here also,' etc. In the sense of peacefulness: by the pacification of opposing states. In the sense of sublimity: by being distinguished by a special development of meditation, by its nature of being unafflicted, and by its excellence; sublime also means brought to prominence by a special condition. Felt happiness is happiness that is actual feeling. Unfelt happiness is so called because insofar as there is freedom from suffering, to that extent it is called happiness. Alternatively, cessation deserves to be so called because it thoroughly 'eats' and 'digs up' bodily and mental affliction, since suffering ceases there for as long as seven days. Therefore, it is said: 'in the sense of happiness, which is reckoned as the state of freedom from suffering.'

91. Yasmiṃ yasmiṃ bhave, cittuppāde, avatthāya vā niddukkhabhāvo, dukkhassa paṭipakkhatā anupalabbhanena dukkhavivittaṃ, taṃ sukhasmiṃyeva paññapeti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

91. In whatever existence, arising of consciousness, or state there is freedom from suffering—being secluded from suffering through the non-apprehension of suffering or its opposite—that is designated as included in happiness. The rest is easily understood.

Bahuvedanīyasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Bahuvedanīya Sutta is completed.

10. Apaṇṇakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta

93. Nānāvidhāti [V 2.0050] nānāvidhadiṭṭhikā samaṇabrāhmaṇāti pabbajjāmattena samaṇā, jātimattena brāhmaṇā ca. Dassananti diṭṭhi. Gahitanti abhinivissa gahitaṃ. Iti te attano dassanaṃ gahetukāmā pucchanti. Vinā dassanena loko na niyyātīti vimokkhabhāvanāya ekena dassanena vinā loko saṃsāradukkhato na nigacchati. Ekadiṭṭhiyampi patiṭṭhātuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu saddhākārābhāvato. Tathā hi te imāya desanāya saraṇesu patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Yasmā aviparīte saddheyyavatthusmiṃ uppannasaddhā “ākāravatī”ti adhippetā, tasmā yo loke aviparītadhammadesanā, ayamevesāti pavattā maggasādhanagatāya saddhāya kāraṇabhāvato tannissayā saddhā, sā ākāravatīti vuttā. Avatthusmiñhi saddhā ayuttakāraṇatāya na ākāravatī. Ākāravatīti ettha vatī-saddo na kevalaṃ atthitāmattadīpako, atha kho atisayatthadīpako pāsaṃsatthadīpako vā daṭṭhabbo. Tena ākāravatīti saddheyyavatthuvasena atisayakāraṇavatīti vā pāsaṃsakāraṇavatīti vā [M 2.0052] ayamettha attho. Apaṇṇakoti ettha yathā kañci atthaṃ sādhetuṃ āraddhassa payogo viraddho, tattha akārako viya hoti punapi ārabhitabbatāya. Aviraddho pana atthassa sādhanato apaṇṇako, evaṃ ayampi dhammo abhibhavitvā pavattanato ekaṃsato “apaṇṇako”ti vutto. Tenāha “aviraddho advejjhagāmī ekaṃsagāhiko”ti.

93. 'Of various kinds' means ascetics and brahmins of various views—ascetics merely by their going forth, and brahmins merely by birth. 'View' means a speculative view. 'Held' means grasped with adherence. Thus they ask, desiring to grasp their own view. 'Without a view the world is not led forth' means: without the one view that is the development of liberation, the world does not go forth from the suffering of saṃsāra. They were unable to become established even in a single view because they lacked a basis for faith. For through this teaching they became established in the refuges. Because faith that has arisen in an unerring object of faith is intended as 'well-grounded,' the faith dependent on the unerring teaching of the Dhamma is called 'well-grounded,' as it is the cause for the faith that pertains to the accomplishment of the path. For faith in an improper object is not well-grounded because its cause is unsuitable. Herein, in the word 'well-grounded' (ākāravatī), the suffix -vatī does not merely indicate possession, but should be seen as indicating superiority or praiseworthiness. Thus, the meaning here is that 'well-grounded' means possessing a superior or praiseworthy cause by way of its object of faith. The Incontrovertible (apaṇṇaka): Just as when the effort of one who has started to accomplish some purpose is frustrated, he is like a non-doer because he has to start all over again, but when it is not frustrated, because he accomplishes his purpose, it is 'unfailing' (apaṇṇaka); so too this Dhamma, because it proceeds by overcoming, is definitely called 'incontrovertible.' Hence it is said: 'unfrustrated, leading to what is certain, to be adopted definitely.'

94. Tabbipaccanīkabhūtāti tassā micchādiṭṭhiyā paccanīkabhūtā.

94. Being opposed to that means being opposed to that wrong view.

95. Nesanti kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Akusalato nikkhantabhāveti asaṃkiliṭṭhabhāve. Ānisaṃsoti suddhavipākatā. Visuddhipakkhoti visuddhibhāvo pariyodātatā. Abhūtadhammassa diṭṭhibhāvassa saññāpanā ācikkhanā abhūtadhammasaññāpanā. Sāvajjesu paramavajje micchādassane paggahaṇanti kuto susīlyassa paggahoti āha – “micchādassanaṃ gaṇhantasseva susīlyaṃ pahīnaṃ hotī”ti. Micchādiṭṭhiādayoti ettha micchāsaṅkappo paralokābhāvacintā, micchāvācā paralokābhāvavādabhūto musāvādo, ariyānaṃ paccanīkatādayo. Aparāparaṃ uppajjanavasenāti punappunaṃ citte uppajjanavasena. Pāpakā akusalā dhammāti paccavekkhaṇasaññāpanādikāle uppajjanakā tathāpavattā akusalakhandhā.

95. They do not seek wholesome qualities. In the state of having departed from the unwholesome means in the state of being undefiled. Benefit means purity of result. The side of purification means the state of purity, brilliance. The making known and explaining of a non-existent thing as a view is the making known of a non-existent thing. Undertaking what is blameworthy, the supreme blame of wrong view—how can there be an undertaking of good morality? He says: 'For one who grasps wrong view, good morality is itself abandoned.' Wrong view, etc.: here wrong intention is the thought of the non-existence of the other world; wrong speech is the falsehood that constitutes the assertion of the non-existence of the other world; opposition to the noble ones, and so on. By way of arising successively means by way of arising again and again in the mind. Evil, unwholesome qualities means the unwholesome aggregates that arise and proceed in such a way at the time of reviewing, making known, etc.

Kaliggahoti [V 2.0051] anatthapariggaho. So pana yasmā diṭṭheva dhamme abhisamparāyañca parājayo hotīti āha “parājayaggāho”ti. Dussamattoti ettha du-saddo “samādinno”ti etthāpi ānetvā yojetabboti āha “dupparāmaṭṭho”ti. Yathā dupparāmaṭṭho hoti, evaṃ samādinno dussamatto dusamādinno vutto. Sakavādameva pharitvāti attano natthikavādameva “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti (ma. ni. 2.187; 3.27-28) avadhārento aññassa okāsaadānavasena pharitvā. Tenāha “adhimuccitvā”ti. “Sambuddho”tiādi adhimuccanākāradassanaṃ. Riñcatīti viveceti apaneti. Tenāha “vajjetī”ti.

A losing throw is the grasping of what is disadvantageous. But because this is a defeat both in this very life and in the life to come, it is called 'the grasp of defeat.' Wrongly held (dussamatto): here the prefix du- should also be brought over and connected with 'undertaken' (samādinno); hence it is said 'wrongly affected' (dupparāmaṭṭho). Just as it is wrongly affected, so being undertaken, it is called dussamatto, that is, 'wrongly undertaken' (dusamādinno). Pervading with his own doctrine: having determined his own nihilistic doctrine—'This alone is true, all else is false'—he pervades with it by not giving an opportunity to another. Hence it says, 'having become intent on.' The words 'the Fully Enlightened One,' etc., show the way of becoming intent. He forsakes means he separates from, he removes. Hence it says, 'he avoids.'

96. Kaṭaggahoti kataṃ sabbaso siddhimeva katvā gahaṇaṃ. So pana jayalābho hotīti vuttaṃ “jayaggāho”ti. Suggahitoti suṭṭhukaraṇavasena gahito. Suparāmaṭṭhoti suṭṭhu parāparaṃ āsevanavasena āmaṭṭho[M 2.0053]. Ubhayenapi tassa kammassa katūpacitabhāvaṃ dasseti, sotthibhāvāvahattañca saggupapattisaṃvattanato pāpasabhāvapahānato ca.

96. A winning throw is a grasp that takes something as completely accomplished. But since this is the acquisition of victory, it is called 'the grasp of victory.' Well-grasped means grasped by way of being well done. Well-affected means affected by way of being repeatedly cultivated. By both, it shows that the kamma has been done and accumulated, and that it brings well-being, because it leads to rebirth in heaven and because it involves the abandoning of an evil nature.

97. Sahatthā karontassāti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.166; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.3.211) sahattheneva karontassa. Nissaggiyathāvarādayopi idha sahatthakaraṇeneva saṅgahitā. Pacanaṃ dahanaṃ vibādhananti āha “daṇḍena pīḷentassā”ti. Sokaṃ sayaṃ karontassāti parassa sokakāraṇaṃ sayaṃ karontassa, sokaṃ vā uppādentassa. Parehi attano vacanakarehi. Sayampi phandatoti parassa vibādhanapayogena sayampi phandato. Atipātayatoti padaṃ suddhakattuatthe hetukattuatthe ca vattatīti āha “hanantassapi hanāpentassāpī”ti.

97. 'Doing it with one's own hand' means doing it with one's very own hand. Offenses entailing forfeiture, those concerning immovable property, and so on, are also included here by the act of doing it with one's own hand. 'Cooking, burning, tormenting': this is said to mean 'oppressing with a stick.' 'Causing grief oneself' means personally causing another's grief, or else producing grief. 'By others' means by those who act on one's word. 'One trembles oneself' means one trembles oneself through the application of tormenting another. The word 'atipātayati' applies to the meaning of both killing and causing to be killed, thus it is said: 'of one who kills and of one who causes to be killed.'

Gharassa bhitti anto bahi ca sandhitā hutvā ṭhitā gharasandhi. Kiñcipi asesetvā niravasesameva lopoti nillopo. Ekāgāre niyutto vilopo ekāgāriko. Parito sabbaso panthe hananaṃ paripantho. Pāpaṃ na karīyati pubbe asato uppādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā, tasmā natthi pāpaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ sattā pāpaṃ paṭipajjantīti āha – “sattā pana karomāti evaṃsaññino hontī”ti. Evaṃ kirassa hoti “imesañhi sattānaṃ hiṃsādikiriyā na attānaṃ phusati tassa niccatāya nibbikārattā, sarīraṃ pana acetanaṃ kaṭṭhakaliṅgarūpamaṃ, tasmiṃ vikopitepi na kiñci pāpa”nti. Khuranemināti nisitakhuramayaneminā. Gaṅgāya dakkhiṇadisā appatirūpadeso, uttaradisā patirūpadesoti adhippāyena “dakkhiṇañce”tiādi vuttanti “dakkhiṇatīre manussā kakkhaḷā”tiādimāha.

A 'house-joint' (gharasandhi) is the wall of a house, standing joined inside and out. 'Utter destruction' (nillopo) is destruction without remainder, leaving nothing behind. The plundering (vilopo) committed against a single house (ekāgāre) is 'a single-house [plunderer]' (ekāgāriko). 'Waylaying' (paripantho) is striking on the path all around. Evil is not done, for what is non-existent cannot be produced; therefore, there is no evil. If so, how do beings engage in evil? It is said: 'Beings, however, have the perception, “We are doing it.”' Thus, it is for him: 'For these beings, actions such as harming do not touch the self because of its permanence and immutability. The body, however, is insentient, like a piece of wood or a clod of earth; even if it is violated, there is no evil.' 'With a razor-rimmed wheel' means with a wheel-rim made of a sharp razor. The southern region of the Ganges is an unsuitable place, while the northern region is a suitable place. With this intention, 'If to the south,' etc., was said. Thus it is said: 'On the southern bank people are harsh,' etc.

Mahāyāganti [V 2.0052] mahāvijitayaññasadisaṃ mahāyāgaṃ. Sīlasaṃyamenāti kāyikavācasikasaṃvarena. Saccavacanenāti saccavācāya. Tassa visuṃ vacanaṃ loke garutarapuññasammatabhāvato. Yathā hi pāpadhammesu musāvādo garu, evaṃ puññadhammesu saccavācā. Tenāha bhagavā – “ekaṃ dhammamatītassā”tiādi (dha. pa. 176). Vuttanayenevāti kaṇhapakkhe vuttanayena. Tattha hi – “natthi pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo”ti āgataṃ, idha “atthi puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo”ti āgataṃ, ayameva viseso. Sesaṃ vuttasadisamevāti [M 2.0054] “tesametaṃ pāṭikaṅkha”nti evamādiṃ sandhāya vadati, taṃ heṭṭhā purimavārasadisaṃ.

'A great sacrifice' means a great sacrifice similar to the great victory sacrifice. 'By restraint in virtue' means by bodily and verbal restraint. 'By truthful speech' means by truthful speech. This is mentioned separately because in the world it is considered a very weighty merit. For just as false speech is a weighty thing among evil qualities, so truthful speech is among meritorious qualities.
