Therefore the Blessed One said: 'For one who has transgressed the one thing…,' and so on. 'By the method already stated' means by the method stated for the dark side. For there it is given: 'There is no evil, there is no source of evil,' while here it is given: 'There is merit, there is a source of merit.' This is the only difference. 'The rest is similar to what was stated': this he says referring to 'this is to be expected of them,' and so on, which is similar to the previous section.

100. Ubhayenāti hetupaccayapaṭisedhavacanena. Saṃkilesapaccayanti saṃsāre paribbhamanena kilinnassa malinabhāvassa kāraṇaṃ. Vuttavipariyāyena visuddhipaccayanti saddattho veditabbo. Balantiādīsu sattānaṃ saṃkilesāvahaṃ vodānāvahañca ussāhasaṅkhātaṃ balaṃ vā, sūravīrabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ vīriyaṃ vā, purisena kattabbo purisathāmo vā, so eva paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanappattiyā purisaparakkamo vā natthi na upalabbhati.

100. 'By both' means by the statement that denies both cause and condition. 'The condition for defilement' is the cause of the state of being stained and impure through wandering in saṃsāra. The meaning of the term 'the condition for purification' should be understood as the opposite of what was stated. In such terms as 'strength,' etc., there is no strength (bala), defined as the effort (ussāha) that brings about defilement and purification for beings; or energy (vīriya), defined as the state of a hero or a brave man; or manly stamina (purisathāma), which is what is to be done by a man; or manly exertion (purisaparakkama), which is that very thing for the purpose of reaching and ascending to higher and higher states. It does not exist, it is not found.

Satvayogato, rūpādīsu sattavisattatāya ca sattā. Pāṇanato assāsapassāsavasena pavattiyā pāṇā. Te pana so ekindriyādivasena vibhajitvā vadatīti āha “ekindriyo”tiādi. Aṇḍakosādīsu bhavanato bhūtāti vuccantīti āha “aṇḍakosa…pe… vadantī”ti. Jīvanato pāṇaṃ dhārento viya vaḍḍhanato jīvāti evaṃ sattapāṇabhūtajīvesu saddattho veditabbo. Natthi etesaṃ saṃkilesavisuddhīsu vasoti avasā. Natthi nesaṃ balaṃ vīriyañcāti abalā avīriyā. Niyatatāti acchejjasuttāvutābhejjamaṇi viya niyatapavattanatāya gatijātibandhapajahavasena niyāmo. Tattha tattha gamananti channaṃ abhijātīnaṃ tāsu tāsu gatīsu upagamanaṃ samavāyena samāgamo. Sabhāvoyevāti yathā kaṇṭakassa tikkhatā, kabiṭṭhaphalānaṃ parimaṇḍalatā, migapakkhīnaṃ vicittākāratā, evaṃ sabbassapi lokassa hetupaccayena vinā tathā tathā pariṇāmo, ayaṃ sabhāvoyeva akittimoyeva. Tenāha “yena hī”tiādi.

They are 'beings' (sattā) because of their connection with existence and because of their attachment and clinging to forms and so on. They are 'breathers' (pāṇā) from breathing, because of their proceeding by way of inhalation and exhalation. But he speaks of them by dividing them according to having one faculty and so on; thus he says 'one-facultied,' etc. They are called 'creatures' (bhūtā) because of coming to be (bhavana) in eggs and the like; thus it is said: 'in an egg-shell… etc… they say.' They are 'living beings' (jīvā) from living (jīvana), from growing as if sustaining the life-breath. Thus the meaning of the terms 'being,' 'breather,' 'creature,' and 'living being' should be understood. They have no power (vaso) over their defilement and purification, thus they are 'powerless' (avasā). They have no strength or energy, thus they are 'without strength' (abalā) and 'without energy' (avīriyā). 'Fixedness' (niyatatā) is a fixed course (niyāmo) because of its fixed proceeding—like the unbreakable gem mentioned in the Acchejjasutta—by way of abandoning the bonds of destiny and birth. 'Going here and there' is the approach of the six classes of birth to their respective destinies, a coming together through combination. 'It is just their nature': just as sharpness is the nature of a thorn, roundness of wood-apple fruits, and variegated forms of beasts and birds, so the transformation of the entire world happens in such and such a way without cause or condition. This is just its nature, uncreated. Therefore he said: 'For by this…,' etc.

Sakuṇe hanatīti sākuṇiko, tathā sūkariko. Luddoti aññopi yo koci māgaviko nesādo. Pāpakammapasutatāya kaṇhābhijāti nāma. Bhikkhūti sākiyā bhikkhū, macchamaṃsakhādanato nīlābhijātīti vadanti. Ñāyaladdhepi paccaye bhuñjamānā ājīvakasamayassa vilomagāhitāya “paccayesu kaṇṭake pakkhipitvā khādantī”ti vadanti. Eke pabbajitā[V 2.0053], ye savisesaṃ attakilamathānuyogamanuyuttā. Tathā [M 2.0055] hi te kaṇṭake vattentā viya hontīti kaṇṭakavuttikāti vuttā. Ṭhatvā bhuñjanadānapaṭikkhepādivatasamāyogena paṇḍaratarā. Acelakasāvakāti ājīvakasāvake vadati. Te kira ājīvakaladdhiyā visuddhacittatāya nigaṇṭhehipi paṇḍaratarā. Nandādayo hi tathārūpāya paṭipattiyā pattabbā, tasmā nandādayo nigaṇṭhehi ājīvakasāvakehi ca paṇḍaratarāti vuttā “sukkābhijātī”ti.

One who kills birds is a 'fowler' (sākuṇiko); likewise, a 'pork-butcher' (sūkariko). 'Cruel hunter' (luddo) refers to any other hunter, such as a deer-stalker (māgaviko) or a trapper (nesādo). Because of their addiction to evil deeds, this is called the 'dark class of birth' (kaṇhābhijāti). 'Monks' means the Sakyan monks; they say this is the 'blue class of birth' (nīlābhijāti) because they eat fish and meat. Even when they are eating requisites obtained rightly, because this is taken as contrary to the Ājīvaka doctrine, they say: 'They eat after putting thorns in their requisites.' Some renunciants are those who are especially devoted to the practice of self-mortification. Indeed, since they are as if living on thorns, they are called 'those of thorny practice' (kaṇṭakavuttikā). Through undertaking vows such as eating while standing, refusing gifts, and so on, they are 'whiter.' 'Disciples of the unclothed' (acelakasāvakā) refers to the disciples of the Ājīvakas. They, it seems, because of the purity of mind in the Ājīvaka doctrine, are whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas. For Nandā and others are to be attained by such a practice; therefore Nandā and others, being whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas and the Ājīvaka disciples, are said to be of the 'bright class of birth' (sukkābhijāti).

Ayametesaṃ laddhīti sākuṇikādibhāvūpagamanena kaṇhābhijātiādīsu dukkhaṃ sukhañca paṭisaṃvedentā anukkamena mahākappānaṃ cullāsītisahassāni khepetvā ājīvakabhāvūpagamanena paramasukkābhijātiyaṃ ṭhatvā saṃsārato sujjhantīti ayaṃ tesaṃ niyati ājīvakānaṃ laddhi.

This is their doctrine: by adopting the state of fowlers and the like, experiencing pain and pleasure in the dark classes of birth and the like, and gradually passing through eighty-four thousand great eons, they then adopt the state of Ājīvakas, stand in the supreme bright class of birth, and are purified from saṃsāra. This is the fixed doctrine of the Ājīvakas.

“Natthi dinna”nti vadanto natthiko dānassa phalaṃ paṭikkhipatīti āha – “natthikadiṭṭhi vipākaṃ paṭibāhatī”ti. Tathā ceva heṭṭhā saṃvaṇṇitaṃ “natthikadiṭṭhi hi natthitamāhā”ti. Ahetukadiṭṭhi ubhayanti kammaṃ vipākañca ubhayaṃ. So hi “ahetū apaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti visujjhantī”ti vadanto kammassa viya vipākassapi saṃkilesavisuddhīnaṃ paccayattābhāvavacanato tadubhayaṃ paṭibāhati nāma. Vipāko paṭibāhito hoti asati kamme vipākābhāvato. Kammaṃ paṭibāhitaṃ hoti asati vipāke kammassa niratthakabhāvāpattito. Atthatoti sarūpena. Ubhayapaṭibāhakāti visuṃ visuṃ taṃtaṃdiṭṭhitā vuttāpi sabbe te natthikādayo natthikadiṭṭhiādivasena paccekaṃ tividhadiṭṭhikā eva ubhayapaṭibāhakattā. “Ubhayapaṭibāhakā”ti hi hetuvacanaṃ. Ahetukavādā cātiādi paṭiññāvacanaṃ. Yo hi vipākapaṭibāhanena natthikadiṭṭhiko, so atthato kammapaṭibāhanena akiriyadiṭṭhiko, ubhayapaṭibāhanena ahetukadiṭṭhiko ca hoti. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo.

The nihilist (natthiko), by saying, 'There is nothing given,' denies the fruit of giving; thus it is said: 'The nihilist view obstructs the result.' Similarly, it is explained below: 'For the nihilist view declares non-existence.' The view of causelessness obstructs both, that is, both kamma and its result. For one who says, 'Beings are defiled and purified without cause, without condition,' indeed obstructs both of them, since he states that kamma and its result are not the condition for defilement and purification. The result is obstructed because when there is no kamma, there is no result. Kamma is obstructed because when there is no result, kamma becomes meaningless. 'In reality' (atthato) means in its own nature. 'Because they obstruct both': although they are spoken of separately according to their respective views, all of them—the nihilists and so on—are each holders of the three views (nihilism, etc.) because they obstruct both. For 'obstructers of both' is a statement of reason. 'Those with a causeless view, etc.' is a statement of the thesis. For whoever is a holder of the nihilist view by obstructing the result, is in reality a holder of the inefficacy-of-action view by obstructing kamma, and a holder of the causelessness view by obstructing both. The same method applies to the other two cases.

Sajjhāyantīti taṃ diṭṭhidīpakaṃ ganthaṃ uggahetvā paṭhanti. Vīmaṃsantīti tassa atthaṃ vicārenti. Tesantiādi vīmaṃsanākāradassanaṃ. Tasmiṃ ārammaṇeti yathāparikappitakammaphalābhāvadīpake “natthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattāya laddhiyā ārammaṇe. Micchāsati santiṭṭhatīti “natthi dinna”ntiādivasena [M 2.0056] anussavūpaladdhe atthe tadākāraparivitakkanehi saviggahe viya sarūpato cittassa paccupaṭṭhite cirakālaparicayena “evameta”nti nijjhānakkhamabhāvūpagamanena nijjhānakkhantiyā tathā gahite punappunaṃ tatheva āsevantassa bahulīkarontassa micchāvitakkena samādiyamānā micchāvāyāmupatthambhitā ataṃsabhāvaṃ “taṃsabhāva”nti gaṇhantī micchāsatīti laddhanāmā taṃladdhisahagatā taṇhā santiṭṭhati[V 2.0054]. Cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hotīti yathāvuttavitakkādipaccayalābhena tasmiṃ ārammaṇe avaṭṭhitatāya anekaggaṃ pahāya ekaggaṃ appitaṃ viya hoti. Micchāsamādhipi hi paccayavisesehi laddhabhāvanābalehi kadāci samādhānapatirūpakiccakaro hotiyeva vālavijjhanādīsu viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Javanāni javantīti anekakkhattuṃ tenākārena pubbabhāgiyesu javanavāresu pavattesu sabbapacchime javanavāre satta javanāni javanti. Paṭhamajavane pana satekicchā honti, tathā dutiyādīsūti dhammasabhāvadassanametaṃ, na pana tasmiṃ khaṇe tesaṃ satekicchabhāvāpādanaṃ kenaci sakkā kātuṃ.

"They recite it" means they learn that text which illuminates their view and recite it. "They investigate" means they reflect on its meaning. The words "for them," etc., show the manner of investigation. "In that object" means in the object of that conviction which proceeds by way of "there is no giving," etc., illuminating the non-existence of the fruit of kamma as has been conceived. "Wrong mindfulness is established" means this: when an object apprehended through oral tradition, such as "there is no giving," is present to the mind in its own nature as if it were concrete through reflections of that kind, and it is grasped thus through acquiescence in meditative thought because, through long familiarity, one has come to a state of being able to reflect on it as "it is so"; for one who repeatedly resorts to it and cultivates it, the craving associated with that conviction becomes established. This craving is called "wrong mindfulness" because, being undertaken with wrong thought and supported by wrong effort, it grasps what is not its true nature as "its true nature." "The mind becomes one-pointed" means that by obtaining the conditions of thought, etc., as stated, the mind, having abandoned its lack of one-pointedness, becomes one-pointed, as if absorbed in that object due to its being established there. For even wrong concentration, when its power of development is obtained through specific conditions, can sometimes perform a function resembling that of concentration, as should be seen in such cases as piercing a hair. "The impulsions run" means that after the impulsion-moments have occurred many times in that way in the preliminary impulsion-series, in the very last impulsion-series seven impulsions run. But in the first impulsion they are remediable, and likewise in the second, etc. This is a display of the nature of phenomena, but at that moment no one is able to bring about their state of being remediable.

Tatthāti tesu tīsu micchādassanesu. Koci ekaṃ dassanaṃ okkamatīti yassa ekasmiṃyeva abhiniveso āsevanā ca pavattā, so ekaṃyeva dassanaṃ okkamati. Yassa pana dvīsu, tīsupi vā abhinivesanā pavattā, so dve tīṇi okkamati. Etena yā pubbe ubhayapaṭibāhanatāmukhena vuttā atthasiddhā sabbadiṭṭhikatā, sā pubbabhāgiyā. Yā pana micchattaniyāmokkanti bhūtā, sā yathāsakaṃ paccayasamudāgamasiddhito bhinnārammaṇānaṃ viya visesādhigamānaṃ aññamaññaṃ ekajjhaṃ anuppattiyā asaṃkiṇṇā evāti dasseti. Ekasmiṃ okkantepītiādinā tissannampi diṭṭhīnaṃ samānabalataṃ samānaphalatañca dasseti, tasmā tissopi cetā ekassa uppannā aññamaññaṃ abbokiṇṇā eva, ekāya vipāke dinne itarā anubalappadāyikā honti. Vaṭṭakhāṇu nāmāti idaṃ vacanaṃ neyyatthaṃ, na nītatthanti taṃ vivaritvā dassetuṃ kiṃ panesātiādi vuttaṃ, akusalaṃ nāmetaṃ abalaṃ dubbalaṃ, na kusalaṃ viya mahābalanti āha – “ekasmiṃyeva attabhāve niyato”ti. Aññathā sammattaniyāmo viya micchattaniyāmopi accantiko siyā. Yadi evaṃ vaṭṭakhāṇukajotanā kathanti āha “āsevanavasena panā”tiādi, tasmā yathā “sakiṃ nimuggo [M 2.0057] nimuggova hotī”ti (a. ni. 7.15) vuttaṃ, evaṃ vaṭṭakhāṇukajotanā. Yādise hi paccaye paṭicca ayaṃ taṃtaṃdassanaṃ okkanto puna kadāci tappaṭipakkhe paccaye paṭicca tato sīsukkhipanamassa na hotīti na vattabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “yebhuyyenā”ti.

"Therein" means in those three wrong views. "Someone enters upon one view" means that one for whom adherence and practice occur in only one view enters upon just that one view. But one for whom adherence occurs in two or even three enters upon two or three. By this he shows that the holding of all views, an established meaning mentioned previously by way of rejecting both alternatives, is preliminary. But the descent into the fixed course of wrongness, being what it is, is shown to be unconfused because, like the special attainments with their different objects, they do not arrive at convergence with one another since they are established by the coming together of their respective conditions. By the words "Even when one has entered upon one," he shows that all three views are equal in strength and equal in fruit. Therefore, even if these three arise for one person, they remain unmixed with each other; when one gives its fruit, the others provide support. "The stake of the round" is a statement requiring interpretation, not one of explicit meaning. To explain it, the words "What then is this?" etc., were stated. This is unwholesome, weak, feeble; it is not powerful like the wholesome. He says: "Fixed in just one existence." Otherwise, like the fixed course of rightness, the fixed course of wrongness would also be absolute. If so, how does the illustration of the stake of the round apply? He says: "But through the force of practice," etc. Therefore, just as it is said, "Once submerged, he remains submerged" (AN 7.15), so too is the illustration of the stake of the round. For it should not be said that because this person has entered upon some particular view depending on certain conditions, he will never again lift his head from it by depending on contrary conditions. Hence it is said, "for the most part."

Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ saṃsārakhāṇubhāvassapi paccayo akalyāṇajano, tasmā. Bhūtikāmoti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthānaṃ vasena attano guṇehi vaḍḍhikāmo. Yaṃ panettha keci vadanti “yathā cirakālabhāvanāya paripākūpagamaladdhabalattā upanissayakusalā akusale sabbaso samucchindanti, evaṃ akusaladhammā tatopi cirakālabhāvanāsambhavato laddhabalā hutvā kadāci kusaladhammepi samucchindanti. Evañca katvā daḷhamicchābhinivesassa micchādiṭṭhikassa vaṭṭakhāṇukabhāvajotanāpi [V 2.0055] samatthitā hotī”ti yathā taṃ “vassabhaññānaṃ diṭṭhī”ti, taṃ na, micchattaniyatadhammānaṃ cirakālabhāvanāmattena na paṭipakkhassa pajahanasamatthatā, atha kho dhammatāsiddhena paccayavisesāhitasāmatthiyena attano pahāyakasabhāvena pahāyakabhāvo bhāvanākusalānaṃyeva vutto, akusalānaṃyeva ca pahātabbabhāvo “dassanena pahātabbā”tiādinā nayena, akusalānaṃyeva dubbalabhāvo “abalānaṃ balīyantī”tiādinā (su. ni. 776; mahāni. 5) (yuttināpi nāmato vā adhigamaniyo āloko ālokabhāvato bāhirāraṇekā viya na cettha paṭiññatte bhāvesatā sotuno āsaṃkitabbā visesavassa sādhetabbato sāmaññassa ca sotubhāvena adhippetattā veda-saddassa lopo dīpe sabhāve sādhane yathā taṃ saddayabhāvassa nāpi visuddhakaanumānādivirodhasambhāvato. Na hi sakkā antarālokassa bāhirālokassa viya rūpakāyaṃ upādāya rūpatā cakkhuviññeyyattādike patiṭṭhāpetuṃ sakkāti vuttaṃ, nanupi antarāloko aviggahattā vedanā viyāti saddheva ñāṇālokassa avijjandhakārā viya vidhamaniyabhāve sabbesampi kusaladhammānaṃ kenacipi akusaladhammena samucchindaniyatā siddhāva hoti). Vaṭṭakhāṇukacodanāya yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttamevāti tiṭṭhatesā bālajanavikatthanā.

"Therefore" means: because an unvirtuous person is a condition even for being a stake in saṃsāra, therefore... "One desiring well-being" means one who desires to grow in one's own qualities by way of benefits in the present life, benefits in future lives, and the ultimate good. But here some say: "Just as wholesome states that are a support, having gained strength from being developed for a long time, completely eradicate unwholesome states, so too unwholesome states, having gained strength because they can be developed for an even longer time, sometimes eradicate wholesome states. And this being so, the illustration of the stake of the round is justified even for one with firm adherence to wrong view." That is not so, like the view of the Vassabhaññas. For states fixed in wrongness are not capable of abandoning their opposite merely by being developed for a long time. Rather, the nature of abandoning is spoken of only for wholesome states developed in meditation, which have the nature of abandoning through a power produced by a specific condition established by the nature of things. And only the unwholesome is to be abandoned, according to the method beginning "to be abandoned by vision." And only the unwholesome is weak, according to the method beginning "the strong crush the weak" (SNip 776; Mahāni 5). (The following parenthetical passage in the Pali text is obscure and likely corrupt.) Whatever should be said in response to the objection concerning the stake of the round has already been stated above. So let this boasting of fools stand.

103. Jhānacittamayāti [M 2.0058] rūpāvacarajjhānacittena nibbattā. Tathā hi tesaṃ visesena jhānamanasā nibbattattā “manomayā”ti vuttā, avisesena pana abhisaṅkhāramanasā sabbepi sattā manomayā eva. Saññāmayāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tenāha “arūpajjhānasaññāyā”ti. Ayanti rūpitābhāvapaṭipajjanakapuggalo. Appaṭiladdhajjhānoti anadhigatarūpajjhāno. Tassapīti takkinopi. Rūpajjhāne kaṅkhā natthi anussavavasena laddhavinicchayattā.

103. "Made of the jhāna-mind" means produced by the fine-material sphere jhāna-mind. Indeed, because they are produced specifically by the jhāna-mind, they are called "mind-made"; but in a general sense, all beings are mind-made by the mind that forms volitions. The same method applies here to "made of perception." Hence he says, "by the perception of the formless jhāna." "This one" means the person who is practicing for the non-existence of what is formed. "One who has not obtained jhāna" means one who has not attained the fine-material jhānas. "For him too" means even for the reasoner. There is no doubt about the fine-material jhānas because a decision has been reached through oral tradition.

104. Sārāgāyāti sarāgabhāvāya. Santiketi samīpe, na thāmagatā diṭṭhinātidūrattā sarāgā, na sampayuttattā. Sā hi na thāmagatā vaṭṭapariyāpannesu dhammesu rajjatīti viññāyatīti āha – “rāgavasena vaṭṭe rajjanassā”ti. Sabbepi saṃyojanā taṇhāvaseneva sambhavantīti āha – “taṇhāvasena saṃyojanatthāyā”ti. Āruppe panassa kaṅkhā natthīti anussavavasena laddhanicchayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kāmaṃ duggatidukkhānaṃ ekantasaṃvattanena natthikadiṭṭhiādīnaṃ apaṇṇakatā pākaṭā eva, nippariyāyena pana anavajjassa atthassa ekantasādhakaṃ apaṇṇakanti katvā codanā, sāvajjassapi atthassa sādhane ekaṃsikabhāvaṃ gahetvā parihāro. Tenāha “gahaṇavasenā”tiādi. Tena ruḷhīvasena “natthi dinna”ntiādīni apaṇṇakaṅgāni jātānīti dasseti.

104. "For lust" means for the state of being with lust. "Nearby" means in the vicinity. The view is lustful because it is not too far away, not because it is associated with lust; it is not a strong lust. For that view, when not strong, lusts for things included in the round. Hence he says, "of lusting for the round by way of lust." All fetters arise through the power of craving. Hence he says, "for the purpose of fettering by way of craving." "But for him there is no doubt about the formless attainments": this is said with reference to a decision reached through oral tradition. Granted, the unsoundness of nihilistic views and so on is evident because they lead exclusively to the suffering of the bad destinations. But the objection is made on the grounds that an incontestable teaching is one that invariably accomplishes a blameless goal, while the rebuttal takes the one-sidedness in accomplishing even a blameworthy goal. Hence he says, "by way of grasping," etc. By this he shows that by way of convention, statements like "there is no giving" have become parts of an incontestable teaching.

105. Heṭṭhā [V 2.0056] tayo puggalāva hontīti attantapo parantapoti imasmiṃ catukke heṭṭhā tayo puggalā honti. Yathāvuttā pañcapi puggalā duppaṭipannāva, tato atthikavādādayo pañcapuggalā sammāpaṭipannatāya imasmiṃ catukke eko catutthapuggalova hoti. Etamatthaṃ dassetunti idha heṭṭhā vuttapuggalapañcakadvayaṃ imasmiṃ catukke eva saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti vibhāgena duppaṭipattisuppaṭipattiyo dassetuṃ bhagavā imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhīti. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

105. "There are three persons below" means that in this tetrad, the three persons below—the self-tormentor, the tormentor of others, and the one who torments both—are found. The five persons mentioned are all wrongly practicing. Then, of the five persons beginning with the affirmationist, because of their right practice, only one—the fourth person—is in this tetrad. "To show this meaning": The Blessed One began this discourse to show wrong practice and right practice by way of division, since the two pentads of persons mentioned above are included in this very tetrad. Whatever is not analyzed here in terms of meaning is easy to understand.

Apaṇṇakasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Concealed Meaning of the Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca gahapativaggavaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the Gahapativagga is concluded.

2. Bhikkhuvaggo

2. The Chapter on the Bhikkhus

1. Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda Sutta

107. Ambalaṭṭhikāyanti [M 2.0059][V 2.0057] ettha ambalaṭṭhikā vuccati sujāto taruṇambarukkho, tassa pana avidūre kato pāsādo idha “ambalaṭṭhikā”ti adhippeto. Tenāha “veḷuvanavihārassā”tiādi. Padhānagharasaṅkhepeti bhāvanāgehappakāre yogīnaṃ geheti attho. Tikhiṇova hoti, na tassa tikhiṇabhāvo kenaci kātabbo sabhāvasiddhattā. Evameva attano vimuttiparipācanakammunā tikkhavisadabhāvappattiyā ayampi āyasmā…pe… tattha vihāsi. Pakatipaññattamevāti pakatiyā paññattaṃ buddhānaṃ upagamanato puretarameva cārittavasena paññattaṃ.

107. Regarding Ambalaṭṭhikā: here ambalaṭṭhikā is said to be a well-grown, young mango tree, but a mansion built not far from it is what is meant here by 'Ambalaṭṭhikā.' Therefore, he said, 'of the Bamboo Grove Monastery,' and so on. The phrase Padhānagharasaṅkhepe means: in a type of meditation hall, a dwelling for yogis. He is sharp by nature; his sharpness does not need to be produced by anyone, as it is established by his intrinsic nature. Just so, this venerable one... dwelt there, having attained a state of sharpness and clarity through the kamma of maturing his own liberation. Regarding Pakatipaññattameva: it was established by nature, meaning it was established by way of custom even before the advent of the Buddhas.

108. Udakaṃ anena dhīyati, ṭhapīyati vā etthāti udakādhānaṃ. Udakaṭṭhānanti ca khuddakabhājanaṃ. “Ovādadānatthaṃ āmantesī”ti vatvā taṃ panassa ovādadānaṃ na idheva, atha kho bahūsu ṭhānesu bahukkhattuṃ pavattitanti tāni tāni saṅkhepato dassetvā idha saṃvaṇṇanatthaṃ “bhagavatā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

108. Water is held by this, or it is placed in this, hence it is an udakādhāna (water-container). And an udakaṭṭhāna (water-stand) is a small vessel. Having said, 'He addressed him for the purpose of giving an exhortation,' yet his giving of this exhortation did not occur only here; rather, it took place in many places on many occasions. Having briefly indicated those instances, the phrase 'for by the Blessed One,' and so on, is stated here for the purpose of commentary.

Tattha sabbabuddhehi avijahitanti iminā sabbesaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsane kumārapañhā nāma hotīti dasseti. Ekekato paṭṭhāya yāva dasakā pavattā dasa pucchā etassāti dasapucchaṃ, ekekato paṭṭhāya yāva dasakā ekuttaravasena pavattaṃ vissajjanatthāya pañcapaṇṇasavissajjanaṃ sāmaṇerapañhanti sambandho. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ paramatthajotikāyaṃ khuddakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (khu. pā. aṭṭha. 4.kumārapañhavaṇṇanā) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Anādīnavadassitāya abhiṇhaṃ musā samudācaraṇato “piyamusāvādā”ti vuttaṃ, udakāvasesachaḍḍanaudakādhānanikujjanaukkujjanadassanasaññitā catasso udakādhānūpamāyo sabbassa yuddhakammassa akaraṇakaraṇavasena dassitā dve hatthiupamāyo.

Herein, 'not abandoned by all Buddhas' shows that in the dispensation of all Buddhas there are what are called the 'Youth's Questions.' There are ten questions for him, proceeding from one up to a set of ten, hence 'Ten Questions.' For the purpose of answering, there are fifty-five answers proceeding by increments of one from one up to a set of ten, hence 'Novice's Questions'—this is the connection. Whatever should be said here should be understood in the way stated in the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha (Khp-a 4, Commentary on the Youth's Questions). Because of not seeing the danger and frequently engaging in falsehood, it is called 'fond of false speech.' The four similes of the water-container—designated by showing the discarding of the remaining water, the overturning of the water-container, and the setting of it upright—and the two similes of the elephant are shown by way of doing and not doing all the actions of battle.

Tattha [V 2.0058] rāhulasuttanti suttanipāte āgataṃ rāhulasuttaṃ (su. ni. 337 ādayo). Abhiṇhovādavasena vuttanti iminā antarantarā taṃ suttaṃ kathetvā bhagavā theraṃ ovadatīti dasseti. Idañca panāti idaṃ yathāvuttaṃ bhagavato taṃtaṃkālānurūpaṃ attano ovādadānaṃ sandhāya. Bījanti aṇḍaṃ. Passasi nūti [M 2.0060] nu-saddo anujānane, nanu passasīti attho. Saccadhammaṃ laṅghitvā ṭhitassa kiñcipi akattabbaṃ nāma pāpaṃ natthīti āha – “sampajānamusāvāde saṃvararahitassa opammadassanatthaṃ vuttā”ti. Tathā hi –

Herein, the Rāhula Sutta means the Rāhula Sutta that comes in the Suttanipāta (Snp 337ff.). 'Spoken by way of frequent exhortation' shows that the Blessed One admonished the elder by teaching that sutta from time to time. And this refers to the Blessed One's giving of exhortation to him appropriate to the particular occasion, as has been said. Bīja (seed) means egg. Regarding Passasi nu: the particle nu is in the sense of seeking agreement; the meaning is, 'Surely you see?' He says that for one who stands having transgressed the true Dhamma, there is no evil that he would not do. This is stated to show a simile for one who is without restraint in regard to deliberate false speech. For thus it is said:

“Ekaṃ dhammamatītassa, musāvādissa jantuno;

Vitiṇṇaparalokassa, natthi pāpamakāriya”nti. (dha. pa. 176);

For one who has transgressed the one law, a person who speaks falsely, and who is unconcerned about the next world, there is no evil he would not do. (Dhp 176)

Uruḷhavāti uruḷho hutvā ussito. So pana damavasena abhiruyha vaḍḍhito ārohanayogyo ca hotīti āha “abhivaḍḍhito ārohasampanno”ti. Āgatāgateti attano yogyapadesaṃ āgatāgate. Paṭisenāya phalakakoṭṭhakamuṇḍapākārādayoti paṭisenāya attano ārakkhatthāya ṭhapite phalakakoṭṭhake ceva uddhacchadapākārādike ca. Etaṃ padesanti etaṃ parasenāpadesaṃ. Ettakenāti olokanamattena. Tassa olokanākāradassaneneva. Satampi sahassampi senānīkaṃ dvedhā bhijjati, tīrapātikaṃ madditaṃ hutvā padātā hutvā dvedhā hutvā palāyanti. Kaṇṇehi paharitvāti pageva sarānaṃ āgamanasaddaṃ upadhāretvā yathā vego na hoti, evaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā tehi paharitvā pātanaṃ. Paṭihatthipaṭiassātiādinā paccekaṃ pati-saddo yojetabboti. Dīghāsilaṭṭhiyāti dīghalatāya asilaṭṭhiyā.

Regarding Uruḷhavā: having grown large, it is raised up. However, having been tamed, trained, and grown, it becomes suitable for riding; hence it is said, 'well-grown and accomplished in riding.' Regarding Āgatāgate: coming again and again to a place suitable for itself. Regarding Paṭisenāya phalakakoṭṭhakamuṇḍapākārādayo: for the opposing army, wooden ramparts and roofless surrounding walls, etc., established for one's own protection. Etaṃ padesaṃ means: that region of the enemy army. Regarding Ettakena: merely by looking. Just by seeing the manner of its looking. An army of a hundred or a thousand is split in two; being crushed on the bank, trampled, becoming foot-soldiers, being split in two, they flee. Regarding striking with the ears: having first discerned the sound of approaching arrows, and having roused oneself so that there is no impetuosity, one strikes with them and fells them. Regarding Paṭihatthipaṭiassā etc.: the prefix paṭi- should be connected with each term individually. Regarding Dīghāsilaṭṭhiyā: with a long sword-staff.

Karaṇeti kammakaraṇe. Maññati hatthāroho. Ayamuggaranti tādise kāle gahitamuggaraṃ. Oloketvāti ñāṇacakkhunā disvā, abhiṇhaṃ sampajaññaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti attho.

Regarding Karaṇe: in the doing of the deed. The elephant-rider thinks. Regarding Ayamuggaraṃ: the mace taken up at such a time. Regarding Oloketvā: having seen with the eye of wisdom, that is, having established clear comprehension again and again—this is the meaning.

109. Sasakkanti passituṃ yuttaṃ katvā ussāhaṃ janetvā na karaṇīyaṃ, tādisaṃ niyamato akattabbaṃ hotīti āha “ekaṃseneva na kātabba”nti. Paṭisaṃhareyyāsīti karaṇato saṅkocaṃ āpajjeyyāsi. Yathābhūto asanto nivatto akaronto nāma hotīti āha “nivatteyyāsi mā kareyyāsī”ti. Anupadeyyāsīti anubalappadāyī bhaveyyāsi. Tenāha “upatthambheyyāsī”ti. Taṃ pana anubalappadānaṃ upatthambhanaṃ punappunaṃ karaṇamevāti āha “punappunaṃ kareyyāsī”ti[M 2.0061]. Sikkhamānoti taṃyeva adhisīlasikkhaṃ tannissayañca sikkhādvayaṃ sikkhanto sampādento.

109. Regarding Sasakkaṃ: having made an effort and generated enthusiasm, one sees that it is not proper to be done. Such a thing is definitely not to be done, hence he said, 'it should absolutely not be done.' Regarding Paṭisaṃhareyyāsi: you should shrink back from doing it. One who has turned back and is not doing it is, as it were, non-existent in that respect. Hence he said, 'you should turn back, you should not do it.' Regarding Anupadeyyāsi: you should become one who gives it additional strength. Therefore, he said, 'you should support it.' But that giving of additional strength, that supporting, is just doing it again and again. Hence he said, 'you should do it again and again.' Regarding Sikkhamāno: training in and accomplishing that very training in the higher virtue and the two trainings dependent on it.

111. Kittake [V 2.0059] pana ṭhāneti kittake ṭhāne pavattāni. Avidūre eva pavattānīti dassento “ekasmiṃ purebhatteyeva sodhetabbānī”ti āha. Evañhi tāni susodhitāni honti suparisuddhāni. Paresaṃ appiyaṃ garuṃ gārayhaṃ, yathāvuttaṭṭhānato pana aññaṃ vā kammaṭṭhānamanasikāreneva kāyakammādīni parisodhitāni hontīti na gahitaṃ. Paṭighaṃ vāti ettha vā-saddena asamapekkhaṇe mohassa saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

111. Regarding Kittake pana ṭhāne: in how many places do they occur? Showing that they occur not far away, he said, 'they should be purified during a single forenoon meal.' For thus they become well-purified, thoroughly pure. What is unpleasing, serious, and reprehensible to others. However, apart from the aforesaid basis, it is not taken up that bodily actions and so on are purified simply by non-attention to another meditation subject. Regarding Paṭighaṃ vā: here, by the word vā, the inclusion of delusion in the sense of non-circumspection should be understood.

112. Vuttanayena kāyakammādiparisodhanaṃ nāma idheva, na ito bahiddhāti āha “buddhā…pe… sāvakā vā”ti. Te hi atthato samaṇabrāhmaṇā vāti. Tasmāti yasmā sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhasāvakehi āruḷhamaggo, rāhula, mayā tuyhaṃ ācikkhito, tasmā. Tena anusikkhantena tayā evaṃ sikkhitabbanti ovādaṃ adāsi. Sesaṃ vuttanayattā suviññeyyameva.

112. The purification of bodily action and so on, in the way stated, is right here, not outside of this. This is what is meant by 'Buddhas... or disciples.' For they are in meaning recluses and brahmins. Regarding Tasmā: because this path, ascended by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples, has been explained by me to you, Rāhula, therefore... He gave the exhortation: 'Therefore, training in accordance with it, you should train thus.' The rest is easy to understand as it follows the method already stated.

Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā

The Elucidation of the Concealed Meaning in the Commentary on the Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda Sutta.

Samattā.

Completed.

2. Mahārāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Greater Discourse of Advice to Rāhula

113. Iriyāpathānubandhanenāti [V 2.0060] iriyāpathagamanānubandhanena, na paṭipattigamanānubandhanena. Aññameva hi buddhānaṃ paṭipattigamanaṃ aññaṃ sāvakānaṃ. Vilāsitagamanenāti – “dūre pādaṃ na uddharati, na accāsanne pādaṃ nikkhipati, nātisīghaṃ gacchati nātisaṇika”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.4.243; udā. aṭṭha. 76; sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.285) vuttena sabhāvasīlena buddhānaṃ cāturiyagamanena. Tadeva hi sandhāya “pade padaṃ nikkhipanto”ti vuttaṃ. Padānupadikoti rāhulattherassapi lakkhaṇapāripūriyā tādisameva gamananti yattakaṃ padesaṃ antaraṃ adatvā bhagavato piṭṭhito gantuṃ āraddho, sabbattha tameva gamanapadānupadaṃ gacchatīti padānupadiko.

113. “By following the posture” means by following the movement of the posture, not by following the course of practice. For the course of practice of the Buddhas is one thing, and that of the disciples is another. “With a graceful gait” means with the naturally graceful gait of the Buddhas, described thus: “He does not lift his foot too far, nor place it down too near; he does not walk too quickly nor too slowly,” etc. It is with reference to this that it was said, “placing one foot after the other.” “One who follows step by step” (padānupadiko): because of the perfection of his characteristics, the Elder Rāhula’s gait was also just like that. Having begun to walk behind the Blessed One without leaving a gap, he walks everywhere following that very gait step by step; thus he is a padānupadiko.

Vaṇṇanābhūmi [M 2.0062] cāyaṃ tattha bhagavantaṃ therañca anekarūpāhi upamāhi vaṇṇento “tattha bhagavā”tiādimāha. Nikkhantagajapotako viya virocitthāti padaṃ ānetvā yojanā. Evaṃ taṃ kesarasīho viyātiādīsupi ānetvā yojetabbaṃ. Tārakarājā nāma cando. Dvinnaṃ candamaṇḍalānantiādi parikappavacanaṃ, buddhāveṇikasantakaṃ viya buddhānaṃ ākappasobhā ahosi, aho sirīsampattīti yojanā.

This is the ground for description. Here, describing the Blessed One and the elder with various similes, he says, “There the Blessed One…,” and so on. The connection is made by supplying the phrase: “he shone like a young elephant that has come forth.” Similarly, in such phrases as “like a maned lion,” the verb should be supplied and connected. The moon is called the king of stars. The phrase “of two moon-disks,” and so on, is a hypothetical statement. The connection is: the beauty of the Buddhas’ appearance was like a possession unique to the Buddhas; “Oh, what glorious fortune!”

Ādiyamānāti gaṇhanti. “Pacchā jānissāmā”ti na ajjupekkhitabbo. Idaṃ na kattabbanti vutteti idaṃ pāṇaatipātanaṃ na kattabbanti vutte idaṃ daṇḍena vā leḍḍunā vā viheṭhanaṃ na kattabbaṃ, idaṃ pāṇinā daṇḍakadānañca antamaso kujjhitvā olokanamattampi na kattabbamevāti nayasatenapi nayasahassenapi paṭivijjhati, tathā idha tāva sammajjanaṃ kattabbanti vuttepi tattha paribhaṇḍakaraṇaṃ vihāraṅgaṇasammajjanaṃ kacavarachaḍḍanaṃ vālikāsamakiraṇanti evamādinā nayasatena nayasahassena paṭivijjhati. Tenāha – “idaṃ kattabbanti vuttepi eseva nayo”ti. Paribhāsanti tajjanaṃ. Labhāmīti paccāsīsati.

“They take it up” means they grasp it. One should not be indifferent, thinking, “We will know later.” When it is said, “This should not be done”—when it is said, “Destroying life should not be done”—one understands in a hundred ways, in a thousand ways, that this means that harming with a stick or a clod should not be done, striking with the hand or giving a beating should not be done, and even merely looking with anger should not be done at all. Similarly, when it is said here, “Sweeping should be done,” one understands in a hundred ways, in a thousand ways, that this includes putting things in order, sweeping the monastery grounds, throwing out rubbish, scattering sand, and so on. Therefore he said: “Even when it is said, ‘This should be done,’ this is the method.” “Rebuke” means threatening. “I will obtain” means one hopes for.

Sabbametanti sabbaṃ etaṃ mayi labbhamānaṃ sikkhākāmataṃ. Abhiññāyāti jānitvā. Sahāyoti raṭṭhapālattheraṃ sandhāyāha. So hi bhagavatā saddhāpabbajitabhāve etadagge ṭhapito. Dhammārakkhoti [V 2.0061] satthu saddhammaratanānupālako dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko. Pettiyoti cūḷapitā. Sabbaṃ me jinasāsananti sabbampi buddhasāsanaṃ mayhameva.

“All this” means all this desire for training that is obtainable by me. “Having directly known” means having known. “Companion”: he says this with reference to the Elder Raṭṭhapāla, for he was placed by the Blessed One at the head of those who have gone forth out of faith. “Guardian of the Dhamma” means the protector of the Teacher’s jewel of the good Dhamma, the treasurer of the Dhamma. “Paternal uncle” means a father’s younger brother. “All the Dispensation of the Conqueror is mine” means the entire Dispensation of the Buddha is mine alone.

Chandarāgaṃ ñatvāti chandarāgaṃ mama citte uppannaṃ ñatvā. Aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūleti vihārapariyante aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūlaṭṭhāne anucchavike.

“Having known sensual lust” means having known: “Sensual lust has arisen in my mind.” “At the foot of a certain tree” means at a suitable place at the foot of a certain tree on the outskirts of the monastery.

Tadāti aggasāvakehi pasādāpanakāle. Aññakammaṭṭhānāni caṅkamanairiyāpathepi piṭṭhipasāraṇakālepi samijjhanti, na evamidanti āha – “idamassa etissā nisajjāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ anucchavika”nti. Ānāpānassatinti ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ.

“Then” means at the time of inspiring confidence in the chief disciples. Other meditation subjects succeed even in the posture of walking or when stretching the back, but this one does not; thus he said: “This meditation subject is suitable for this sitting posture.” “Mindfulness of breathing” means the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing.

Samasīsī hotīti sace samasīsī hutvā na parinibbāyati. Paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti no ce paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti. Khippābhiññoti khippaṃ lahuṃyeva pattabbachaḷabhiñño.

“He becomes one with a level head”: if, having become such, he does not attain final Nibbāna, he realizes the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha; if he does not realize the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha… “One of quick direct knowledge” means one who is to attain the six direct knowledges quickly and swiftly.

Paripuṇṇāti [M 2.0063] soḷasasu ākāresu kassacipi atāpanena sabbaso puṇṇā. Subhāvitāti samathabhāvanāya vipassanābhāvanāya ca anupubbasampādanena subhāvitā. Gaṇanāvidhānānupubbiyā āsevitattā anupubbaṃ paricitā.

“Perfected” means completely perfected in the sixteen aspects by not neglecting any of them. “Well-developed” means well-developed through the gradual accomplishment of the development of serenity and the development of insight. “Familiarized in sequence” means it has been repeatedly practiced and become familiar in sequence according to the method of counting.

Omānaṃ vāti avajānanaṃ uññātanti evaṃvidhaṃ mānaṃ vā. Atimānaṃ vāti “kiṃ imehi, mameva ānubhāvena jīvissāmī”ti evaṃ atimānaṃ vā kuto janessatīti.

“Or disparagement”: this kind of conceit, that is, disdain or contempt. “Or excessive pride”: whence would he generate such excessive pride as thinking, “What are these to me? I will live by my own power”?

114. Visaṅkharitvāti visaṃyutte katvā, yathā saṅgākārena gahaṇaṃ na gacchati, evaṃ vinibhuñjitvāti attho. Mahābhūtāni tāva vitthāretu, sammasanūpagattā, asammasanūpagaṃ ākāsadhātuṃ atha kasmā vitthāresīti āha “upādārūpadassanattha”nti. Āpodhātu sukhumarūpaṃ. Itarāsu oḷārikasukhumatāpi labbhatīti āha “upādārūpadassanattha”nti. Heṭṭhā cattāri mahābhūtāneva kathitāni, na upādārūpanti tassa panettha lakkhaṇahāranayena ākāsadassanena dassitatā veditabbā. Tenāha “iminā mukhena taṃ dassetu”nti. Na kevalaṃ upādārūpaggahaṇadassanatthameva ākāsadhātu vitthāritā, atha kho pariggahasukhatāyapīti dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Tattha paricchinditabbassa rūpassa niravasesapariyādānatthaṃ “ajjhattikenā”ti visesanamāha. Ākāsenāti ākāsadhātuyā gahitāya. Paricchinnarūpanti tāya paricchinditakalāpagatampi pākaṭaṃ hoti vibhūtaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti.

114. “Having dismantled” means having disjoined them, having separated them so that they are not grasped as a composite; this is the meaning. Let him first expand on the great elements, since they are accessible to comprehension. But why did he then expand on the space element, which is not accessible to comprehension? He said: “For the purpose of showing derived form.” The water element is subtle form. In the others, both coarseness and subtlety are found. Thus he said: “For the purpose of showing derived form.” Previously, only the four great elements were discussed, not derived form; it should be understood that the latter is shown here by showing space through the method of adducing characteristics. Therefore he said: “To show it by this means.” He says, “And moreover,” etc., to show that the space element was expanded upon not only for the purpose of showing the grasp of derived form, but also for the sake of ease of comprehension. There, for the purpose of completely including without remainder the form to be delimited, he stated the qualification “internal.” “By space” means when the space element has been grasped. “Delimited form” means that what is comprised in the material groups delimited by it becomes manifest, appearing distinctly.

Idāni [V 2.0062] vuttamevatthaṃ sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ gāthāya dasseti. Tassāti upādāyarūpassa. Evaṃ āvibhāvatthanti evaṃ paricchinnatāya ākāsassa vasena vibhūtabhāvatthaṃ. Tanti ākāsadhātuṃ.

Now, for the sake of easy comprehension, he shows this same meaning in a verse. “Of that” means of derived form. “Thus for the purpose of manifestation” means for the purpose of its becoming manifest by means of space due to its being delimited. “It” means the space element.

118. Ākāsabhāvaṃ gatanti catūhi mahābhūtehi asamphuṭṭhānaṃ tesaṃ paricchedakabhāvena ākāsanti gahetabbataṃ gataṃ, ākāsameva vā ākāsagataṃ yathā “diṭṭhigataṃ (dha. sa. 381; mahāni. 12), atthaṅgata”nti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.130) ca. Ādinnanti imanti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi ādinnaṃ. Tenāha “gahitaṃ parāmaṭṭha”nti. Aññattha kammajaṃ “upādinna”nti vuccati, na tathā idhāti āha “sarīraṭṭhakanti attho”ti. Pathavīdhātuādīsu [M 2.0064] vuttanayenevāti mahāhatthipadopame (ma. ni. 1.300 ādayo) vuttanayadassanaṃ sandhāya vadati.

118. “Gone to the state of space” means it has gone to a state of being graspable as ‘space’ because it is the delimiter of those things untouched by the four great elements; or it is simply space that has ‘gone to space,’ as in “gone to a view” (Dhs §381; Mahānid 12) and “gone to setting” (i.e., disappeared) (AN-a 1:130). “Grasped” means this, which is grasped by craving and views. Therefore he said: “Seized, affected.” Elsewhere, what is kamma-born is called `upādinna` (clung-to form), but not so here; thus he says: “The meaning is the body-octet.” “In the same way as stated for the earth element, etc.”: he says this referring to the method shown in the Great Simile on the Elephant’s Footprint (MN 28).

119. Tādibhāvo nāma niṭṭhitakiccassa hoti, ayañca vipassanaṃ anuyuñjati, atha kimatthaṃ tādibhāvatā vuttāti? Pathavīsamatādilakkhaṇācikkhaṇāhi vipassanāya sukhappavattiatthaṃ. Tenāha “iṭṭhāniṭṭhesū”tiādi. Gahetvāti kusalappavattiyā okāsadānavasena pariggahetvā. Na patiṭṭhitoti na nissito na laggo.

119. The state of being ‘such’ belongs to one who has finished his task, but this one is practicing insight; for what reason, then, is the state of being ‘such’ mentioned? For the purpose of the smooth progress of insight through the indication of such characteristics as impartiality like the earth. Therefore he said: “In the desirable and undesirable,” etc. “Having taken” means having taken up by way of giving an opportunity for the arising of what is wholesome. “Not established” means not dependent, not clinging.

120. Brahmavihārabhāvanā asubhabhāvanā ānāpānassatibhāvanā ca upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā pāpento vipassanāya pādakabhāvāya aniccādisaññāya vipassanābhāvena ussakkitvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahattādhigamāya hotīti “mettādibhāvanāya pana hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Yattha katthaci sattesu saṅkhāresu ca paṭihaññanakilesoti āghātabhāvameva vadati ñāyabhāvato aññesampi. Asmimānoti rūpādike paccekaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahetvā “ayamahamasmī”ti evaṃ pavattamāno.

120. It was said, “But it is by the development of loving-kindness, etc.,” because the development of the divine abodes, the development of foulness, and the development of mindfulness of breathing—while one is attaining either access concentration or absorption—serve as a foundation for insight; and having striven with the development of insight by means of the perception of impermanence, etc., they lead to the attainment of arahantship by the sequence of the path. “The defilement of aversion towards any beings or formations whatsoever”: this refers to the state of hatred itself, and by implication, to others as well. “The conceit ‘I am’” is that which proceeds by grasping form, etc., individually or collectively, thus: “This I am.”

121. Idaṃ kammaṭṭhānanti ettha gaṇanādivasena āseviyamānā assāsapassāsā yogakammassa patiṭṭhānatāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha pana tathāpavatto manasikāro bhāvanā. Ettha ca tasseva therassa bhagavatā bahūnaṃ kammaṭṭhānānaṃ desitattā caritaṃ anādiyitvā kammaṭṭhānāni sabbesaṃ puggalānaṃ sappāyānīti ayamattho siddho, atisappāyavasena pana kammaṭṭhānesu vibhāgakathā kathitāti veditabbā.

121. “This is the meditation subject”: Here, the in-and-out breaths, being practiced by way of counting, etc., are the meditation subject because they are the basis for the yogi’s work. The attention that proceeds in such a way is the development. And here, since the Blessed One taught many meditation subjects to that same elder, the point is established that meditation subjects are suitable for all persons, without taking temperament into account. It should be understood, however, that the discussion of the division of meditation subjects is made on the basis of extreme suitability.

Mahārāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Greater Discourse of Advice to Rāhula is completed.

3. Cūḷamālukyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary to the Cūḷamālukya Sutta.

122. Evaṃ [V 2.0063] ṭhapitānīti “sassato loko”tiādinayappavattāni diṭṭhigatāni aniyyānikatāya na byākātabbāni na kathetabbāni, evaṃ ṭhapanīyapakkhe ṭhapitāni ceva niyyānikasāsane chaḍḍanīyatāya paṭikkhittāni ca, apicettha atthato paṭikkhepo eva byākātabbato. Yathā eko [M 2.0065] kammakilesavasena itthattaṃ āgato, tathā aparopi aparopīti satto tathāgato vuccatīti āha – “tathāgatoti satto”ti. Taṃ abyākaraṇaṃ mayhaṃ na ruccatīti yadi sassato loko, sassato lokoti, asassato loko, asassato lokoti jānāmāti byākātabbameva, yaṃ pana ubhayathā abyākaraṇaṃ, taṃ me cittaṃ na ārādheti ajānanahetukattā abyākaraṇassa. Tenāha – “ajānato kho pana apassato etadeva ujukaṃ, yadidaṃ na jānāmi na passāmī”ti. Sassatotiādīsu sassatoti sabbakāliko, nicco dhuvo avipariṇāmadhammoti attho. So hi diṭṭhigatikehi lokīyanti ettha puññapāpatabbipākā, sayaṃ vā tabbipākākarādibhāvena aviyuttehi lokīyatīti lokoti adhippeto. Etena cattāropi sassatavādā dassitā honti. Asassatoti na sassato, anicco addhuvo bhedanadhammoti attho, asassatoti ca sassatabhāvapaṭikkhepena ucchedo dīpitoti sattapi ucchedavādā dassitā honti. Antavāti parivaṭumo paricchinnaparimāṇo, asabbagatoti attho. Tena “sarīraparimāṇo, aṅguṭṭhaparimāṇo, yavaparimāṇo paramāṇuparimāṇo attā”ti (udā. aṭṭha. 54; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.76-77) evamādivādā dassitā honti.

122. Thus set aside: The speculative views that proceed in the manner of “the world is eternal,” etc., should not be declared or spoken of because they do not lead to liberation. Thus they are both set aside in the category of what is to be set aside and rejected in the liberating teaching because they are to be discarded. Moreover, here it is precisely the rejection in terms of meaning that is to be declared. Just as one being has come to this state through kamma and defilements, so too another and another—thus a being is called a Tathāgata. He said: “A Tathāgata is a being.” That non-declaration does not please me: If the world is eternal, it should be declared, “The world is eternal.” If the world is not eternal, it should be declared, “The world is not eternal.” But the non-declaration in both cases does not satisfy my mind, because the non-declaration is due to not knowing. Therefore he said: “For one who does not know or see, this alone is straightforward: ‘I do not know, I do not see.’” In such phrases as eternal, “eternal” means existing at all times, permanent, stable, and not subject to change; this is the meaning. For by those holding such views, it is regarded as the world wherein are merit, demerit, and their results; or it is regarded as the world by those who are not separate from the causes of their results. This is what is meant by world. By this, the four kinds of eternalism are shown. Not eternal means not eternal, impermanent, unstable, and subject to dissolution; this is the meaning. And by “not eternal,” through the rejection of an eternal state, annihilationism is indicated; thus the seven kinds of annihilationism are shown. Finite means circumscribed, of limited measure; not all-pervading is the meaning. By this, such views as “the self is the size of the body, the size of a thumb, the size of a barley grain, or the size of an atom” are shown.

Tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti tathāgato jīvo attā maraṇato imassa kāyassa bhedato paraṃ uddhaṃ hoti atthi saṃvijjatīti attho. Etena sassatabhāvamukhena soḷasa saññīvādā, aṭṭha asaññīvādā, aṭṭha ca nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā dassitā honti. Na hotīti natthi na upalabbhati. Etena ucchedavādo dassito hoti. Apica hoti ca na ca hotīti atthi natthi cāti. Etena ekaccasassatavādo dassito. Neva hoti na na hotīti pana iminā amarāvikkhepavādo dassitoti veditabbaṃ. Bhagavatā pana aniyyānikattā anatthasaṃhitāni imāni dassanānīti tāni na byākatāni, taṃ abyākaraṇaṃ sandhāyāha ayaṃ thero “taṃ me na ruccatī”ti. Sikkhaṃ paṭikkhipitvā yathāsamādinnasikkhaṃ pahāya.

The Tathāgata exists after death: this means the Tathāgata—the living being, the self—exists, is present, after death, beyond the breakup of this body; this is the meaning. By this, through the gateway of an eternal state, the sixteen views of those who hold the self to be percipient, the eight views of those who hold it to be non-percipient, and the eight views of those who hold it to be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient are shown. Does not exist: he is not, is not found. By this, annihilationism is shown. Both exists and does not exist: he is and is not. By this, semi-eternalism is shown. Neither exists nor does not exist: by this, it should be understood, the doctrine of the eel-wrigglers is shown. But by the Blessed One these views were not declared because they do not lead to liberation and are not connected with the goal. It was with reference to this non-declaration that this elder said: “This does not please me.” Having rejected the training: having abandoned the training as undertaken.

125. Tvaṃ [M 2.0066] neva [V 2.0064] yācakoti ahaṃ bhante bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ carissāmītiādinā. Na yācitakoti tvaṃ mālukyaputta mayi brahmacariyaṃ carātiādinā.

125. You were not the one who asked: by saying, ‘Venerable sir, I will live the holy life under the Blessed One,’ and so on. Nor were you asked: by my saying, ‘Come, Mālukyaputta, live the holy life under me,’ and so on.

126. Parasenāya ṭhitena purisena. Bahalalepanenāti bahalavilepanena. Mahāsupiyādi sabbo muduhidako veṇuviseso saṇho. Maruvāti makaci. Khīrapaṇṇinoti khīrapaṇṇiyā, yassā chindanamatte paṇṇe khīraṃ paggharati. Gacchanti gacchato jātaṃ sayaṃjātagumbato gahitanti adhippāyo. Sithilahanu nāma dattā kaṇṇo pataṅgo. Etāya diṭṭhiyā sati na hotīti “sassato loko”ti etāya diṭṭhiyā sati maggabrahmacariyavāso na hoti, taṃ pahāya eva pattabbato.

126. By a man standing in another’s army. With a thick smearing: with a thick anointment. Mahāsupiya, etc., all refers to a particular kind of soft, smooth bamboo called muduhidaka. Maruvā: a sandfly. Khīrapaṇṇin: of the khīrapaṇṇī plant, from the leaf of which milk flows out as soon as it is cut. Gacchanti: born as one goes, taken from a self-grown bush, is the meaning. Loose-jawed is the name for a scraper, an ear, a grasshopper. When this view exists, it is not: when this view, “the world is eternal,” exists, the living of the holy life for the path does not come to be, because that view must be abandoned for it to be attained.

127. Attheva jātītiādinā etā diṭṭhiyo paccekampi saṃsāraparibrūhanā kaṭasivaḍḍhanā nibbānavibandhanāti dasseti.

127. By the passage beginning, ‘When there is birth…’ he shows that these views, even individually, augment saṃsāra, increase the charnel ground, and are a fetter to Nibbāna.

128. Tasmātihāti idaṃ aṭṭhāne uddhaṭaṃ, ṭhāneyeva pana “vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabba”nti imassa parato katvā saṃvaṇṇetabbaṃ. Attano phalena araṇīyato anugantabbato kāraṇampi “attho”ti vuccatīti āha “kāraṇanissita”nti. Tenāha “brahmacariyassa ādimattampī”ti. Pubbapadaṭṭhānanti paṭhamārambho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

128. Therefore: This has been extracted out of place; it should be placed after the phrase ‘should be understood by way of the opposite of what was said’ and then explained. Because a cause is to be pursued (araṇīyato) and followed up for its own fruit, it is also called ‘purpose’ (attha). Thus he said ‘dependent on cause.’ Therefore he said: ‘even the mere beginning of the holy life.’ The initial basis: the first commencement. The rest is easy to understand.

Cūḷamālukyasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Obscure Meaning of the Commentary on the Cūḷamālukya Sutta is completed.

4. Mahāmālukyasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Mahāmālukya Sutta

129. Oraṃ [V 2.0065] vuccati kāmadhātu, tattha pavattiyā saṃvattanato oraṃ bhajantīti orambhāgiyāni, heṭṭhimamaggavajjhatāya orambhāge heṭṭhākoṭṭhāse bhajantīti orambhāgiyāni ka-kārassa ya-kāraṃ katvā. Tenāha “heṭṭhākoṭṭhāsikānī”tiādi. Kammunā hi vaṭṭena ca dukkhaṃ saṃyojentīti saṃyojanāni, orambhāgiyasaññitāni saṃyojanāni yassa appahīnāni, tasseva vaṭṭadukkhaṃ. Yassa pana tāni pahīnāni, tassa taṃ natthīti. Appahīnatāya anusetīti ariyamaggena asamucchinnatāya kāraṇalābhe [M 2.0067] sati uppajjati, appahīnabhāvena anuseti. Anusayamāno saṃyojanaṃ nāma hotīti anusayattaṃ pharitvā pavattamāno pāpadhammo yathāvuttenatthena saṃyojanaṃ nāma hoti. Etena yadi pana anusayato saṃyojanaṃ pavattaṃ, tathāpi ye te kāmarāgādayo “anusayā”ti vuccanti, teyeva bandhanaṭṭhena saṃyojanānīti dasseti.

129. The lower part (oraṃ) is called the sense-sphere. Because they conduce to existence there, they are called 'belonging to the lower part' (orambhāgiyāni). Or, because they are to be abandoned by the lower paths, they partake of the lower portion (orambhāge), the lower part (heṭṭhākoṭṭhāse); thus they are called 'belonging to the lower part' (orambhāgiyāni), with the 'ka' being changed to 'ya'. Hence, it is said, 'belonging to the lower part,' etc. By kamma and the round, they bind to suffering—thus, they are called 'fetters.' For one whose fetters designated as orambhāgiyāni are not abandoned, for him alone does the suffering of the round exist. But for one who has abandoned them, that does not exist. 'Lies latent due to not being abandoned' means that when the occasion arises, it arises because it has not been uprooted by the noble path; it lies latent due to not being abandoned. An unwholesome state, spreading and occurring by pervading the state of latency, is called a 'fetter' in the sense explained. By this, it is shown that even if a fetter arises from a latent tendency, nevertheless those very states of sensual desire, etc., which are called 'latent tendencies,' are themselves called 'fetters' in the sense of binding.

Evaṃ santepīti yadeva orambhāgiyasaṃyojanaṃ bhagavatā pucchitaṃ, tadeva therenapi vissajjitaṃ, tathāpi ayaṃ laddhi sannissayā. Tattha dosāropanāti dassetuṃ “tassa vāde”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samudācārakkhaṇeyevāti pavattikkhaṇe eva. Na hi sabbe vattamānā kilesā saṃyojanatthaṃ pharantīti adhippāyo. Tenāti tena kāraṇena, tathāladdhikattāti attho. Cintesi “dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti yojanā. Attano dhammatāyevāti ajjhattāsayeneva. Visaṃvāditāti satthu cittassa anārādhanena vivecitā. Evamakāsi evaṃ dhammaṃ desāpesi.

Even so, whatever lower fetters the Blessed One asked about, the elder answered about those same; yet this belief is based on dependence. Therein, to show the imputation of fault, “in his doctrine,” and so forth, is stated. At the very moment of manifestation—precisely at the moment of occurrence. For the intention is that not all defilements arising in the present reach the level of fetters. Therefore—for that reason, meaning because of holding such a view. He thought: “I will teach the Dhamma.” By his own nature—simply by his inner inclination. Being at variance—being separated due to not pleasing the Teacher's mind. Thus he acted—thus he had the Dhamma taught.

130. Sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhitenāti pariyuṭṭhānasamatthasakkāyadiṭṭhikena. Tathābhūtañca cittaṃ tāya diṭṭhiyā vigayhitaṃ ajjhotthaṭañca nāma hotīti āha “gahitena abhibhūtenā”ti. Diṭṭhinissaraṇaṃ nāma dassanamaggo tena samucchinditabbato, so pana nibbānaṃ āgamma taṃ samucchindati, tasmā vuttaṃ “diṭṭhinissaraṇaṃ nibbāna”nti. Avinoditā anīhaṭāti padadvayenapi samucchedavasena appahīnattaṃyeva vadati. Aññaṃ saṃyojanaṃ añño anusayoti vadanti, sahabhāvo nāma aññena hoti. Na hi tadeva tena sahāti vuccatīti tesaṃ adhippāyo. Aññenāti atthato aññena. Avatthāmattato yadipi avayavavinimutto samudāyo natthi, avayavo pana samudāyo na hotīti so samudāyato añño evāti sakkā vattunti yathāvuttassa parihārassa appāṭihīrakataṃ āsaṅkitvā pakkhantaraṃ āsallitaṃ “athāpi siyā”tiādinā. Pakkhantarehi parihārā [V 2.0066] hontīti yathāvuttañāyenapi añño puriso athāpi siyā, ayaṃ panettha añño dosoti āha “yadi tadevā”tiādi. Athāpi siyā tuyhaṃ yadi parivitakko īdiso yadi tadeva saṃyojanantiādi. Imamatthaṃ sandhāyāti paramatthato so eva [M 2.0068] kileso saṃyojanamanusayo ca, bandhanatthaappahīnatthānaṃ pana attheva bhedoti imamatthaṃ sandhāya.

130. “Obsessed with identity view” means by one with an identity view capable of obsession. Such a mind is seized and overwhelmed by that view, hence it is said, “seized and overpowered.” The escape from views is the path of seeing, by which it is to be eradicated; that path eradicates it upon reaching Nibbāna, therefore it is said, “the escape from views is Nibbāna.” “Not dispelled, not removed”—these two terms both indicate that it has not been abandoned by way of eradication. Some say a fetter is one thing, a latent tendency another. Coexistence occurs with another, for it is not said that the very same thing is ‘with’ itself—that is their intention. “Another” means different in sense. Even if, in terms of mere state, there is no aggregate apart from its components, a component is not the aggregate—thus, it can be said that it is different from them. Fearing that the aforesaid refutation is not unassailable, an alternative position is suggested with “or it might be so,” and so on. Refutations are made through alternative positions. As previously explained, another person might say, “or it might be so,” but here this is another fault—thus it is said, “if it is the very same,” and so on. “Or it might be so for you to have such a thought: if it is the very same fetter,” and so on. This is said with reference to the meaning: ultimately, that very defilement is both a fetter and a latent tendency, but in terms of the function of bondage and the state of non-abandonment, there is a difference in meaning—this is the intended meaning.

132. Tacacchedo viya samāpatti kilesānaṃ samāpattivikkhambhanassa sāracchedassa anusayassa dūrabhāvato. Pheggucchedo viya vipassanā tassa āsannabhāvato. Evarūpā puggalāti abhāvitasaddhādibalatāya dubbalanāmakāyā puggalā, yesaṃ sakkāyanirodhāya…pe… nādhimuccati. Evaṃ daṭṭhabbāti yathā so dubbalako puriso, evaṃ daṭṭhabbo so puriso gaṅgāpāraṃ viya sakkāyapāraṃ gantuṃ asamatthattā. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkhassa attho veditabbo.

132. Attainment is like cutting the bark, because the suppression of defilements by attainment is far from the latent tendency, which is the cutting of the heartwood. Insight is like cutting the sapwood, because of its nearness to eradication. Such individuals are those called ‘weak’ due to their undeveloped faith and other faculties, whose minds are not resolved for the cessation of identity. Thus it should be regarded: just as that weak man is unable to cross to the further shore of the Ganges, so should that person be regarded as unable to reach the further shore of identity. The meaning of the bright side should be understood in the opposite way.

133. Upadhivivekenāti iminā upadhivivekāti karaṇe nissakkananti dasseti, upadhivivekāti vā hetumhi nissakkavacanassa upadhivivekenāti hetumhi karaṇavacanena pañcakāmaguṇaviveko kathito. Kāmaguṇāpi hi upadhīyati ettha dukkhanti upadhīti vuccantīti. Thinamiddhapaccayā kāyavijambhitādibhedaṃ kāyālasiyaṃ. Tatthāti antosamāpattiyaṃ samāpattiabbhantare jātaṃ. Taṃ pana samāpattipariyāpannampi apariyāpannampīti tadubhayaṃ dassetuṃ “antosamāpattikkhaṇeyevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Rūpādayo dhammeti rūpavedanādike pañcakkhandhadhamme. Na niccatoti iminā niccapaṭikkhepato tesaṃ aniccatamāha. Tato eva udayavayantato vipariṇāmato tāvakālikato ca te aniccāti jotitaṃ hoti. Yañhi niccaṃ na hoti, taṃ udayabbayaparicchinnaṃ jarāya maraṇena cāti dvedhā vipariṇataṃ ittarakhaṇameva ca hoti. Na sukhatoti iminā sukhapaṭikkhepato tesaṃ dukkhatamāha, ato eva abhiṇhaṃ paṭipīḷanato dukkhavatthuto ca te dukkhāti jotitaṃ hoti. Udayabbayavantatāya hi te abhiṇhaṃ paṭipīḷanato nirantaradukkhatāya dukkhasseva ca adhiṭṭhānabhūtāti. Paccayayāpanīyatāya rogamūlatāya ca rogato. Dukkhatāsūlayogitāya kilesāsucipaggharaṇato uppādajarābhaṅgehi uddhumātapakkabhijjanato ca gaṇḍato. Pīḷājananato antotudanato dunnīharaṇato ca avaddhiāvahato aghavatthuto ca aserībhāvato ābādhapadaṭṭhānatāya ca ābādhato. Avasavattanato avidheyyatāya parato[M 2.0069]. Byādhijarāmaraṇehi palujjanīyatāya palokato. Sāmīnivāsīkārakavedakaadhiṭṭhāyakavirahato suññato. Attapaṭikkhepaṭṭhena anattato, rūpādidhammāpi na ettha attā hontīti anattā, evaṃ ayampi na attā hotīti anattā. Tena [V 2.0067] abyāpārato nirīhato tucchato anattāti dīpitaṃ hoti. Lakkhaṇattayameva avabodhatthaṃ ekādasahi padehi vibhajitvā gahitanti dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

133. By ‘seclusion from attachments’ (upadhivivekena), it is shown that this is renunciation in the instrumental sense. Or, by the word ‘upadhivivekā’ in the sense of cause, the seclusion from the five strands of sensual pleasure is stated by the instrumental word ‘upadhivivekena’ in the sense of cause. For the strands of sensual pleasure are also called attachments, as suffering is placed upon them. Bodily laziness, such as stretching the limbs, etc., is caused by sloth and torpor. “Therein” refers to what arises within the attainment, inside the absorption. To show both that which is included in the attainment and that which is not, it is said, “even at the moment of the attainment,” etc. “Phenomena such as form, etc.” refers to the five aggregates, such as form, feeling, etc. By “not permanent” – through this rejection of permanence, their impermanence is stated. From this it is illuminated that they are impermanent due to their arising and passing away, their changeability, and their momentary nature. For what is not permanent is limited by arising and passing away, is changed in two ways by aging and death, and exists only for a brief moment. By “not happiness” – through this rejection of happiness, their suffering is stated. From this it is illuminated that they are suffering due to their constant oppression and their nature as a basis of suffering. For due to their nature of arising and passing away, they are constantly oppressive, continuously of the nature of suffering, and are the foundation of suffering itself. Because they are maintained by conditions and are the root of disease, they are like a disease. Due to their connection with the stake of suffering and oozing the impurity of defilements, and because they are split open by birth, aging, and destruction, they are like a boil. Because they generate affliction, are an internal goad, are difficult to remove, bring about decline, are a basis for misery, are not one's own, and serve as a ground for illness, they are an affliction. Because they are not under one's own power and are not compliant, they are other. Due to being destroyed by sickness, aging, and death, they are perishable. Being devoid of an owner, resident, agent, experiencer, or controller, they are empty. In the sense of rejecting self, they are not-self. Even phenomena like form, etc., are not a self here—thus, they are not-self. Similarly, this too is not a self—thus, it is not-self. Therefore, it is shown that ‘not-self’ means without activity, without agency, and void. To show that the three characteristics themselves are taken up by dividing them into eleven terms for the sake of comprehension, “therein,” etc., is said.

Antosamāpattiyanti samāpattīnaṃ sahajātatāya samāpattīnaṃ abbhantare. Cittaṃ paṭisaṃharatīti tappaṭibaddhachandarāgādiupakkilesavikkhambhanena vipassanācittaṃ paṭisaṃharati. Tenāha “mocetī”ti. Savanavasenāti “sabbasaṅkhārasamatho”tiādinā savanavasena. Thutivasenāti tatheva thomanāvasena guṇato saṃkittanavasena. Pariyattivasenāti tassa dhammassa pariyāpuṇanavasena. Paññattivasenāti tadatthassa paññāpanavasena. Ārammaṇakaraṇavaseneva upasaṃharati maggacittaṃ. Etaṃ santantiādi pana avadhāraṇanivattitatthadassanaṃ. Yathā vipassanā “etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇīta”ntiādinā asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā cittaṃ upasaṃharati, evaṃ maggo nibbānaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena abhisamento tattha labbhamāne sabbe visese asammohato paṭivijānanto tattha cittaṃ upasaṃharati. Tenāha “iminā pana ākārenā”tiādi. So tattha ṭhitoti so adandhavipassano yogī tattha tāya aniccādilakkhaṇattayārammaṇāya vipassanāya ṭhito. Sabbasoti tassa maggassa adhigamāya nibbattitasamathavipassanāsu. Asakkonto anāgāmī hotīti heṭṭhimamaggavahāsu eva samathavipassanāsu chandarāgaṃ pahāya aggamaggavahāsu tāsu nikantiṃ pariyādātuṃ asakkonto anāgāmitāyameva saṇṭhāti.

“Within the attainment” means inside the attainments, because of being co-arisen with them. “Withdraws the mind” means one withdraws the insight mind by suppressing defilements such as desire and lust connected to it. Hence it is said, “it releases.” “By way of hearing” refers to hearing through phrases like “the stilling of all formations.” “By way of praise” means similarly through commendation, by summarizing the virtues. “By way of learning” refers to thoroughly learning that Dhamma. “By way of designation” means making known its meaning. The path-mind directs solely by way of making it an object. “This is peaceful,” etc., however, is the showing of a meaning that transcends determination. Just as insight directs the mind toward the unconditioned element with phrases like “this is peaceful, this is sublime,” so too the path, realizing Nibbāna by way of direct experience and penetration, directs the mind there, understanding without delusion all the special qualities obtainable there. Hence it is said, “in this way,” etc. “Established there” means that yogī with swift insight is established there in that insight which has as its object the three characteristics of impermanence, etc. “Of all” refers to the serenity and insight developed for the attainment of that path. “Unable, he becomes a non-returner” means that, having abandoned desire and lust in the serenity and insight that lead to the lower paths, he is unable to fully overcome craving for those that lead to the highest path, and thus is established only in the state of a non-returner.

Samatikkantattāti samathavasena vipassanāvasena cāti sabbathāpi rūpassa atikkantattā. Tenāha “ayañhī”tiādi. Anenāti yoginā. Taṃ atikkammāti idaṃ yo vā paṭhamaṃ pañcavokārabhavapariyāpanne dhamme sammadeva sammasitvā te vivajjetvā tato arūpasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā arūpadhamme sammasati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenāha “idāni arūpaṃ sammasatī”ti.

By ‘having transcended’ (samatikkantattā) is meant because of having transcended form in every way, by way of both serenity and insight. Therefore, it is said, “For this one,” etc. By this one—by the yogī. “Having transcended that”—this is said with reference to one who, having first rightly comprehended the phenomena included in the five-constituent existence, and having turned away from them, then enters a formless attainment and comprehends the formless phenomena. Therefore, it is said, “Now he comprehends the formless.”

Samathavasena [M 2.0070] gacchatoti samathappadhānaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ anuyuñjantassa. Cittekaggatā dhuraṃ hotīti tassa vipassanābhāvanāya tathā pubbe pavattattā vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā samādhippadhānā hoti, maggepi cittekaggatā dhuraṃ hoti, samādhindriyaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ balavaṃ hoti. So cetovimutto nāmāti so ariyo cetovimutto nāma hoti. Vipassanāvasena gacchatoti “samathavasena gacchato”ti ettha vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Ayañca puggalavibhāgo suttantanayena idhābhihito pariyāyo nāma, abhidhammanayena parato kīṭāgirisuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ dassayissāma. Ayaṃ sabhāvadhammoyevāti pubbabhāgapaṭipadā samathappadhānā ce samādhi dhuraṃ, vipassanāpadhānā ce paññā dhuranti ayaṃ dhammasabhāvoyeva, ettha kiñci na āsaṅkitabbaṃ.

"One who proceeds by way of serenity" means one who practices the preliminary path with serenity as predominant. "Unification of mind is the yoke" means that for him, because insight meditation has previously proceeded in that way, the insight leading to emergence has concentration as its predominant factor. Even on the path, unification of mind is the yoke, and the faculty of concentration is foremost and strong. "He is called one liberated by mind" means that noble one is called one liberated by mind. "One who proceeds by way of insight" should be understood according to the method stated here for "one who proceeds by way of serenity." This classification of individuals, stated here according to the Suttanta method, is called a method of exposition; we will explain it later in the commentary on the Kīṭāgiri Sutta according to the Abhidhamma method. "This is simply the nature of things" means that if the preliminary path has serenity as predominant, concentration is the yoke; and if insight is predominant, wisdom is the yoke. This is simply the nature of things—nothing should be doubted here.

Indriyaparopariyattaṃ [V 2.0068] indriyavemattatā. Tenāha “indriyanānattaṃ vadāmī”ti. Indriyanānattatā kāraṇanti idaṃ dasseti – aniccādivasena vipassanābhiniveso viya samathavasena vipassanāvasena ca yaṃ pubbabhāgagamanaṃ, taṃ appamāṇaṃ taṃ vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanaṃ, yassa samādhi dhuraṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ balavaṃ hoti, so ariyo cetovimutti nāma hoti. Yassa paññā dhuraṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ balavaṃ hoti so ariyo paññāvimutto nāma hoti. Idāni tamatthaṃ buddhivisiṭṭhena nidassanena dassento “dve aggasāvakā”tiādimāha, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

The varying maturity of faculties is the diversity of faculties. Therefore, he said, "I speak of the diversity of faculties." He shows that the diversity of faculties is the cause: just as there is the inclination towards insight by way of impermanence and so on, so too is the preliminary proceeding by way of serenity and by way of insight immeasurable. As for that insight leading to emergence: for one for whom concentration is the yoke, foremost, and strong, that noble one is called liberated by mind. For one for whom wisdom is the yoke, foremost, and strong, that noble one is called liberated by wisdom. Now, showing that meaning with an example distinguished by wisdom, he said, "the two chief disciples," and so on. That is indeed easy to understand.

Mahāmālukyasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Mahāmālukyasutta is complete.

5. Bhaddālisuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Bhaddāli Sutta

134. Asiyatīti [V 2.0069] asanaṃ, bhuñjanaṃ bhojanaṃ, asanassa bhojanaṃ asanabhojanaṃ, āhāraparibhogo, ekasmiṃ kāle asanabhojanaṃ ekāsanabhojanaṃ. So pana kālo sabbabuddhānaṃ sabbapaccekabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇavasena pubbaṇho eva idhādhippetoti āha “ekasmiṃ purebhatte asanabhojana”nti. Vippaṭisārakukkuccanti “ayuttaṃ vata mayā kataṃ, yo attano sarīrapakatiṃ ajānanto ekāsanabhojanaṃ bhuñji, yena me idaṃ sarīraṃ kisaṃ jātaṃ brahmacariyānuggaho nāhosī”ti evaṃ [M 2.0071] vippaṭisārakukkuccaṃ bhaveyya. Etaṃ sandhāya satthā āha, na bhaddālimeva tādisaṃ kiriyaṃ anujānanto. Itarathāti yadi ekaṃyeva bhattaṃ dvidhā katvā tato ekassa bhāgassa bhuñjanaṃ ekadesabhuñjanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Ko sakkotīti ko evaṃ yāpetuṃ sakkoti. Atītajātiparicayopi nāma imesaṃ sattānaṃyeva anubandhatīti āha “atīte”tiādi. Viravantassevāti anādare sāmivacanaṃ. Taṃ madditvāti “ayaṃ sikkhā sabbesampi buddhānaṃ sāsane āciṇṇaṃ, ayañca bhikkhu imaṃ sikkhatevā”ti vatvā taṃ bhaddāliṃ tassa vā anussāhapavedanaṃ abhibhavitvā. Bhikkhācāragamanatthaṃ na vitakkamāḷakaṃ agamāsi, vihāracārikaṃ caranto tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ bhagavā gacchati.

134. "Asana" means eating; "bhojana" means food or eating. "Asanabhojana" is the eating of food, the consumption of food. "Ekāsanabhojana" is the eating of food at one time. That time, through the constant practice of all Buddhas and all Paccekabuddhas, is here intended to be only the forenoon. Hence it is said, "eating food at one time in the forenoon." "Regret and remorse" would be: "Indeed, I have done what is improper—not knowing my own bodily constitution, I ate a single meal, whereby this body of mine has become emaciated and there was no support for the holy life." Thus, regret and remorse would arise. Referring to this, the Teacher spoke, not approving of such an action for Bhaddāli alone. "Otherwise" means if eating one part after having divided a single meal in two is intended as "partial eating." "Who is capable?" means who is able to maintain themselves in this way? The habit from past lives indeed follows these very beings; hence he said, "in the past," etc. "Of him who was protesting" is a genitive of disregard. "Having subdued him" means having said, "This training is practiced in the dispensation of all the Buddhas, and this monk is indeed training in it," thus overpowering Bhaddāli or his declaration of lack of enthusiasm. For the purpose of going on alms-round, he did not go to the Vitakkamāḷaka; while wandering on his monastery tour, the Blessed One went to his dwelling place.

135. Dūsayanti garahanti etenāti doso, aparādho, so eva kucchitabhāvena dosako. Garahāya pavattiṭṭhānato okāso. Tenāha – “etaṃ okāsaṃ etaṃ aparādha”nti. Dukkarataranti patikāravasena atisayena dukkaraṃ. Aparādho hi na khamāpentaṃ yathāpaccayaṃ vitthārito hutvā duppatikāro hoti. Tenāha “vassañhī”tiādi.

135. One defiles and censures by means of this, thus it is a 'dosa' (fault), an offense. That itself, through its contemptible nature, is a fault. An 'okāsa' (occasion) is a basis for the arising of censure. Hence he said: "this occasion, this offense." "More difficult to do" means exceedingly difficult by way of remedy. For an offense, when one does not ask for forgiveness, becomes difficult to redress, having been expanded according to conditions. Hence it is said: "for the rains," etc.

Alaggitvāti imampi nāma apanītaṃ akāsīti evaṃ avinetvā, taṃ taṃ tassa hitapaṭipattiṃ nivāraṇaṃ katvāti attho. Ñāyapaṭipattiṃ aticca eti pavattatīti accayo, aparādho, purisena madditvā pavattito aparādho atthato purisaṃ aticca abhibhavitvā pavatto nāma hoti. Tenāha “accayo maṃ, bhante, accagamā”ti. Avasesapaccayānaṃ samāgame eti phalaṃ etasmā uppajjati pavattati cāti samayo, hetu yathā “samudāyo”ti āha “ekaṃ kāraṇa”nti. Yaṃ panettha bhaddālittherassa aparipūrakāritāya bhikkhuādīnaṃ jānanaṃ, tampi kāraṇaṃ katvā “ahaṃ kho, bhante, na ussahāmī”tiādinā vattabbanti dasseti.

"Not having adhered" means not having trained in this way, and thus creating an obstruction to his own various beneficial practices, so that it is said of him, "He has abandoned even this." "Accayo" (transgression) is so called because it goes beyond or proceeds past right practice; it is an offense. An offense committed by a person is, in meaning, said to have occurred by transgressing against and overpowering that person. Therefore, he said, "A transgression, venerable sir, has overcome me." "Samayo" (occasion) is when, with the convergence of the remaining conditions, the result comes from it, arises, and proceeds; it is a cause, just as "samudāya" (origin) is. He said "a single reason." He shows that the fact that the monks and others knew of the Elder Bhaddāli's failure to fulfill the training should also be made a reason and stated with words such as, "I, venerable sir, am unable."

136. Ekacittakkhaṇikāti [V 2.0070] paṭhamamaggacittakkhaṇena ekacittakkhaṇikā. Evaṃ āṇāpetuṃ na yuttanti saṅkamatthāya āṇāpetuṃ na yuttaṃ payojanābhāvato. Anāciṇṇañcetaṃ buddhānaṃ, yadidaṃ padasā akkamanaṃ. Tathā hi –

136. "Lasting for a single mind-moment" means lasting for a single mind-moment by means of the mind-moment of the first path. "It is not proper to command thus" means it is not proper to command for the sake of crossing over, because there is no purpose. And this is not the practice of Buddhas, that is, stepping on someone step by step. For thus it is said:

“Akkamitvāna maṃ buddho, saha sissehi gacchatu;

Mā naṃ kalalaṃ akkamittha, hitāya me bhavissatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.53);

"Having stepped upon me, let the Buddha proceed with his disciples; Let him not tread upon the mire; it will be for my benefit." (Bv. 2.53)

Sumedhapaṇḍitena [M 2.0072] paccāsīsitaṃ na kataṃ. Yathāha –

The aspiration made by the wise Sumedha was not in vain.

“Dīpaṅkaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Ussīsake maṃ ṭhatvāna, idaṃ vacanamabravī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.60);

"Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the receiver of offerings, having stood at my head, spoke these words." (Bv. 2.60)

Bhagavatā āṇatte sati tesampi evaṃ kātuṃ na yuttanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Etesaṃ paṭibāhituṃ yuttanti idaṃ aṭṭhānaparikappanavaseneva vuttaṃ.
