Na hi buddhānaṃ kātuṃ āraddhaṃ nāma kiccaṃ kehici paṭibāhituṃ yuttaṃ nāma atthi paṭibāhituṃyeva akaraṇato. Sammattaniyāmassa anokkantattā vuttaṃ “bāhirako”ti.

Even when the Blessed One had commanded, it was not proper for them to act thus; here too, the same principle applies. The statement "it is proper to obstruct them" is spoken only by way of supposing an impossible case. For there is indeed no task undertaken by the Buddhas that it is proper for anyone to obstruct, precisely because they do not do what should be obstructed. It is called "external" because it has not entered the fixed course of rightness.

137. Na kammaṭṭhānaṃ allīyatīti cittaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ na otarati.

137. "It does not adhere to the meditation subject" means the mind does not enter into the meditation subject.

140. Punappunaṃ kārentīti daṇḍakammapaṇāmanādikāraṇaṃ punappunaṃ kārenti. Sammāvattamhi na vattatīti tassā tassā āpattiyā vuṭṭhānatthaṃ bhagavatā paññattasammāvattamhi na vattati. Anulomavatte na vattatīti yena yena vattena saṅgho anulomiko hoti, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ anulomavatte na vattati vilomameva gaṇhāti, paṭilomena hoti. Nitthāraṇakavattamhīti yena vattena saṅgho anulomiko hoti, sāpattikabhāvato nitthiṇṇo hoti, tamhi nitthāraṇavattasmiṃ na vattati. Tenāha “āpattī”tiādi. Dubbacakaraṇeti dubbacassa bhikkhuno karaṇe.

140. "They repeatedly make them do" means they repeatedly make them perform acts such as staff-punishment and bowing down. "He does not conduct himself in right conduct" means he does not conduct himself in the right conduct prescribed by the Blessed One for the purpose of rising from this or that offense. "He does not conduct himself in conformable conduct" means he does not conduct himself in whatever conduct by which the Sangha is conformable; he adopts only what is contrary, he is contrary. "In the conduct for rehabilitation" means he does not conduct himself in that conduct for rehabilitation by which the Sangha becomes conformable and he is crossed over from the state of being one who has an offense. Hence it is said, "offenses," etc. "In the making of one difficult to admonish" means in the case of a monk who is difficult to admonish.

144. Yāpetīti vattati, sāsane tiṭṭhatīti attho. Abhiññāpattāti “asuko asuko ca thero sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo bahussuto”tiādinā abhiññātabhāvaṃ pattā adhigataabhiññātā.

144. "He maintains himself" means he continues; the meaning is he remains in the Dispensation. "Having attained recognition" means having attained the state of being recognized by such means as "such and such an elder is virtuous, of noble qualities, very learned," etc.; they have acquired recognition.

145. Sattesu hāyamānesūti kilesabahulatāya paṭipajjanakasattesu parihāyantesu paṭipathesu [V 2.0071] jāyamānesu. Antaradhāyati nāma tadādhāratāya. Diṭṭhadhammikā parūpavādādayo. Samparāyikā apāyadukkhavisesā. Āsavanti tena tena paccayena pavattantīti āsavā. Nesanti parūpavādādiāsavānaṃ. Teti vītikkamadhammā.

145. “When beings are declining” means when beings capable of practice are deteriorating due to the abundance of defilements, and wrong paths are arising. “Disappears” means it does so because of its foundation. “Present-life” refers to blame from others and so on. “Future-life” refers to the particular sufferings of the lower realms. They are called “cankers” because they flow forth due to this and that condition. “Of these” refers to the cankers such as blame from others. “Those” are states of transgression.

Akālaṃ dassetvāti sikkhāpadapaññattiyā akālaṃ dassetvā. Uppattinti āsavaṭṭhāniyānaṃ dhammānamuppattiṃ. Sikkhāpadapaññattiyā kālaṃ, tāva [M 2.0073] senāsanāni pahonti, tena āvāsamacchariyādihetunā sāsane ekacce āsavaṭṭhāniyā dhammā na uppajjanti. Iminā nayenāti iminā pana hetunā padasodhammasikkhāpadānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

“Having shown the untimely” means having shown that it was not the right time for the laying down of the training rule. “The arising” means the arising of states that are grounds for cankers. The time for the laying down of the training rule is when dwellings are abundant; thus, due to reasons such as avarice regarding dwellings, certain states that are grounds for cankers do not arise in the Dispensation. “By this method” means by this reason, the inclusion of the training rules of the Dhamma, word by word, should be understood.

Yasanti kittisaddaṃ parivārañca. Sāgatattherassa nāgadamanakittiyasādivasena surāpānasaṅkhāto āsavaṭṭhāniyo dhammo uppajji.

“Fame” means the sound of renown and also a retinue. In the case of the elder Sāgata, due to his fame for taming the Nāga and so on, a state that is a basis for cankers, known as drinking liquor, arose.

Rasena rasaṃ saṃsandetvāti upādinnakaphassarasena anupādinnakaphassarasaṃ saṃsandetvā.

“Mixing taste with taste” means mixing the taste of clung-to contact with the taste of unclung-to contact.

146. Na kho, bhaddāli, eseva hetu, atha kho aññampi atthīti dassento bhagavā “apicā”tiādimāha. Tena dhammassa sakkaccasavane theraṃ niyojeti.

146. “Not only, Bhaddāli, is this the reason, but there is also another.” Thus showing this, the Blessed One said, “Moreover,” and so on. By that, he directs the elder to listen carefully to the Dhamma.

147. Visevanācāranti adantakiriyaṃ. Parinibbāyatīti vūpasammati. Tattha adantakiriyaṃ pahāya danto hoti. Yugassāti rathadhurassa.

147. “Behaving like a wild one” means unrestrained behavior. “Is fully extinguished” means is calmed. There, having abandoned unrestrained behavior, one becomes restrained. “Of the yoke” means of the chariot yoke.

Anukkameti anurūpaparigame. Tadavatthānurūpaṃ pādānaṃ ukkhipane nikkhipane ca. Tenāha “cattāro pāde”tiādi. Rajjubandhanavidhānenāti pādato bhūmiyā mocanavidhānena. Evaṃ karaṇatthanti yathā asse nisinnasseva bhūmiṃ gahetuṃ sakkā, evaṃ cattāro pāde tathā katvā attano niccalabhāvakaraṇatthaṃ. Maṇḍaleti maṇḍaladhāvikāyaṃ. Pathavīkamaneti pathaviṃ phuṭṭhamattena gamane. Tenāha “aggaggakhurehī”ti. Okkantakaraṇasminti okkantetvā parasenāsammaddana okkantakaraṇe. Ekasmiṃ ṭhāneti catūsu pādesu yattha katthaci ekasmiṃ ṭhāne gamanaṃ codentīti attho, so panettha sīghataro adhippeto. Davatteti mariyādākopanehi nānappayojane, parasenāya pavattamahānādapaharaṇehi attho. Tenāha “yuddhakālasmi”ntiādi.

“Gradually trains” means in suitable training. According to that stance, in the lifting and placing of the feet. Hence it is said, “four feet,” and so on. “By the method of tying with reins” means by the method of releasing the feet from the ground. “For the purpose of doing so” means just as one seated on a horse can grasp the ground, so too, for the purpose of making oneself steady by having made the four feet thus. “In a circle” means in running in a circle. “Touching the ground” means in moving by just touching the ground. Hence it is said, “with the very tips of the hooves.” “For the purpose of trampling” means for the purpose of trampling, having trampled and crushed the enemy’s army. “In one place” means urging movement to any one place among the four feet; this is the meaning. Here, however, the faster is intended. “Gallops” means for various purposes, such as breaking boundaries, and for overpowering the great noise made by the enemy’s army. Hence it is said, “at the time of battle,” and so on.

Raññā jānitabbaguṇeti yathā rājā assassa guṇe jānāti, evaṃ tena jānitabbaguṇakāraṇaṃ [V 2.0072] kāreti. Assarājavaṃseti dussahaṃ dukkhaṃ patvāpi yathā ayaṃ rājavaṃsānurūpakiriyaṃ na jahissati, evaṃ sikkhāpane. Sikkhāpanameva hi sandhāya sabbattha “kāraṇaṃ kāretī”ti vuttaṃ tassa karaṇakārāpanapariyāyattā.

“Qualities to be known by the king” means: just as the king knows the qualities of a horse, so he has it perform the action that makes its qualities known to him. “Of royal horse lineage” means: in training it so that, even having met with unbearable suffering, it will not abandon conduct befitting the royal lineage. For it is precisely with reference to training that it is everywhere said, “he has the action performed,” because this is a synonym for doing and causing to be done.

Yathā [M 2.0074] uttamajavo hotīti javadassanaṭṭhāne yathā hayo uttamajavaṃ na hāpesi, evaṃ sikkhāpeti. Uttamahayabhāve, yathā uttamahayo hotīti kammakaraṇakāle attano uttamasabhāvaṃ aniguhitvā avajjetvā yathā atthasiddhi hoti, evaṃ paramajavena sikkhāpeti. Yathā kiriyā vinā dabbampi vinā kiriyaṃ na bhavati, evaṃ daṭṭhabbanti dassetuṃ “tattha pakatiyā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“So that it becomes of utmost speed” means: he trains it so that at the place for displaying speed the horse does not lose its supreme speed. In the state of being a superior horse, so that it becomes a superior horse: he trains it with supreme speed so that at the time of performing a task, without concealing or abandoning its own supreme nature, there is accomplishment of the goal. To show that just as there is no action without a substance, nor a substance without action, so it should be understood, it is said, “there, by nature,” and so on.

Tatrāti tasmiṃ pakatiyā uttamahayasseva uttamahayakāraṇārahattā uttamajavapaṭipajjane. Māsakhādakaghoṭakānanti māsaṃ khāditvā yathā tathā viguṇakhaluṅgakānaṃ. Valañjakadaṇḍanti raññā gahetabbasuvaṇṇadaṇḍaṃ. Dhātupatthaddhoti attanāva samuppāditadhātuyā upatthambhito hutvā.

“There” means: in that undertaking of supreme speed, because by nature only a superior horse is fit for the training of a superior horse. “Of horses that eat beans” means of inferior hacks that eat beans just as they come. “The staff for use” means the golden staff to be taken by the king. “Stiffened by the element” means having been supported by the element produced by oneself.

Uttame sākhalyeti paramasakhilabhāve sakhilavācāya eva dametabbatāya. Tenāha “muduvācāya hī”tiādi.

“In supreme friendliness” means: in the state of utmost friendliness, because it is to be tamed by friendly speech alone. Hence it is said, “for by soft speech,” and so on.

Arahattaphalasammādiṭṭhiyāti phalasamāpattikāle pavattasammāñāṇaṃ. Sammāñāṇaṃ pubbe vuttasammādiṭṭhiyevāti pana idaṃ phalasammādiṭṭhibhāvasāmaññena vuttaṃ. Keci pana “paccavekkhaṇañāṇa”nti vadanti, taṃ na yujjati “asekkhenā”ti visesitattā. Tampi asekkhañāṇanti ce? Evampi nippariyāya sekkhaggahaṇe pariyāyasekkhaggahaṇaṃ na yuttameva, kiccabhedena vā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ekā eva hi sā paññā nibbānassa paccakkhakiriyāya sammādassanakiccaṃ upādāya “sammādiṭṭhī”ti vuttā, sammājānanakiccaṃ upādāya “sammāñāṇa”nti. Aññātāvindriyavasena vā sammādiṭṭhi, paññindriyavasena sammāñāṇanti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Maggaphalāvahāya desanāya saṅkhepatova āgatattā vuttaṃ “ugghaṭitaññupuggalassa vasenā”ti.

“With the right view of the fruit of arahantship” means the right knowledge that occurs at the time of the attainment of the fruit. But that right knowledge is the same as the right view mentioned before—this is said because of the commonality of being the right view of the fruit. Some, however, say it is “reviewing knowledge,” but that is not correct because it is specified as “by one beyond training.” If it is said that this too is the knowledge of one beyond training, even so, when “one in training” is taken in its direct sense, it is not proper to take it in a figurative sense. Or it should be understood that this is stated because of a difference in function. For that wisdom is one and the same: with respect to the function of right seeing by the direct realization of Nibbāna, it is called “right view”; with respect to the function of right knowing, it is called “right knowledge.” Or the meaning here should be understood thus: right view is in the sense of the faculty of final knowledge, and right knowledge is in the sense of the faculty of wisdom. Because the discourse that brings the path and fruit has come only briefly, it is said, “by way of a person of quick understanding.”

Bhaddālisuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

Here ends the Elucidation of the Concealed Meaning in the Commentary on the Bhaddāli Sutta.

6. Laṭukikopamasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Laṭukikopama Sutta

148. Mahāudāyittheroti [V 2.0073] kāḷudāyilāḷudāyittherehi añño mahādehatāya mahāudāyīti sāsane paññāto thero. Apahari apaharati apaharissatīti apahattā. Tekāliko hi ayaṃ [M 2.0075] saddo. Upahattāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Apahārakoti apanetā. Upahārakoti upanetā.

148. The elder Mahāudāyi: an elder known in the Dispensation as Mahāudāyi because of his large body, different from the elders Kāḷudāyi and Lāḷudāyi. “He took away, he takes away, he will take away”: thus `apahattā`. For this word refers to the three times. The same method applies also to `upahattā`. `Apahāraka` means one who removes. `Upahāraka` means one who brings near.

149. Yanti bhummatthe paccattavacanaṃ, tena ca anantaraniddiṭṭhasamayo paccāmaṭṭhoti āha “yasmiṃ samaye”ti. Na bhagavantaṃ paṭiccāti na bhagavantaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā.

149. The word `yaṃ` is a singular expression in the locative sense. And by it the time just indicated is referred to; thus it says, “at which time.” “Not on account of the Blessed One” means not making the Blessed One the object.

Kammanipphannatthanti attanā āyāciyamānakammasiddhiatthaṃ. Bhavatīti bhū, na bhūti abhū, bhayavasena pana sā itthī “abhu”nti āha. Ātu mātūti ettha yathā –

“For the purpose accomplished by action” means for the purpose of accomplishing the deed being requested by oneself. `Bhū` means ‘being’; `abhū` means ‘not being.’ But out of fear that woman said `abhu`. Here, regarding `ātu mātū`, it is as follows:

“Aṅgā aṅgā sambhavasi, hadayā adhijāyase;

Attā eva putta nāmāsi, sa jīva saradosata”nti. –

“From my every limb you are born, from my heart you are produced; you are indeed myself, my son by name. May you live for a hundred autumns!”

Ādīsu putto “attā”ti vuccati kulavasena santāne pavattanato. Evaṃ pitāpi “puttassa attā”ti vuccati. Yasmā “bhikkhussa attā mātā”ti vatthukāmā bhayavasena “ātu mātū”ti āha. Tenāha “ātūti pitā”tiādi.

In such texts, a son is called ‘self’ because he continues the lineage in the family line. Similarly, a father is also called ‘the self of the son.’ Since the one desiring the object of sensual pleasure, out of fear of saying, “The mother is the self of the bhikkhu,” said `ātu mātū`, hence it is said, “`ātu` means father,” and so on.

150. Evamevanti idaṃ garahatthajotananipātapadanti vuttaṃ “garahanto āhā”ti. Tathā hi naṃ vācakasaddeneva dassento “idhekacce moghapurisā”ti āha. Āhaṃsūti tesaṃ tathā vacanassa avicchedena pavattidīpananti āha “vadantī”ti. Kiṃ panimassa appamattakassāti pahātabbavatthuṃ avamaññamānehi vuttaṃ. Tenāha “kiṃ panā”ti. Hetumhi jotetabbe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ yathā “anussavassa hetu, ajjhenassa hetū”ti. Tenāha “appamattakassa hetū”ti. Nanu apassantena viya asuṇantena viya bhavitabbanti? Satthārā nāma appamattakesu dosesu apassantena viya ca asuṇantena viya ca bhavitabbanti tesaṃ adhippāyena vivaraṇaṃ. Tesu cāti sikkhākāmesu ca. Appaccayaṃ upaṭṭhāpentīti ānetvā sambandhitabbanti dasseti. Tesanti ye “moghapurisā”ti vuttā puggalā, tesaṃ. Gale baddhaṃ mahākaṭṭhanti gale olambetvā baddhaṃ rukkhadaṇḍamāha. [V 2.0074] Pūtilatāyāti galociyā. Pārājikavatthu viya duppajahaṃ hotīti chandakappahānavasena taṃ pajahituṃ na sakkoti.

150. “Similarly”: this is a particle that illuminates the meaning of censure; thus it is said, “he spoke while censuring.” For, indicating this with the very word that expresses it, he said, “Here, some foolish men.” “They said” (`āhaṃsu`): this shows the uninterrupted occurrence of their speaking thus; hence he says, “they say” (`vadanti`). “But what of this trifling matter?”: this was said by those who look down upon the thing to be abandoned. Hence he says, “But what?” And when a cause is to be illuminated, this is a genitive expression, as in “the cause of tradition, the cause of study.” Hence he says, “the cause of a trifling matter.” “Should one not act as if not seeing, as if not hearing?” This is an explanation according to their intention, that “The Teacher should indeed act as if not seeing and as if not hearing in the case of minor faults.” “And in them” means and in those who desire training. “They establish distrust”: this shows that they bring it up and connect it. “Of them” means of those persons who are called “foolish men.” “A great log tied at the neck” means a wooden log hung and tied at the neck. “With a rotting creeper” means with a `galocī` creeper. “It becomes as hard to abandon as a matter entailing defeat” means one is not able to abandon it by way of abandoning desire.

151. Anussukkāti [M 2.0076] tassa pahātabbassa pahāne ussukkarahitā. Apaccāsīsanapakkheti tāya paradattavuttitāya kassaci paccayassa kutoci apaccāsīsakapakkhe ṭhitā hutvā suppajahaṃ hoti, na tassa pahāne bhāriyaṃ atthi.

151. “Not eager” (`anussukka`) means without eagerness in abandoning what should be abandoned. “In the faction of not hoping” (`apaccāsīsanapakkhe`) means: because of that livelihood dependent on what is given by others, being in the faction that does not hope for any requisite from anywhere, it is easy to abandon; there is no burden in abandoning it.

152. Daliddo duggato. Assakoti asāpateyyo. Gehayaṭṭhiyoti gehachadanassa ādhārā, tā ujukaṃ tiriyaṃ ṭhapetabbadaṇḍā. Samantato bhittipādesu ṭhapetabbadaṇḍā maṇḍalā. Kākātidāyinti ito cito kākehi atipātavasena uḍḍetabbaṃ. Tenāha “yattha kiñcidevā”tiādi. Sūrakākāti kākānaṃ uḍḍepanākāramāha. Naparamarūpanti hīnarūpaṃ. Vilīvamañcakoti tālavettakādīhi vītamañcako. Sā panassa santānānaṃ chinnabhinnatāya oluggaviluggatā, tathā sati sā visamarūpā hotīti āha “oṇatā”tiādi. So puggalo lūkhabhojī hotīti āha “dhaññaṃ nāma kudrūsako”ti. Samakālaṃ vapitabbatāya samavāpakaṃ, yathāutu vapitabbabījaṃ. Jāyikāti kucchitā bhariyā, sabbattha garahāyaṃ ka-saddo. So vatāhaṃ pabbajeyyanti sohaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā pabbajeyyaṃ, yohaṃ puriso nāma assaṃ vatāti pabbajjāvasena attano purisaṃ bodheyya. Taṃsabhāve ṭhitassa bodhā na tu dukkarā, sā khaṭopikā. Sā kumbhī. Meṇḍakaseṭṭhino aḍḍhateḷasāni koṭṭhāgārasatāni viya.

152. Poor, wretched. `Assaka` means without property. `Gehayaṭṭhi` (house-posts) are the supports for the house roof; they are posts to be set up straight and crosswise. The circular beams are posts to be placed all around at the base of the walls. `Kākātidāyin` means to be driven away from here and there by crows attacking. Hence it is said, “wherever anything,” and so on. `Sūrakāka` describes the manner of being driven away by crows. “Not of the highest form” means an inferior form. `Vilīvamañcaka` means a bed woven with palm leaves, cane, and the like. But because its frame is broken and shattered, it is rickety and dilapidated. That being so, it is uneven in form; hence it is said, “sagging,” and so on. That person is one who eats coarse food; hence it is said, “the grain is `kudrūsaka`.” `Samavāpakaṃ`: because it should be sown at the same time, it is seed to be sown according to the season. `Jāyikā` means a contemptible wife; the suffix `-ka` everywhere has the sense of censure. “Would that I might go forth!” means “Having shaved off my hair and beard, I would go forth.” “I, who am indeed a man!” means that by way of going forth he would awaken his own manliness. For one established in that state, awakening is not difficult. That is the gruel-scum. That is the pot. Like the twelve and a half hundred storehouses of the treasurer Meṇḍaka.

153. Suvaṇṇanikkhasatānanti anekesaṃ suvaṇṇanikkhasatānaṃ. Cayoti santānehi nicayo avīci niccappabandhanicayo. Tenāha “santānato katasannicayo”ti.

153. “Of hundreds of gold `nikkhas`” means of many hundreds of gold `nikkhas`. “Heap” (`cayo`) means an accumulation by continuities, an uninterrupted, continuous, connected accumulation. Hence it is said, “an accumulation made from continuity.”

154. Heṭṭhā kiñcāpi appajahanakā paṭhamaṃ dassitā, pajahanakā padhānā, tesañca vasenettha puggalacatukkaṃ dassitaṃ. Te tañceva pajahantīti pajahanakā paṭhamaṃ gahitā. Rāsivasenāti “idhudāyi ekacco puggalo”tiādinā catukke āgatavibhāgaṃ anāmasitvā “te te”ti pacuravasena vuttaṃ. Tenāha “na pāṭiyekkaṃ vibhattā”ti. Avibhāgena gahitavatthūsu vibhāgato gahaṇaṃ lokasiddhametanti dassetuṃ “yathā nāmā”tiādi [M 2.0077] vuttaṃ. Pajahanakapuggalāti “te tañceva pajahantī”ti evaṃ pajahanakapuggalā eva.

154. Although the non-abandoners were shown first, the abandoners are the principal ones, and a fourfold classification of persons is shown here with reference to them. The abandoners are taken first because of the phrase, 'they abandon just that.' By 'in terms of aggregates,' it is said in an abundant manner, 'those, those,' without referring to the classification given in the fourfold section beginning, 'Here, Udāyin, a certain person...' Therefore it is said, 'not individually distinguished.' To show that taking things by distinction where they are taken without distinction is a worldly convention, it is said, 'just as...' and so on. By 'persons who abandon,' it means just those persons who abandon, in the sense of 'they abandon just that.'

Upadhianudhāvanakāti upadhīsu anuanudhāvanakā upadhiyo ārabbha pavattanakā. Vitakkāyevāti [V 2.0075] kāmasaṅkappādivitakkāyeva. Indriyanānattatāti vimuttiparipācakānaṃ indriyānaṃ paropariyattaṃ. Tassa hi vaseneva te cattāro puggalā jātā. Aggamaggatthāya vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā yāva na taṃ maggena samugghātenti, tāva nappajahanti nāma. Iti heṭṭhimā tayopi ariyā appahīnassa kilesassa vasena “nappajahantī”ti vuttā, pageva puthujjanā. Vuttanayena pana vipassanaṃ maggena ghaṭentā te cattāro janā aggamaggakkhaṇe pajahanti nāma. Te eva tattha sīghakārino khippaṃ pajahanti nāma, tenāha “tatthā”tiādi.

By 'pursuit of substrates of clinging' (`upadhianudhāvanakā`) is meant the continuous pursuit of the substrates of clinging, arising with the substrates of clinging as their basis. By 'merely thoughts' (`vitakkāyeva`) is meant just thoughts such as those of sensual desire and so on. By 'diversity of faculties' (`indriyanānattatā`) is meant the varying degrees of maturity of the faculties that lead to liberation. Indeed, it is by its power that these four types of individuals are born. Until they generate zeal for insight aimed at the supreme path, and eradicate defilements with that path, they are said 'not to abandon.' Thus, even the lower three noble ones are said 'not to abandon' due to the presence of unabandoned defilements, let alone ordinary people. But according to the method stated, those four individuals, striving with insight in the path, abandon defilements at the moment of the supreme path. They, being swift in that matter, abandon quickly; hence it is said, 'there,' etc.

Saṃvegaṃ katvā aggiṃ akkantapuriso viya. Maggenāti anukkamāgatena aggamaggena. Mahāhatthipadopameti mahāhatthipadopamasutte (ma. ni. 1.300 ādayo). Tattha hi “tassa dhātārammaṇameva cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati adhimuccatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.302) ettha atitikkhanātitikkha-nātimandaatimanda-puggalavasena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.302) tayo vārā uddhaṭā, tattha majjhimavaseneva pañho kathito. Indriyabhāvaneti indriyabhāvanāsutte, tatthāpi majjhimanayeneva pañho kathito. Tenāha “imesū”tiādi.

Having aroused a sense of urgency, like a man who has stepped into fire. By 'the path' (`maggena`) is meant the successively attained supreme path. By 'like the great elephant’s footprint' (`mahāhatthipadopama`) is meant the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 1.300, etc.). There, it is said, 'His mind plunges, becomes serene, settles, and is resolved upon that very element as its object' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.302). Here, in the commentary (Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 2.302), three instances are extracted based on individuals of very sharp, sharp, dull, and very dull faculties, but the question is discussed according to the middle way. By 'development of the faculties' (`indriyabhāvanā`) is meant the Indriyabhāvanā Sutta, where also the question is discussed according to the middle way. Hence he said, 'among these,' etc.

Tanti “upadhī”ti vuttaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ. Dukkhassa mūlanti sabbassapi vaṭṭadukkhassa kāraṇaṃ. Niggahaṇoti nirupādāno. Tenāha “nittaṇho”ti.

‘That’ refers to the five aggregates, which are called `upadhi` (substrates of clinging). By 'root of suffering' (`dukkhassa mūlaṃ`) is meant the cause of all suffering in the cycle of existence. By `niggahaṇa` is meant `nirupādāna` (without fuel/clinging). Hence it is said, 'without craving.'

155. Ye pajahantīti “te tañceva pajahantī”ti evaṃ vuttapuggalā. Te ime nāma ettake kilese pajahantīti ye te puthujjanā lābhino ca pañca kāmaguṇe ettake taṃtaṃjhānādivatthuke ca taṃtaṃmaggavajjhatāya paricchinnattā ettake kilese pajahanti. Ye nappajahantīti ettha vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Asucisukhaṃ kāyāsucisannissitattā. Anariyehīti aparisuddhehi. Paṭilābhato bhāyitabbaṃ kilesadukkhagatikattā. Vipākato bhāyitabbaṃ apāyadukkhagatikattā. Gaṇatopi kilesatopi vivittasukhanti gaṇasaṅgaṇikato ca kilesasaṅgaṇikato [M 2.0078] ca vivittasukhaṃ. Rāgādivūpasamatthāyāti rāgādivūpasamāvahaṃ sukhaṃ. Na bhāyitabbaṃ sampati āyatiñca ekantahitabhāvato.

155. By 'those who abandon' (`ye pajahanti`) are meant the individuals spoken of as 'they abandon just that.' By 'these are those who abandon such and such defilements' are meant those ordinary people who, having gained the five strands of sense pleasure and various things based on jhāna and so on, abandon such and such defilements because they are delimited by being subject to abandonment by the respective paths. By 'those who do not abandon' (`ye nappajahanti`) the meaning should be understood according to the method explained here. 'Impure pleasure' (`asucisukhaṃ`) is so called because it is dependent on the impurity of the body. By 'by the ignoble' (`anariyehi`) is meant by the impure. One should fear its acquisition (`paṭilābhato`) because it leads to the suffering of defilements and to bad destinations. One should fear its result (`vipākato`) because it leads to the suffering of the lower realms. By 'secluded happiness' (`vivittasukhaṃ`) is meant happiness secluded from association with crowds and from association with defilements. By 'for the pacification of lust, etc.' (`rāgādivūpasamatthāya`) is meant happiness that leads to the pacification of lust, etc. One should not fear it (`na bhāyitabbaṃ`) because it is solely conducive to welfare both in the present and in the future.

156. Iñjitasminti paccatte bhummavacananti āha “iñjana”ntiādi. Iñjati tenāti iñjitaṃ, tassa tassa jhānassa khobhakaraṃ oḷārikaṃ jhānaṅgaṃ. Catutthajjhānaṃ aniñjanaṃ sannisinnābhāvato. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “ṭhite āneñjappatte”ti (dī. ni. 1.244-245; ma. ni. 1.384-386; pārā. 12-13).

156. Regarding `iñjitasmiṃ` (in the agitated), it is said that this is a locative expression, meaning 'agitation' (`iñjana`), and so on. That by which one is shaken is `iñjitaṃ` (agitated), meaning the coarse jhāna factor that disturbs each jhāna. The fourth jhāna is `aniñjana` (unagitated) because of the absence of agitation. As it is said: 'Standing, attained to the immovable' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.244–245; Majjhima Nikāya 1.384–386; Pārājika 12–13).

Alaṃ-saddo [V 2.0076] yuttatthopi hoti – “alameva nibbindituṃ, alaṃ vimuccitu”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.272; saṃ. ni. 2.124, 128, 134, 143), tasmā analaṃ anusaṅgaṃ kātuṃ ayuttanti attho. Tenāha “akattabbaālayanti vadāmī”ti. Sanniṭṭhānanti sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ alaṃ ettāvatāti ussāhapaṭippassambhanavasena sanniṭṭhānaṃ na kātabbanti yojanā. Uddhambhāgiyasaññitaṃ aṇuṃ vā orambhāgiyasaññitaṃ thūlaṃ vā, rūparāgoti evarūpaṃ aṇuṃ vā kāmāsavo paṭighanti evarūpaṃ thūlaṃ vā, mudunā pavattiākāravisesena appasāvajjaṃ, kammabandhanaṭṭhena vā appasāvajjaṃ, tabbipariyāyato mahāsāvajjaṃ veditabbaṃ. Nātitikkhapaññassa vasena desanāya pavattattā “neyyapuggalassa vasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbaso hi pariyādinnanikantikassa ariyapuggalassa vasena saññāvedayitanirodhassa āgatattā “arahattanikūṭeneva niṭṭhāpitā”ti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ panettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

The word 'alaṃ' (enough/sufficient) is also used in the sense of 'proper' or 'suitable'—as in 'it is proper to become disenchanted, it is proper to be liberated' (Dī. Ni. 2.272; Saṃ. Ni. 2.124, 128, 134, 143). Therefore, 'analaṃ anusaṅgaṃ kātuṃ' means it is improper to make an attachment. Hence it is said, 'I say it is an attachment that should not be made' (akattabbaālayaṃ). By 'final determination' (sanniṭṭhānaṃ) is meant that one should not make a final determination by way of relaxing effort, thinking, 'This much is enough for the right practice.' Whether subtle, pertaining to the higher realms, or gross, pertaining to the lower realms—such as the subtle lust for form, or the gross, such as the taint of sensual desire and aversion—that which is slightly blameworthy due to the mild nature of its occurrence or because it creates little karmic bondage should be understood as highly blameworthy when considered in the opposite way. It is said 'for the sake of the person to be guided' (neyyapuggalassa vasena) because the teaching proceeds for the sake of one whose wisdom is not yet sharp. Indeed, since the cessation of perception and feeling is attained by a noble person who has completely overcome craving, it is said, 'It is concluded only by the pinnacle of arahantship.' As for what is not explicitly explained here in terms of meaning, that should be easily understood.

Laṭukikopamasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Laṭukikopama Sutta is complete.

7. Cātumasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Cātumā Sutta

157. Yathāupanissayenāti [V 2.0077] yo yo upanissayo yathāupanissayo, tena yathāupanissayena sammāpayogena. Patiṭṭhahissanti sāsane patiṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhissanti. Vasanaṭṭhānānīti vassaggādivasena vasanaṭṭhānāni. Saṇṭhāpayamānāti suvibhattabhāvena ṭhapentā.

157. ‘According to the requisite condition’ (yathāupanissayena) means whatever requisite condition there is, according to that requisite condition, with that proper application. ‘They will be established’ (patiṭṭhahissanti) means they will gain a firm footing in the Dispensation. ‘Dwelling places’ (vasanaṭṭhānāni) refers to dwelling places in terms of the rains-residence, and so forth. ‘Setting up’ (saṇṭhāpayamānā) means establishing in a well-divided manner.

Avinibbhogasaddanti vinibhuñjitvā gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyasaddaṃ. Vacīghosopi hi bahūhi ekaccaṃ pavattito ṭhānato ca dūrataro kevalaṃ mahānigghoso [M 2.0079] eva hutvā sotapathamāgacchati. Macchavilopeti macche vilumpitvā viya gahaṇe, macchānaṃ vā nayane.

‘The sound that cannot be distinguished’ (avinibbhogasadda) refers to a sound that cannot be grasped separately. For even a vocal sound, when uttered by many together from a place far away, comes to the ear merely as a great noise. ‘Fish-plunder’ (macchavilopa) means either seizing as if plundering fish, or the leading of fish.

158. Vavassaggattheti nicchayatthe, idaṃ tāva amhehi vuccamānavacanaṃ ekantasotabbaṃ, pacchā tumhehi kātabbaṃ karothāti adhippāyo. Vacanaparihāroti tehi sakyarājūhi vuttavacanassa parihāro. Lesakappanti kappiyalesaṃ. Dhuravahāti dhuravāhino, dhorayhāti attho. Pādamūlanti upacāraṃ vadati. Vigacchissatīti hāyissati. Paṭippharitoti na bhagavato sammukhāva, sakyarājūnaṃ puratopi vippharitova hoti.

158. ‘Vavassaggatthe’ means in the sense of certainty, that is, determination. The intention is: ‘First, this statement made by us should be listened to completely; afterward, you should do what is to be done.’ ‘Vacanaparihāro’ means the avoidance of the words spoken by those Sakyan kings. ‘Lesakappa’ refers to a suitable pretext. ‘Dhuravaha’ means burden-bearers, that is, those who carry the yoke. ‘Pādamūla’ refers to the vicinity. ‘Vigacchissati’ means it will decline. ‘Paṭippharito’ means it was spread abroad not only in the presence of the Blessed One, but also before the Sakyan kings.

159. Abhinandatūti abhimukho hutvā pamodatu. Abhivadatūti abhirūpavasena vadatu. Pasādaññathattanti appasādassa vipariṇāmo hīnāyāvattanasaṅkhātaṃ parivattanaṃ, tenāha “vibbhamantānaṃ. Vipariṇāmaññathatta”nti. Kāraṇūpacārena sassesu bījapariyāyoti āha “bījānaṃ taruṇānanti taruṇasassāna”nti. Taruṇabhāveneva tassa bhāvino phalassa abhāvena vipariṇāmo.

159. ‘Abhinandatu’ means may he rejoice, having turned towards it. ‘Abhivadatu’ means may he speak in a suitable manner. ‘Pasādaññathatta’ means the alteration of faith, that is, the change into lack of faith, a transformation described as turning to a lower state; hence it is said, ‘of those deviating, the alteration is the change.’ By way of causal metaphor, ‘the way of seeds in the case of crops’ means, he says, ‘of the young seeds,’ that is, ‘of young crops.’ Due to their youth, there is transformation because of the absence of the future fruit.

160. Kattabbassa saraseneva karaṇaṃ cittaruciyaṃ, na tathā parassa ussādanenāti āha – “pakkosiyamānānaṃ gamanaṃ nāma na phāsuka”nti. Mayampi bhagavā viya diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāreneva viharissāmāti dīpeti pakatiyā vivekajjhāsayabhāvato viraddho āgatassa bhārassa avahanatoyeva. Tenāha “attano bhārabhāvaṃ na aññāsī”ti.

160. The doing of what ought to be done is pleasing to the mind when done spontaneously, not so when incited by another; hence it is said, ‘going is not pleasant for those who are summoned.’ ‘We too, like the Blessed One, will dwell with a pleasant abiding in this very life’—this demonstrates that, due to his natural inclination for seclusion, he failed precisely by having to bear the burden that had come to him. Hence it is said, ‘he did not know his own state of being a burden.’

161. Kasmā [V 2.0078] ārabhīti? Sappāyato. Pañcasatā hi bhikkhū abhinavā, tasmā tesaṃ ovādadānatthaṃ bhagavā imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhīti.

161. Why did he begin? Because it was appropriate. For there were five hundred new monks, so the Blessed One began this discourse for the purpose of giving them instruction.

162. Kodhupāyāsassāti ettha kujjhanaṭṭhena kodho, sveva cittassa kāyassa ca atippamaddanamathanuppādanehi daḷhaṃ āyāsaṭṭhena upāyāso. Anekavāraṃ pavattitvā attanā samavetaṃ sattaṃ ajjhottharitvā sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ adatvā anayabyasanapāpanena kodhupāyāsassa ūmisadisatā daṭṭhabbā. Tenāha “kodhupāyāse”tiādi.

162. ‘Of anger and distress’ (Kodhupāyāsassa): Here, ‘kodha’ is anger in the sense of being angry, and that very thing is ‘upāyāsa’ (distress) in the sense of intense affliction, through producing excessive crushing and torment of the mind and body. The wave-like nature of anger and distress should be understood in this way: having arisen repeatedly, it overwhelms the being possessed of it, does not allow them to lift their head, and leads them to misfortune and ruin. Hence it is said, ‘in anger and distress,’ and so forth.

163. Odarikattena khāditoti odarikabhāvena āmisagedhena micchājīvena jīvikākappanena nāsitasīlādiguṇatāya khāditadhammasarīro.

163. ‘Consumed by gluttony’ (Odarikattena khādito) means his body of Dhamma is devoured, as his virtues such as morality have been destroyed by gluttony, greed for material things, and making a living through wrong livelihood.

164. Pañcakāmaguṇāvaṭṭe [M 2.0080] nimujjitvāti ettha kāmarāgābhibhūte satte ito ca etto, etto ca itoti evaṃ manāpiyarūpādivisayasaṅkhāte āvaṭṭe attānaṃ saṃsāretvā yathā tato bahibhūte nekkhamme cittampi na uppādeti, evaṃ āvaṭṭetvā byasanāpādanena kāmaguṇānaṃ āvaṭṭasadisatā daṭṭhabbā. Tenāha “yathā hī”tiādi.

164. ‘Having sunk into the whirlpool of the five strands of sensual pleasure’ (Pañcakāmaguṇāvaṭṭe nimujjitvā): Here, the whirlpool-like nature of sensual pleasures should be understood by how they cause ruin. Beings overcome by sensual desire make themselves transmigrate in the whirlpool of pleasing forms and other sense objects, from here to there and from there to here, so that they do not even arouse the mind toward renunciation, which lies outside of it. Hence it is said, ‘just as,’ and so forth.

165. Rāgānuddhaṃsitenāti rāgena anuddhaṃsitena. Caṇḍamacchaṃ āgammāti susukādicaṇḍamacchaṃ āgamma. Mātugāmaṃ āgammāti mātugāmo hi yonisomanasikārarahitaṃ adhīrapurisaṃ itthikuttabhūtehi attano hāvabhāvavilāsehi abhibhuyya gahetvā dhīrajātiyampi attano rūpādīhi palobhanavasena anavasesaṃ attano upakāradhamme sīlādike sampādetuṃ asamatthaṃ karonto anayabyasanaṃ pāpeti. Tenāha – “mātugāmaṃ āgamma uppannakāmarāgo vibbhamatī”ti.

165. ‘Not overcome by lust’ (Rāgānuddhaṃsitena) means not overcome by lust. ‘Approaching a fierce fish’ (Caṇḍamacchaṃ āgamma) refers to approaching a fierce fish such as a porpoise, and so forth. ‘Approaching a woman’ (Mātugāmaṃ āgamma) means that a woman overpowers a man of weak character who lacks wise attention with her feminine wiles and allure, and by enticing even a man of firm character with her form and so on, she renders him incapable of fully accomplishing his own beneficial qualities such as morality, and thus leads him to misfortune and ruin. Hence it is said: ‘Through approaching a woman, arisen sensual lust causes one to go astray.’

Bhayaṃ nāma yattha bhāyitabbavatthu, tattha otarantasseva hoti, na anotarantassa, taṃ otaritvā bhayaṃ vinodetvā tattha kiccaṃ sādhetabbaṃ, itarathā catthasiddhi na hotīti imamatthaṃ upamopamitabbasarūpavasena dassetuṃ “yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha udakaṃ nissāya ānisaṃso pipāsavinayanaṃ sarīrasuddhi pariḷāhūpasamo kāyautuggāhāpananti evamādi. Sāsanaṃ nissāya ānisaṃso pana saṅkhepato vaṭṭadukkhūpasamo, vitthārato pana sīlānisaṃsādivasena anekavidho, so visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.9) vuttanayena veditabbo. Vuttappakāro ānisaṃso hoti tāni bhayāni abhibhuyya pavattassāti adhippāyo. Imāni abhāyitvāti imāni kodhūpāyāsādibhayāni [V 2.0079] abhibhuyya pavattitvā abhāyitvā. Kodhūpāyāsādayo hi bhāyati etasmāti bhayanti vuttā. Theroti mahādhammarakkhitatthero. Kāmaṃ pahānābhisamayakālo eva sacchikiriyābhisamayo, sammādiṭṭhiyā pana saṃkilesavodānadhammesu kiccaṃ asaṃkiṇṇaṃ katvā dassetuṃ samānakālikampi asamānakālikaṃ viya vuttaṃ “taṇhāsotaṃ chinditvā nibbānapāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ na sakkotī”ti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Fear arises only where there is an object to be feared; it arises for one who enters into it, not for one who does not. One must enter into it, dispel the fear, and accomplish what needs to be done; otherwise, success is not achieved. To illustrate this point through the nature of a simile and that which is compared to it, the passage beginning with ‘just as’ (yathā) was stated. Here, the benefits derived from water include quenching thirst, cleansing the body, relieving heat, making the body buoyant, and so forth. The benefit derived from the Teaching, in brief, is the cessation of the suffering of the round of rebirth; in detail, it is manifold, by way of the benefits of virtue and so forth, and should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.9). The intended meaning is that such benefits arise for one who proceeds having overcome those fears. ‘Not fearing these’ (Imāni abhāyitvā) means having proceeded without fear, having overcome these fears such as anger and distress. For anger, distress, and so forth, are called ‘fears’ because one is afraid of them. ‘The elder’ (Thero) refers to the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita. Although the time of the full understanding of abandoning is indeed the full understanding of realization, in order to show that right view performs its task regarding defiling and purifying states without confusion, what is simultaneous is spoken of as if it were not simultaneous, as in: ‘One cannot see the far shore of Nibbāna without having cut off the stream of craving.’ The rest is easily understood.

Cātumasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Cātuma Sutta is complete.

8. Naḷakapānasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Naḷakapāna Sutta

166. Yattha [V 2.0080][M 2.0081] bodhisattapamukho vānaro naḷakena pānīyaṃ pivi, sā pokkharaṇī, tassāmanto bhūmippadeso, tattha niviṭṭhagāmo ca “naḷakapāna”nteva paññāyittha, idha pana gāmo adhippetoti āha “naḷakapāneti evaṃnāmake gāme”ti. Idāni tamatthaṃ āgamanato paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ “pubbe kirā”ti āraddhaṃ. Paññavāti itikattabbatāya paññāya paññavā.

166. The pond where the Bodhisatta, as the chief monkey, drank water with a reed, the land surrounding it, and the village established there, became known as ‘Naḷakapāna’. Here, however, the village is intended, thus it is said: ‘in a village named Naḷakapāna’. Now, to show that meaning from its origin, the passage ‘Formerly, it is said…’ is begun. ‘Wise’ (paññavā) means possessing wisdom by virtue of the wisdom concerning what ought to be done.

Thūladīghabahulabhāvena mahatīhi dāṭhikāhi samannāgatattā mahādāṭhiko. “Udakarakkhaso aha”nti vatvā vānarānaṃ kañci amuñcitvā “sabbe tumhe mama hatthagatā”ti dassento “tumhe pana sabbe khādissāmī”ti āha. Dhami…pe… piviṃsūti bodhisattena gahitanaḷo anavaseso abbhantare sabbasandhīnaṃ nibbādhena ekacchiddo ahosi. Neva maṃ tvaṃ vadhissasīti udakarakkhasa tvaṃ vadhitukāmopi mama purisathāmena na vadhissasi.

Because he was endowed with large tusks, due to their thickness, length, and abundance, he was called Mahādāṭhika. Saying, ‘I am a water demon,’ and not releasing any of the monkeys, showing them, ‘All of you are in my grasp,’ he said, ‘But I will devour all of you.’ ‘They drank’ (piviṃsu): The reed grasped by the Bodhisatta became a single hollow tube throughout, due to all its internal joints being unobstructed. ‘You will not kill me’: O water demon, even if you desire to kill me, you will not kill me, for you cannot overcome my manly strength.

Evaṃ pana vatvā mahāsatto “ayaṃ pāpo ettha pānīyaṃ pivante aññepi satte mā bādhayitthā”ti karuṇāyamāno “ettha jāyantā naḷā sabbe apabbabandhā ekacchiddāva hontū”ti adhiṭṭhāya gato. Tenāha “tato paṭṭhāyā”tiādi.

Having spoken thus, the Great Being, feeling compassion, thought: ‘May this evil one not harm other beings who drink water here.’ Having resolved, ‘May all the reeds growing here be without joints and have a single hollow,’ he departed. Hence it is said, ‘From that time onward,’ and so forth.

167. Anuruddhappamukhā bhikkhū bhagavatā “kacci tumhe anuruddhā”ti pucchitāti thero “taggha mayaṃ, bhante”ti āha.

167. When the monks headed by Anuruddha were asked by the Blessed One, ‘Are you, Anuruddhas, getting along?’, the elder replied, ‘Indeed, venerable sir, we are.’

Sace pabbajati, jīvitaṃ labhissati, no aññathāti raññā pabbajjāya abhinītāti rājābhinītā. Corābhinītāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Corānaṃ mūlaṃ chindanto “kaṇṭakasodhanaṃ karissāmī”ti. Ājīvikāyāti ājīvena jīvitavuttiyā. Imesu pana anuruddhattherādīsu.

‘If he goes forth, he will gain his life; otherwise not’—thus he was urged to go forth by the king; hence, ‘urged by the king’ (rājābhinītā). Similarly, the same method applies to ‘urged by thieves’ (corābhinītā). Cutting off the root of the thieves, thinking, ‘I will perform a clearing of thorns.’ ‘By livelihood’ (ājīvikāya) means by a way of life, a means of living. But in these cases, regarding elders such as Anuruddha and others.

Vivekanti pubbakālikakiriyappadhānaṃ “abyāpajjaṃ upeta”ntiādīsu viyāti āha – “viviccā”ti, viviccitvā vivitto hutvā vinā hutvāti attho. Pabbajitakiccanti pabbajitassa sāruppakiccaṃ. Samaṇakiccanti samaṇabhāvakaraṇakiccaṃ. Yadaggena hi pabbajitakiccaṃ [V 2.0081] kātuṃ na sakkoti tadaggena samaṇabhāvakarampi kiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Tenāha “so yevā”tiādi.

The word ‘seclusion’ (vivekaṃ) primarily indicates a preceding action, as in phrases like ‘endowed with non-ill-will’ (abyāpajjaṃ upetaṃ), and so forth. Thus it is said: ‘having secluded’ (viviccā), meaning having withdrawn, having become secluded, being without. ‘The duty of one gone forth’ (pabbajitakiccaṃ) is the appropriate duty of a monastic. ‘The duty of an ascetic’ (samaṇakiccaṃ) is the duty that makes one an ascetic. For to the extent that one cannot perform the duty of one gone forth, to that extent one also cannot perform the duty that makes one an ascetic. Hence it is said, ‘That very one…’ and so forth.

168. Appaṭisandhike [M 2.0082] tāva byākaronto pavattīsu ṭhānaṃ atītoti katvā upapattīsu byākaroti nāma tattha paṭisandhiyā abhāvakittanato. Mahantatuṭṭhinoti vipulapamodā.

168. First, when explaining the state of no relinking in rebirth, he does so by treating its place in the ongoing round of existence as past, and explains it in terms of rebirths, thereby mentioning the absence of relinking there. ‘Of great satisfaction’ (mahantatuṭṭhino) means of abundant delight.

169. Imassāti “assā”ti padassa atthavacanaṃ. Imassa ṭhitassa āyasmato sāmaṃ diṭṭho vā hoti anussavasuto vāti yojanā. Samādhipakkhikā dhammā dhammāti adhippetā, samādhi pana evaṃvihārīti ettha vihārasaddena gahito. Evaṃvimuttāti ettha pana vimuttisaddena phalavimutti gahitā. Caratopīti samathavipassanācārena caratopi viharantassapi. Upāsakaupāsikāṭhānesu labbhamānampi arahattaṃ appakabhāvato pāḷiyaṃ anuddhaṭanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

169. ‘Of this’ (imassa) is the statement of meaning for the word ‘assa’. The connection is: ‘Of this venerable one, who is present, it is either seen by oneself or heard through tradition.’ By ‘states’ (dhammā), ‘states associated with concentration’ (samādhipakkhikā dhammā) are intended. Concentration, however, is included here by the word ‘dwelling’ (vihāra) in the phrase ‘dwells thus’ (evaṃvihārī). In ‘thus liberated’ (evaṃvimutta), the liberation of fruition is included by the word ‘liberation’ (vimutti). ‘Even while walking’ (caratopi) means even while behaving or living with the conduct of serenity and insight. It should be understood that even though arahantship is attainable in the state of laymen and laywomen, it is not cited in the Pāḷi due to its rarity. The rest is easily understood.

Naḷakapānasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the Commentary on the Naḷakapāna Sutta is complete.

9. Goliyānisuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Goliyāni Sutta.

173. Padasamācāroti [V 2.0082] taṃtaṃpaccayabhedadassanāya vigatattā pakārehi daliddasamācāro sithilasamācāroti attho. Yasmā pana tādiso samācāro thiro daḷho nāma na hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “dubbalasamācāro”ti. “Sākhasamācāro”ti vā pāṭho, tattha tattha lagganaṭṭhena sākhāsadisasīloti attho. Tenāha “oḷārikācāro”ti. Paccayesu sāpekkhoti paccayesu sāpekkhatāya eva hissa oḷārikācāratā veditabbā. Garunā kismiñci vutte gāravavasena patissavanaṃ patisso, patissavacanabhūtaṃ taṃsabhāgañca yaṃ kiñci gāravanti attho. Saha patissenāti sappatissena, sappatissavena ovādasampaṭicchanena. Patissīyatīti vā patisso, garukātabbo, tena saha patissenāti sabbaṃ pubbe viya. Tenāha “sajeṭṭhakenā”ti. Serivihāro nāma attappadhānavāso. Tenāha “niraṅkusavihārenā”ti.

173. ‘Padasamācāra’ means poor conduct or lax conduct, because it is devoid of insight into the distinctions among the various requisites. Since such conduct is not firm or strong, it is called ‘weak conduct’ (dubbalasamācāra). Alternatively, the reading is ‘sākhasamācāra’, meaning conduct resembling a branch in that it gets attached here and there. Hence it is said, ‘coarse conduct’ (oḷārikācāra). ‘Dependent on requisites’ (paccayesu sāpekkho): his coarse conduct should be understood precisely by his dependence on requisites. When something is said by a senior, ‘patissa’ means respectful assent given out of respect; it means any respectful act which is of the nature of a respectful reply and shares its character. ‘With respect’ (saha patissena) means with respectful assent, with respectful acceptance of advice. Alternatively, ‘patissa’ is one who is to be respected, one who should be revered; then ‘with respect’ (saha patissena) is all as before. Hence it is said, ‘with a senior’ (sajeṭṭhakena). ‘Independent living’ (serivihāro) means a dwelling with oneself as the authority. Hence it is called ‘a dwelling without restraint’ (niraṅkusavihārena).

Anupakhajjāti anupakaḍḍhitvā. Garuṭṭhāniyānaṃ antaraṃ anāpucchā anupavisitvāti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha yo”tiādi vuttaṃ.

‘Anupakhajjā’ means without encroaching. To explain the meaning of entering among those worthy of respect without asking leave, the passage ‘whoever there’ (tattha yo), and so forth, is stated.

Ābhisamācārikanti [M 2.0083] abhisamācāre bhavaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti āha “vattapaṭipattimattampī”ti. Nātikālasseva saṅghassa purato pavisitabbaṃ, na pacchā paṭikkamitabbanti adhippāyena atikāle ca gāmappaveso atidivā paṭikkamanañca nivāritaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “na atipāto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Uddhaccapakatikoti vibbhantacitto. Avacāpalyenāti daḷhavātāpahatapallavasadisena lolabhāvena.

‘Ābhisamācārikaṃ’ means pertaining to proper conduct. But what is that? It is said: ‘even a mere matter of duties and observances’ (vattapaṭipattimattampi). The intention is that one should not enter the presence of the Saṅgha too early, nor depart too late. To indicate this, entering the village at too late an hour and returning too late in the day are prohibited; hence it is said: ‘not too early’ (na atipāto), and so forth. ‘Of a restless nature’ (uddhaccapakatiko) means one whose mind is agitated. ‘With unsteadiness’ (avacāpalyena) means with a fickle nature like a leaf struck by a strong wind.

Paññavatāti iminā bhikkhusāruppesu itikattabbesu upāyapaññā adhippetā, na sutamayapaññā. Abhidhamme abhivinaye yogoti iminā bhāvanāpaññāuttarimanussadhamme yogo pakāsito. Yogoti ca paricayo uggaṇhavasena.

By ‘being wise’ (paññavatā) is intended wisdom of means in the duties to be done that are appropriate for a monk, not wisdom derived from learning (sutamayapaññā). By ‘application in the higher Dhamma and higher Vinaya’ (abhidhamme abhivinaye yogo) is revealed the application in the higher-than-human states, which is wisdom from development. And ‘application’ (yogo) means familiarity by way of grasping.

Āruppāti iminā catassopi arūpasamāpattiyo gahitā, tā pana catūhi rūpasamāpattīhi vinā na sampajjantīti āha – “āruppāti ettāvatā aṭṭhapi samāpattiyo vuttā hontī”ti. Kasiṇeti dasavidhe kasiṇe. Ekaṃ parikammakammaṭṭhānanti yaṃ kiñci ekabhāvanā [V 2.0083] parikammadīpanaṃ khandhakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Tenāha “paguṇaṃ katvā”ti. Kasiṇaparikammaṃ pana taggahaṇeneva gahitaṃ hoti, lokiyā uttarimanussadhammā heṭṭhā gahitāti āha “uttarimanussadhammeti iminā sabbepi lokuttaradhamme dassetī”ti. Neyyapuggalassa vasenāti jānitvā vitthāretvā ñātabbapuggalassa vasenāti.

By ‘formless states’ (āruppa) are included all four formless attainments. However, since these are not accomplished without the four form attainments, it is said: ‘By “formless states” (āruppa), thus far, all eight attainments are stated.’ ‘Kasiṇa’ refers to the tenfold kasiṇas. ‘One preliminary meditation object’ (ekaṃ parikammakammaṭṭhānaṃ) is any meditation subject related to the aggregates that illuminates the preliminary work for a single development. Hence it is said, ‘having made it familiar’ (paguṇaṃ katvā). The preliminary work of the kasiṇa is indeed grasped by the very act of taking it up. Since the mundane higher states were included below, it is said: ‘By “higher states beyond the human” (uttarimanussadhamma) are shown all supramundane states.’ ‘By way of the person to be guided’ (neyyapuggalassa vasena) means by way of the person who is to be known, having known and elaborated upon them.

Goliyānisuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the Commentary on the Goliyāni Sutta is complete.

10. Kīṭāgirisuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Kīṭāgiri Sutta.

174. Pañca [V 2.0084] ānisaṃseti appābādhatādike pañca guṇe. Tattha akkhirogakucchirogādīnaṃ abhāvo appābādhatā. Sarīre tesaṃ kuppanadukkhassa abhāvo appātaṅkaṃ. Sarīrassa uṭṭhānasukhatā lahuṭṭhānaṃ. Balaṃ nāma kāyabalaṃ. Phāsuvihāro iriyāpathasukhatā. Anupakkhandānīti duccajanavasena sattānaṃ anupaviṭṭhāni. Sañjānissathāti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, tasmā iti evaṃ ānisaṃsanti attho.

174. He states five benefits, namely, five qualities beginning with freedom from illness. Here, ‘freedom from illness’ (appābādhatā) is the absence of eye diseases, stomach diseases, and so on. ‘Freedom from affliction’ (appātaṅkaṃ) is the absence of the pain of their agitation in the body. ‘Lightness of rising’ (lahuṭṭhānaṃ) is the ease of the body in rising. ‘Strength’ (balaṃ) is physical strength. ‘Comfortable living’ (phāsuvihāro) is ease in the postures. ‘Anupakkhandāni’ means not to be fallen upon; that is, they are not things that are entered into by beings because they are difficult to abandon. Here, in ‘sañjānissathāti’, the word ‘iti’ has the meaning of ‘and so on’; therefore, the meaning is ‘thus are the benefits’.

175. Āvāse niyuttāti āvāsikā tassa anativattanato. Tenāha “nibaddhavāsino”ti, niyatavāsinoti attho. Tannibandhāti [M 2.0084] nibandhaṃ vuccati byāpāro, tattha bandhā pasutā ussukāti tannibandhā. Kathaṃ te tattha nibandhāti āha “akataṃ senāsana”ntiādi. Uppajjanakena kālena pattabbaṃ kālikaṃ so pana kālo anāgato eva hotīti āha “anāgate kāle pattabba”nti.

175. ‘Appointed to the dwelling’ (āvāse niyuttā) means ‘residents’ (āvāsikā), because they do not transgress it. Therefore, it is said, ‘those who dwell fixedly’ (nibaddhavāsino), meaning ‘those who dwell permanently’. ‘Bound to that’ (tannibandhā) means ‘engagement’ (nibandhaṃ) is called ‘activity’ (byāpāro); those who are bound, devoted, and zealous to that are called ‘bound to that’. How are they bound there? He says, ‘unmade lodging’, etc. ‘Kālika’ means what should be obtained at the time of arising; but since that time is always in the future, he says, ‘to be obtained in a future time’.

178. Ettakā vedanā sevitabbāti aṭṭhārasapi nekkhammanissitā vedanā sevitabbā, gehassitā na sevitbbā.

178. ‘These feelings should be cultivated’ (ettakā vedanā sevitabbā) means all eighteen feelings dependent on renunciation should be cultivated; those dependent on household life should not be cultivated.

181. Taṃ kataṃ soḷasavidhassapi kiccassa niṭṭhitattā. Anulomikānīti utusukhabhāvena anurūpāni. Tenāha “kammaṭṭhānasappāyānī”ti. Samānaṃ kurumānāti omattataṃ adhimattatañca pahāya samakiccataṃ sampādentā.

181. That is accomplished because the sixteenfold task is completed. ‘Anulomikāni’ means suitable by way of seasonal comfort. Therefore, it is said, ‘suitable for meditation subjects’. ‘Making equal’ (samānaṃ kurumānā) means abandoning deficiency and excess, accomplishing equanimity in the task.

182. Te dve hontīti te ādito vuttā dve.

182. ‘Those two exist’ (te dve honti) means those two stated from the beginning.

Ubhato (a. ni. ṭī. 3.7.14) ubhayathā ubhohi bhāgehi vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto ekadesasarūpekasesanayena. Tathā hi vuttaṃ abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pu. pa. aṭṭha. 24) “dvīhi bhāgehi dve vāre vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti. Tattha keci tāva therā – “samāpattiyā vikkhambhanavimokkhena, maggena samucchedavimokkhena vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti [V 2.0085] vadanti. Aññe therā – “ayaṃ ubhatobhāgavimutto rūpato muccitvā nāmaṃ nissāya ṭhito puna tato muccanato nāmanissitako”ti vatvā tassa ca sādhakaṃ –

‘Ubhato’ (A.N.Ṭī. 3.7.14) means ‘in both ways’, ‘freed by both parts’; thus, ‘liberated in both ways’ (ubhatobhāgavimutto) is by the principle of retaining one of two similar parts. As stated in the Abhidhamma commentary (Pu. Pa. Aṭṭha. 24): ‘Freed by two parts, twice, thus, ‘liberated in both ways’ (ubhatobhāgavimutto)’. Here, some elders say: ‘He is liberated by suppression through meditative attainment and by eradication through the path; thus, he is ‘liberated in both ways’ (ubhatobhāgavimutto)’. Other elders say: ‘This one liberated in both ways, having been liberated from form, relies on mentality (nāma), and then, being liberated from that too, is called ‘dependent on mentality’ (nāmanissitako)’; having said this, they also provide supporting evidence.

“Acci yathā vātavegena khittā, (upasivāti bhagavā,)

Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkhaṃ;

Evaṃ muni nāmakāyā vimutto,

Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkha”nti. (su. ni. 1080; cūḷani. upasīvamāṇavapucchā 11; upasīvamāṇavapucchāniddesa 43) –

‘Just as a flame, (Upasiva,) blown by the force of the wind, Goes to its end and cannot be reckoned; So too the sage, liberated from the mental body, Goes to its end and cannot be reckoned.’

Imaṃ suttapadaṃ vatvā “nāmakāyato ca rūpakāyato ca suvimuttattā ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti vadanti. Sutte hi ākiñcaññāyatanalābhino upasivabrāhmaṇassa bhagavatā nāmakāyā vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimuttoti akkhātoti. Apare pana “samāpattiyā vikkhambhanavimokkhena [M 2.0085] ekavāraṃ vimutto, maggena samucchedavimokkhena ekavāraṃ vimuttoti evaṃ ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti vadanti. Ettha paṭhamavāde dvīhi bhāgehi vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto. Dutiyavāde ubhatobhāgato vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto. Tatiyavāde pana dvīhi bhāgehi dve vāre vimuttoti ayametesaṃ viseso. Kilesehi vimutto kilesā vā vikkhambhanasamucchedehi kāyadvayato vimuttā assāti ayamattho daṭṭhabbo. Tenāha “dvīhi bhāgehī”tiādi.

Having spoken this verse, they say: ‘Because of being well-liberated from the mental body and the physical body, he is ‘liberated in both ways’ (ubhatobhāgavimutto)’. For in the Sutta, the brahmin Upasiva, who attained the base of nothingness, was declared by the Blessed One as ‘liberated from the mental body’ and thus ‘liberated in both ways’. Others, however, say: ‘He is liberated once through the liberation of suppression by meditative attainment, and once through the liberation of eradication by the path; thus, he is ‘liberated in both ways’ (ubhatobhāgavimutto)’. Here, in the first view, ‘liberated by two parts’ means ‘liberated in both ways’. In the second view, ‘liberated from both parts’ means ‘liberated in both ways’. In the third view, however, ‘liberated by two parts, twice’—this is the distinction among them. The meaning should be understood as: ‘He is liberated from defilements, or the defilements are liberated from the two bodies by suppression and eradication’. Therefore, it is said, ‘by two parts’, etc.

Soti ubhatobhāgavimutto. Kāmañcettha rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānampi arūpāvacarajjhānaṃ viya duvaṅgikaṃ āneñjappattanti vuccati. Taṃ pana padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā arahattaṃ patto ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma na hoti rūpakāyato avimuttattā. Tañhi kilesakāyatova vimuttaṃ, na rūpakāyato, tasmā tato vuṭṭhāya arahattaṃ patto ubhatobhāgavimutto na hotīti āha – “catunnaṃ arūpa…pe… pañcavidho hotī”ti. “Rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādike nirodhasamāpattiante aṭṭha vimokkhe vatvā – “yato ca kho, ānanda, bhikkhu ime aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharati, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti, ayaṃ vuccati, ānanda, bhikkhu ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti yadipi mahānidāne (dī. ni. 2.129-130) vuttaṃ, taṃ pana ubhatobhāgavimuttaseṭṭhavasena vuttanti idha sabbaubhatobhāgavimuttasaṅgahaṇatthaṃ “pañcavidho hotī”ti vatvā “pāḷi panettha…pe… abhidhamme aṭṭhavimokkhalābhino vasena āgatā”ti āha. Idhāpi hi kīṭāgirisutte “idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo…pe… ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti [V 2.0086] arūpasamāpattivasena cattāro ubhatobhāgavimuttā, seṭṭho ca vutto vuttalakkhaṇūpapattito. Yathāvuttesu hi pañcasu purimā cattāro nirodhaṃ na samāpajjantīti pariyāyena ubhatobhāgavimuttā nāma. Aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī anāgāmī taṃ samāpajjitvā tato vuṭṭhāya vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pattoti nippariyāyena ubhatobhāgavimuttaseṭṭho nāma.

He is ‘liberated in both ways’. Although here, even the fourth jhāna of the form realm, like the formless jhāna, is called the attainment of the imperturbable with two factors. However, one who attains arahantship by making that a basis is not called ‘liberated in both ways’ because he is not liberated from the form body. For he is liberated only from the defilement body, not from the form body. Therefore, emerging from that and attaining arahantship, he is not called ‘liberated in both ways’. Hence it is said: ‘Of the four formless… there are five kinds’. Having spoken of the eight liberations, beginning with ‘one with form sees forms’ and ending with the attainment of cessation, it is said: ‘But, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu dwells having touched these eight liberations with the body, and having seen with wisdom, his taints are destroyed—this, Ānanda, is called a bhikkhu ‘liberated in both ways’.’ Although this is stated in the Mahānidāna (Dī. Ni. 2.129-130) as referring to the foremost kind of one liberated in both ways, here, to encompass all kinds of those liberated in both ways, it is said, ‘there are five kinds’, and then it is explained: ‘But the Pali here… in the Abhidhamma, it is given according to one who gains the eight liberations’. Here too, in the Kīṭāgiri Sutta, it is said: ‘Here, bhikkhus, a certain person… liberated in both ways’. Four kinds of those liberated in both ways are described based on formless attainments, and the foremost is stated according to the characteristics of attainment. Among the five mentioned, the first four do not attain cessation; thus, they are called ‘liberated in both ways’ in a figurative sense. One who gains the eight attainments, a non-returner, attains cessation, emerges from it, develops insight, and attains arahantship—this is called the foremost ‘liberated in both ways’ in the literal sense.

Katamo ca puggalotiādīsu katamoti pucchāvacanaṃ, puggaloti asādhāraṇato pucchitabbavacanaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Ekaccoti eko[M 2.0086]. Aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharatīti aṭṭha samāpattiyo sahajātanāmakāyena paṭilabhitvā viharati. Paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontīti vipassanāpaññāya saṅkhāragataṃ, maggapaññāya cattāri saccāni passitvā cattāropi āsavā parikkhīṇā hontīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

In phrases like ‘And what is the person?’, ‘what’ (katamo) is a word of inquiry, and ‘person’ (puggalo) is a word to be inquired about specifically. ‘Here’ (idha) means in this Dispensation. ‘Someone’ (ekacco) means ‘one’. ‘He dwells having touched the eight liberations with his body’ means he attains and dwells having gained the eight attainments with the co-arisen mental body. ‘And through wisdom, having seen, his taints are destroyed’ means that through insight-wisdom he sees conditioned formations, and through path-wisdom he sees the four truths, and thus all four taints are destroyed. This is how the meaning should be understood.

Paññāvimuttoti visesato paññāya eva vimutto, na tassā patiṭṭhānabhūtena aṭṭhavimokkhasaṅkhātena sātisayena samādhināti paññāvimutto. Yo ariyo anadhigataaṭṭhavimokkhena sabbaso āsavehi vimutto, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Adhigatepi hi rūpajjhānavimokkhe na so sātisayasamādhinissitoti na tassa vasena ubhatobhāgavimutto hotīti vuttovāyamattho. Arūpajjhānesu pana ekasmimpi sati ubhatobhāgavimuttoyeva nāma hoti. Tena hi aṭṭhavimokkhekadesena taṃnāmadānasamatthena aṭṭhavimokkhalābhītveva vuccati. Samudāye hi pavatto vohāro avayavepi dissati yathā “sattisayo”ti. Pāḷīti abhidhammapāḷi. Etthāti etissaṃ paññāvimuttikathāyaṃ. Aṭṭhavimokkhapaṭikkhepavasenevāti avadhāraṇena idhāpi paṭikkhepavaseneva āgatabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tenāha “kāyena phusitvā viharatī”ti.

‘Liberated by wisdom’ (paññāvimutto) means specifically liberated solely by wisdom, not by the surpassing concentration known as the eight liberations, which serves as its foundation; thus, he is called ‘liberated by wisdom’. This term refers to a noble one who is entirely liberated from the taints without having attained the eight liberations. Even if one has attained the liberations of the form jhānas, because he is not dependent on surpassing concentration, he is not called ‘liberated in both ways’; this is the meaning stated. However, if even a single formless jhāna has been attained, he is called ‘liberated in both ways’. Therefore, by attaining a portion of the eight liberations that is sufficient to warrant that name, he is indeed called ‘an attainer of the eight liberations’. For conventional usage that applies to the whole is also seen in a part, as in ‘a multitude of spears’. ‘Pāḷi’ means the Abhidhamma Pāḷi. ‘Here’ (ettha) means in this discussion on liberation by wisdom. ‘By way of rejecting the eight liberations’ (aṭṭhavimokkhapaṭikkhepavaseneva) indicates, by way of emphasis, that here too it is presented by way of rejection. Therefore, it is said, ‘he dwells having touched with the body’.

Phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikarotīti phuṭṭhānaṃ anto phuṭṭhanto, phuṭṭhānaṃ arūpajjhānānaṃ anantaro kāloti adhippāyo. Accantasaṃyoge cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ, phuṭṭhānantarakālameva sacchikaroti sacchikātabbopāyenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ vā etaṃ “ekamantaṃ nisīdī”tiādīsu (pārā. 2) viya. Yo hi arūpajjhānena rūpakāyato nāmakāyekadesato ca vikkhambhanavimokkhena vimutto, tena nirodhasaṅkhāto vimokkho ālocito pakāsito viya hoti, na pana kāyena sacchikato, nirodhaṃ pana ārammaṇaṃ katvā ekaccesu āsavesu khepitesu tena so sacchikato hoti, tasmā so sacchikātabbaṃ nirodhaṃ yathāālocitaṃ nāmakāyena sacchikarotīti “kāyasakkhī”ti vuccati, na tu “vimutto”ti ekaccānaṃ āsavānaṃ [V 2.0087] aparikkhīṇattā. Tenāha [M 2.0087] – “jhānaphassaṃ paṭhamaṃ phusati, pacchā nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarotī”ti. Ayaṃ catunnaṃ arūpasamāpattīnaṃ ekekato vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasitvā kāyasakkhibhāvaṃ pattānaṃ catunnaṃ, nirodhā vuṭṭhāya aggamaggappattaanāgāmino ca vasena ubhatobhāgavimutto viya pañcavidho nāma hoti. Tena vuttaṃ abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ “kāyasakkhimhipi eseva nayo”ti.

‘He realizes the contacted end’ (phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikaroti) means ‘the end of what is contacted’ is ‘the contacted end’; the intention is the time immediately following the formless jhānas that have been contacted. And this is a term of application in the sense of ultimate connection; it is said that he realizes it immediately after contact, by the means by which it should be realized. Alternatively, this is a neuter verbal noun in the sense of development, as in phrases like ‘sat down to one side’ (ekamantaṃ nisīdī), etc. (Pārā. 2). For one who is liberated from the form body and a portion of the mental body by the formless jhāna through the liberation of suppression, the liberation called cessation is as if considered and revealed, but not personally realized by the body. However, by making cessation the object and having destroyed some taints, it is then personally realized by him. Therefore, because he personally realizes cessation, which should be realized as considered, with the mental body, he is called a ‘body-witness’ (kāyasakkhī), but not ‘liberated’ (vimutto), because some taints remain undestroyed. Therefore, it is said: ‘First, one experiences the jhāna-contact; afterward, one personally realizes cessation, Nibbāna’. This is fivefold, like the ‘liberated-in-both-ways’ (ubhatobhāgavimutto), consisting of the four types who attain the state of body-witness after emerging from each of the four formless attainments and contemplating formations, and the non-returner who attains the highest path after emerging from cessation. Therefore, it is said in the Abhidhamma Subcommentary: ‘The same method applies even to the body-witness’.

Diṭṭhantaṃ pattoti dassanasaṅkhātassa sotāpattimaggañāṇassa anantaraṃ pattoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Diṭṭhattā patto”tipi pāṭho. Etena catusaccadassanasaṅkhātāya diṭṭhiyā nirodhassa pattataṃ dīpeti. Tenāha “dukkhā saṅkhārā, sukho nirodhoti ñātaṃ hotī”ti. Tattha paññāyāti maggapaññāya. Paṭhamaphalaṭṭhato yāva aggamaggaṭṭhā, tāva diṭṭhippatto. Tenāha “sopi kāyasakkhi viya chabbidho hotī”ti. Yathā pana paññāvimutto pañcavidho vutto, evaṃ ayampi sukkhavipassako, catūhi rūpajjhānehi vuṭṭhāya diṭṭhippattabhāvappattā cattāro cāti pañcavidho hotīti veditabbo. Saddhāvimuttepi eseva nayo. Idaṃ dukkhanti ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito uddhaṃ dukkhanti. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ dukkhasaccanti yāthāvato pajānāti. Yasmā pana taṇhā dukkhaṃ janeti nibbatteti, tato taṃ dukkhaṃ samudeti, tasmā naṃ “ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti yasmā pana idaṃ dukkhaṃ samudayo ca nibbānaṃ patvā nirujjhati appavattiṃ gacchati, tasmā “ayaṃ dukkhanirodho”ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ariyo pana aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo taṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ gacchati, tena “ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadā”ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ettāvatā nānakkhaṇe saccavavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ. Idāni taṃ ekakkhaṇe dassetuṃ “tathāgatappaveditā”tiādi vuttaṃ, tassattho āgamissati.

“One who has attained the view” (diṭṭhippatto) means having attained immediately after the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, which is known as seeing. There is also the reading, “attained through seeing” (diṭṭhattā patto). By this, it indicates the attainment of cessation through the view known as the seeing of the four truths. Hence it is said, “Formations are suffering; cessation is bliss”—this is known. Herein, “by wisdom” refers to the wisdom of the path. From one standing in the first fruition up to one standing in the highest path, one is called “one who has attained the view.” Therefore, it is said, “He too, like the body-witness, is sixfold.” Just as the wisdom-liberated one is described as fivefold, so too this one—the dry-insight meditator, and the four who attain the state of one who has reached the view after emerging from the four form jhānas—becomes fivefold; thus it is to be understood. The same method applies to the faith-liberated one. “This is suffering” means only this much is suffering, not beyond this. “He understands as it really is” means that, excluding craving, he understands the five aggregates of clinging as the truth of suffering as it really is. Since craving generates and produces suffering, from that suffering arises; therefore, he understands as it really is, “This is the origin of suffering.” And since this suffering and its origin cease upon reaching Nibbāna, coming to non-occurrence, he understands as it really is, “This is the cessation of suffering.” The noble eightfold path, moreover, leads to that cessation of suffering; therefore, he understands as it really is, “This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.” Thus far, the determination of the truths at different moments has been shown. Now, to show them in a single moment, it is said, “proclaimed by the Tathāgata,” etc. The meaning of this will follow.

Saddhāya vimuttoti etena sabbathā avimuttassapi saddhāmattena vimuttabhāvo dīpito hoti. Saddhāvimuttoti vā saddhāya adhimuttoti attho. Vuttanayenevāti “sotāpattiphala”ntiādinā vuttanayena. Saddahantassāti “ekaṃsato ayaṃ paṭipadā kilesakkhayaṃ āvahati sammāsambuddhena bhāsitattā”ti evaṃ saddahantassa. Yasmā panassa aniccānupassanādīhi [M 2.0088] niccasaññāpahānavasena bhāvanāya pubbenāparaṃ visesaṃ passato tattha tattha paccakkhatāpi atthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “saddahantassa viyā”ti. Sesapadadvayaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Ettha ca pubbabhāgamaggabhāvanāti vacanena āgamanīyapaṭipadānānattena saddhāvimuttadiṭṭhippattānaṃ paññānānattaṃ hotīti dassitaṃ. Abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyampi (pu. pa. aṭṭha. 28) “nesaṃ kilesappahāne [V 2.0088] nānattaṃ natthi, paññāya nānattaṃ atthiyevā”ti vatvā – “āgamanīyanānatteneva saddhāvimutto diṭṭhippattaṃ na pāpuṇātīti sanniṭṭhānaṃ kata”nti vuttaṃ.

“Liberated by faith” (saddhāya vimutto)—by this, it is shown that even one who is not completely liberated has a state of liberation through mere faith. Or, “liberated by faith” means one who is resolved through faith. “In the way stated” refers to the way stated by “the fruit of stream-entry,” and so on. “Of one who has faith” refers to one who has faith thus: “This path surely leads to the destruction of defilements because it was spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One.” Moreover, since for one who sees successive distinctions in his development by abandoning the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence, etc., there is also direct experience in various respects, it is therefore said, “as if having faith.” The remaining two phrases are synonyms of this. Here, by the statement “the development of the preliminary part of the path,” it is shown that there is a diversity of wisdom among those who are liberated by faith and those who have attained the view, due to the diversity of the path to be approached. In the Abhidhamma Commentary as well, it is said: “There is no diversity in their abandoning of defilements, but there is indeed diversity in wisdom.” And further: “It is concluded that the one liberated by faith does not reach the state of one who has attained the view, precisely because of the diversity of the path to be approached.”

Paññāsaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ adhimattatāya pubbaṅgamaṃ hutvā pavattaṃ anussaratīti dhammānusārī. Tenāha “dhammo”tiādi. Saddhaṃ anussarati saddhāpubbaṅgamaṃ maggaṃ bhāvetīti imamatthaṃ “eseva nayo”ti atidisati. Paññaṃ vāhetīti paññāvāhī, paññaṃ sātisayaṃ pavattetīti attho. Tenāha “paññāpubbaṅgamaṃ ariyamaggaṃ bhāvetī”ti. Saddhāvāhinti ettha vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Ubhatobhāgavimuttādikathāti ubhatobhāgavimuttādīsu āgamanato paṭṭhāya vattabbakathā. Etesanti yathāvuttānaṃ ubhatobhāgavimuttādīnaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ kīṭāgirisutte. Nanu ca aṭṭhasamāpattilābhivasena ubhatobhāgavimutto kāyasakkhīādayo ca abhidhamme āgatā, kathamidha arūpajjhānalābhīvaseneva uddhaṭāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “yasmā”tiādi.

“One who follows the Dhamma” (dhammānusārī) means one who follows the Dhamma, which is reckoned as wisdom, which proceeds having become foremost through its great intensity. Therefore, it is said: “Dhamma,” and so on. The meaning “one who follows faith, develops the path with faith as its forerunner” is extended by “this is the same method.” “One who is borne by wisdom” (paññāvāhī) means one who makes wisdom proceed exceedingly. Therefore, it is said: “One develops the noble path with wisdom as its forerunner.” Regarding “one who is borne by faith” (saddhāvāhī), the meaning should be understood in the way explained. The discussion on the liberated-in-both-ways, etc., refers to the explanation to be given concerning the liberated-in-both-ways and others, starting from the scriptural passage. “These” refers to the aforementioned liberated-in-both-ways and others. “Here” means in this Kīṭāgiri Sutta. Now, since the liberated-in-both-ways, the body-witness, and others are mentioned in the Abhidhamma as those who have obtained the eight attainments, how then are they singled out here merely as those who have obtained the formless jhānas? Anticipating this objection, it is said: “Because,” and so on.

Phusitvā patvā. Paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontīti na āsavā paññāya passīyanti, dassanakāraṇā paññāya parikkhīṇā “disvā paññāya parikkhīṇā”ti vuttā. Dassanāyattaparikkhayattā eva hi dassanaṃ āsavānaṃ khayassa purimakiriyā hotīti. Tathāgatena paveditāti bodhimaṇḍe nisīditvā tathāgatena paṭividdhā viditā pacchā paresaṃ pākaṭīkatā. “Catusaccadhammā”ti vatvā tadantogadhattā sīlādīnaṃ “imasmiṃ ṭhāne sīlaṃ kathita”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Atthenāti avippaṭisārādipayojanena tasmiṃ tasmiṃ pītiādikena atthena. Kāraṇenāti sappurisūpanissayādinā kāraṇena tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samādhiādipadaṭṭhānatāya sīlādi [M 2.0089] kāraṇe. Ciṇṇacaritattāti saddhāciṇṇabhāvena sambodhāvahabhāve. Tattha tattha vicaritā visesena caritā, tesu tena paññā suṭṭhu carāpitāti attho. Patiṭṭhitā hoti maggena āgatattā. Mattāya parittappamāṇena. Olokanaṃ khamanti, paññāya gahetabbataṃ upenti.

Having touched, having attained. “And for him, having seen with wisdom, the taints are exhausted” means that the taints are not seen by wisdom; rather, because they are exhausted by wisdom for the reason of seeing, it is said, “having seen, exhausted by wisdom.” For it is because their exhaustion is dependent on seeing that seeing is the preliminary action for the destruction of the taints. “Proclaimed by the Tathāgata” means realized and known by the Tathāgata while sitting at the seat of awakening, and later made manifest to others. Having spoken of “the phenomena of the Four Truths,” because virtue and so on are included within them, it is said, “in this place, virtue is spoken of,” and so on. “By meaning” refers to the purpose of non-remorse, etc., and to joy, etc., as the meaning in each case. “By reason” refers to the reason of relying on good people, etc., and because virtue, etc., serve as the proximate cause for concentration, etc., in each case. “Through cultivated conduct” refers to the state of bringing about awakening through the nature of having practiced faith. “Practiced in various respects, especially practiced” means that among them, wisdom is well-exercised by that person. “It is established” because it has come by way of the path. “By a measure” means by a small amount. “They are fit for inspection” means they come to be graspable by wisdom.

Tayoti kāyasakkhidiṭṭhippattasaddhāvimuttā. Yathāṭhitova pāḷiattho, na tattha kiñci niddhāretvā vattabbaṃ atthīti suttantapariyāyena avuttaṃ vadati. Tassa maggassāti sotāpattimaggassa yaṃ kātabbaṃ, tassa adhigatattā. Upari pana tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ atthāya sevamānā anulomasenāsanaṃ, bhajamānā kalyāṇamitte, samannānayamānā indriyāni anupubbena bhāvanāmaggappaṭipāṭiyā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissanti maggassa anekacittakkhaṇikatāyāti ayamettha suttapadese pāḷiyā attho.

They are the three: the body-witness, the one who has attained to the view, and the one liberated by faith. The meaning of the Pāli stands as it is; nothing further should be determined or stated there. Thus, it speaks of what is not stated by the Suttanta method. ‘Of that path’ means of the path of stream-entry, because what is to be done by it has been attained. But for the sake of the three higher paths, by resorting to suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and harmonizing the faculties, they will gradually attain arahantship through the sequence of the path of development, because the path consists of many moments of consciousness. This is the meaning of the Pāli here in this passage of the sutta.

Imameva [V 2.0089] pāḷiṃ gahetvāti “katamo ca puggalo saddhānusārī”ti maggaṭṭhe puggale vatvā “imassa kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave”tiādinā tesaṃ vasena anulomasenāsanasevanādīnaṃ vuttattā imameva yathāvuttaṃ pāḷipadesaṃ gahetvā “lokuttaradhammo bahucittakkhaṇiko”ti vadati. So vattabboti so vitaṇḍavādī evaṃ vattabbo. Yadi maggaṭṭhapuggale vatvā anulomikasenāsanasevanādi pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti maggasamaṅgino eva hutvā te tathā paṭipajjanti, evaṃ sante senāsanapaṭisaṃyuttarūpādivipassanaggahaṇasmiṃ tava matena maggasamaṅgino eva āpajjeyyuṃ, na cetaṃ evaṃ hoti, tasmā suttaṃ me laddhanti yaṃ kiñci mā kathehīti vāretabbo. Tenāha “yadi aññena cittenā”tiādi. Tattha evaṃ santeti nānācitteneva senāsanapaṭisevanādike sati. Tattha pāḷiyaṃ yadi lokuttaradhammasamaṅgino eva pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgikālepi lokuttarasamaṅgitaṃ sace sampaṭicchasi, satthārā saddhiṃ paṭivirujjhasi suttavirodhadīpanato. Tenāha “satthārā hī”tiādi. Dhammavicāraṇā nāma tuyhaṃ avisayo, tasmā yāguṃ pivāhīti uyyojetabbo.

Taking up this very Pāli passage: having spoken of the person at the path stage with ‘And what person is a faith-follower?’ and because it is stated, beginning with ‘Indeed, monks, of this one,’ that they resort to suitable lodgings and so on, taking up this very Pāli passage as explained, he says, ‘The supramundane Dhamma consists of many moments of consciousness.’ That one should be told thus; that sophist should be addressed thus: ‘If, having spoken about the person at the path stage, the resorting to suitable lodgings and so on is stated in the Pāli, then those endowed with the path would practice accordingly. If that were the case, then according to your view, those endowed with the path would also be engaged in insight connected with dwellings, visible form, and so on; but it is not so. Therefore, he should be stopped with, “Do not say just anything, thinking, ‘I have understood the sutta.’”’ Hence it is said, ‘If with another mind,’ and so on. This being the case, when there is resorting to dwellings and so on with different minds. There, in the Pāli, if you accept that one is endowed with the supramundane Dhamma even at the time of being endowed with the five consciousnesses, you contradict the Teacher, as is shown by the contradiction with the sutta. Hence it is said, ‘For with the Teacher,’ and so on. The investigation of the Dhamma is not your domain; therefore, you should be dismissed with, ‘Go drink your gruel.’

183. Ādikenevāti paṭhameneva. Anupubbasikkhāti anupubbeneva pavattasikkhāya. Tenāha “karaṇatthe paccattavacana”nti.
