Saddhā jātā etassāti saddhājāto, agyāhitātipakkhepena jāta-saddassa pacchāvacanaṃ[M 2.0090]. Evametanti adhimuccanaṃ okappaniyasaddhā. Santike nisīdati upaṭṭhānavasena. Sādhukaṃ katvā dhāretīti yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ vācuggatakaraṇavasena taṃ paguṇaṃ katvā sāravasena dhāreti. Chando jāyatīti dhammesu nijjhānakkhamesu ime dhamme bhāvanāpaññāya paccakkhato ussāmīti kattukamyatākusalacchando jāyati. Ussahatīti chando uppādamatte aṭṭhatvā tato bhāvanārambhavasena ussahati. Tulayatiti sammasanavasena saṅkhāre. Tīraṇavipassanāya tulayantoti tīraṇapariññāya jānitvā upari pahānapariññāya vasena paritulayanto paṭijānanto. Maggapadhānaṃ padahatīti maggalakkhaṇaṃ padhānikaṃ maggaṃ padahati. Pesitacittoti nibbānaṃ pati pesitacitto. Nāmakāyenāti maggappaṭipāṭiyā taṃtaṃmaggasampayuttanāmakāyena. Na pana kiñci āhāti dūratāya samānaṃ na kiñci vacanaṃ bhagavā āha te daḷhataraṃ niggaṇhituṃ.

183. ‘Ādikeneva’ means from the very beginning. ‘Anupubbasikkhā’ refers to training that proceeds gradually. Hence it is said, ‘the personal ending in the sense of instrument.’ ‘Saddhājāto’ means one in whom faith has arisen; the word ‘jāta’ is placed after, with the insertion of ‘agyāhita’ etc. ‘Evametaṃ’ refers to the faith of conviction and trust. ‘Sits nearby’ means by way of attending. ‘Having mastered it well, he retains it’ means having made the Dhamma he has heard proficient through verbal recitation, he retains it by grasping its essence. ‘Desire arises’ means that in regard to the Dhammas, which are fit for reflection, the wholesome desire to act arises, thinking, ‘I will strive to realize these Dhammas directly through the wisdom of development.’ ‘He exerts himself’ means that after desire has arisen, he then exerts himself by commencing development. ‘He weighs’ means he examines the formations through contemplation. ‘Weighing with discerning insight’ means knowing with the understanding of discrimination, and then, by way of the understanding of abandoning, fully weighing and acknowledging them. ‘He strives the path-striving’ means he strives the principal striving that is the characteristic of the path. ‘With mind dispatched’ means his mind is dispatched toward Nibbāna. ‘By the mental body’ means by the mental body associated with each respective path in the sequence of the path. ‘But he says nothing’ means the Blessed One says nothing, as if from a distance, to restrain them more firmly.

184. Paṇena vohārena byākaraṇaṃ paṇaviyā, paṇaviyā abhāvena opaṇaviyā, na upetīti na yujjati. Tanti idaṃ idha adhippetaṃ paṇo paṇaviyaṃ dassetuṃ. Tayidaṃ sabbaṃ bhagavā “mayaṃ kho, āvuso, sāyañceva bhuñjāmā”ti assajipunabbasukehi vuttaṃ sikkhāya avattanabhāvadīpanavacanaṃ sandhāya vadati.

184. Paṇaviyā is an explanation by way of a wager or transaction. The absence of paṇaviyā is opaṇaviyā. ‘Na upeti’ means ‘it does not fit’ or ‘it is not appropriate’. Here, this text is intended to show ‘paṇa’ as ‘paṇaviyā’. All this the Blessed One speaks with reference to the statement made by Assaji and Punabbasuka, “We, friend, eat in the evening,” which clarifies their non-observance of the training.

Ukkhipitvāti [V 2.0090] sīsena gahetvā viya samādāya. Anudhammoti anurūpo sabhāvo, sāvakabhāvassa anucchavikā paṭipatti. Rohanīyanti viruḷhibhāvaṃ. Siniyhati ettha, etena vāti sineho, kāraṇaṃ. Taṃ ettha atthīti sinehavantaṃ, pādakanti attho. Taco ekaṃ aṅganti taco vīrapakkhabhāve ekamaṅgaṃ. Padhānaṃ anuyuñjantassa hi tace palujjamānepi taṃnimittaṃ avosānaṃ anāpajjanakasseva vīriyassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ sesesu vattabbaṃ. Tenāha – “arahattaṃ appatvā na vuṭṭhahissāmīti evaṃ paṭipajjatī”ti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

‘Ukkhipitvā’ means having undertaken, as if taking it up with the head. ‘Anudhamma’ means the corresponding nature, the fitting practice for discipleship. ‘Rohanīya’ means the state of growing, flourishing. Affection (`sineho`) is that wherein or whereby one is affectionate (`siniyhati`); it is a cause. That which possesses this is `sinehavantaṃ`, meaning a foundation. ‘The skin is one factor’ means the skin is one factor in the state of heroic effort. For one who is constantly striving, even when the skin is perishing, it is a factor, a cause, of energy that does not give up on that account. The same should be stated for the rest. Therefore it was said: ‘He practices thus: “Without attaining Arahantship, I will not rise up.”’ The rest is easily understood.

Kīṭāgirisuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition clarifying the hidden meaning of the Kīṭāgiri Sutta is complete.

Niṭṭhitā ca bhikkhuvaggavaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the Bhikkhu Vagga is completed.

3. Paribbājakavaggo

3. The Chapter on Wanderers

1. Tevijjavacchasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Tevijjavaccha Sutta

185. Tatthāti [V 2.0091][M 2.0091] ekapuṇḍarīkasaññite paribbājakārāme. Anāgatapubbo lokiyasamudāhāravasena “cirassaṃ kho, bhante”tiādinā vuccati, ayaṃ panettha āgatapubbataṃ upādāya tathā vutto. Bhagavā hi kesañci vimuttijananatthaṃ, kesañci indriyaparipākatthaṃ, kesañci visesādhigamatthaṃ kadāci titthiyārāmaṃ upagacchati. Ananuññāya ṭhatvāti ananujānitabbe ṭhatvā. Anujānitabbaṃ siyā anaññātassa ñeyyassa abhāvato. Yāvatakañhi ñeyyaṃ, tāvatakaṃ bhagavato ñāṇaṃ, yāvatakañca bhagavato ñāṇaṃ tāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ. Tenevāha – “na tassa adiṭṭhamidhatthi kiñci, atho aviññātamajānitabba”ntiādi (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 32; paṭi. ma. 1.121). Sabbaññutaññāṇena hi bhagavā āvajjetvā pajānāti. Vuttañhetaṃ “āvajjanapaṭibaddhaṃ buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇa”nti (mi. pa. 4.1.2). Yadi evaṃ “caraṃ samāhito nāgo, tiṭṭhaṃ nāgo samāhito”ti (a. ni. 6.43) idaṃ suttapadaṃ kathanti? Vikkhepābhāvadīpanapadametaṃ, na anāvajjanenapi ñāṇānaṃ pavattiparidīpanaṃ. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vitthārato vuttameva.

185. ‘There’ means in the wanderers’ park named Ekapuṇḍarīka. ‘Never having come before’ is said by way of worldly convention, as in the expression, ‘It has been a long time, venerable sir,’ but here it is spoken of thus with reference to his having come before. For the Blessed One sometimes approaches the parks of sectarians for the sake of liberating some, maturing the faculties of others, or helping some achieve distinction. ‘Standing without permission’ means standing in a place where permission is required. But for him, nothing requires permission, because there is nothing to be known that is not already known. For whatever is to be known, that much is the Blessed One’s knowledge, and whatever is the Blessed One’s knowledge, that much is to be known. Hence it is said: ‘There is nothing here unseen by him, nor anything unknown or unknowable’ (Mahāni. 156; Cūḷani. Dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 32; Paṭi. Ma. 1.121). The Blessed One knows by adverting with his omniscient knowledge. As it is said: ‘The knowledge of the Blessed One is connected with adverting’ (Mi. Pa. 4.1.2). If so, how is the sutta passage ‘Walking, the nāga is composed; standing, the nāga is composed’ (A. Ni. 6.43) to be understood? This passage illustrates the absence of distraction, not the manifestation of knowledge without adverting. What should be said here has already been explained in detail below.

186. Yāvadevāti idaṃ yathāruci pavatti viya aparāparuppattipi icchitabbāti tadabhāvaṃ dassento āha – “sakiṃ khīṇānaṃ āsavānaṃ puna khepetabbābhāvā”ti. Paccuppannajānanaguṇanti idaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇassa paribhaṇḍañāṇaṃ anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ anādiyitvā vuttaṃ, tassa pana vasena anāgataṃsañāṇaguṇaṃ dassetīti vattabbaṃ siyā.

186. ‘Yāvadeva’ here means that even if one wishes for repeated occurrences according to their liking, their absence is shown by stating, ‘because for those whose taints are destroyed once, there is no need to destroy them again.’ ‘Paccuppannajānanaguṇa’ refers to the quality of knowing the present, stated without taking into account the divine eye knowledge and the knowledge of the future, which are its accessory knowledges. However, it could be said that by means of it, the quality of the knowledge of the future is also indicated.

Gihiparikkhāresūti vatthābharaṇādidhanadhaññādigihiparikkhāresu. Gihiliṅgaṃ pana appamāṇaṃ, tasmā gihibandhanaṃ chinditvā dukkhassantakarā hontiyeva. Sati pana dukkhassantakiriyāya gihiliṅge te na tiṭṭhantiyevāti dassento “yepī”tiādimāha. Sukkhāpetvā samucchinditvā. Arahattaṃ [V 2.0092] pattadivaseyeva pabbajanaṃ vā parinibbānaṃ vāti ayaṃ nayo na sabbasādhāraṇoti āha “bhūmadevatā pana tiṭṭhantī”ti. Tattha kāraṇavacanaṃ [M 2.0092] “nilīyanokāsassa atthitāyā”ti. Araññapabbatādipavivekaṭṭhānaṃ nilīyanokāso. Sesakāmabhaveti kāmaloke. Laḷitajanassāti ābharaṇālaṅkāranaccagītādivasena vilāsayuttajanassa.

"In the requisites of a householder" means in the requisites of a householder, such as clothing, ornaments, wealth, grain, and so on. But the signs of a householder are immeasurable; therefore, having cut off the bonds of household life, they certainly become enders of suffering. Indeed, when there is the ending of suffering, they do not remain in those signs of a householder—showing this, he said, "even those..." and so on. Having caused them to wither and having completely cut them off. This principle that on the very day of attaining arahantship, there is either ordination or final Nibbāna, is not universal, thus he said, "but the earth deities remain." Here, the reason is stated: "because there is a place of concealment." A secluded place, such as a forest or mountain, is a place of concealment. The rest, in the sensual realm, means in the kāma-world. "Of pleasure-loving people" means of people given to amusements by way of adornments, ornaments, dancing, singing, and so on.

Sopīti “so aññatra ekenā”ti vutto sopi. Karato na karīyati pāpanti evaṃ na kiriyaṃ paṭibāhati. Yadi attānaṃyeva gahetvā katheti, atha kasmā mahāsatto tadā ājīvakapabbajjaṃ upagacchīti āha “tadā kirā”tiādi. Tassapīti na kevalaṃ aññesaṃ eva pāsaṇḍānaṃ, tassapi. Vīriyaṃ na hāpesīti tapojigucchavādaṃ samādiyitvā ṭhito virāgatthāya taṃ samādiṇṇavattaṃ na pariccaji, satthusāsanaṃ na chaḍḍesi. Tenāha – “kiriyavādī hutvā sagge nibbattatī”ti.

`Sopi` refers to the one spoken of as 'he, apart from one'. 'For the doer, evil is not done'; thus, he does not reject the doctrine of action. If he speaks taking only himself, then why did the Great Being at that time undertake the ascetic life of the Ājīvakas? He says, 'At that time, indeed,' and so on. 'For him too' means: not only for other heretics, but for him too. 'He did not diminish effort' means: having adopted the doctrine of austerity and revulsion, he stood firm for the sake of dispassion, did not relinquish that adopted practice, and did not discard the Teacher's instruction. Therefore, it is said: 'Being a proponent of action, he is reborn in heaven.'

Tevijjavacchasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The explanation of the profound meaning in the commentary on the Tevijjavacchasutta is complete.

2. Aggivacchasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Aggivaccha Sutta

187. Lokassa [V 2.0093] sassatatāpavattipaṭikkhepavasena pavatto vādo ucchedavādo eva hotīti sassataggāhābhāve ucchedaggāhabhāvato puna paribbājakena “asassato loko”ti vadantena ucchedaggāho pucchito, bhagavatāpi so eva paṭikkhittoti āha “dutiye nāhaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhiko”ti. Antānantikādivasenāti ettha antānantikaggahaṇena antavā loko anantavā lokoti imaṃ vādadvayamāha. Ādi-saddena “taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”ntiādivādacatukkaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, itaraṃ pana dvayaṃ sarūpeneva gahitanti. Paṭikkhepo veditabboti “tatiye nāhaṃ antavādiṭṭhiko, catutthe nāhaṃ anantavādiṭṭhiko”ti evamādinā paṭikkhepo veditabbo. “Hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti ayampi sassatavādo, so ca kho aparantakappikavasena, “sassato loko”ti pana pubbantakappikavasenāti ayametesaṃ viseso. “Na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti ayampi ucchedavādo, so ca kho sattavasena, “asassato loko”ti pana sattasaṅkhāravasenāti vadanti.

187. The view that arises by rejecting the eternal occurrence of the world is indeed annihilationism, because when there is no grasping of eternalism, there is the grasping of annihilationism. Therefore, when the wanderer, in saying "The world is not eternal," asked about the grasping of annihilationism, the Blessed One rejected even that, saying, "Secondly, I do not hold the annihilationist view." 'By way of finite and infinite, etc.' means: here, by the term 'finite and infinite,' he refers to the two views: "The world is finite" and "The world is infinite." By the word "etc." he includes the fourfold views such as "The soul is the same as the body," etc. The other two, however, are taken in their own form. The rejection is to be understood thus: "Thirdly, I do not hold the view that the world is finite; fourthly, I do not hold the view that the world is infinite," and so on. "The Tathāgata exists after death"—this too is eternalism, and that is with regard to speculating about the future, whereas "The world is eternal" is with regard to speculating about the past—this is their distinction. "The Tathāgata does not exist after death"—this too is annihilationism, and that is with regard to a being, whereas they say that "The world is not eternal" is with regard to a being's conditioned phenomena.

189. Sappatibhayaṃ [M 2.0093] uppajjanato saha dukkhenāti sadukkhaṃ. Tenāha “kilesadukkhenā”tiādi. Tesaṃyevāti kilesadukkhavipākadukkhānaṃyeva. Saupaghātakanti sabādhaṃ. Saupāyāsanti saparissamaṃ saupatāpaṃ sapīḷaṃ. Sapariḷāhanti sadarathaṃ.

189. Because it arises with fear, 'with suffering' means `sadukkhaṃ`. Hence it is said, "with the suffering of defilements," and so on. "Of those very things" means only of the suffering of defilements and the suffering of results. "With injury" means with affliction. "With distress" means with exertion, with torment, with oppression. "With feverish heat" means with torment.

Kiñci diṭṭhigatanti imā tāva aṭṭha diṭṭhiyo mā hontu, atthi pana, bho gotama, yaṃ kiñci diṭṭhigataṃ gahitaṃ. Na hi tāya diṭṭhiyā vinā kañci samayaṃ pavattetuṃ yujjatīti adhippāyena pucchati. Apaviddhanti samucchedappahānavasena chaḍḍitaṃ. Paññāya diṭṭhanti vipassanāpaññāsahitāya maggapaññāya bhagavatā paṭividdhaṃ. Yattha uppajjanti, taṃ sattaṃ mathenti sammaddantīti mathitāti āha “mathitānanti tesaṃyeva vevacana”nti. Kañci dhammanti rūpadhammaṃ arūpadhammaṃ vā. Anupādiyitvāti aggahetvā.

'Any view' means: Let these eight views be for now; but is there, good Gotama, any view whatsoever that is held? He asks with the intention: 'For it is not fitting to propound any doctrine without that view.' 'Rejected' means abandoned by way of abandonment through cutting off. 'Seen with wisdom' means penetrated by the Blessed One with the wisdom of the path accompanied by insight wisdom. Because where they arise, they torment and crush that being, they are called 'tormented'; he said that 'tormented' is a synonym for those very things. 'Any phenomenon' means either a material phenomenon or an immaterial phenomenon. 'Without clinging' means without grasping.

190. Na upetīti saṅkhaṃ na gacchatīti atthoti āha “na yujjatī”ti. Anujānitabbaṃ siyā anupādāvimuttassa kañcipi uppattiyā abhāvato. “Evaṃ vimuttacitto na upapajjatī”ti kāmañcetaṃ sabhāvapavedanaṃ parinibbānaṃ, eke pana ucchedavādino “mayampi ‘satto āyatiṃ na upapajjatī’ti vadāma, samaṇo gotamopi tathā vadatī”ti ucchedabhāveyeva patiṭṭhahissanti, tasmā bhagavā [V 2.0094] “na upapajjatīti kho vaccha na upetī”ti āha. “Upapajjatī”ti pana vutte sassatameva gaṇheyyāti yojanā. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Appatiṭṭhoti ucchedavādādivasena patiṭṭhārahito. Anālamboti tesaṃyeva vādānaṃ olambārammaṇassa abhāvena anālambo. Sukhapavesanaṭṭhānanti tesaññeva vādānaṃ sukhapavesanokāsaṃ mā labhatūti. Ananuññāya ṭhatvāti “na upapajjatī”tiādinā anujānitabbāya paṭiññāya ṭhānahetu. Anuññampīti anujānitabbampi dutiyapañhaṃ paṭikkhipi. Pariyatto pana dhammo atthato paccayākāro evāti āha “dhammoti paccayākāradhammo”ti. Aññattha payogenāti imamhā niyyānikasāsanā aññasmiṃ micchāsamaye pavattappayogena, aniyyānikaṃ vividhaṃ micchāpaṭipattiṃ paṭipajjantenāti attho. “Aññavādiyakenā”tipi pāṭho, paccayākārato aññākāradīpakaācariyavādaṃ paggayha tiṭṭhantenāti attho.

190. 'Does not apply' means 'does not come into reckoning,' hence it is said, 'it is not fitting.' It might be permissible because, for one liberated without clinging, there is no possibility of any arising. The statement, "Thus, with a mind liberated, he does not reappear," is indeed a declaration of the natural state of Nibbāna. However, some annihilationists might say, "We too declare, 'A being does not reappear in the future,' and the ascetic Gotama says the same," thus establishing themselves firmly in annihilationism. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Vaccha, 'does not reappear' does not apply." If it were said, "he reappears," they would grasp it as eternalism—this is the connection. The same method applies to the remaining two alternatives. 'Unsupported' means devoid of a basis by way of annihilationist views and so on. 'Without a support' means being so due to the absence of a supporting object for those very views. 'A place for easy entry' means: so that they may not obtain an opportunity for easy entry into those very views. 'Standing without consenting' means: because of standing by a proposition that is not to be consented to, such as 'he does not reappear,' etc. 'Even what should be consented to' means: he rejected even the second question, which was to be assented to. The Dhamma, however, when completely mastered, is in meaning the way of conditions—hence it is said, 'Dhamma means the Dhamma of the way of conditions.' 'By application elsewhere' means: by application in another wrong doctrine outside this teaching that leads to release, that is, by one who engages in diverse wrong practices that do not lead to release. 'By one of another doctrine' is also a reading, meaning 'by one who stands holding onto the doctrines of teachers who declare a way that is different from the way of conditions.'

191. Appaccayoti [M 2.0094] anupādāno, nirindhanoti attho.

191. 'Without a condition' means without clinging; this is the meaning of 'without fuel'.

192. Yena rūpenāti yena bhūtupādādibhedena rūpadhammena. Taṃ rūpaṃ tappaṭibaddhasaṃyojanappahānena khīṇāsava-tathāgatassa pahīnaṃ anuppattidhammataṃ āpannaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “anuppādadhamma”ntiādi. Aññesaṃ jānanāya abhāvaguṇatāya guṇagambhīro. “Ettakā guṇā”ti pamāṇaṃ gaṇhituṃ na sakkuṇeyyo. “Īdisā etassa guṇā”ti pariyogāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya duppariyogāḷhoti. Dujjānoti agādhatāya gambhīro “ettakāni udakaḷhakasatānī”tiādinā pametuṃ na sakkāti appameyyo, tato eva dujjāno. Evamevānti yathā mahāsamuddo gambhīro appameyyo dujjāno, evameva khīṇāsavopi guṇavasena, tasmā ayaṃ rūpādiṃ gahetvā rūpītiādivohāro bhaveyya, parinibbutassa pana tadabhāvā tathā paññāpetuṃ na sakkā, tato taṃ ārabbha upapajjatītiādi na yujjeyya. Yathā pana vijjamāno eva jātavedo byattena purisena nīyamāno puratthimādidisaṃ gatoti vucceyya, na nibbuto, evaṃ khīṇāsavopīti dassento “evamevā”tiādimāha.

192. "By which form" means by which form-phenomenon, distinguished by divisions such as primary and derived elements. That form, through the abandonment of the fetters connected with it, is abandoned for the Tathāgata whose taints are destroyed, having attained the nature of non-arising. Therefore, it is said in the Pāli text, "of non-arising nature," and so on. Due to the quality of being unknowable to others, he is profound in qualities. One would not be able to grasp the measure, thinking, "So many are his virtues." Because of the inability to fathom, thinking "Such are his virtues," he is hard to fathom. "Hard to know" means he is profound because of his unfathomable depth. Because one cannot measure, saying "So many hundreds of water-pots," and so on, he is immeasurable, and therefore hard to know. In the same way—just as the great ocean is deep, immeasurable, and hard to know, so too is the one whose taints are destroyed, in terms of his virtues. Therefore, this designation 'one with form,' etc., might exist with respect to form and so on. But for one who is fully extinguished, since that does not exist, it is not possible to designate him thus. Hence, to say that he arises with reference to that would not be fitting. Just as when an existing fire is being led by a skilled person, it might be said to have gone to the eastern direction, etc., but not when it is extinguished, so too is the one whose taints are destroyed. Illustrating this, he says, "in the same way," and so on.

Aniccatāti ettha aniccatāgahaṇaṃ asāranidassanaṃ. Tena yathā so sālarukkho sākhāpalāsādiasārāpagamena suddho sāre patiṭṭhito, evamayaṃ dhammavinayo sāsavasaṅkhātaasāravigamena lokuttaradhammasāre patiṭṭhitoti dasseti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Herein, the taking up of impermanence is an illustration of the absence of essence. Just as that sal tree, with the removal of its non-essential parts such as branches and leaves, stands established in its pure essence, so too this Dhamma-Vinaya, with the removal of the non-essence known as 'that with taints,' is established in the supramundane Dhamma-essence. The rest is easily understood.

Aggivacchasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The explanation of the hidden meaning in the Aggivaccha Sutta Commentary is complete.

3. Mahāvacchasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Mahāvaccha Sutta

193. Saha [V 2.0095] kathā etassa atthīti sahakathī, “mayaṃ pucchāvasena tumhe vissajjanavasenā”ti evaṃ sahapavattakathoti attho. Etasseva kathitāni, tattha paṭhame vijjāttayaṃ desitaṃ, dutiye agginā dassitanti tevijjavacchasuttaṃ aggivacchasuttanti nāmaṃ visesetvā vuttaṃ. Sīghaṃ laddhiṃ na vissajjenti, yasmā saṅkhārānaṃ niyatoyaṃ vināso anaññasamuppādo, hetusamuppannāpi na cirena nijjhānaṃ khamanti, na lahuṃ. Tenāha “vasātela [M 2.0095] …pe… sujjhantī”ti. Pacchimagamanaṃ ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā. Yaṭṭhiṃ ālambitvā udakaṃ tarituṃ otaranto puriso “yaṭṭhiṃ otaritvā udake patamāno”ti vutto. Kammapathavasena vitthāradesananti saṃkhittadesanaṃ upādāya vuttaṃ. Tenāha “mūlavasena cetthā”tiādi. Vitthārasadisāti kammapathavasena idha desitadesanāva mūlavasena desitadesanaṃ upādāya vitthārasadisā. Vitthāradesanā nāma natthīti na kevalaṃ ayameva, atha kho sabbāpi buddhānaṃ nippariyāyena ujukena niravasesato vitthāradesanā nāma natthi desanāñāṇassa mahāvisayatāya karaṇasampattiyā ca tajjāya mahānubhāvattā sabbaññutaññāṇassa. Sabbaññutaññāṇasamaṅgitāya hi avasesapaṭisambhidānubhāvitāya aparimitakālasambhatañāṇasambhārasamudāgatāya kadācipi parikkhayānarahāya anaññasādhāraṇāya paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāya pahūtajivhāditadanurūparūpakāyasampattisampadāya vitthāriyamānā bhagavato desanā kathaṃ parimitā paricchinnā bhaveyya, mahākāruṇikatāya pana bhagavā veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ tattha tattha parimitaṃ paricchinnaṃ katvā niṭṭhapeti. Ayañca attho mahāsīhanādasuttena (ma. ni. 1.146 ādayo) dīpetabbo. Sabbaṃ saṃkhittameva attajjhāsayavasena akathetvā bodhaneyyapuggalajjhāsayavasena desanāya niṭṭhāpitattā. Na cettha dhammasāsanavirodho pariyāyaṃ anissāya yathādhammaṃ dhammānaṃ bodhitattā sabbalahuttā cāti.

193. One who has conversation with him is called ‘sahakathī,’ meaning ‘We ask, and you answer,’ thus indicating a dialogue that proceeds together. It is taught in this sutta: in the first, the threefold knowledge is taught; in the second, it is shown by fire. Thus, the Tevijjavaccha Sutta and the Aggivaccha Sutta are mentioned, specifying the name. They do not quickly relinquish their views, since this destruction of formations is fixed, not produced by another cause; and even though arisen from causes, they do not endure for long, nor do they perish quickly. Therefore, it is said: ‘Like sesame oil... they are purified.’ The final going is because knowledge has reached maturity. Just as a man descending to cross water, holding a staff, is said to be ‘descending with the staff and falling into the water.’ The detailed teaching by way of the course of action is stated with reference to a brief teaching. Therefore, it is said: ‘By way of the root here,’ and so on. It is similar to a detailed teaching: for the teaching given here by way of the course of action is similar to a detailed teaching, taking up the teaching given by way of the root. There is no such thing as a detailed teaching: not only this, but indeed all the teachings of the Buddhas, being direct, straightforward, and without remainder, are not called a detailed teaching due to the vast scope of the knowledge of teaching, the perfection of means, and the great power of the knowledge of omniscience arising from it. For the Blessed One’s teaching, being endowed with omniscient knowledge, enhanced by the remaining analytical knowledges, arisen from the accumulation of knowledge gathered over immeasurable time, never liable to exhaustion, unique analytical knowledge of inspired speech, and the perfection of a body adorned with a broad tongue and other corresponding marks—how could it be limited or confined when expounded? Yet, out of great compassion, the Blessed One completes it in a measured and defined way, suited to the inclinations of those to be taught in each instance. This meaning should be explained by the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta (MN 1.146 etc.). All is indeed brief, for the teaching is completed not by speaking according to one’s own intention, but according to the inclinations of those persons capable of being enlightened. And there is no contradiction with the teaching of the Dhamma here, because the principles are taught in accordance with the Dhamma, without relying on indirect expression, and because all is easily understood.

194. Satta dhammā kāmāvacarā sampattasamādānaviratīnaṃ idhādhippetattā.

194. The seven qualities are of the sense sphere, because abstinences as accomplishments and as undertakings are intended here.

Aniyametvāti “sammāsambuddho, sāvako”ti vā niyamaṃ visesena akatvā. Attānameva…pe… veditabbaṃ, tathā hi paribbājako “tiṭṭhatu bhavaṃ gotamo”ti āha.

‘Without specifying’ means not making a specific designation such as ‘a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One or a disciple.’ It should be understood as referring to oneself... For thus the wanderer said: ‘Let the venerable Gotama stay.’

195. Satthāva [V 2.0096] arahā hoti paṭipattiyā pāripūribhāvato. Tasmiṃ byākateti tasmiṃ “ekabhikkhupi sāvako”tiādinā suṭṭhu pañhe kathite.

195. The Teacher is indeed an Arahant because of the perfection of his practice. 'When that was explained' means: when the question, beginning with ‘Is there even one bhikkhu who is a disciple?’, was well spoken.

196. Sampādakoti paṭipattisampādako.

196. ‘Sampādaka’ means one who accomplishes the practice.

197. Sekhāya [M 2.0096] vijjāyāti sekhalakkhaṇappattāya maggapaññāya sātisayaṃ katvā karaṇavasena vuttā, phalapaññā pana tāya pattabbattā kammabhāvena vuttā. Tenāha “heṭṭhimaphalattayaṃ pattabba”nti. Imaṃ panettha aviparītamatthaṃ pāḷito eva viññāyamānaṃ appaṭivijjhanato vitaṇḍavādī “yāvatakaṃ sekhena pattabbaṃ, anuppattaṃ taṃ mayā”ti vacanalesaṃ gahetvā “arahattamaggopi anena pattoyevā”ti vadati. Evanti idāni vuccamānāya gāthāya.

197. ‘By the knowledge of a trainee’ means the wisdom of the path that has attained the characteristics of a trainee, spoken of with excellence by way of agency. But the wisdom of the fruit is spoken of in terms of object, because it is to be attained by that. Therefore, it is said: ‘The lower three fruits are to be attained.’ Here, though this unperverted meaning is understood from the Pāli itself, the sophist, not having penetrated it, seizing upon a trace of a saying, ‘Whatever is to be attained by a trainee, that I have attained,’ says, ‘Even the path to Arahantship has been attained by this trainee.’ ‘Thus’ refers to the verse now being spoken.

Kilesāni pahāya pañcāti pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanasaṅkhāte saṃkilese pahāya pajahitvā, pahānahetu vā. Paripuṇṇasekhoti sabbaso vaḍḍhitasekhadhammo. Aparihānadhammoti aparihānasabhāvo. Na hi yassa phātigatehi sīlādidhammehi parihāni atthi, samādhimhi paripūrakāritāya cetovasippatto. Tenāha “samāhitindriyo”ti. Aparihānadhammattāva ṭhitatto.

‘Having abandoned the five defilements’ means having abandoned, having given up, the defilements known as the five lower fetters, or it is the cause of abandoning. ‘A perfected trainee’ means one whose trainee qualities are perfected in every way. ‘Not subject to decline’ means one whose nature is not subject to decline. For there is no decline in one whose virtues and other qualities have reached fulfillment, who has attained mastery of mind through perfecting concentration. Therefore, it is said: ‘With faculties composed.’ Because of being by nature not subject to decline, one is steadfast.

Anāgāminā hi asekhabhāvāvahā dhammā paripūretabbā, na sekhabhāvāvahāti so ekantaparipuṇṇe sekho vutto. Etaṃ na buddhavacananti “maggo bahucittakkhaṇiko”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ na buddhavacanaṃ anantarekantavipākadānato, bahukkhattuṃ pavattane payojanābhāvato ca lokuttarakusalassa, “samādhimānantarikaññamāhu (khu. pā. 6.5; su. ni. 228), na pāraṃ diguṇaṃ yantī”ti (su. ni. 719) evamādīni suttapadāni etassatthasādhakāni. Orambhāgiyasaṃyojanappahānena sekkhadhammaparipūribhāvassa vuttatāya attho tava vacanena virujjhatīti. Assa āyasmato vacchassa.

For by a Non-returner, the qualities leading to the state of a non-trainee must be perfected, not those leading to the state of a trainee; thus, he is called a trainee who is absolutely perfected. ‘This is not the word of the Buddha’ means this statement, ‘The path has many moments of consciousness,’ is not the word of the Buddha because the supramundane wholesome gives an immediate and certain result, and because there is no purpose for it to occur many times. ‘They say concentration is immediately successive’ (Khp 6.5; Sn 228), ‘They do not go to the far shore a second time’ (Sn 719), and such sutta passages support this meaning. The meaning that the trainee qualities are perfected through the abandonment of the lower fetters is contradicted by your statement. This is the Venerable Vaccha’s statement.

198. Abhiññā vā kāraṇanti yañhi taṃ tatra tatra sakkhibhabbatāsaṅkhātaṃ iddhividhapaccanubhavanādi, tassa abhiññā kāraṇaṃ. Atha iddhividhapaccanubhavanādi abhiññā, evaṃ sati abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Avasāne chaṭṭhābhiññāya pana arahattaṃ. Ettha ca yasmā paṭhamasutte āsavakkhayo adhippeto, āsavā khīṇā eva, na puna khepetabbā, tasmā tattha “yāvadevā”ti na vuttaṃ. Idha phalasamāpatti adhippetā, sā ca punappunaṃ samāpajjīyati, tasmā “yāvadevā”ti vuttaṃ. Tato eva hi “arahattaṃ vā kāraṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Tañhi “kudāssu [V 2.0097] nāmāhaṃ tadāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharissāmi, [M 2.0097] yadariyā etarahi upasampajja viharantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.465; 3.307) anuttaresu vimokkhesu pihaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā abhiññā nibbattentassa kāraṇaṃ, tayidaṃ sabbasādhāraṇaṃ na hotīti sādhāraṇavasena naṃ dassento “arahattassa vipassanā vā”ti āha.

198. ‘Or direct knowledge is the cause’ means that which is called the ability to witness here and there—such as experiencing the kinds of psychic powers—has direct knowledge as its cause. Then, if experiencing psychic powers and so on is direct knowledge, in that case, the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge is the cause. Finally, for the sixth direct knowledge, arahantship is the cause. Here, because the destruction of the taints is intended in the first discourse, and the taints are indeed destroyed, not to be destroyed again, therefore, ‘only up to that extent’ is not stated there. Here, the attainment of fruition is intended, and it is entered into again and again, thus ‘only up to that extent’ is stated. For that very reason, it is said: ‘or arahantship is the cause.’ For that is the cause for one who, having aroused longing for the unsurpassed liberations by thinking, ‘When, indeed, shall I enter and dwell in that base which the noble ones now enter and dwell in?’ (MN 1.465; 3.307), generates direct knowledge. Since this is not common to all, to show it in a general way, it is said: ‘or insight for the sake of arahantship.’

200. Paricaranti nāma vippakatabrahmacariyavāsattā. Pariciṇṇo hoti sāvakena nāma satthu dhamme kattabbā paricariyā sammadeva niṭṭhāpitattā. Tenāha “iti…pe… thero evamāhā”ti. Tesaṃ guṇānanti tesaṃ asekkhaguṇānaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

200. ‘They attend upon’ means due to living an incomplete holy life. ‘Attended upon by the disciple’ means the service to be performed in the Teacher’s Dhamma has been rightly fulfilled. Therefore, it is said: ‘Thus... the elder spoke thus.’ ‘Their qualities’ refers to their qualities as non-trainees. The rest is easily understood.

Mahāvacchasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of the hidden meaning in the Commentary on the Mahāvaccha Sutta is complete.

4. Dīghanakhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Dīghanakha Sutta

201. Khananaṃ [V 2.0098] khataṃ, sūkarassa khataṃ ettha atthīti sūkarakhatā, sūkarassa vā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde paṭhamaṃ khataṃ upādāya sūkarakhatā, tāya. Evaṃnāmaketi evaṃ itthiliṅgavasena laddhanāmake. Paṃsudhoteti dhotapaṃsuke. Otaritvā abhiruhitabbanti pakatibhūmito anekehi sopānaphalakehi otaritvā puna leṇadvāraṃ katipayehi abhiruhitabbaṃ.

201. "Dug up" means excavated. "Sūkarakhatā" means either there was an excavation dug by a pig here, or it is named after the first excavation done by a pig in this Buddha’s dispensation, by that. "Thus-named" means thus named in the feminine gender. "Dust-washed" means with the dust washed off. "Having descended, one must ascend" means descending from the natural ground by means of many step-planks and ascending again to the cave entrance by a few.

Ṭhitakovāti mātulassa ṭhitattā tattha sagāravasapatissavasena ṭhitakova. Kiñcāpi sabba-saddo avisesato anavasesapariyādāyako, vatthuadhippāyānurodhī pana saddappayogoti tamatthaṃ sandhāya paribbājako “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti āha. Yā loke manussaupapattiyotiādikā upapattiyo, tā anatthasamudāgatā tattha tattheva sattānaṃ ucchijjanato, tasmā samayavādīhi vuccamānā sabbā āyatiṃ uppajjanaupapatti na hoti. Jalabubbuḷakā viya hi ime sattā tattha tattha samaye uppajjitvā bhijjanti, tesaṃ tattha paṭisandhi natthīti assa adhippāyo. Tenāha “paṭisandhiyo”tiādi. Assa adhippāyaṃ muñcitvāti yenādhippāyena paribbājako “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti āha, taṃ tassa adhippāyaṃ jānantopi ajānanto viya hutvā tassa akkhare tāva dosaṃ dassentoti [M 2.0098] padesasabbaṃ sandhāya tena vuttaṃ, sabbasabbavisayaṃ katvā tattha dosaṃ gaṇhanto. Yathā loke kenaci “sabbaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ musā”ti vutte tassa vacanassa sabbantogadhattā musābhāvo āpajjeyya, evaṃ imassapi “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti vadato tathā pavattā diṭṭhipi nakkhamatīti atthato āpannameva hoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “esāpi te diṭṭhi nakkhamatī”ti. Yathā pana kenaci “sabbaṃ vuttaṃ musā”ti vutte adhippāyānurodhinī saddappavatti, tassa vacanaṃ muñcitvā tadaññesameva musābhāvo ñāyāgato, evamidhāpi “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti vacanato yassā diṭṭhiyā vasena “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti tena vuttaṃ, taṃ diṭṭhiṃ muñcitvā tadaññameva yathādhippetaṃ sabbaṃ nakkhamatīti ayamattho ñāyāgato, bhagavā pana vādīvaro sukhumāya āṇiyā thūlaṃ āṇiṃ nīharanto viya upāyena tassa diṭṭhigataṃ nīharituṃ tassa adhippāyena avatvā saddavasena tāva labbhamānaṃ dosaṃ dassento “yāpi kho te”tiādimāha. Tena vuttaṃ – “assa adhippāyaṃ muñcitvā akkhare tāva dosaṃ dassento”ti.

"Standing firm" means that because of his uncle's standing, he stood there with reverence and deference. Although the word 'all' is generally inclusive and exhaustive, the usage of words depends on the intended meaning. Referring to that meaning, the wanderer said, 'All is not pleasing to me.' The rebirths in the world, such as human rebirth, are accompanied by disadvantage because beings are annihilated in those very states. Thus, according to the proponents of such theories, all future arising and rebirth do not occur. Like bubbles in water, these beings arise and burst in their respective moments—there is no rebirth-linking for them there. This is his intention; hence the statement 'rebirth-linking' and so on. "Setting aside his intended meaning" means that, although knowing the intention with which the wanderer said, 'All is not pleasing to me,' acting as if not knowing, the Buddha first pointed out the fault in his words by taking what was said with reference to a partial 'all' and making it a matter concerning a universal 'all' to find fault. Just as in the world, if someone says, 'All that is said is false,' the statement itself would be false because it encompasses everything, so too for this wanderer who says, 'All is not pleasing to me,' it follows in meaning that his view itself is also not pleasing. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'This view of yours is also not pleasing.' Just as, on the other hand, when someone says, 'All that is said is false,' the usage of words follows the intended meaning, and setting aside that statement, only the falsity of other statements is logically established; so too here, from his statement 'All is not pleasing to me,' the meaning is logically established that, setting aside the very view by means of which he said this, everything else as intended is not pleasing. But the Blessed One, a skilled debater, like one extracting a thick peg with a fine one, skillfully drew out his view without addressing his intended meaning. Instead, He first pointed out the fault obtainable from the words themselves, saying, 'Whatever view you hold...' Hence it is said: 'Setting aside his intended meaning, He first pointed out the fault in the words.'

Paribbājako [V 2.0099] pana yaṃ sandhāya “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti mayā vuttaṃ, “ayaṃ so”ti yathāvuttadosapariharaṇatthaṃ tasmiṃ atthe vuccamāne esa doso sabbo na hoti, evampi samaṇo gotamo mama vāde dosameva āropeyyāti attano ajjhāsayaṃ niguhitvā yathāvuttadosaṃ pariharitukāmo “esā me”tiādimāha. Tattha tampassa tādisamevāti yaṃ “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti gahitaṃ vatthu, tampi tādisameva bhaveyyāti. Ayañca sabbantogadhadiṭṭhi mayhampi diṭṭhivatthu, taṃ me khameyyavāti. Yasmā pana “esāpi diṭṭhi tuyhaṃ nakkhamatī”ti yāpi diṭṭhi vuttā bhavatā gotamena, sāpi mayhaṃ nakkhamati, tasmā sabbaṃ me nakkhamatevāti paribbājakassa adhippāyo. Tenāha – “taṃ pariharāmīti saññāya vadatī”ti. Tathā ca vakkhati “tasmāpi ucchedadiṭṭhi mayhaṃ nakkhamatī”ti. “Esā me diṭṭhī”ti yā ṭhitibhūtā diṭṭhi, tāya “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti panettha sabbaggahaṇena gahitattā āha – “atthato panassa esā diṭṭhi na me khamatīti āpajjatī”ti. Ayaṃ dosoti dassento āha “yassa panā”tiādi. Esāti diṭṭhi. Rucitanti diṭṭhidassanena abhinivisitvā rocetvā gahitaṃ. Tena hi diṭṭhiakkhamena arucitena bhavitabbanti sati diṭṭhiyā akkhamabhāve tato tāya gahitāya khameyya rucceyya yathā, evaṃ sabbassa akkhamabhāveti [M 2.0099] aparabhāge sabbaṃ khamati ruccatīti āpajjati. Na panesa taṃ sampaṭicchatīti esa “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti evaṃ vadanto ucchedavādī taṃ vuttanayena sabbassa khamanaṃ ruccanaṃ na sampaṭicchati. Ñāyena vuttamatthaṃ kathaṃ na sampaṭicchatīti āha “kevalaṃ tassāpi ucchedadiṭṭhiyā ucchedameva gaṇhātī”ti. Sabbesañhi dhammānaṃ āyatiṃ uppādaṃ aruccitvā taṃ sandhāya ayaṃ “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti vadati, ucchedadiṭṭhikesu ca ucchinnesu kuto ucchedadiṭṭhisabhāvoti.

The wanderer, however, with reference to what was said by himself, 'All is not pleasing to me,' and thinking 'this is it,' sought to avoid the aforesaid fault. Concealing his own inclination and wishing to avoid the fault, he said, 'This is my view,' etc., reasoning thus: 'When that meaning is stated, this fault is not entirely present; even so, the ascetic Gotama would just impute a fault to my statement.' Therein, 'that too for him is just the same' means that the matter taken up as 'All is not pleasing to me' would also be just the same. And this view that encompasses everything is also a matter for my view; may that be pleasing to me. But because the view stated by the venerable Gotama, 'This view too is not pleasing to you,' is also not pleasing to me, therefore the wanderer's intention is 'Everything is indeed not pleasing to me.' Hence it is said: 'He speaks with the perception, "I am avoiding that."' And so he will say, 'Therefore, the annihilationist view is also not pleasing to me.' 'This is my view' refers to the established view. Because it is included by the taking of 'all' in 'All is not pleasing to me,' it is said: 'But in meaning, it follows that for him "this view is not pleasing to me."' Pointing out that this is the fault, it is said, 'But for whom,' etc. 'This' refers to the view. 'Pleasing' means it is grasped by adhering to and approving of it through seeing the view. Therefore, the view should be not pleasing and not approved of. If the view is not pleasing, how could that which is grasped by it be pleasing and approved of? Thus, if everything is not pleasing, it follows that on the other side, everything is pleasing and approved of. But he does not accept that. This annihilationist who says, 'All is not pleasing to me,' does not accept the pleasing and approval of everything in the aforesaid manner. How does he not accept the meaning stated logically? It is said: 'He merely grasps the annihilation of that very annihilationist view.' For, not approving of the future arising of any phenomena, with reference to that he says, 'All is not pleasing to me.' And when the annihilationists themselves are annihilated, whence the nature of the annihilationist view?

Tenāti tena kāraṇena, yasmā idhekacce sattā īdisaṃ diṭṭhiṃ paggayha tiṭṭhanti, tasmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pajahanakena vā cittena ekajjhaṃ gahetvā pajahanakehi appajahanake niddhāretuṃ bhagavā “ato…pe… bahutarā”ti avocāti āha – “pajahanakesu nissakka”nti yathā “pañcasīlehi pabhāvanā paññavantatarā”ti. “Bahū”ti vatvā na kevalaṃ bahū, atha kho ativiya bahūti dassento “bahutarā”ti āha. “Bahū hī”ti nayidaṃ nissakkavacanaṃ, atha kho paccattavacanaṃ. Kathaṃ hi-saddoti āha “hi-kāro nipātamatta”nti. Anissakkavacanaṃ tāva tassa pajahanakānaṃ bahubhāvato tepi parato “bahutarā”ti vuccīyanti. Mūladassananti ye tādisaṃ dassanaṃ paṭhamaṃ upādiyanti, tajjātikameva pacchā gahitadassanaṃ. Vijātiyañhi paṭhamaṃ gahitadassanaṃ appahāya vijātiyassa gahaṇaṃ na sambhavati viruddhassa abhinivesassa saha anavaṭṭhānato[V 2.0100]. Aviruddhaṃ pana mūladassanaṃ avissajjitvā visayādibhedabhinnaṃ aparadassanaṃ gahetuṃ labbhati. Tenāha “ettha cā”tiādi.

'Therefore' means for that reason: because some beings here hold such a view and persist in it, therefore it is said. Or, having grasped it all at once with a mind that abandons, the Blessed One spoke 'from this... and so on... more numerous' in order to distinguish those who abandon from those who do not. Thus it is said: 'a statement of comparison regarding those who abandon,' as in 'those who are established in the five precepts are wiser.' Having said 'many,' not merely many, but to show an exceedingly great number, he said 'more numerous.' 'For many'—this is not a statement of comparison, but rather an absolute statement. How so? He says the particle 'hi' is merely an expletive. The non-comparative statement ('many') is due to the abundance of those who abandon, and they are later called 'more numerous'. 'Root-seeing' means that those who first adopt such a view, later grasp only a view of that same kind. For without abandoning a first-grasped view of one kind, it is impossible to grasp a view of another kind, because conflicting adherence cannot coexist. But without giving up a non-conflicting root-view, one can grasp another view differing in object and so forth. Hence he said, 'and here,' and so on.

Tattha kiñcāpi ekaccasassatavādo sassatucchedābhinivesānaṃ vasena yathākkamaṃ sassatucchedaggāhanajātiko, ucchedaggāhena pana sassatābhinivesassa taṃgāhena ca asassatābhinivesassa virujjhanato ubhayatthapi “ekaccasassataṃ vā gahetuṃ na sakkā”ti vuttaṃ, tathā “sassataṃ vā ucchedaṃ vā na sakkā gahetu”nti ca. Mūlasassatañhi paṭhamaṃ gahitaṃ. Āyatanesupi yojetabbanti paṭhamaṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ sassatanti gahetvā aparabhāge na kevalaṃ cakkhāyatanameva sassataṃ, sotāyatanampi sassataṃ, ghānāyatanādipi sassatanti gaṇhātītiādinā yojetabbaṃ. Āyatanesupīti pi-saddena dhātūnaṃ indriyānampi gāho daṭṭhabbo. Idaṃ sandhāyāti [M 2.0100] “mūle sassata”ntiādinā vuttapaṭhamaggāhassa samānajātiyaṃ aparaggāhaṃ sandhāya.

Here, although the doctrine of partial eternalism, due to adherence to eternalism and annihilationism, becomes sequentially a type of grasping of eternalism and annihilationism, yet because the grasping of annihilationism contradicts the adherence to eternalism, and that grasping contradicts the adherence to non-eternalism, it is said in both cases that 'one cannot grasp even partial eternalism,' and also 'one cannot grasp either eternalism or annihilationism.' For the root eternalism is first grasped. Regarding the sense bases as well, it should be applied thus: first, the eye base is taken as eternal, and subsequently, not only the eye base is eternal, but also the ear base is eternal, and the nose base and so on are eternal—thus one grasps. By the word 'pi' in 'āyatanesupi' (in the sense bases also), the grasping of the elements and faculties should also be understood. This is said with reference to the subsequent grasping of the same kind as the initial grasping stated as 'root eternalism,' and so on.

Dutiyavāre paṭhamavāre vuttasadisaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tattha ādīnavaṃ disvāti “yadi rūpaṃ sassataṃ siyā, nayidaṃ ābādhāya saṃvatteyya. Yasmā ca kho idaṃ rūpaṃ asassataṃ, tasmā abhiṇhapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena udayavayavantatāya rūpaṃ aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ, sassatābhiniveso micchā”tiādinā tattha sassatavāde ādīnavaṃ dosaṃ disvā. Oḷārikanti tasmā paṭipīḷanaṭṭhena ayāthāvaggāhatāya rūpaṃ na saṇhaṃ oḷārikameva. Vedanādīnampi aniccādibhāvadassanaṃ rūpavedanāādīnaṃ samānayogakkhamattā. Vissajjetīti pajahati.

In the second instance, it should be understood in the same way as stated for the first instance. Here, 'having seen the danger' means: having seen the danger, the fault, in the doctrine of eternalism in this way: 'If form were eternal, it would not conduce to affliction. But because this form is not eternal, therefore, on account of its constant oppression and its nature of arising and passing away, form is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen; adherence to eternalism is wrong,' and so on. 'Coarse' means that because of its nature of oppression and because it is wrongly grasped, form is not subtle, but is indeed coarse. The seeing of the state of impermanence and so on with regard to feelings and the rest is due to form, feelings, and so on being suitable for the same application. 'He relinquishes' means he abandons.

Tisso laddhiyoti sassatucchedaekaccasassatadiṭṭhiyo. Yasmā sassatadiṭṭhikā vaṭṭe rajjanassa āsannā. Tathā hi te olīyantīti vuccanti, bhavābhavadiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena imesaṃ sattānaṃ saṃsārato sīsukkhipanaṃ natthīti etāva tisso visesato gahetabbā.

'Three doctrines' means the views of eternalism, annihilationism, and partial eternalism. For those who hold the eternalist view are close to finding delight in the cycle of rebirth. Indeed, they are said to be 'those who lag behind,' for due to their views of existence and non-existence, there is no lifting the head from saṃsāra for these beings. For this reason, these three should be especially understood.

Idhalokaṃ paralokañca atthīti jānātīti ettāvatā sassatadassanassa appasāvajjatākāraṇamāha, vaṭṭaṃ assādeti, abhinandatīti iminā dandhavirāgatāya. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. Idhalokaṃ paralokañca atthīti jānātīti iminā tāsu tāsu gatīsu sattānaṃ saṃsaraṇaṃ paṭikkhipatīti dasseti, sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ atthīti jānātīti iminā kammaphalaṃ. Kusalaṃ na karotīti iminā kammaṃ, akusalaṃ karonto na bhāyatīti iminā puññāpuññāni sabhāvato jāyantīti dasseti. Vaṭṭaṃ assādeti abhinandati tanninnabhāvato[V 2.0101]. Sīghaṃ laddhiṃ jahituṃ na sakkoti vaṭṭupacchedassa aruccanato. Ucchedavādī hi tasmiṃ bhave ucchedaṃ maññati. Tato paraṃ idhalokaṃ paralokañca atthīti jānāti sukatadukkaṭānaṃ phalaṃ atthīti jānāti kammaphalavādībhāvato. Yebhuyyena hi ucchedavādī sabhāvaniyatiyadicchābhinivesesu aññatrābhiniveso hoti. Sīghaṃ dassanaṃ pajahati vaṭṭābhiratiyā abhāvato. Pāramiyo pūretuṃ sakkonto paccekabuddho hutvā, lokavohāramatteneva so sammāsambuddho hutvā parinibbāyatīti yojanā. Asakkontoti buddho hotuṃ asakkonto. Abhinīhāraṃ [M 2.0101] katvā aggasāvakādibhāvassa abhinīhāraṃ sampādetvā. Sāvako hutvāti aggasāvako mahāsāvako hutvā, tatthāpi tevijjo chaḷabhiñño paṭisambhidāppatto vā sukkhavipassako eva vā buddhasāvako hutvā parinibbāyati. Sabbamidaṃ ucchedavādino kalyāṇamittanissayena sammattaniyāmokkamane khippavirāgatādassanatthaṃ āgataṃ. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi.

By the words 'He knows that this world and the other world exist,' he states the reason for the eternalist view being the least blameworthy. By 'He delights in the cycle, he rejoices,' he indicates slowness in becoming dispassionate. Therefore, it is said, 'Thus,' and so on. By 'He knows that this world and the other world exist,' it is shown that he does not reject the wandering of beings in various destinations. By 'He knows that the fruit of good and evil deeds exists,' he indicates the fruit of kamma. He delights in the cycle and rejoices due to his inclination towards it. He is unable to quickly abandon the doctrine, because he does not approve of the cutting off of the cycle. For an annihilationist conceives of annihilation in that very existence. Beyond that, he knows that this world and the other world exist, and he knows that the fruit of good and evil deeds exists, because he is one who holds the doctrine of the fruit of kamma. For the most part, an annihilationist is one who adheres to views of inherent nature, determinism, or chance, or has some other adherence. He quickly abandons the view due to a lack of delight in the cycle. The connection is as follows: one who is able to fulfill the perfections, having become a Paccekabuddha, or having become a Perfectly Enlightened One, attains parinibbāna merely through worldly convention. 'One who is unable' means one who is unable to become a Buddha. Having made an aspiration, having accomplished the aspiration for the state of a chief disciple and so on, 'having become a disciple' means having become a chief disciple or a great disciple—and in that case, whether one with the threefold knowledge, the six higher knowledges, or the analytical knowledges, or even a bare-insight practitioner—having become a disciple of the Buddha, he attains parinibbāna. All this is stated to show the swift dispassion of an annihilationist who enters the fixed course of rightness through reliance on a good spiritual friend. Therefore, it is said, 'Thus,' and so on.

202. Kañjiyenevāti āranāḷena. Kañjiyasadisena ucchedadassanena. Pūritoti paripuṇṇajjhāsayo. Soti paribbājako. Appahāyāti abhinditvā. Viggahoti kalaho idameva saccaṃ, moghamaññanti aññamaññaṃ viruddhaggāhoti katvā. Vivādanti viruddhavādaṃ. Vighātanti virodhahetukaṃ cittavighātaṃ. Vihesanti viggahavivādanimittaṃ kāyikaṃ cetasikañca kilamathaṃ. Ādīnavaṃ disvāti etāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ evarūpo ādīnavo, aniyyānikabhāvatāya pana sampati āyatiñca mahādīnavoti evaṃ ādīnavaṃ disvā.

202. 'With sour gruel' means with fermented rice-gruel. 'Like sour gruel' refers to the view of annihilationism. 'Filled' means one whose disposition is perfected. 'He' means the wanderer. 'Not having abandoned' means not having broken through. 'Quarrel' means a dispute, holding mutually opposing views with the thought, 'This alone is true, the other is false.' 'Dispute' means contradictory speech. 'Vexation' means mental vexation caused by opposition. 'Harassment' means the physical and mental fatigue on account of quarrels and disputes. 'Having seen the danger' means having seen the danger in this way: 'Such is the danger of these views; and because they do not lead to emancipation, there is great danger both at present and in the future.'

205. “Esohamasmi, eso me attā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.241; saṃ. ni. 3.8) kāyaṃ anvetīti kāyanvayo, soyeva, tassa vā samūho kāyanvayatā, kāyapaṭibaddho kileso. Tenāha “kāyaṃ…pe… attho”ti.

205. With the words 'This I am, this is my self,' and so on (Majjhima Nikāya 1.241; Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.8), it follows after the body, thus it is 'body-following' (kāyanvayo). That very thing, or a collection of it, is 'the state of body-following' (kāyanvayatā). It is a defilement connected with the body. Therefore, it is said, 'the body... and so on... is the meaning.'

Asammissabhāvanti asaṅkarato vavatthitabhāvaṃ. Tena tāsaṃ yathāsakaṃ paccayānaṃ uppajjitvā vigamaṃ dasseti. Evañhi tāsaṃ kadācipi saṅkaro natthi. Tenāha “tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho”tiādi. Sarūpaṃ aggahetvā “aññā vedanā”ti aniyamena vuttattā tameva vigamaṃ dassento “anuppannāva honti antarahitā vā”ti āha. Sarūpato niyametvā vuccamāne kāci anuppannā vā hoti, kāci antarahitā vāti. Cuṇṇavicuṇṇabhāvadassanatthanti khaṇe khaṇe bhijjamānabhāvadassanatthaṃ.

'The state of being unmixed' means the state of being distinct due to non-conmixture. By this, it shows their passing away after having arisen from their respective conditions. For in this way, there is never any mixing of them. Therefore, it is said, 'Herein, this is the meaning in brief,' and so on. Because 'another feeling' is said indeterminately, without grasping its specific nature, showing that very passing away, he said, 'they either have not yet arisen or have disappeared.' When speaking determinately according to its specific nature, some would not have arisen, while others would have disappeared. 'For the purpose of showing the state of being crushed to powder' means for the purpose of showing the state of breaking up moment by moment.

Na kenaci [V 2.0102] saṃvadatīti kenaci puggalena saddhiṃ diṭṭhirāgavasena saṃkiliṭṭhacitto na vadati. Tenāha “sassataṃ gahetvā”tiādi. Na vivadatīti viruddhabhāvo hutvā na vivadati. Parivattetvāti ucchedaṃ gahetvā ekaccasassataṃ gahetvā evaṃ vuttanayena tayopi vādā parivattetvā yojetabbā[M 2.0102]. Tena voharatīti tena lokavohārena lokasamaññaṃ anatidhāvanto satto puriso puggalotiādinā voharati, na pana ito bāhirakā viya abhinivisati. Tenāha “aparāmasanto”ti. Kañci dhammanti rūpādīsu ekaṃ dhammampi. Parāmāsaggāhena aggaṇhantoti “nicca”ntiādinā, “etaṃ mamā”tiādinā ca dhammasabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā parato āmasitvā gahaṇena aggaṇhanto.

'He does not converse with anyone' means he does not speak with any person with a mind defiled by lust for views. Therefore, it is said, 'having grasped eternalism,' and so on. 'He does not dispute' means he does not dispute by becoming an opponent. 'Having revolved' means: having grasped annihilationism, having grasped partial eternalism—thus, all three doctrines should be applied in turn in the manner stated. 'He makes use of' means he makes use of that worldly convention, not overrunning worldly designation, speaking of 'a being,' 'a man,' 'a person,' and so on; but he does not adhere to it like an outsider. Therefore, he said, 'not misapprehending.' 'Any phenomenon' means any one phenomenon among form and so on. 'Not grasping with the grasp of misapprehension' means not grasping by way of misapprehending it from another angle, transgressing the intrinsic nature of the phenomenon with thoughts such as 'permanent,' and so on, or 'this is mine,' and so on.

Katāvīti katakicco. So vadeyyāti khīṇāsavo bhikkhu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāresu sabbaso samucchinnesupi ahaṃ vadāmīti vadeyya. Tattha ahanti niyakajjhattasantāne. Mamanti tassa santakabhūte vatthusmiṃ lokaniruḷhe. Samaññanti tattha sukusalatāya loke samaññā kusalo viditvā. Vohāramattenāti kevalaṃ paccekabuddho hutvā mahābodhipāramiyo pūretuṃ asakkonto sāvako hutvā desavohāramattena na appahīnataṇho viya andhaputhujjano abhinivesanavasena.

'Accomplished' means one who has done what was to be done. 'He might speak' means a monk whose cankers are destroyed, although 'I-making' and 'mine-making' are completely cut off in every way, might say, 'I speak.' Therein, 'I' refers to one's own personal continuity. 'Mine' refers to a thing belonging to him that is established in the world's usage. 'Designation' means that, being skilled in worldly designation, he knows it well due to his great skill therein. 'Merely by way of expression' means that one who, being unable to fulfill the perfections for great enlightenment, becomes a Paccekabuddha or a disciple, speaks merely by way of the region's expression, not by way of adherence like a blind ordinary person whose craving is not abandoned.

206. Sassatādīsūti sassatābhinivesādīsu. Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānanti niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ. Sassataṃ abhiññāyāti sassatadiṭṭhiṃ samudayato atthaṅgamato assādato nissaraṇato abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya paṭivijjhitvā. Pahānanti accantappahānaṃ samucchedaṃ. Rūpassa pahānanti rūpassa tappaṭibaddhasaññojanappahānena pahānaṃ. Anuppādanirodhena niruddhehi āsavehi aggahetvāva cittaṃ vimucci. “Āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccī”ti ettha kiñcipi aggahetvā asesetvā. Soḷasa paññāti mahāpaññādikā soḷasa paññā. Caturaṅgasamannāgatoti puṇṇauposathadivasatā, kenaci anāmantitameva anekasatānaṃyeva anekasahassānaṃ vā bhikkhūnaṃ sannipatitatā, sabbesaṃ ehibhikkhubhāvena upasampannatā, chaḷabhiññatā cāti. Tenāha “tatrimāni aṅgānī”tiādi. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

206. “Sassatādīsūti” means in regard to adherence to eternalism, etc. “Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānanti” is a genitive expression used for specification. “Sassataṃ abhiññāyāti” means having penetrated the eternalist view with superior wisdom regarding its origin, cessation, gratification, and escape. “Pahānanti” means final abandonment, eradication. “Rūpassa pahānanti” means the abandonment of form through the abandonment of the fetters connected with it. The mind was liberated without grasping, through the taints that have ceased by non-arising cessation. In the phrase “Āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccīti,” it means without grasping anything, without remainder. “Soḷasa paññāti” refers to the sixteen kinds of wisdom, such as great wisdom. “Caturaṅgasamannāgatoti” means endowed with four factors: it being the full-moon Uposatha day; the gathering of many hundreds or even thousands of monks without being invited by anyone; all of them having been ordained with the ‘Come, monk’ formula; and their possession of the six higher knowledges. Hence it is said, “Herein, these are the factors,” etc. Whatever herein is not differentiated in meaning should be easily understood.

Dīghanakhasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The commentary on the Dīghanakha Sutta, elucidating its hidden meaning, is complete.

5. Māgaṇḍiyasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta

207. Dve [M 2.0103] māgaṇḍiyāti dve [V 2.0103] māgaṇḍiyanāmakā. Devagabbhasadisanti devānaṃ vasanaovarakasadisaṃ. Etaṃ vuttanti “bhāradvājagottassa brāhmaṇassa agyāgāre tiṇasanthārake”ti etaṃ vuttaṃ. Na kevalaṃ taṃ divasamevāti yaṃ divasaṃ māgaṇḍiyo paribbājako tiṇasanthārakaṃ paññattaṃ, na kevalaṃ taṃ divasameva bhagavā yenaññataro vanasaṇḍo, tenupasaṅkamīti yojanā. Gāmūpacāreti gāmasamīpe. Saññāṇaṃ katvāti saññāṇaṃ katvā viya. Na hi bhagavato tassa saññāṇakaraṇe payojanaṃ atthi.

207. “Dve māgaṇḍiyāti” means two individuals named Māgaṇḍiya. “Devagabbhasadisanti” means like a dwelling chamber of the gods. “Etaṃ vuttanti” refers to this which was said: “In the fire-hut of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, on a grass spread.” “Na kevalaṃ taṃ divasamevāti”: on the day the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya prepared the grass spread, it was not only on that day that the Blessed One approached a certain forest grove—this is the connection. “Gāmūpacāreti” means in the vicinity of the village. “Saññāṇaṃ katvāti” means as if having made a sign. For the Blessed One had no purpose in making a sign to him.

Samaṇaseyyānurūpanti samaṇassa anucchavikā seyyā. Pāsaṃsattho hi ayaṃ rūpa-saddo. Tenāha “imaṃ tiṇasanthāraka”ntiādi. Anākiṇṇoti viluḷito aghaṭṭito. Hatthapādasīsehi tattha tattha pahaṭena na calito abhinno, acalitattā eva abhinnaṃ attharaṇaṃ. Paricchinditvā paññatto viyāti ayaṃ chekena cittakārena cintetvā tulikāya paricchinnalekhāya paricchinditvā likhitā cittakataseyyā viya. Bhūnaṃ vuccati vaḍḍhitaṃ, taṃ hantīti bhūnahuno. Tenāha “hatavaḍḍhino”ti. Taṃ panāyaṃ cakkhādīsu saṃvaravidhānaṃ vaḍḍhihananaṃ maññati. Tenāha “mariyādakārakassā”ti. Brūhetabbanti uḷāravisayūpahārena vaḍḍhetabbaṃ pīṇetabbaṃ. Taṃ pana ananubhūtānubhavanena hotīti āha “adiṭṭhaṃ dakkhitabba”nti. Anubhūtaṃ pana apaṇītaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “diṭṭhaṃ samatikkamitabba”nti. Sesavāresupi eseva nayo. Paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānavādī kiresa paribbājako, tasmā evaṃ chasu dvāresu vaḍḍhiṃ paññapeti. Yasmā yaṃ channampi cakkhādīnaṃ yathāsakaṃ visayaggahaṇaṃ paṭikkhipanto lokassa avaḍḍhitaṃ vināsameva paññapeti, tasmā so sayampi vaḍḍhihato hatavaḍḍhito.

A bed suitable for an ascetic means a bed fitting for a recluse. For this word `rūpa` is used in a laudatory sense. Hence it is said, “this grass spread,” etc. “Anākiṇṇoti” means not disarranged, not disturbed. It is not moved or broken by being struck here and there with hands, feet, or head; because it is unmoved, the spread is unbroken. “Paricchinditvā paññatto viyāti” means like a painted bed, conceived by a skilled artist and drawn with a brush with a demarcated line, having been marked out. “Bhūna” is said to mean growth; one who destroys that is a `bhūnahuno`. Hence, it is said, “of one who has destroyed growth” (hatavaḍḍhino). But this one considers the establishment of restraint in the eye, etc., to be the destruction of growth. Hence, it is said, “of one who makes a boundary” (mariyādakārakassa). “Brūhetabba” means it should be augmented, nourished by the presentation of sublime objects. But that comes about through experiencing the unexperienced; thus it is said, “the unseen should be seen” (adiṭṭhaṃ dakkhitabba). But the experienced is inferior; thus it is said, “the seen should be transcended” (diṭṭhaṃ samatikkamitabba). In the remaining instances, too, this is the method. This wanderer, it seems, is a proponent of the highest Nibbāna in this very life. Therefore, he prescribes growth in these six doors. Because, by rejecting the grasping of their respective objects by all six—the eye and so on—he prescribes only non-growth and destruction for the world, therefore he himself is one whose growth is destroyed, a destroyer of growth.

Saṃkilesato ārakattā ariyo niyyānikadhammabhāvato ñāyo dhammo. Vajjalesassapi abhāvato kusalo. Tenāha “parisuddhe kāraṇadhamme anavajje”ti. Uggatassāti uccakulīnatādinā uḷārassa. Mukhe ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvāti mukhena saṃyato hutvā. Ambajambūādīni gahetvā viya apūrayamānoti ambajambūādīni aññamaññavisadisāni viya pūraṇakathānayena yaṃ kiñci akathetvā. Tenāha “mayā kathitaniyāmenā”ti.

The Dhamma is noble (ariyo) because it is far from defilements, and it is the method (ñāyo) because it is a doctrine that leads out. It is wholesome (kusalo) because of the absence of even a trace of fault. Hence it is said, “in the pure, causal Dhamma, which is blameless” (parisuddhe kāraṇadhamme anavajje). “Uggatassāti” means of one who is eminent due to high birth, etc. “Mukhe ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvāti” means having become restrained in speech. “Apūrayamānoti” means not speaking just anything, in the manner of filling up by taking mangoes, rose-apples, etc., which are dissimilar to one another. Hence it is said, “according to the method spoken by me” (mayā kathitaniyāmena).

208. Phalasamāpattiyā [M 2.0104][V 2.0104] vuṭṭhitoti divāvihārato vuṭṭhitoti attho. Divāvihāropi hi “paṭisallāna”nti vuccati “rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādī”tiādīsu (pārā. 18). Bhagavā hi phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhānuttarakālaṃ tesaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ sutvā divāvihārato vuṭṭhāya tattha gato. Saṃvego nāma sahottappañāṇaṃ, taṃ nibbindanavasenapi hoti, saṃveganissitaṃ sandhāyāha “pītisaṃvegena saṃviggo”ti. So pana yasmā purimāvatthāya calanaṃ hoti cittassa, tasmā āha “calito kampito”ti. Tikhiṇasotena purisenāti bhagavantaṃ sandhāyāha.

208. “Having emerged from the attainment of fruition” (phalasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhito) means having risen from daytime abiding. For daytime abiding is also called “seclusion” (paṭisallāna), as in such passages as “to one gone to a solitary place, in seclusion, such a reflection of the mind arose” (Pārā. 18). Indeed, the Blessed One, having heard their conversation at the time immediately after emerging from the attainment of fruition, rose from daytime abiding and went there. Spiritual urgency (saṃvega) is knowledge together with moral dread; it also occurs by way of disenchantment. Referring to that which is based on spiritual urgency, it is said, “stirred with joyous urgency” (pītisaṃvegena saṃviggo). But because that is a stirring of the mind from its previous state, it is said, “shaken and stirred” (calito kampito). “By a man with a sharp ear” (Tikhiṇasotena purisena) is said in reference to the Blessed One.

209. Dhammadesanaṃ ārabhi yathā vineyyadamanakusalo vasanaṭṭhānaṭṭhenāti idaṃ āramitabbabhāvassa bhāvalakkhaṇavacanaṃ. Āramati etthāti ārāmo, rūpaṃ ārāmo etassāti rūpārāmaṃ, tato eva tanninnabhāvena rūpe ratanti rūparataṃ, tena sammo duppattiyā rūpena sammuditanti rūpasammuditaṃ, tadetaṃ tadabhihatajavanakiccaṃ tattha āropetvā vuttaṃ. Dantantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Dantaṃ damitaṃ. Nibbisevananti vigatavisukāyikaṃ. Guttanti satiyā guttaṃ. Rakkhitanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Saṃvutanti apanītaṃ pavesanivāraṇena. Tenāha “pihita”nti.

209. With the meaning of 'dwelling place' (vasanaṭṭhānaṭṭhena): this is a statement of the characteristic nature of that which is to be delighted in. One delights (āramati) here (ettha), thus it is a pleasance (ārāmo). Form is a pleasance for one (rūpaṃ ārāmo etassa), thus 'delighting in form' (rūpārāmaṃ). From that very inclination towards it, one is fond of (ratanti) form, thus 'fond of form' (rūparataṃ). Through that, being wrongly attained, one is overjoyed (sammuditanti) by form, thus 'overjoyed by form' (rūpasammuditaṃ). This is said by ascribing to it the function of impulsion struck by that. In the case of 'tamed' (danta), etc., the method is the same. Tamed (dantaṃ) means subdued (damitaṃ). “Nibbisevananti” means devoid of sensual craving. “Guttanti” means guarded by mindfulness. “Rakkhitanti” is a synonym for that. “Saṃvutanti” means removed by the prevention of entry. Hence it is said, “closed” (pihita).

210. Uppajjanapariḷāhanti uppajjanakilesapariḷāhaṃ. Kiṃ vacanaṃ vattabbaṃ assāti rūpārammaṇaṃ anubhavitvā samudayādipahānaṃ pariggaṇhitvā parinibbinditvā virajjitvā yo vimutto, tattha kiṃ vuddhihatapariyāyo avassaṃ labhati na labhatīti pucchati. Paribbājako tādise sārabaddhavimuttike vuddhihatoti na vadeyyāti āha “na kiñci, bho, gotamā”ti.

210. “The fever of arising” (Uppajjanapariḷāha) means the fever of defilements that are arising. He asks: What should be said about one who, having experienced a form-object, having grasped the abandonment of its origin, etc., having become disenchanted and dispassionate, is liberated—in that case, does he necessarily gain or not gain the designation 'one whose growth is destroyed'? The wanderer would not say of such a one, who is liberated and bound to the essence, that his growth is destroyed. Thus he says, “Not anything, good Gotama” (na kiñci, bho, gotamā).

211. Teti tayā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Vassaṃ vāso vassaṃ uttarapadalopena, vassituṃ arahatīti vassiko, vassakāle nivāsānucchavikoti attho.

211. “Te” means `tayā` (by you), or this is simply the reading. `Vassaṃ vāso` becomes `vassaṃ` by elision of the final member of the compound. One who is fit to dwell during the rains (vassituṃ arahati) is `vassiko`; the meaning is 'suitable for residence in the rainy season'.

Nātiucco hoti nātinīcoti gimhiko viya ucco, hemantiko viya nīco na hoti, atha kho tadubhayavemajjhalakkhaṇatāya nātiucco hoti nātinīco. Nātitanūnīti [M 2.0105] hemantikassa viya na khuddakāni. Nātibahūnīti gimhikassa viya na atibahūni. Missakānevāti hemantikagimhikesu vuttalakkhaṇavomissakāni. Uṇhapavesanatthāyāti niyūhesu purebhattaṃ pacchābhattañca patitasūriyobhāsavasena uṇhassa abbhantarapavesanatthāya. Bhittiniyūhāni nīharīyantīti [V 2.0105] dakkhiṇapasse bhittīsu niyūhāni nīharitvā karīyanti. Vipulajālānīti puthulachiddāni. Udakayantānīti udakavāhakayantāni.

“It is not too high and not too low” means it is not high like a summer dwelling, nor low like a winter dwelling; rather, because its characteristic is to be midway between both, it is not too high and not too low. “Not too small” means they are not small in number like those of a winter dwelling. “Not too numerous” means they are not very numerous like those of a summer dwelling. “Mixed” means intermingled with the characteristics described for winter and summer dwellings. “For the purpose of warmth entering” means for the purpose of warmth entering inside the gables before and after the meal, by means of the sunlight falling on them. “Gables on the wall are extended” means gables are made by extending them from the walls on the southern side. “With large lattices” means with wide openings. “Water machines” means water-drawing machines.

Nīluppalagacchake katvāti vikasitehi nīluppalehi gacchake naḷinike katvā. Gandhakalalanti gandhamissakakaddamaṃ. Yamakabhittīti yugaḷabhitti, tassā antare nāḷi, yato udakaṃ abhiruhati. Lohanāḷinti lohamayayantanāḷiṃ. Jālanti tambalohamayaṃ jālaṃ. Heṭṭhā yantaṃ parivattentīti heṭṭhābhāge udakayantaṃ gamenti. Udakaphusite temente vivaṇṇatā māhosīti nīlapaṭaṃ nivāseti. Divākāleti divasavelāya. Ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto viharāmīti etena attano phalasamāpattivihāro bhagavatā dassitoti āha – “tāya ratiyā ramamānoti idaṃ catutthajjhānikaphalasamāpattiratiṃ sandhāya vutta”nti.

“Nīluppalagacchake katvā” means having made a small pond a cluster with fully bloomed blue lotuses. “Gandhakalala” means mud mixed with fragrant substances. “Yamakabhitti” means paired walls; between them is a channel through which water rises. “Lohanāḷi” means a pipe of a metal mechanism. “Jāla” means a net made of copper. “Heṭṭhā yantaṃ parivattenti” means they set the water wheel in motion below. “Udakaphusite temente vivaṇṇatā māhosīti” means ‘Lest its being wetted by splashing water cause discoloration,’ he covers it with a blue cloth. “Divākāle” means during the daytime. “Ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto viharāmi” means ‘I dwell internally with a pacified mind’; with this, the Blessed One shows his abiding in fruition attainment—thus it is said: “tāya ratiyā ramamāno” (delighting in that pleasure) refers to the joy of the fruition attainment of the fourth jhāna.

212. Mahā ca nesaṃ papañcoti nesaṃ rājūnaṃ mahāpapañco rājiddhivasena sabbadā sampattivisayo ca, anubhavituṃ na labhantīti adhippāyo. Mante gavesantā vicaranti, na bhogasukhaṃ. Gaṇanā nāma acchinnagaṇanā, na vigaṇagaṇanā na paṇagaṇanā. Āvaṭṭoti yathādhigate dibbe kāme pahāya kāmahetu āvaṭṭo nivatto parivattito bhaveyya. Evaṃ mānusakā kāmāti yathā koci kusaggena udakaṃ gahetvā mahāsamudde udakaṃ mineyya. Tattha mahāsamudde udakameva mahantaṃ vipulaṃ paṇītañca, evaṃ dibbānaṃ kāmānaṃ samīpe upanidhāya mānusakā kāmā appamattakā oramattakā nihīnā, dibbāva kāmā mahantā vipulā uḷārā paṇītā. Samadhigayhāti sammā adhigamanavasena niggayha dibbampi sukhaṃ hīnaṃ katvā tiṭṭhati.

212. “And great is their proliferation (papañco)”: for those kings, a great proliferation occurs due to royal power, always within the sphere of their attainments, yet they do not get to enjoy them—this is the meaning. They wander about seeking counsel, not the pleasure of wealth. “Gaṇanā” means continuous counting, not scattered counting or commercial counting. “Āvaṭṭo” means turning back: it is as if, having abandoned the divine sensual pleasures one has obtained, one might turn back, revert, or revolve for the sake of sensual pleasures. “Thus, human sensual pleasures (mānusakā kāmā)” are like someone taking water with the tip of a kusa grass blade and trying to measure the water in the great ocean. There, the water in the great ocean is itself vast, abundant, and excellent; similarly, when compared to divine sensual pleasures, human sensual pleasures are insignificant, trivial, and inferior, while divine sensual pleasures are vast, abundant, sublime, and excellent. “Samadhigayhāti” means by way of right attainment, having subdued even divine pleasure and rendered it inferior, one abides.

213. Ārogyahetukaṃ sukhaṃ assa atthīti sukhī, taṃ panassa rogavigamatovāti āha “paṭhamaṃ dukkhito pacchā sukhito”ti. Serī nāma attādhīnavuttīti āha “serī ekako bhaveyyā”ti. Attano vaso [M 2.0106] sayaṃvaso, so etassa atthīti sayaṃvasī. Aṅgārakapallaṃ viya kāmavatthupariḷāhahetuto. Tacchetvāti ghaṭṭetvā, kaṇḍūyitvāti attho.

213. “Ārogyahetukaṃ sukhaṃ assa atthīti sukhī” means ‘He has happiness caused by health,’ thus he is happy; but that comes from the departure of disease—thus it is said, “first afflicted, later happy” (paṭhamaṃ dukkhito pacchā sukhito). “Serī nāma attādhīnavuttīti” means ‘serī’ is one who lives independently—thus it is said, “serī ekako bhaveyyā” (an independent one would be alone). One who is his own master is self-mastered; he has this, therefore he is `sayaṃvasī` (self-mastered). Like a pit of embers: because of the torment caused by the objects of sensual pleasure. “Tacchetvāti” means having rubbed, that is, having scratched.

214. Yena kāyo madhurakajāto hoti, taṃ kira kuṭṭhaṃ chaviṃ vināseti, cammaṃ chiddajātaṃ viya hoti. Tenevāha “upahatakāyappasādo”ti. Paccalatthāti paṭilabhi. Avijjābhibhūtatāya virodhipaccayasamāyogena paññindriyassa upahatattā. Āyatiṃ dukkhaphalatāya etarahi ca kilesadukkhabahulatāya kāmānaṃ dukkhasamphassatā, tadubhayasaṃyuttesu tesu ca taṃ asallakkhitvā [V 2.0106] ekantasukhābhiniveso viparītasaññāya, na kevalāya sukhavedanāya sukhāti pavattasaññī.

214. That by which the body becomes pleasant, it is said that leprosy destroys the skin, making the hide as if perforated. Therefore, it is said, “with impaired bodily sensitivity” (upahatakāyappasādo). “Paccalatthāti” means he obtained in return (paṭilabhi). Due to being overwhelmed by ignorance, through association with opposing conditions, the faculty of wisdom is impaired. Because sensual pleasures bear the fruit of suffering in the future and are abundant with the suffering of defilements at present, contact with them is suffering; and not recognizing this in them, which are connected with both, one adheres to them as exclusively pleasant—this is a distorted perception, not merely the perception that proceeds as ‘pleasant’ from a pleasant feeling.

215. Tānīti kuṭṭhasarīre vaṇamukhāni. Asucīnīti asubhāni. Duggandhānīti vissagandhāni. Pūtīnīti kuṇapabhūtāni. Idānīti etarahi. Nakhehi vippatacchanaaggiparitāpanehi atinippīḷanakāle pāṇakā…pe… paggharanti, tena vedanā tanukā hoti. Evanti vuttanayena vedanāya tanukabhāvato.

215. “Tānīti” means the openings of the wounds on the leprous body. “Asucīnīti” means unlovely. “Duggandhānīti” means having a rank smell. “Pūtīnīti” means having become like a corpse. “Idānīti” means at this time. At the time of excessive pressing, scraping with nails, and heating with fire, the creatures… ooze out, and by that the feeling becomes slight. “Evanti” means due to the slightness of the feeling in the way described.

Ārogyabhāve dhanalābhādilābhuppattito, asati ca ārogye lābhassa niratthakabhāvato, diṭṭhadhammikādisabbasampattīnaṃ lābhassa nimittabhāvato ca ārogyaparamā lābhā. Nibbāne sukhuppattito, asati ca nibbānādhigame tādisassa sukhassa anupalabbhanato, sabbasaṅkhatavivittattā ca sabbaso ca saṃsāradukkhābhāvato, adhigate ca tasmiṃ sakalavaṭṭadukkhābhāvato ca nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ. Pubbabhāgamaggānanti kāyānupassanādibhedabhinnānaṃ ariyamaggassa pubbabhāgiyānaṃ maggānaṃ. Tesañca amatagāmitā nāma tanninnatāvaseneva sacchikiriyāvasenāti āha “pubbabhāgagamaneneva amatagāmina”nti. Aṭṭhaṅgiko ariyamaggo khemo sabbaparissayasamugghātanena anupaddutattā, taṃsamaṅgīnaṃ sabbaso anupaddutattā taṃsamaṅgīnaṃ sabbaso anupaddavahetuto ca. Laddhivasena gahitāti sassatavādādīhi kevalaṃ tesaṃ laddhivasena tathā gahitā. Khemaamatagāminanti iminā hi “khemaṃamatagāmina”nti vibhattialopena niddeso, attho pana vibhattilopena daṭṭhabboti dasseti.

Because when there is health, gains such as wealth arise, and without health, gains are meaningless; and because health is the cause for acquiring all attainments, beginning with those in this present life, health is the highest of gains. Because happiness arises in Nibbāna, and without the attainment of Nibbāna such happiness is not found; and because it is secluded from all conditioned things and completely devoid of the suffering of saṃsāra; and because upon attaining it, all the suffering of the cycle of existence is absent, Nibbāna is the supreme happiness. “Of the preliminary paths” means of the paths that are the preliminary part of the Noble Path, differentiated by divisions such as the contemplation of the body. And their “leading to the deathless” is by way of their inclination towards it and by way of their realization; hence it is said, “they lead to the deathless simply by being the preliminary path.” The Noble Eightfold Path is safe because it is unassailed through the eradication of all dangers, and because for one endowed with it there is complete freedom from harm, and it is the cause of a complete absence of calamity for them. “Grasped by way of acquisition” means it is grasped thus by eternalists and others merely by way of their acquired view. With “khemaamatagāminanti,” he shows that the designation “khemaṃamatagāminaṃ” is made with an elision of the case ending, but the meaning should be understood as if the case ending were not elided.

216. Anomajjatīti [M 2.0107] anu anu omajjati. Aparāparaṃ hatthaṃ heṭṭhā otārento majjati.

216. “Anomajjatīti” means he repeatedly rubs down. Again and again, lowering his hand downward, he rubs.

217. Chekanti ghanabhāvena vītaṃ. Ghanamaṭṭhabhāvena sundaraṃ hotīti āha “sampanna”nti. Sādhūhi paramappicchasantuṭṭhehi lāto gahitoti sāhuḷi. Saṅkāracoḷakaṃ niccakāḷakaṃ.

217. “Chekanti” means densely woven. Because it is beautiful due to its dense and smooth nature, he says “sampanna” (perfect). “Sāhuḷi” is so called because it is received and taken by the virtuous, who are of few wishes and supremely content. “Saṅkāracoḷakaṃ” is a rag from a rubbish heap, which is always black.

218. Tattha tattha rujanaṭṭhena vibādhanaṭṭhena rogova bhūto. Vipassanāñāṇenapi sikhāppattena ārogyaṃ ekadesena passati, nibbānañca vaṭṭapaṭipakkhatoti āha “vipassanāñāṇañcevā”ti.

218. Here and there, it has become a disease in the sense that it hurts and oppresses. Even with insight knowledge that has reached its peak, one sees health in part, and Nibbāna as the counterpart to the cycle of existence; hence it is said, “and even insight knowledge.”

219. Antarāti [V 2.0107] paṭhamuppatti jarāmaraṇānaṃ vemajjhe. Upahatoti pittasemhādidosehi dūsitabhāvena kathito. Pittādidose pana bhesajjasevanāya nivattento upahataṃ paṭipākatikaṃ karonto cakkhūni uppādeti nāma. Vinaṭṭhānīti anuppattidhammataṃ āpannāni.

219. “Antarā” means in the middle, between the first arising and aging and death. “Upahato” (afflicted) is spoken of as being corrupted by disorders such as bile and phlegm. But by counteracting the disorders such as bile through the use of medicine, restoring what was afflicted to its natural state, one is said to “produce” eyes. “Vinaṭṭhāni” (destroyed) means they have attained the state of non-arising.

220. Pubbe vutte sāhuḷiyacīre. Vaṭṭe anugatacittenāti anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe anādīnavadassitāya anugāmicittena.

220. Regarding the previously mentioned `sāhuḷiya` robe. “Vaṭṭe anugatacittena” means with a mind that follows along with the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra because of not seeing the danger in it.

221. Dhammassāti nibbānassa. Anudhammanti anurūpaṃ niyyānadhammaṃ. Tenāha “anucchavikaṃ paṭipada”nti. Pañcakkhandheti pañcupādānakkhandhe dasseti. “Dīgharattaṃ vata, bho”tiādinā pāḷiyaṃ vivaṭṭaṃ dassitaṃ. Tenāha “upādānanirodhāti vivaṭṭaṃ dassento”ti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.
