221. “Dhammassāti” means of Nibbāna. “Anudhammanti” means the suitable Dhamma of deliverance. Hence it is said, “the suitable practice.” By “the five aggregates,” he indicates the five aggregates subject to clinging. In the Pāli, by the phrase beginning, “Dīgharattaṃ vata, bho” (For a long time, indeed, sirs), the turning away from the cycle is shown. Hence it is said, “showing the turning away by ‘the cessation of clinging.’” The rest is easily understood.

Māgaṇḍiyasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta is complete.

6. Sandakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Sandaka Sutta.

223. Devena [V 2.0108] vassena kato sobbho devakatasobbho. Tenāha “vasso…pe… rahado”ti. Guhāti paṃsuguhā pāsāṇaguhā missakaguhāti tisso guhā. Tattha paṃsuguhā udakamuttaṭṭhāne ahosi ninnaṭṭhānaṃ pana udakena ajjhotthataṃ. Umaṅgaṃ katvāti heṭṭhā suduggaṃ katvā. Anamataggiyaṃ [M 2.0108] paccavekkhitvāti “na kho so sattāvāso sulabharūpo, yo iminā dīghena addhunā anāvuṭṭhapubbo”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.160) idañca taḷākaṃ mayā vutthapubbaṃ bhavissati, tampi ṭhānaṃ so ca attabhāvo apaññattikabhāvaṃ gatoti evaṃ anamataggiyaṃ paccavekkhitvā tādisaṃ ṭhānaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Iminā nayena samuddapabbatadassanādīsupi paccavekkhaṇāvidhi veditabbo.

223. A `devakatasobbho` is a pool made by divine rain. Hence it is said, “rain… a lake.” “Guhā” (cave) means three kinds of caves: an earth cave, a rock cave, and a mixed cave. Among them, the earth cave was in a place where water was discharged, while the low-lying area was flooded with water. “Umaṅgaṃ katvāti” means having made the area below very difficult to traverse. “Anamataggiyaṃ paccavekkhitvāti” means having reflected on the beginningless past, considering: “Indeed, an abode for beings is not easily found that one has not dwelt in before in this long stretch of time,” and so forth (MN 1.160), and “This lake, too, may have been a place I have dwelt in before, but that place and that existence have now passed into a state of non-manifestation.” Having thus reflected on the beginningless past, it is proper to go to such a place. By this method, the way of reflection should be understood also in regard to seeing the ocean, mountains, and so on.

Uccaṃ nadamānāyāti uccaṃ katvā saddaṃ karontiyā kāmassādabhavassādādivatthunti “ayañca ayañca kāmo iṭṭho kanto manāpo, asuko bhavo iṭṭho kanto manāpo, evamayaṃ loko piyehi piyataro”ti evaṃ kāmassādabhavassādalokassādādisaṅkhātaṃ vatthuṃ. Duggatito saṃsārato ca niyyāti etenāti niyyānaṃ, saggamaggo mokkhamaggo ca, taṃ niyyānaṃ arahati, niyyāne vā niyuttāti niyyānikā, niyyānaṃ vā phalaṃ etissā atthīti niyyānikā, vacīduccaritādisaṃkilesato niyyātīti vā niyyānīyā, ī-kārassa rassattaṃ ya-kārassa ca ka-kāraṃ katvā niyyānikā, cetanāya saddhiṃ samphappalāpā veramaṇi. Tappaṭipakkhato aniyyānikā, tassā bhāvo aniyyānikattaṃ, tasmā aniyyānikattā. Tiracchānabhūtāti tirokaraṇabhūtā. Gehassitakathāti kāmapaṭisaṃyuttakathā. Kammaṭṭhānabhāveti aniccatāpaṭisaṃyuttacatusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāve. Saha atthenāti sātthakaṃ, hitapaṭisaṃyuttanti attho. Visikhāti gharasanniveso, visikhāgahaṇena ca tannivāsino gahitā “gāmo āgato”tiādīsu (sārattha. ṭī. 1.ācariyaparamparakathāvaṇṇanā) viya. Tenevāha “sūrā samatthā”ti “saddhā pasannā”ti ca. Kumbhaṭṭhānappadesena kumbhadāsiyo vuttāti āha “kumbhadāsikathā vā”ti.

“She makes a loud noise” means she produces a sound loudly, referring to objects such as the gratification of sensual pleasures, the gratification of existence, and the gratification of the world, as in: “This and that sensual pleasure is dear, delightful, and pleasing; such an existence is dear, delightful, and pleasing; thus, this world is dearer than the dear.” That by which one is led out from a wretched state and from saṃsāra is called “deliverance” (niyyāna), which is the path to heaven and the path to liberation. One who is worthy of that deliverance, or one engaged in deliverance, is called “niyyānikā.” Alternatively, “niyyānikā” is that which has deliverance as its fruit, or that which leads out from verbal misconduct and other defilements—this is “niyyānīyā,” which becomes “niyyānikā” by shortening the vowel ‘ī’ and changing ‘y’ to ‘k.’ It is abstaining from frivolous talk along with the intention. Its opposite is “aniyyānikā,” and its state is “aniyyānikattaṃ”; therefore, it is because of its nature of not leading out. “Behaving like animals” means being of the nature of obscuring. “Household talk” refers to talk connected with sensual pleasures. “Developing meditation subjects” means developing the meditation subjects connected with impermanence and the four truths. “With meaning” means purposeful, connected with benefit. “Visikhā” refers to a residential area, and by the term visikhā, its inhabitants are also included, as in phrases like “the village has come,” and so forth (Sārattha. Ṭī. 1.ācariyaparamparakathāvaṇṇanā). Thus, it is said: “The heroes are capable,” and “the faithful are devoted.” By mentioning the Kumbhaṭṭhāna area, female slaves are referred to; hence it is said: “Or talk about female slaves.”

228. Vohāro viya tesaṃ tathā vohāramattaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ “brahmacariyavāse”ti. Akatāti samena, visamena vā kenaci hetunā na katā na vihitā. Katavidho karaṇavidhi natthi [V 2.0109] etesanti akaṭavidhā. Padadvayenapi loke kenaci hetupaccayena nesaṃ anibbattataṃ dasseti. Iddhiyāpi na nimmitāti kassaci iddhimato cetovasippattassa devassa, issarādino vā iddhiyāpi na nimmitā. Animmātāti kassaci animmāpitā. Rūpādijanakabhāvanti rūpasaddādīnaṃ paccayabhāvaṃ, rūpādayopi pathaviyādīhi [M 2.0109] appaṭibaddhavuttikāti tassa adhippāyo. Yathā pabbatakūṭaṃ kenaci anibbattitaṃ kassaci ca anibbattanakaṃ, evametepīti āha “pabbatakūṭā viya ṭhitāti kūṭaṭṭhā”ti. Yamidaṃ bījato aṅkurādi jāyatīti vuccati, taṃ vijjamānameva tato nikkhamati nāvijjamānaṃ, aññathā aññatopi aññassa upaladdhi siyāti adhippāyo. Evaṃ ṭhitāti evaṃ nibbikārā ṭhitā. Ubhayenapīti atthadvayenapīti vadanti. “Kūṭaṭṭhā esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitā”ti padadvayenapi. Tesaṃ sattannaṃ kāyānaṃ. Ṭhitattāti nibbikārābhāvena ṭhitattā. Na calantīti vikāraṃ nāpajjanti. Vikārābhāvato hi tesaṃ sattannaṃ kāyānaṃ esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitatā. Aniñjanañca atthato pakatiyā avaṭṭhānamevāti dassetuṃ “na vipariṇāmentī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā avipariṇāmadhammattā eva te aññamaññaṃ na byābādhenti. Sati hi vikāraṃ āpādetabbatāya byābādhakatāpi siyā, tathā anuggahetabbatāya anuggāhakatāti tadabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “nāla”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

228. Just as in common speech, it is said by way of merely taking the conventional usage: “in the holy life.” “Not made” means not created or established by any cause, whether equal or unequal. “Without a method of creation” means no method of making or process of creation exists for them. These two words also show that they are not produced by any cause or condition in the world. “Not even created by psychic power” means not fashioned by the psychic power of any deity who has attained mastery over the mind, nor by any ruler or the like, even if they possess psychic power. “Uncreated” means not caused to be created by anyone. “The state of generating form, etc.” means they are not a condition for form, sound, etc.; and the meaning is that form, etc., also have their functions not bound to earth and other elements. Just as a mountain peak is not produced by anyone nor is a producer for anyone, so too are these; hence it is said, “They stand like mountain peaks, firm at their core.” That which is said to arise from a seed, such as a sprout, comes forth from what exists, not from what does not exist; otherwise, the acquisition of one thing from another would be possible—this is the intended meaning. “Thus they stand” means they stand without alteration. “By both” means by both meanings, they say, and also by the two phrases: “firm at their core” and “steadfastly established.” Of those seven bodies. “Because they stand” means because they remain without alteration. “They do not waver” means they do not undergo change. Indeed, due to the absence of change, those seven bodies are steadfastly established at their core. And to show that “unshaken” means, in essence, their natural state of remaining, it is said: “They do not transform.” Likewise, because they are not subject to transformation, they do not harm one another. For if they were subject to being altered, there could also be harming; and likewise, if they were subject to being supported, there could be supporting. To show the absence of this, the text states: “They are not able…” and so on.

Pathavī eva kāyekadesattā pathavīkāyo. Hantuṃ vā ghātetuṃ vā samattho nāma natthi jīvasattamānaṃ kāyānaṃ niccatāya nibbikārabhāvato, eteneva nesamahantabbatā aghātetabbatā atthato vuttāyevāti daṭṭhabbā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “sattannaṃtveva kāyāna”ntiādi. Sotuṃ vā sāvetuṃ vā samattho nāma natthīti paccekaṃ nesaṃ savanesu asamatthattā tadekadesādīsupi asamatthataṃ dīpeti. Yadi koci hantā natthi, kathaṃ satthappahāroti āha “yathā muggarāsiādīsū”tiādi. Kevalaṃ saññāmattameva hoti, hananaghātanādi pana paramatthato nattheva kāyānaṃ avikopanīyabhāvatoti adhippāyo. Kevalaṃ takkamattena niratthakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ dīpetīti etena yasmā takkikā niraṅkusatāya parikappanassa yaṃ kiñci attanā parikappitaṃ sārato maññamānā tatheva abhinivissa takkadiṭṭhiggāhaṃ gaṇhanti, tasmā na tesaṃ diṭṭhivatthusmiṃ viññūhi vicāraṇā kattabbāti dasseti. Kecīti sārasamāsācariyā. Pañcindriyavasenāti pañcarūpindriyavasena. Kammanti laddhi kammabhāvena supākaṭattā. Avaṅkakathātāraṇādikā dvāsaṭṭhi paṭipadā. Ekasmiṃ kappeti ekasmiṃ mahākappe.

The earth, being a part of the body, is the earth-body. There is no one capable of killing or destroying, since the bodies of living beings are permanent and unchangeable. By this, their unkillability and indestructibility are implicitly stated in meaning, so it should be understood. Thus it is said, "There are indeed seven kinds of bodies," and so forth. There is no one capable of hearing or making others hear, for they are individually incapable of hearing, which also shows their inability in those partial aspects. If no killer exists, how is there a strike with a weapon? It is said, "Just as with a heap of clubs," and so forth. It is merely a matter of perception, but in ultimate truth, there is no actual killing or destruction, as bodies are unalterable. This is the meaning. It merely illustrates a pointless view based on reasoning alone. By this, it is shown that since logicians, unrestrained in their assumptions, consider whatever they conceive to be essential and thus grasp at speculative views, the wise should not engage in examining the substance of their views. Some—referring to the teachers of essentialism. By means of the five faculties—that is, through the five material faculties. Kamma—understood as the doctrine of action due to its evident ripening. Distortions, disputes, and the like—the sixty-two paths. In one aeon—in one great aeon.

Purisabhūmiyoti [M 2.0110] padhānapuggalena niddeso, itthīnampetā bhūmiyo icchanteva. Bhikkhu ca pannakotiādi tesaṃ pāḷiyeva. Tattha pannakoti bhikkhāya vicaraṇakoti vadanti, tesaṃ vā paṭipattiṃ [V 2.0110] paṭipannako. Jinoti jiṇṇo, jarāvasena nihīnadhātukoti vadanti, attano vā paṭipattiyā paṭipakkhaṃ jinitvā ṭhito. So kira tathābhūto kassacipi dhammaṃ na katheti, tenāha “na kiñci āhā”ti. Alābhinti “so na kumbhimukhā paṭiggaṇhatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.394) nayena vuttaalābhahetusamāyogena alābhiṃ. Tato eva jighacchādubbalaparetatāya sayanaparāyaṇaṃ samaṇaṃ pannabhūmīti vadati.

The realm of men is designated by reference to the principal individual; women also desire these realms. And "bhikkhu" and "pannakoti," etc., are their Pāli terms. There, "pannakoti" means, they say, the limit of wandering for alms, or one who has undertaken their practice. "Jina" means aged, weakened in elements due to old age, they say, or one who has conquered the opposition through his own practice and stands firm. It is said that such a one does not teach the Dhamma to anyone; therefore, it is said, "He says nothing." "Without gain" refers to one who lacks gain due to the combination of causes for lacking, as stated in the manner of "He does not receive from the mouth of a pot," etc. (Dī. Ni. 1.394). From that very state, overcome by hunger and weakness, resorting to lying down, the ascetic is called "one who has reached the pannabhūmi."

Ājīvavuttisatānīti sattānaṃ ājīvabhūtāni jīvikāvuttisatāni. Pasuggahaṇena eḷakajāti gahitā, migaggahaṇena rurugavayādisabbamigajāti. Bahū devāti cātumahārājikādibrahmakāyikādivasena nesaṃ antarabhedavasena bahū devā. Tattha cātumahārājikānaṃ ekacco antarabhedo “mahāsamayasuttena” (dī. ni. 2.331 ādayo) dīpetabbo. Mānusāpi anantāti dīpadesakulavaṃsājīvādivibhāgavasena mānusāpi anantabhedā. Pisācā eva pesācā, te aparapetādayo mahantā veditabbā.

"The hundred livelihood practices" means the hundred means of livelihood that are the livelihoods of beings. By the inclusion of cattle, the species of goats is included; by the inclusion of deer, all species like the ruru and gavaya are included. "Many devas" refers to the many devas from the Cātummahārājika to the Brahmakāyika, according to their internal divisions. There, a certain internal division of the Cātummahārājikas should be explained by the "Mahāsamaya Sutta" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.331, and so forth). "Humans too are countless" means humans are of endless variety due to divisions of island, country, clan, lineage, livelihood, and so on. Pisācas are indeed pesācas; they should be understood as great, such as aparapetas and others.

Chaddantadahamandākiniyo kuḷīramucalindanāmena vadati. Gaṇṭhikāti pabbagaṇṭhikā. Paṇḍitopi…pe… uddhaṃ na gacchati, kasmā? Sattānaṃ saṃsaraṇakālassa niyatabhāvato.

Chaddanta, Daha, and Mandākinī are spoken of by the names Kuḷīra and Mucalinda. "Gaṇṭhikā" means a mountain peak. Even the wise... do not go upwards. Why? Because the wandering time of beings is fixed.

Aparipakkaṃ saṃsaraṇanimittaṃ sīlādinā paripāceti nāma sīghaṃyeva visuddhippattiyā. Paripakkaṃ phussa phussa patvā patvā paripakkabhāvāpādanena byantiṃ karoti nāma. Suttaguḷeti suttavaṭṭiyaṃ. Nibbeṭhiyamānameva paletīti upamāya sattānaṃ saṃsāro anukkamena khīyateva, na tassa vaddhīti dasseti paricchinnarūpattā.

An unripened cause of wandering is ripened by morality, etc., for the sake of quickly attaining purification. A ripened one, repeatedly contacting and reaching, is brought to a state of full ripeness and destroyed. "Suttaguḷa" means a ball of thread. "Unraveling, it wastes away" – by this simile, he shows that the wandering of beings gradually diminishes and does not increase, because of its limited nature.

229. Niyativāde pakkhipantoti sabbaññutaṃ paṭijānitvāpi padesaññutāya asampāyamāno tattha attano aññāṇakiriyaṃ pariharituṃ asakkonto ca “evamesā niyatī”ti niyativāde pakkhipanto.

229. "One who throws it into the doctrine of determinism" means one who, even after claiming omniscience, fails when it comes to partial knowledge and, being unable to conceal his act of ignorance in that matter, throws it into the doctrine of determinism, saying, 'This is how it is determined.'

230. Dhammakathāya [M 2.0111] apassayabhūto anussavo etassa atthīti anussavī, tenevassa apassayavādaṃ dassetuṃ “anussavanissito”ti āha. Savanaṃ saccatoti yaṃ kiñci anussavaṃ, taṃ savanaṃ saccanti gahetvā ṭhito. Piṭakasampadāyāti ganthasampādanena, tādisaṃ ganthaṃ paguṇaṃ vācuggataṃ katvā taṃ nissāya dhammaṃ katheti. Tenāha “vaggapaṇṇāsakāyā”tiādi.

230. One for whom there is hearsay (anussava) that has become the foundation for his Dhamma talk is called an 'anussavī.' To show his doctrine of reliance on that foundation, it is said, 'dependent on hearsay.' 'Hearing is truth' means he is established in taking whatever hearsay he hears as truth. 'By accomplishment in the Piṭaka' means by the accomplishment of texts; having made such a text proficient and memorized, he teaches the Dhamma relying on it. Hence it is said, 'from the group of fifty,' and so forth.

232. Mandapaññoti [V 2.0111] parittapañño. Momūhoti sammuyhako. “Evantipi me no”tiādinā vividho nānappakāro khepo vācāya paravādānaṃ khīpanaṃ vācāvikkhepo, taṃ vācāvikkhepaṃ, na marati na pacchijjati yathāvutto vādavikkhepo etāyāti amarā, tattha pavattā diṭṭhi amarāvikkhepo, taṃ amarāvikkhepaṃ. Apariyantavikkhepanti “evampi me no”tiādinā pucchitassa apariyosāpanavasena vikkhepaṃ. Ito cito ca sandhāvati ekasmiṃ sabhāve anavaṭṭhānato. Gāhaṃ na upagacchatīti micchāgāhatāya uttaravidhānāya purimapakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā gāhaṃ na upagacchati. Amarāsadisāya amarāya vikkhepoti amarāvikkhepo.

232. "Mandapañño" means one with little wisdom. "Momūho" means utterly deluded. By means of "'Even so, for me, no,' and so on," there is various and diverse evasion, the refutation of others' arguments by speech, which is verbal evasion; because of this, the aforesaid verbal evasion does not die or get cut off—thus, it is called "amarā" (deathless). The view that arises there is "amarāvikkhepo" (deathless evasion); that is an endless evasion. Endless evasion means evasion by way of not bringing to a conclusion what has been asked with phrases like "'Even so, for me, no,'" and so forth. He runs here and there, due to not being established in a single nature. "He does not take a grasp" means: for the sake of a wrong grasp for a future refutation, he sets aside the former position and does not take a grasp. Evasion like an eel (amarā) is called "amarāvikkhepo."

Idaṃ kusalanti ettha iti-saddo pakārattho, iminā pakārenāti attho. Amarāvikkhepiko yathā kusale, evaṃ aññasmiṃ yaṃ kiñci kenaci pucchitaṃ atthaṃ attano aruccanatāya “evantipi me no”tiādinā tattha tattha vikkhepaññeva āpajjati, tasmā “evantipi me no”tiādi tattha tattha pucchitākārapaṭisedhanavasena vikkhipanākāradassanaṃ. Nanu cettha vikkhepavādino vikkhepapakkhassa ananujānanaṃ vikkhepapakkhe avaṭṭhānaṃ yuttanti? Na, tatthāpi tassa sammūḷhassa paṭikkhepavaseneva vikkhepavādassa pavattanato. Tena vuttaṃ “no”ti. Tathā hi sañcayo belaṭṭhaputto raññā ajātasattunā sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ puṭṭho paralokattikādīnaṃ paṭisedhanamukhena vikkhepaṃ byākāsi.

In "This is wholesome," the word "iti" has the sense of manner, meaning "in this way." The Amarāvikkhepika (evasive wrangler), just as with the wholesome, so too when asked about anything else by anyone, due to his own dislike, resorts only to evasion in every instance with phrases like "Even so, for me, no," and so forth. Therefore, phrases like "Even so, for me, no," and so forth demonstrate the manner of evasion by way of rejecting the form of the question wherever it is asked. Now, one might ask: "Is it not appropriate here for the exponent of evasion to not approve of the side of evasion, to not stand on the side of evasion?" No, because even there, that deluded one's doctrine of evasion proceeds only by way of rejection. Hence, it is said: "No." For example, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, when asked by King Ajātasattu about the visible fruit of asceticism, explained by way of evasion, through rejecting questions about the afterlife and so on.

Etthāha – “nanu cāyaṃ sabbopi amarāvikkhepiko kusalādayo dhamme paralokattikādīni ca yathābhūtaṃ anavabujjhamāno tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭho samāno pucchāya vikkhepamattaṃ āpajjati, tassa kathaṃ diṭṭhigatabhāvo. Na hi avattukāmassa viya pucchitamatthaṃ ajānantassa vikkhepakaraṇamattena [M 2.0112] tassa diṭṭhigatikatā yuttā”ti? Vuccate – na heva kho pucchāya vikkhepakaraṇamattena tassa diṭṭhigatikatā, atha kho micchābhinivesavasena. Sassatābhinivesena micchābhiniviṭṭhoyeva hi puggalo mandabuddhitāya kusalādidhamme paralokattikādīni ca yāthāvato appaṭipajjamāno attanā aviññātassa atthassa paraṃ viññāpetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya musāvādabhayena ca vikkhepaṃ āpajjatīti. Atha vā puññapāpānaṃ tabbipākānañca anavabodhena asaddahanena ca tabbisayāya pucchāya vikkhepakaraṇaṃyeva sundaranti khantiṃ ruciṃ uppādetvā abhinivisantassa uppannā visuṃyeva sā ekā diṭṭhi sattabhaṅgadiṭṭhi viyāti daṭṭhabbā, indriyabaddhato ca tatiyaṭṭhānabhāve dassito.

Here it is said: "But is it not the case that any Amarāvikkhepika, not truly understanding skillful and other states, and matters like the afterlife, etc., merely resorts to evasion when asked various questions? How then is it a case of holding a wrong view? For someone who does not wish to speak or does not know the meaning of what is asked, mere evasion does not justify attributing a wrong view to them." It is replied: It is not merely by the act of evading questions that this constitutes holding a wrong view, but rather it is due to wrong adherence. Indeed, a person wrongly adhering through adherence to eternalism, with weak intellect, not properly grasping skillful and other states or matters like the afterlife, etc., resorts to evasion because they are unable to explain to another the meaning they themselves do not understand, and out of fear of lying. Alternatively, due to not comprehending merit and demerit and their results, and lacking faith in those matters, one develops a liking and preference for evasion in response to questions concerning them, finding mere evasion appealing, and adheres to it. Thus, that one view arises quite separately, like the sevenfold predication view, and should be seen as such. Moreover, it is shown as the third position due to being bound by the faculties.

234. Sannidhikārakaṃ [V 2.0112] kāmeti ettha anindriyabaddhāni adhippetānīti tilataṇḍulādiggahaṇaṃ, tassa lokassa appasādaparihāratthaṃ kadāci taṇḍulanāḷiādisaṅgahaṇakaraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “tilataṇḍulādayo paññāyantī”ti.

234. Regarding "He desires accumulating goods," here, things not bound by the faculties are intended, thus the collecting of sesame seeds, rice, and so on is meant. It is said with reference to the occasional act of collecting a measure of rice or similar things for the purpose of avoiding the displeasure of the world, hence "sesame seeds, rice, and the like are specified."

236. Ājīvakā matā nāmāti ime ājīvakā sabbaso sammāpaṭipattirahitā micchā eva ca paṭipajjamānā adhisīlasaṅkhātassa sīlajīvitassa abhāvena matā nāma. Puttamatāti mataputtā. Samaṇe gotame brahmacariyavāso atthīti samaṇaṃ eva gotamaṃ parisuddho suparipuṇṇo takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāvaho brahmacariyavāso atthi. Etenettha dhammasudhammatādidīpanena buddhasubuddhatañca dīpeti, aññattha natthīti iminā bāhirakesu tassa abhāvaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

236. "The Ājīvakas are called dead": these Ājīvakas, being entirely devoid of right practice and practicing only wrongly, are called dead because of the absence of the life of virtue, known as higher virtue. "Puttamatā" means having dead sons. "In the ascetic Gotama, there is the holy life": only in the ascetic Gotama is there a holy life that is perfectly pure, complete, and which, for one who practices it, rightly leads to the destruction of suffering. Here, by this explanation of the excellence of the Dhamma and so forth, he also shows the perfect enlightenment of the Buddha; by "elsewhere it does not exist," he indicates its absence among outsiders. The rest is easily understood.

Sandakasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Sandaka Sutta is complete.

7. Mahāsakuludāyisuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta

237. Abhiññātāti [V 2.0113] ediso ediso cāti abhilakkhaṇavasena ñātā. Appasaddassa vinīto, appasaddatāya mandabhāṇitāya vinītoti ca appasaddavinītoti vuccamāne aññena vinītabhāvo dīpito hoti, bhagavā pana sayambhuñāṇena sayameva vinīto. Tasmā pāḷiyaṃ “appasaddavinīto”ti na vuttaṃ. Tenāha “na hi bhagavā aññena vinīto”ti.

237. "Well-known" means known by way of specific characteristics, such as "of this sort and that sort." When it is said "disciplined due to being of few words" (appasaddavinīto), meaning disciplined due to being of few words, that is, of gentle speech, the state of being disciplined by another is shown. But the Blessed One was disciplined by himself through self-arisen knowledge. Therefore, in the Pāli text, "disciplined due to being of few words" is not said. Hence it is stated, "For the Blessed One was not disciplined by another."

238. Hiyyodivasaṃ [M 2.0113] upādāya tato āsannāni katipayāni divasāni purimāni nāma honti, purimānīti ca pubbakāni, atītānīti attho. Tato paranti yathā vuttaatītadivasato anantaraṃ paraṃ purimataraṃ atisayena purimattā. Iti imesu dvīsu pavattito yathākkamaṃ purimapurimatarabhāvo, evaṃ santepi yadettha “purimatara”nti vuttaṃ, tato pabhuti yaṃ yaṃ oraṃ, taṃ taṃ paraṃ, yaṃ yaṃ paraṃ, taṃ taṃ “purimatara”nti vuttaṃ hoti. Kutūhalayuttā sālā kutūhalasālā yathā “ājaññaratho”ti. Ime dassanādayo.

238. Starting from the day before yesterday, a few days near to that are called "former days" (purimāni), which means "preceding" (pubbakāni), meaning "past" (atītāni). Beyond that, further back than the aforesaid past days, is "even more former" (purimatara) due to being exceedingly former. Thus, in these two cases, the state of being former and more former proceeds in sequence. Even so, when it is said "more former" (purimatara), from that point onward, whatever is nearer in time is called "later" (paraṃ), and whatever is later is called "more former" (purimatara). A hall endowed with curiosity is a "curiosity hall," just as in "a thoroughbred chariot." These are examples like 'viewing' and so on.

Ayathābhūtaguṇehīti ayathābhūtaṃ micchādīpitaatthamatteneva ugghositaguṇehi samuggato ghosito. Taranti atikkamanti etenāti titthaṃ, aggamaggo. Diṭṭhigatikamaggo pana ayathābhūtopi tesaṃ tathā vitaraṇaṃ upādāya titthanti voharīyatīti taṃ karontā titthakarā. Osaratīti pavisati.

"With qualities that are not as they really are" means with qualities proclaimed, loudly proclaimed, that are not as they really are, merely for the sake of a falsely illuminated meaning. "They cross over" (taranti), they surpass (atikkamanti) by means of this, thus it is a "ford" (titthaṃ); it is the supreme path. However, the path of wrong views, though not as it really is, is called a "ford" on account of their crossing in such a way; those who make it are called "ford-makers" (titthakarā). "One enters" (osarati) means one enters (pavisati).

239. Sahitanti pubbāparāviruddhaṃ. Na kiñci jātanti paṭiññādosahetudosaudāharaṇadosaduṭṭhadosatāya na kiñci jātaṃ. Tenāha “āropito te vādo”ti. Vadanti tena paribhāsantīti vādo doso. Sabhāvakkosenāti sabhāvato pavattakoṭṭhāsena.

239. "Coherent" (sahitaṃ) means non-contradictory between what precedes and what follows. "Nothing has arisen" (na kiñci jātaṃ) means nothing has arisen due to the faultiness of the fault of the thesis, the fault of the reason, and the fault of the example. Hence, it is said, "Your thesis is refuted." "Thesis" (vādo) means fault (doso), because by that they speak (vadanti), they censure (paribhāsanti). "By natural reproach" (sabhāvakkosena) means by way of the naturally proceeding portion.

240. Pīḷeyyāti madhubhaṇḍena saha bhājane pīḷetvā dadeyya. Sabrahmacārīhi sampayojetvāti sahadhammikehi viheṭhanapayogaṃ katvā, tenāha “vivādaṃ katvā”ti.

240. "One would crush" (pīḷeyya) means one would crush it in a vessel together with a pot of honey and give it. "Having incited his fellow practitioners" (sabrahmacārīhi sampayojetvā) means having made a harmful application with his co-religionists; hence, it is said, "having created a dispute."

241. Itarītarenāti paṇītato itarena. Tenāha “lāmakalāmakenā”ti.

241. "By the one and the other" (itarītarena) means by that which is other than the excellent, i.e., by the inferior. Hence, it is said, "by the base and contemptible."

242. Bhattakosakenāti [V 2.0114] kosakabhattena, khuddakasarāvabhattakenāti attho. Beluvamattabhattāhārāti billapamāṇabhattabhojanā. Oṭṭhavaṭṭiyāti mukhavaṭṭiyā. Sabbākārenevāti sabbappakāreneva. Anappāhāroti na vattabbo kadāci appāhāroti katvā. Tattha ativiya aññehi avisayhaṃ appāhārataṃ bhagavato dassetuṃ “padhānabhūmiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Mayāti nissakkavacanaṃ. Visesatarāti tena dhammena visesavantatarā.

242. 'With a meal bowl' (bhattakosakena) means with food in a bowl (kosakabhattena), that is, with food in a small dish. 'Eating a meal the size of a beluva fruit' (beluvamattabhattāhārā) means consuming food the size of a beluva fruit (billapamāṇabhattabhojanā). 'With a lip ring' (oṭṭhavaṭṭiyā) means with a mouth rim (mukhavaṭṭiyā). 'In every way' (sabbākāreneva) means in every manner (sabbappakāreneva). 'Not one with insufficient food' (anappāhāro) means it should not be said that he ever had insufficient food. There, to show the Blessed One's extreme frugality with food, which was unendurable by others, it is said, 'on the ground of striving,' etc. 'By me' (mayā) is a word indicating certainty. 'More distinguished' (visesatarā) means more distinguished by that Dhamma.

Vatasamādānavaseneva [M 2.0114] paṃsukūlaṃ dhārentīti paṃsukūlikāti āha – “samādinnapaṃsukūlikaṅgā”ti, saddattho pana “visuddhimagge” (visuddhi. 1.24) vuttanayena veditabbo. Piṇḍapātikā sapadānacārinotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Tattha tattha satthena chinditattā satthalūkhāni. Yaṃ yaṃ sappāyaṃ, tasseva gahaṇaṃ uccinanti āha “uccinitvā…pe… thiraṭṭhānameva gahetvā”ti. Alābulomasānīti alābulomāni viya sukhumatarāni cīvarasuttaṃsūni etesaṃ santīti alābulomasāni. Pātitasāṇapaṃsukūlanti kaḷevarena saddhiṃ chaḍḍitasāṇamayaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ, yaṃ tumbamatte puḷave odhunitvā satthā gaṇhi.

Because they wear rag-robes by way of undertaking a vow, they are called 'paṃsukūlika' (rag-robe wearers); thus it is said, 'one who has undertaken the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes.' The literal meaning, however, should be understood according to the method explained in the Visuddhimagga. This same method applies also to terms like 'piṇḍapātika' (alms-food eater) and 'sapadānacārin' (one who goes on alms round without omission). Because they are cut here and there with a knife, they are knife-roughened. They collect and take only what is suitable; thus it is said, 'having collected... taking only the firm part.' 'Alābulomasāni' means: they have robe-threads as fine as the down of a gourd; therefore they are called 'alābulomasāni.' 'Pātitasāṇapaṃsukūla' means a rag-robe made of hemp discarded together with a corpse, which the Teacher took after shaking it out from a putrid mass the size of a gourd.

“Yathāpi bhamaro puppha”ntiādinā (dha. pa. 49) vuttaṃ madhukarabhikkhācāravataṃ “piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāya pabbajjā”ti (mahāva. 73, 128) vacanato bhikkhūnaṃ pakatibhūtaṃ vatanti vuttaṃ “uñchāsake vate ratā”ti. Vata-saddo cettha pakativatasaṅkhātaṃ sakavataṃ vadati. Tenāha “uñchācariyasaṅkhāte bhikkhūnaṃ pakativate”ti. Uccanīcagharadvāraṭṭhāyinoti mahantakhuddakagehānaṃ bahidvārakoṭṭhakaṭṭhāyino. Kabaramissakaṃ bhattaṃ saṃharitvāti kaṇājakamissakaṃ bhattaṃ sampiṇḍitvā. Ummārato paṭṭhāyāti gharummārato paṭṭhāya.

'Just as the bee from the flower...' (Dhp. 49) etc. speaks of the practice of the alms-round like a honeybee, and 'The going forth is in dependence on morsels of food from the alms-bowl' (Mhv. 73, 128) speaks of the vow that has become the nature of bhikkhus; this is what is meant by 'delighting in the vow of gleaning.' Here, the word 'vata' refers to one's own vow, known as the natural vow. Therefore he said: 'in the natural vow of bhikkhus, known as the practice of gleaning.' 'Standing at the doors of high and low houses' means standing at the outer gate-chambers of large and small houses. 'Having gathered variegated food' means having collected food mixed with broken rice. 'Beginning from the threshold' means beginning from the house's threshold.

Cīvarānuggahatthanti cīvarānurakkhaṇatthaṃ. Ettha ca yasmā buddhā nāma sadevake loke anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ, sā cassa puññakkhettatā paramukkaṃsagatā, tasmā sattānaṃ tādisaṃ upakāraṃ ācikkhitvā te ca anuggaṇhantā gahapaticīvaraṃ sādiyanti, catupaccayasantose pana ne paramukkaṃsagatā evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'For the sake of supporting the robe' means for the protection of the robe. And here, because the Buddhas are the unsurpassed field of merit in the world with its devas, and this quality of being a field of merit has reached the highest excellence, therefore, having explained such a benefit to beings and while supporting them, they accept a householder's robe. However, it should be understood that in contentment with the four requisites, they have indeed reached the highest excellence.

244. Sappaccayanti sahetukaṃ sakāraṇaṃ hutvā dhammaṃ desetīti ayamettha attho. Codako pana adhippāyaṃ ajānanto “kiṃ panā”tiādimāha. Itaro “no na desetī”tiādinā adhippāyaṃ vivarati. Nidānanti cettha ñāpakaṃ uppattikāraṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, tañca tassa tassa anuppattiyuttassa atthassa paṭipakkhaharaṇato “sappāṭihāriya”nti vuccatīti āha “purimassevetaṃ [V 2.0115] vevacana”nti. Rāgādīnaṃ vā paṭiharaṇaṃ paṭihāriyaṃ, tadeva pāṭihāriyaṃ, saha pāṭihāriyenāti sappāṭihāriyaṃ. Rāgādipaṭisedhavaseneva hi satthā dhammaṃ deseti.

244. 'With a condition' (sappaccayaṃ) means: having a cause, having a reason, he teaches the Dhamma—this is the meaning here. The accuser, however, not knowing the intention, says, 'But what...?' and so on. The other reveals the intention with, 'No, he does not teach...' and so on. Here, by 'origin' (nidāna) is intended the indicative cause, the cause of arising. And since that removes the opposing factors for each meaning that is fit to arise, it is called 'with a miracle' (sappāṭihāriya). Thus it is said: 'This is just a synonym for the former.' Alternatively, the removal of lust and so on is a 'miracle' (paṭihāriya); that itself is 'pāṭihāriya.' 'With a miracle' (sappāṭihāriya) means 'with pāṭihāriya.' For the Teacher teaches the Dhamma precisely by way of negating lust and so on.

245. Tassa [M 2.0115] tassa pañhassāti yaṃ yaṃ pañhaṃ paro abhisaṅkharitvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchati, tassa tassa pañhassa. Upari āgamanavādapathanti vissajjane kate tato upari āgacchanakaṃ vādamaggaṃ. Visesetvā vadantoti vattati, “bho gotama, vattumarahatī”ti attano vādabhedanatthaṃ āhataṃ kāraṇaṃ attano māraṇatthaṃ āvudhaṃ nidassento viya visesetvā vadanto pahārakena vacanena. Antarantareti mayā vuccamānakathāpabandhassa antarantare. Dadeyya vadeyya. Evarūpesu ṭhānesūti paravādīhi saddhiṃ vādapaṭivādaṭṭhānesu. Te niggahetuṃ mayā desitaṃ suttapadaṃ ānetvā mamayeva anusāsaniṃ ovādaṃ paccāsīsanti.

245. 'For each and every question' means: for whatever question another prepares, approaches the Blessed One, and asks. 'The path of argument that comes after' means the path of debate that comes after the answer has been given. 'Speaking distinctively': saying, 'Venerable Gotama, you should speak,' he speaks distinctively with striking words, as if displaying a weapon brought for his own destruction, a reason brought to defeat his own thesis. 'In the intervals' means in the intervals of the connected discourse being spoken by me. 'He would give' means he would speak. 'In such situations' means in situations of debate and counter-debate with opponents. In order to censure me, they bring a passage from a sutta taught by me and expect instruction and advice from me myself.

246. Sampādemīti manorathaṃ sampādemi. Paripūremīti ajjhāsayaṃ paripūremi. Adhisīleti adhike uttamasīle. Sāvakasīlato ca paccekabuddhasīlato ca buddhānaṃ sīlaṃ adhikaṃ ukkaṭṭhaṃ paramukkaṃsato anaññasādhāraṇabhāvato. Tenāha “buddhasīlaṃ nāma kathita”nti. Ṭhānuppattikapaññāti tattha tattha ṭhānaso uppannapaññā. Tenāha “tatthā”tiādi. Avasesā paññāti idha pāḷiyaṃ āgatā anāgatā ca yathāvuttañāṇadvayavinimuttā paññā.

246. 'I accomplish' means I accomplish my aspiration. 'I fulfill' means I fulfill my intention. 'In higher virtue' means in superior, supreme virtue. The virtue of the Buddhas is higher and more excellent than the virtue of disciples and paccekabuddhas, because it is supremely pre-eminent and not shared by others. Therefore it is said, 'The virtue of the Buddhas is spoken of.' 'Wisdom that arises according to the situation' means wisdom that has arisen appropriately in each case. Therefore he said, 'there,' etc. 'The remaining wisdom' means the wisdom—whether it appears in the Pāli text here or not—that is distinct from the two kinds of knowledge mentioned.

247. Visesādhigamānanti satipaṭṭhānādīnaṃ adhigandhabbavisesānaṃ. Abhiññā nāma cha abhiññā, tāsu ukkaṭṭhaniddesena chaḷabhiññārahatova aggamaggapaññā idha abhiññāti adhippetā, tassa vosānaṃ pariyosānaṃ pāramī paramukkaṃsāti avakaṃsāti ca aggaphalaṃ vuccatīti āha “abhiññā…pe… arahattaṃ pattā”ti.

247. 'Of the attainment of distinctions' means of the special attainments to be realized, such as the foundations of mindfulness. 'Direct knowledge' refers to the six direct knowledges. Among them, by way of supreme designation, the wisdom of the highest path of an Arahant possessing the six direct knowledges is intended here by 'direct knowledge.' Its ending, its conclusion, its perfection, its supreme excellence, and its culmination is called the highest fruit. Thus it is said: 'direct knowledge… having attained Arahantship.'

Upāyapadhāneti ariyaphalādhigamanassa upāyabhūte padhāne. “Anuppannapāpakānuppādādiatthā”ti gahitā tatheva honti, taṃ atthaṃ sādhentiyevāti etassa atthassa dīpako sammā-saddoti yathāadhippetatthassa anuppannapāpakānuppādādino upāyabhūte, padhānaupāyabhūteti attho. Sammā-saddassa vā yoniso atthadīpakataṃ sandhāya “yoniso padhāne”ti vuttaṃ. Chandaṃ janetīti kattukamyatākusalacchandaṃ uppādeti pavatteti vā. Vāyamatīti payogaparakkamaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti kāyikacetasikavīriyaṃ karoti. Cittaṃ ukkhipatīti [M 2.0116] teneva sahajātavīriyena kosajjapakkhato cittaṃ ukkhipati. Padahatīti sammappadhānabhūtaṃ vīriyaṃ pavatteti. Paṭipāṭiyā panetāni cattāri padāni āsevanābhāvanābahulīkammasātaccakiriyāhi [V 2.0116] yojetabbāni. “Padahatī”ti vā iminā āsevanādīhi saddhiṃ sikhāpattaṃ ussoḷhivīriyaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Vaḍḍhiyā paripūraṇatthanti yāvatā bhāvanāpāripūriyā paripūraṇatthaṃ. Yā ṭhitīti yā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭipakkhavigamena avaṭṭhiti. So asammosoti so avināso. Yaṃ vepullanti yo sabbaso vipulabhāvo mahantatā. Bhāvanāpāripūrīti bhāvanāya paripūritā. Atthotipi veditabbaṃ purimapacchimapadānaṃ samānatthabhāvato.

'In the effort that is a means' means in the effort that is a means for the attainment of the noble fruit. The phrase 'for the non-arising of unarisen evil...' etc. is taken just so, as they accomplish that meaning. The word 'right' (sammā) illuminates this, meaning that the effort is a means for the intended purpose of the non-arising of unarisen evil, etc.; it is the effort that is a means. Or, with reference to the word 'right' illuminating the meaning properly, it is said 'in the proper effort.' 'He generates desire' means he produces or sets in motion the wholesome desire to act. 'He strives' means he makes an effort of exertion. 'He arouses energy' means he makes bodily and mental energy. 'He exerts his mind' means with that co-nascent energy, he lifts his mind from the side of laziness. 'He strives' means he sets in motion the energy that constitutes right striving. These four terms, in sequence, should be connected with the actions of cultivation, development, making much of, and continuous application. Or, by this word 'strives', the vigorous energy that has reached its peak should be connected with cultivation and so on. 'For the sake of increase and fulfillment' means for the sake of fulfillment by means of the completion of development. 'That stability' means the persistence of wholesome states through the removal of their opposites. 'That non-confusion' means that non-perishing. 'That abundance' means the state of being extensive in every way, greatness. 'Completion of development' means fulfilled by development. This meaning should also be understood, because the preceding and succeeding terms are synonymous.

Pubbabhāgapaṭipadā kathitātaṃtaṃvisesādhigamassa paṭipadāvibhāvanāya āraddhattā. Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppajjanena anatthāvahatā nāma natthīti vuttaṃ – “uppajjamānā”ti vacanaṃ uppannānaṃ rāsantarabhāvena gahitattā. Tathā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppajjanenāti vuttaṃ – anuppajjamānāti vacanaṃ uppannānaṃ rāsantarabhāvena gahitattā. Nirujjhamānāti paṭipakkhasamāyogena vinassamānā, na khaṇanirodhavasena nirujjhamānā.

The preliminary practice has been discussed because it was undertaken to clarify the path for achieving various specific attainments. It is said that there is no bringing of harm by the non-arising of unwholesome states—the word 'arising' is taken as referring to their being included in a mass of already arisen states. Similarly, concerning the arising of wholesome states, it is said that the word 'arising' is taken as referring to their being included in a mass of already arisen states. 'Ceasing' means being destroyed through the association of opposing factors, not ceasing through momentary cessation.

Lobhādayo veditabbā, ye āraddhavipassakānaṃ uppajjanārahā. Sakiṃ uppajjitvāti sabhāvakathanamattametaṃ. Ekavārameva hi maggo uppajjati. Nirujjhamānoti saraseneva nirujjhamāno. Na hi tassa paṭipakkhasamāyogo nāma atthi. Phalassāti anantarakāleva uppajjanakaphalassa. Paccayaṃ datvāva nirujjhatīti iminā maggo sampati āyatiñca ekanteneva atthāvahoti dasseti. Purimasmimpīti “anuppannā me kusalā dhammā anuppajjamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyu”nti etasmiṃ tatiyavārepi. “Samathavipassanā gahetabbā”ti vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ, taṃ pana maggassa anuppannatāya sabbhāvato, anuppajjamāne ca tasmiṃ vaṭṭānatthasabbhāvatoti maggassapi sādhāraṇabhāvato na yuttanti paṭikkhipati. Yadi samathavipassanānampi anuppatti anatthāvahā, maggassa anuppattiyā vattabbaṃ natthīti.

Greed and the like, which are liable to arise in those who have initiated insight, should be understood. 'Having arisen once'—this is merely a statement of its nature, for the path arises only once. 'Ceasing' means ceasing by its own nature, for it has no association with an opposing factor. 'Of the fruit' means of the fruit that arises in the immediately subsequent moment. 'Having given the condition, it ceases'—by this, it shows that the path is entirely beneficial both in the present and in the future. 'In the previous case also' refers to this third instance: 'Unarisen wholesome states, by not arising, would lead to harm.' It is said in the commentary that serenity and insight should be taken up, but he rejects this as not fitting. For this is also common to the path, since the path is as yet unarisen, and when it does not arise, there is certainly harm for the round of existence. If even the non-arising of serenity and insight is harmful, what need be said of the non-arising of the path?

Mahantaṃ[M 2.0117], gāravaṃ hoti, tasmā “saṅghagāravena yathāruci vandituṃ na labhāmī”ti saṅghena saha na nikkhami. Ettakaṃ dhātūnaṃ nidhānaṃ nāma aññatra natthi, mahādhātunidhānato hi nīharitvā katipayā dhātuyo tattha tattha cetiye upanītā, idha pana rāmagāmathūpe vinaṭṭhe nāgabhavanaṃ paviṭṭhā doṇamattā dhātuyo upanītā. Atimandāni noti nanu ativiya mandāni.

Great is the reverence; therefore, thinking, “Due to reverence for the Sangha, I cannot pay homage as I wish,” he did not leave with the Sangha. Nowhere else is there such a great deposit of relics. For from the great deposit of relics, a few relics were taken and placed here and there in various shrines. But here, when the Rāmagāma stupa was ruined, relics amounting to a doṇa measure, which had entered the Nāga abode, were brought. 'Are they not extremely slow?' means, 'Are they not indeed very slow?'

Saṃvijjitvāti “kathañhi nāma mādiso īdisaṃ anatthaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti saṃvegaṃ janetvā. Īdisaṃ nāma mādisaṃ ārabbha vattabbanti kiṃ vadatīti taṃ vacanaṃ anādiyanto.

'Having been stirred' means having generated a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking: 'How indeed could one like me come to such misfortune?' 'Disregarding that statement' means not taking to heart the statement, thinking: 'What is he saying, that such a thing is said concerning one like me?'

Santasamāpattito [V 2.0117] aññaṃ santhambhanakāraṇaṃ balavaṃ natthīti tato parihīno sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ patiṭṭhā kathaṃ bhavissatīti āha “santāya…pe… na sakkotī”ti. Na hi mahārajjuyā chinnāya suttatantū santhambhetuṃ sakkontīti. Samathe dassetvā tena samānagatikā imasmiṃ visaye vipassanāpīti iminā adhippāyenāha “evaṃ uppannā samathavipassanā…pe… saṃvattantī”ti.

There is no stronger cause for firm establishment than the attainment of peace. Therefore, for one who is deficient in it, how can there be a footing in right practice? Thus it is said: “Through peace... one is not able.” Indeed, when a great rope is cut, a cotton thread is not able to hold it together. Having shown this in the case of serenity, he says with the intention that insight also has the same course in this matter: “Thus arisen serenity and insight... lead to...”

Kāsāvanti kāsāvavatthaṃ. Kacchaṃ pīḷetvā nivatthanti pacchimaṃ ovaṭṭikaṃ pīḷento viya daḷhaṃ katvā nivatthaṃ addasaṃsūti yojanā.

'Kāsāva' means a saffron-colored garment. 'Wearing it with the loin-cloth fold tightened': the construction is that they saw him wearing it firmly, as if pressing down the final fold of the lower garment.

Vuttanayenāti (a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.394) “kāmā nāmete aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā”tiādinā vatthukāmakilesakāmesu ādīnavadassanapubbakanekkhammapaṭipattiyā chandarāgaṃ vikkhambhayato samucchindantassa ca “anuppanno ca kāmāsavo na uppajjatī”tiādinā heṭṭhā sabbāsavasuttavaṇṇanādīsu (ma. ni. 1.15 ādayo; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.15 ādayo) vuttanayena. Ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavitvā niruddhavipākoti tadārammaṇamāha. Anubhavitvā bhavitvā ca vigataṃ bhūtavigataṃ. Anubhūtabhūtā hi bhūtatāsāmaññena bhūta-saddena vuttā. Sāmaññameva hi upasaggena visesīyatīti. Anubhūtasaddo ca kammavacanicchāya abhāvato anubhavakavācako daṭṭhabbo. Vipāko ārammaṇe uppajjitvā niruddho bhutvāvigatoti vattabbataṃ arahati, [M 2.0118] vikappagāhavasena rāgādīhi tabbipakkhehi ca akusalaṃ kusalañca kammaṃ ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavitvā vigatanti vattabbataṃ arahati. Yathāvutto pana vipāko kevalaṃ ārammaṇarasānubhavanavaseneva pavattatīti anubhavitvā vigatattā nippariyāyeneva vutto, tassa ca tathā vuttattā kammaṃ bhavitvā vigatapariyāyena, yaṃ “uppannānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya, uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā”ti ettha “uppanna”nti gahetvā taṃsadisānaṃ pahānaṃ, vuddhi ca vuttā. Vipaccituṃ okāsakaraṇavasena uppatitaṃ atītakammañca tato uppajjituṃ āraddho anāgato vipāko ca “okāsakatuppanno”ti vutto. Yaṃ uppannasaddena vināpi viññāyamānaṃ uppannaṃ sandhāya “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sañcetanikāna”ntiādi (a. ni. 10.217, 219) vuttaṃ.

'By the method stated' refers to the method stated in the sub-commentary (A. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1.394), beginning with 'These sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,' whereby one suppresses and eradicates sensual desire by the practice of renunciation, which is preceded by seeing the danger in sensual pleasures as objects and as defilements; and also by the method stated in the commentaries on the Sabbāsava Sutta and other texts (M.N. 1.15ff; M.N.A. 1.15ff), beginning with 'the unarisen influx of sensuality does not arise.' 'The result having ceased after experiencing the flavor of the object' refers to the registering consciousness (tadārammaṇa). 'Gone after having been experienced and having become' is bhūtavigata. For what has been experienced and has become is called by the word bhūta in the general sense of 'having become.' Indeed, it is the general meaning that is specified by the prefix. And the word anubhūta should be understood as having an active sense, due to the absence of an intended passive meaning. The result, having arisen in relation to the object and then ceased, is fit to be described as 'having become and passed away.' And due to grasping at concepts, unwholesome and wholesome kamma, along with their opposites, having experienced the flavor of the object, are fit to be described as 'passed away.' However, the aforementioned result occurs solely by way of experiencing the flavor of the object; and because it has passed away after having been experienced, it is stated directly. And because it is stated thus, kamma is stated indirectly as 'having become and passed away.' This is why in the passage 'for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states and for the stability of arisen wholesome states,' by taking the word 'arisen,' the abandoning and growth of similar states are mentioned. Past kamma that has occurred by creating an opportunity to ripen, and the future result that has begun to arise from it, are called 'opportunity-arisen.' And that which is understood as 'arisen' even without the word 'arisen' being used is what is referred to in statements like: 'Monks, of intentional actions... I say...' (A.N. 10.217, 219).

Tesūti vipassanāya bhūmibhūtesu khandhesu. Anusayitakilesāti anusayavasena pavattā appahīnā maggena pahātabbā kilesā adhippetā. Tenāha “atītā…pe… na vattabbā”ti. Tesañhi ambarukkhopamāya vattamānāditā na vattabbā maggena pahātabbānaṃ tādisassa vibhāgassa anuppajjanato. Appahīnāva hontīti iminā appahīnaṭṭhena anusayaṭṭhoti dasseti. Idaṃ [V 2.0118] bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāmāti idaṃ tesu khandhesu uppattirahakilesajātaṃ tāya eva uppattirahatāya bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāma, tebhūmakabhūmiladdhā nāma hotīti attho. Tāsu tāsu bhūmīsūti manussadevādiattabhāvasaṅkhātesu upādānakkhandhesu. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ santāne anuppattianāpāditatāya asamugghātitā. Ettha ca laddhabhūmikaṃ bhūmiladdhanti vuttaṃ aggiāhito viya.

“In these” refers to the aggregates, which serve as the ground for insight. 'Latent defilements' means the defilements that persist by way of latency, are unabandoned, and are to be abandoned by the path. Hence it is said, “past… etc.… cannot be spoken of.” For of these defilements to be abandoned by the path, 'present, etc.' cannot be spoken, as in the simile of the mango tree, because such a distinction does not arise. By 'they are simply unabandoned,' he shows that the meaning of 'latency' is the meaning of 'unabandoned.' “This is called ‘arisen having gained a ground’” means that this class of defilements, which is liable to arise in those aggregates, is called “arisen having gained a ground” precisely because of its liability to arise; the meaning is that it is “gained on the ground of the three realms.” “In those various grounds” refers to the aggregates of clinging, designated as states of individual existence such as human, divine, etc. In each continuum, they are uneradicated due to not having occurred and not having been produced. And here, what has obtained a ground is called 'ground-gained,' like fire that has been taken up.

Okāsakatuppanna-saddepi ca okāso kato etenāti okāso kato etassāti ca atthadvayepi kata-saddassa paranipāto daṭṭhabbo. Āhatakhīrarukkho viya nimittaggāhavasena adhiggahitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, anāhatakhīrarukkho viya avikkhambhitatāya antogadhakilesaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Nimittaggāhakāvikkhambhitakilesā vā puggalā āhatānāhatakhīrarukkhasadisā. Purimanayenevāti avikkhambhituppanne viya “imasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne nuppajjissantīti na vattabbā. Kasmā? Asamugghātitattā”ti yojetvā vitthāretabbaṃ.

And in the word 'okāsakatuppanna' (opportunity-arisen), the posterior placing of the word 'kata' should be understood in both meanings: 'an opportunity was made by this' and 'an opportunity was made for this.' Like a milk-tree that has been struck, the object is apprehended by way of grasping a sign; like a milk-tree that has not been struck, the object is one with defilements lurking within due to not being suppressed. Or, individuals who grasp signs or have unsuppressed defilements are like the struck and unstruck milk-trees. 'By the former method' means that, as in the case of what arises from the unsuppressed, it should be connected and elaborated thus: 'It cannot be said, “They will not arise in this place.” Why? Because they have not been eradicated.'”

Vuttaṃ paṭisambhidāmagge. Tattha ca maggena pahīnakilesānameva tidhā navattabbataṃ apākaṭaṃ supākaṭaṃ kātuṃ ajātaphalarukkho upamābhāvena āgato[M 2.0119]. Atītādīnaṃ appahīnatā dassanatthampi “jātaphalarukkhena dīpetabba”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā acchinne rukkhe nibbattārahāni phalāni chinne anuppajjamānāni na kadāci sasabhāvāni ahesuṃ honti bhavissanti cāti tāni atītādibhāvena na vattabbāni, evaṃ maggena pahīnakilesā ca daṭṭhabbā. Yathā chede asati phalāni uppajjissanti, sati ca nuppajjissantīti chedassa sātthakatā, evaṃ maggabhāvanāya ca sātthakatā yojetabbā.

It is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. There, to make very clear what was unclear regarding the fact that the defilements abandoned by the path cannot be spoken of in three ways, the analogy of a tree that has not yet borne fruit is introduced. Also, to show the non-abandonment of those in the past, etc., it is said, 'It should be illustrated with a tree that has borne fruit.' Therein, just as fruits that were capable of arising on an uncut tree do not arise when it is cut, and were never of their own nature, are not, nor will be, and thus cannot be spoken of in terms of past, etc.; in the same way, the defilements abandoned by the path should be regarded. Just as when there is no cutting, fruits will arise, but when there is cutting, they will not arise, thus showing the purposefulness of cutting; in the same way, the purposefulness of developing the path should be connected.

Tepi pajahatiyeva kilesappahāneneva tesampi anuppattidhammatāpādanato. Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassāti paṭisandhiviññāṇassa. Upādinnaanupādinnatoti upādinnakhandhato ceva kilesato ca. Upapattivasena vuṭṭhānaṃ dassetumāha – “bhavavasena panā”tiādi. Ye sotāpannassa satta bhavā appahīnā, tato pañca ṭhapetvā itare dve “sugatibhavekadesā”ti adhippetā. Sugatikāmabhavatoti sugatibhavekadesabhūtakāmabhavato. Arahattamaggo rūpārūpabhavato vuṭṭhāti uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanasamugghātabhāvato. Yadi arahattamaggo eva ariyamaggo siyā, so eva sabbakilese pajaheyya, sabbabhavehipi vuṭṭhaheyya. Yasmā pana odhisova kilesā pahīyanti, tasmā heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimamaggehi pahīnāvasese kilese so pajahati, iti imaṃ sāmatthiyaṃ sandhāya [V 2.0119] “sabbabhavehi vuṭṭhātiyevātipi vadantī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi so eva “vajirūpamo”ti vutto.

It abandons those too, by the very abandoning of defilements, because it brings about for them the state of non-arising. 'Of formations-consciousness' means of rebirth-linking consciousness. 'From the grasped and the ungrasped' means from the aggregates subject to clinging and from the defilements. To show emergence by way of becoming, he says: 'But by way of becoming…' and so on. Of the seven becomings not abandoned by a stream-enterer, setting aside five, the other two are intended as 'a portion of a happy becoming.' 'From a happy sensual becoming' means from the sensual becoming that constitutes a portion of a happy becoming. The path of arahantship emerges from the form and formless becomings because it eradicates the higher fetters. If the path of arahantship were the only noble path, it alone would abandon all defilements and emerge from all becomings. But since defilements are abandoned in stages, it abandons the defilements remaining after abandonment by the lower paths. Therefore, with reference to this capability, it is said: 'some say that it emerges from all becomings indeed.' For it is said to be 'like a diamond.'

Hotu tāva vuttanayena anuppannānaṃ akusalānaṃ anuppādāya, uppannānaṃ uppannasadisānaṃ pahānāya anuppattidhammatāpādanāya maggabhāvanā, atha maggakkhaṇe kathaṃ anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ uppādāya uppannānañca ṭhitiyā bhāvanā hoti ekacittakkhaṇikattā tassāti codeti, itaro “maggappavattiyāyevā”ti parihāramāha. Maggo hi kāmañcekacittakkhaṇiko, tathārūpo panassa pavattiviseso, yaṃ anuppannā kusalā dhammā sātisayaṃ uppajjanti, uppannā ca savisesaṃ pāripūriṃ pāpuṇanti. Tenāha “maggo hī”tiādi. Kiñcāpi ariyamaggo vattamānakkhaṇe anuppanno nāma na hoti, anuppannapubbataṃ upādāya upacāravasena tathā vuccatīti dassetuṃ “anāgatapubbaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ayamevāti ayaṃ maggassa yathāpaccayapavatti [M 2.0120] eva ṭhiti nāmāti, maggasamaṅgī puggalo maggampi bhāvento eva tassa ṭhitiyā bhāvetīti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Let it be granted that, in the way stated, the development of the path is for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states and those similar to them, and for bringing about the state of non-recurrence. But how, at the moment of the path, does the development for the arising of unarisen wholesome states and for the stability of arisen ones occur, given that the path lasts only a single mind-moment? This is the objection. The other gives the reply: 'It is precisely through the occurrence of the path.' For although the path lasts only a single mind-moment, its distinctive mode of occurrence is such that unarisen wholesome states arise with excellence, and arisen ones reach fulfillment with distinction. Hence he says, 'For the path…' and so on. To show that although the noble path is not, in the present moment, something unarisen, it is spoken of in this way figuratively, with reference to its having been previously unarisen, it is said, 'For what was previously unarisen…' and so on. This very occurrence of the path in accordance with its conditions is what is called 'stability.' Thus, it is proper to say that a person endowed with the path, while developing the path, also develops it for its stability.

Upasamamānaṃ gacchatīti vikkhambhanavasena samucchedavasena kilese upasamentaṃ vattati. Pubbabhāgindriyāni eva vā adhippetāni. Tenevāha “kilesūpasamatthaṃ vā gacchatī”ti.

'Going to pacification' means proceeding while pacifying defilements by way of suppression or by way of eradication. Or, the faculties of the preliminary part are intended. Therefore, it is said: 'Or, one who goes for the sake of pacifying defilements.'

248. Adhimuccanaṭṭhenāti (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.129; a. ni. ṭī. 3.8.66) adhikaṃ savisesaṃ muccanaṭṭhena, tenāha “suṭṭhu muccanaṭṭho”ti. Etena satipi sabbassapi rūpāvacarajjhānassa vikkhambhanavasena paṭipakkhato vimuttabhāve yena bhāvanāvisesena taṃ jhānaṃ sātisayaṃ paṭipakkhato vimuccitvā pavattati, so bhāvanāviseso dīpito. Bhavati hi samānajātiyuttopi bhāvanāvisesena pavattiākāraviseso. Yathā taṃ saddhāvimuttato diṭṭhippattassa, tathā paccanīkadhammehi suṭṭhu vimuttatāya eva aniggahitabhāvena nirāsaṅkatāya abhirativasena suṭṭhu adhimuccanaṭṭhenapi vimokkho. Tenāha “ārammaṇe cā”tiādi. Ayaṃ panatthoti ayaṃ adhimuccanattho pacchimavimokkhe nirodhe natthi. Kevalo vimuttattho eva tattha labbhati, taṃ sayameva parato vakkhati.

248. 'In the sense of firm resolve' means in the sense of being released additionally and with distinction; therefore he says, 'the sense of being well-released.' By this is shown that distinctive development by which, even though all fine-material jhānas are in a state of being liberated from opposing factors by way of suppression, that jhāna proceeds by being exceptionally released from opposing factors. For even among those of the same kind, there is a distinctive mode of occurrence due to a distinctive development, just as that of one who has attained vision differs from one liberated by faith. So too, through being well-released from opposing states, and thus by being unconstrained, free from hesitation, and by way of thorough delight, there is liberation also in the sense of firm resolve. Hence he says, 'and in the object…' and so on. But this meaning—this sense of firm resolve—does not exist in the final liberation, which is cessation. There, only the meaning of release is found. That he will explain himself later.

Rūpīti yenāyaṃ sasantatipariyāpannena rūpena samannāgato, taṃ yassa jhānassa hetubhāvena visiṭṭhaṃ rūpaṃ hoti. Yena visiṭṭhena rūpena “rūpī”ti vucceyya rūpī-saddassa atisayatthadīpanato, tadeva sasantatipariyāpannarūpanimittaṃ jhānamiva paramatthato rūpībhāvasādhakanti [V 2.0120] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “ajjhatta”ntiādi. Rūpajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ uttarapadalopena. Rūpānīti panettha purimapadalopo daṭṭhabbo. Tena vuttaṃ “nīlakasiṇādīni rūpānī”ti.

'One with form' means one who is endowed with form included in one's own continuity, which form is distinguished as the cause for that jhāna. It should be understood that the very distinguished form by which one would be called 'one with form'—because this shows the excellent meaning of the word 'rūpī'—that sign of form included in one's own continuity, like the jhāna itself, establishes in an ultimate sense the state of being 'one with form.' Hence he says, 'internal…' and so on. Rūpajjhānaṃ becomes rūpaṃ by elision of the last member. In rūpāni, however, the elision of the first member should be understood. Therefore, it is said, 'the blue kasiṇa and so on are forms.'

Antoappanāyaṃ subhanti ābhogo natthīti iminā pubbābhogavasena adhimutti siyāti dasseti. Evañhettha tathāvattabbatāpatticodanā anavakāsā hoti. Yasmā suvisuddhesu nīlādīsu vaṇṇakasiṇesu tattha katādhikārānaṃ abhirativasena suṭṭhu adhimutti siyā, tasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tathā tatiyo vimokkho saṃvaṇṇito. Yasmā pana mettādivasena pavattamānā bhāvanā satte appaṭikūlato dahati, [M 2.0121] te subhato adhimuccitvāva pavattati, tasmā paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.212) brahmavihārabhāvanā “subhavimokkho”ti vuttā, tayidaṃ ubhayampi tena tena pariyāyena vuttattā na virujjhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By the statement, 'In internal absorption, there is no advertence "beautiful",' he shows that there can be firm resolve by way of preliminary advertence. Thus, in this case, the accusation of being obliged to speak in that way is groundless. Since in the perfectly purified color kasiṇas, such as blue, there can be a firm resolve by way of delight for those who have made a foundation therein, the third liberation is described in that way in the commentary. Moreover, since the development proceeding by way of loving-kindness and so on regards beings as non-repulsive, it proceeds only after having firmly resolved upon them as beautiful. Therefore, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the development of the divine abidings is called the 'liberation of the beautiful.' It should be understood that both of these are not contradictory, because they are stated each in its own way.

Sabbasoti anavasesato. Na hi catunnaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ ekadesopi tattha avasiṭṭhoti. Vissaṭṭhattāti yathāparicchinne kāle nirodhitattā. Uttamo vimokkho nāma ariyeheva samāpajjitabbato, ariyaphalapariyosānattā diṭṭheva dhamme nibbānappattibhāvato ca.

'Completely' means without remainder. For not even a portion of the four immaterial aggregates remains there. 'Because of being relinquished' means because of being ceased at the determined time. It is called the supreme liberation because it is to be attained only by the noble ones, because it culminates in the fruit of arahantship, and because it is the state of having attained Nibbāna in this very life.

249. Abhibhavatīti abhibhu (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.173; a. ni. ṭī. 3.6.61-65) parikammaṃ, ñāṇaṃ vā. Abhibhu āyatanaṃ etassāti abhibhāyatanaṃ, jhānaṃ. Abhibhavitabbaṃ vā ārammaṇasaṅkhātaṃ āyatanaṃ etassāti abhibhāyatanaṃ, jhānaṃ. Ārammaṇābhibhavanato abhibhu ca taṃ āyatanañca yogino sukhavisesānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhāvato manāyatanadhammāyatanabhāvato cātipi sasampayuttaṃ jhānaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ. Tenāha “abhibhavanakāraṇānī”tiādi. Tānīti abhibhāyatanasaññitāni jhānāni. Samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa ābhogo pubbabhāgabhāvanāvasena jhānakkhaṇe pavattaṃ abhibhavanākāraṃ gahetvā pavattoti daṭṭhabbo. Parikammavasena ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī, na appanāvasena. Na hi paṭibhāganimittārammaṇā appanā ajjhattavisayā sambhavati. Taṃ pana ajjhatta parikammavasena laddhaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ asuvisuddhameva hoti, na bahiddhā parikammavasena laddhaṃ viya visuddhaṃ.

249. "Abhibhavati" means 'overcomes' (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.173; A. Ni. Ṭī. 3.6.61-65), referring to preparatory work or knowledge. The sphere of mastery (abhibhāyatana) is the jhāna, for it is the sphere of one who overcomes. Alternatively, its sphere is the sphere (āyatana) to be overcome, designated as the object; hence it is a sphere of mastery, the jhāna. Because it overcomes the object, it is mastery, and because it is a sphere serving as the basis for the meditator's special happiness, and being the mental base (manāyatana) and the mental-object base (dhammāyatana), the associated jhāna is a sphere of mastery. Hence it is said, "the causes of overcoming," etc. "These" refers to the jhānas designated as spheres of mastery. For one who has emerged from the attainment, it should be understood that the advertence proceeds by taking up the mode of overcoming that occurred at the moment of jhāna, by means of the development of the preliminary part. By means of preparatory practice, one perceives form internally, not by means of absorption. For absorption with a counterpart sign as its object is not possible with an internal object. However, the kasiṇa sign attained through internal preparatory practice is not very pure, not pure like one attained through external preparatory practice.

Parittānīti yathāladdhāni suppasarāvamattāni. Tenāha “avaḍḍhitānī”ti. Parittavasenevāti vaṇṇavasena ābhoge vijjamānepi parittavaseneva idamabhibhāyatanaṃ vuttaṃ. Parittatā hettha abhibhavanassa kāraṇaṃ. Vaṇṇābhoge satipi asatipi abhibhāyatanabhāvanā nāma tikkhapaññasseva sambhavati, na itarassāti “ñāṇuttariko puggalo”ti. Abhibhavitvā samāpajjatīti [V 2.0121] ettha abhibhavanaṃ samāpajjanañca upacārajjhānādhigamasamanantarameva appanājhānuppādananti āha “saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ pāpetī”ti. Saha nimittuppādenāti ca appanāparivāsābhāvassa lakkhaṇavacanametaṃ. Yo “khippābhiñño”ti vuccati[M 2.0122], tatopi ñāṇuttarasseva abhibhāyatanabhāvanā. Etthāti etasmiṃ nimitte. Appanaṃ pāpetīti bhāvanā appanaṃ neti.

"Limited" means as obtained, about the size of a small bowl. Therefore it is said, "not enlarged." "By means of the limited" means that even when there is advertence by means of color, this sphere of mastery is spoken of as being by means of the limited. Here, limitedness is the cause for the overcoming. Whether there is advertence to color or not, the development of the sphere of mastery is possible only for one of sharp wisdom, not for others; therefore, it is said, "a person superior in knowledge." "Having overcome, one attains": here, the overcoming and the attainment are the production of absorption-jhāna immediately after the attainment of access concentration. Thus it is said, "here, one attains absorption simultaneously with the arising of the sign." "Simultaneously with the arising of the sign" is a statement characterizing the absence of a preparatory period for absorption. The development of the sphere of mastery is for one who is superior in knowledge, even more so than one who is called "of swift direct knowledge." "Here" means in this sign. "Attains absorption" means the development leads to absorption.

Ettha ca keci “uppanne upacārajjhāne taṃ ārabbha ye heṭṭhimantena dve tayo javanavārā pavattanti, te upacārajjhāna pakkhikā eva, tadanantarañca bhavaṅgaparivāsena upacārāsevanāya ca vinā appanā hoti, saha nimittuppādeneva appanaṃ pāpetī”ti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ. Na hi pārivāsikaparikammena appanāvāro icchito, nāpi mahaggatappamāṇajjhānesu viya upacārajjhāne ekantato paccavekkhaṇā icchitabbā, tasmā upacārajjhānādhigamato paraṃ katipayabhavaṅgacittāvasāne appanaṃ pāpuṇanto “saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ pāpetī”ti vutto. “Saha nimittuppādenā”ti ca adhippāyikamidaṃ vacanaṃ, na nītatthaṃ, adhippāyo vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Here, some say: "When access concentration has arisen, taking that as object, the two or three impulsion-courses that occur at the very end belong to the side of access concentration. Immediately after that, absorption occurs without a preparatory period of life-continuum and without cultivation of access concentration, and one attains absorption simultaneously with the arising of the sign." This is merely their opinion. For an absorption-course is not intended through the preparatory work of a probationary period, nor should reviewing be absolutely required in access concentration as it is in the exalted and immeasurable jhānas. Therefore, one who attains absorption after the attainment of access concentration, at the end of a few life-continuum mind-moments, is said to "attain absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the sign." And the statement "simultaneously with the arising of the sign" is a statement requiring interpretation, not of explicit meaning; its intention should be understood in the way that has been explained.

Na antosamāpattiyaṃ tadā tathārūpassa ābhogassa asambhavato, samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa ābhogo pubbabhāgabhāvanāvasena jhānakkhaṇe pavattaṃ abhibhavanākāraṃ gahetvā pavattoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 204) pana “iminā panassa pubbabhāgo kathito”ti vuttaṃ. Antosamāpattiyaṃ tathā ābhogābhāve kasmā “jhānasaññāyapī”ti vuttanti āha “abhibhava…pe… atthī”ti.

Not during the attainment itself, because at that time such an advertence is impossible. It should be understood that for one who has arisen from attainment, the advertence proceeds by taking up the mode of overcoming that occurred at the moment of jhāna, by means of the development of the preliminary part. However, in the Abhidhamma commentary (DhsA. 204) it is said, "By this, his preliminary part has been described." If there is no such advertence during the attainment itself, why is it said, "even by the perception of jhāna"? The reply is: "overcoming... etc. ... exists."

Vaḍḍhitappamāṇānīti vipulappamāṇānīti attho, na ekaṅguladvaṅgulādivasena vaḍḍhitappamāṇānīti tathā vaḍḍhanassevettha asambhavato. Tenāha “mahantānī”ti.

"Of increased measure" means of vast measure, not increased by one inch or two inches, since such increase is impossible here. Therefore, it is said, "large."

Rūpe saññā rūpasaññā, sā assa atthīti rūpasaññī, na rūpasaññī arūpasaññī. Saññāsīsena jhānaṃ vadati. Rūpasaññāya anuppādanamevettha alābhitā. Bahiddhāva uppannanti bahiddhāvatthusmiṃyeva uppannaṃ. Abhidhamme pana “ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti evaṃ catunnaṃ abhibhāyatanānaṃ āgatattā abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 204) “kasmā pana yathā suttante – ‘ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittānī’tiādi vuttaṃ, evaṃ avatvā [V 2.0122] idha catūsupi abhibhāyatanesu ajjhattaṃ [M 2.0123] arūpasaññitāva vuttā”ti codanaṃ katvā “ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyato”ti kāraṇaṃ vatvā “tattha vā hi idha vā bahiddhārūpāneva abhibhavitabbāni, tasmā tāni niyamato vattabbānīti tatrāpi idhāpi vuttāni. ‘Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī’ti idaṃ pana satthu desanāvilāsamattamevā”ti vuttaṃ.

Perception of form is form-perception. One who has that is a form-perceiver; one who does not have form-perception is a non-form perceiver. He speaks of jhāna with perception as the chief. Here, the non-arising of form-perception is simply a non-acquisition. What arises externally arises only in an external object. In the Abhidhamma, however, it is said: "Internally a non-form perceiver, externally one sees forms, limited, fair and foul, unlimited, fair and foul." Thus, because this pertains to the four bases of mastery, in the Abhidhamma commentary (DhsA. 204), the question is raised: "But why, as in the suttas—'internally a form-perceiver, one sees external forms, limited,' and so on—is it not stated thus here, but in all four bases of mastery, only internal non-form perception is mentioned?" After raising this objection, the reason is given: "Because internal forms cannot be overcome." It is then explained: "For there or here, only external forms are to be overcome. Therefore, those must be stated definitively. Thus, they are stated both there and here. The phrase 'internally a non-form perceiver,' however, is merely an expression of the Teacher's skillful means in teaching."

Ettha ca vaṇṇābhogarahitāni sahitāni ca sabbāni “parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti vuttāni, tathā “appamāṇānī”ti daṭṭhabbāni. Atthi hi eso pariyāyo “parittāni abhibhuyya tāni ce kadāci vaṇṇavasena ābhujitāni honti suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni abhibhuyyā”ti. Pariyāyakathā hi suttantadesanāti. Abhidhamme pana nippariyāyadesanattā vaṇṇābhogarahitāni visuṃ vuttāni, tathā sahitāni. Atthi hi ubhayattha abhibhavanapariyāyoti “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī”tiādinā paṭhamadutiyaabhibhāyatanesu paṭhamavimokkho, tatiyacatutthābhibhāyatanesu dutiyavimokkho, vaṇṇābhibhāyatanesu tatiyavimokkho ca abhibhavanappavattito saṅgahito, abhidhamme pana nippariyāyadesanattā vimokkhābhibhāyatanāni asaṅkarato dassetuṃ vimokkhe vajjetvā abhibhāyatanāni kathitāni, sabbāni ca vimokkhakiccāni jhānāni vimokkhadesanāyaṃ vuttāni. Tadetaṃ “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī”ti āgatassa abhibhāyatanadvayassa abhidhamme abhibhāyatanesu avacanato “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīnañca sabbavimokkhakiccasādhāraṇavacanabhāvato vavatthānaṃ katanti viññāyati.

Here, all those devoid of advertence to color, as well as those accompanied by it, are called "limited, fair and foul," and similarly, they should be understood as "unlimited." For there is this figurative expression: "Having overcome the limited, if on occasion they are adverted to by means of color, they become 'having overcome the fair and foul.'" Indeed, figurative explanation is the teaching of the discourses. In the Abhidhamma, however, because the teaching is non-figurative, those devoid of advertence to color are spoken of separately, and likewise those accompanied by it. For in both cases, there is the mode of overcoming. Thus, by "internally a form-perceiver" and so forth, the first liberation is included in the first and second spheres of mastery, the second liberation in the third and fourth spheres of mastery, and the third liberation in the color spheres of mastery, through the process of overcoming. But in the Abhidhamma, because the teaching is non-figurative, in order to show the liberations and spheres of mastery without confusion, the spheres of mastery are discussed, omitting the liberations, while all the jhānas that have the function of liberation are stated in the teaching on the liberations. Therefore, it is understood that this distinction has been made because the pair of spheres of mastery beginning with "internally a form-perceiver" is not mentioned in the Abhidhamma’s section on the spheres of mastery, and because statements like "one with form sees forms" are common statements fulfilling all the functions of the liberations.

“Ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyato”ti idaṃ abhidhamme katthacipi “ajjhattaṃ rūpāni passatī”ti avatvā sabbattha yaṃ vuttaṃ “bahiddhārūpāni passatī”ti, tassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tena yaṃ aññahetukaṃ, taṃ tena hetunā vuttaṃ, yaṃ pana desanāvilāsahetukaṃ ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññitāya eva abhidhamme vacanaṃ, na tassa aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ maggitabbanti dasseti. Ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyatā ca tesaṃ bahiddhārūpānaṃ viya avibhūtattā, desanāvilāso ca yathāvuttavavatthānavasena veditabbo, veneyyajjhāsayavasena vijjamānapariyāyakathanabhāvato. “Suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti eteneva siddhattā nīlādiabhibhāyatanāni na vattabbānīti ce? Na, nīlādīsu [M 2.0124] katādhikārānaṃ nīlādibhāvasseva abhibhavanakāraṇattā. Na hi tesaṃ parisuddhāparisuddhavaṇṇānaṃ parittatā tadappamāṇatā vā abhibhavanakāraṇaṃ, atha kho nīlādibhāvo evāti. Etesu ca parittādikasiṇarūpesu yaṃ caritassa imāni abhibhāyatanāni ijjhanti, taṃ dassetuṃ “imesu panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The statement 'because internal forms cannot be overcome' is the reason for what is said everywhere in the Abhidhamma—'one sees external forms'—without ever saying 'one sees internal forms.' This shows that what has another cause is stated for that reason, while for the statement in the Abhidhamma of only internal formless perception, which has the grace of the teaching as its cause, no other reason should be sought. The inability to overcome internal forms is due to their being indistinct, like external forms. And the grace of the teaching should be understood according to the distinctions already stated, based on the disposition of those to be trained and the fact that it is a statement of an existing mode. If it is said that since this is established by 'of fair and foul color,' the bases of mastery related to blue, etc., need not be mentioned? No, because for those who have undertaken the practice with blue, etc., the very nature of blue, etc., is the cause of overcoming. For it is not the limitedness or boundlessness of their pure or impure colors that is the cause of overcoming, but rather the nature of blue, etc., itself. And to show for which temperament these bases of mastery succeed among these limited and other kasiṇa forms, it is said, 'But in these...,' etc.

Sabbasaṅgāhikavasenāti [V 2.0123] sakalanīlavaṇṇanīlanidassananīlanibhāsānaṃ sādhāraṇavasena. Vaṇṇavasenāti sabhāvavaṇṇavasena. Nidassanavasenāti passitabbatāvasena. Obhāsavasenāti sappabhāsatāya avabhāsanavasena. Umāpupphanti atasipupphaṃ. Nīlameva hoti vaṇṇasaṅkarābhāvato. Bārāṇasiyaṃ bhavanti bārāṇasiyaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ.

'By way of all-inclusiveness' means by way of being common to all blue colors, blue appearances, and blue radiances. 'By way of color' means by way of its natural color. 'By way of appearance' means by way of being visible. 'By way of radiance' means by way of shining, by way of illuminating. 'Flax flower' means the atasi flower. It is simply blue due to the absence of color mixture. They are of Bārāṇasī; it arose in Bārāṇasī.

Te dhammeti te satipaṭṭhānādidhamme ceva aṭṭhavimokkhadhamme ca. Ciṇṇavasībhāvāyeva tattha abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya pariyosānuttaraṃ sataṃ gatā abhiññāvosānapāramippattā.

'Those dhammas' means the dhammas beginning with the foundations of mindfulness, and also the dhammas of the eight liberations. Through the very state of cultivated mastery, they have gone to the unsurpassed culmination by means of especially distinguished wisdom, having attained the perfection that is the culmination of direct knowledge.

250. Sakalaṭṭhenāti (dī. ni. ṭī. 3.346; a. ni. ṭī. 3.10.25) sakalabhāvena, asubhanimittādīsu viya ekadese aṭṭhatvā anavasesato gahetabbaṭṭhenāti attho. Yathā khettaṃ sassānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhiṭṭhānañca, evameva taṃtaṃsampayuttadhammānanti āha “khettaṭṭhenā”ti. Paricchinditvāti idaṃ uddhaṃ adho tiriyanti yojetabbaṃ. Paricchinditvā eva hi sabbattha kasiṇaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Tena tena kāraṇenāti upariādīsu tena tena kasiṇena. Yathā kinti āha – “ālokamiva rūpadassanakāmo”ti, yathā dibbacakkhunā uddhaṃ ce rūpaṃ daṭṭhukāmo, uddhaṃ ālokaṃ pasāreti, adho ce, adho, samantato ce rūpaṃ daṭṭhukāmo, samantato ālokaṃ pasāreti, evaṃ sabbakasiṇanti attho. Ekassāti pathavīkasiṇādīsu ekekassa. Aññabhāvānupagamanatthanti aññakasiṇabhāvānupagamanadīpanatthaṃ, aññassa vā kasiṇabhāvānupagamanadīpanatthaṃ. Na hi aññena pasāritakasiṇaṃ tato aññena pasāritakasiṇabhāvaṃ upagacchati, evampi nesaṃ aññakasiṇasambhedābhāvo veditabbo. Na aññaṃ pathavīādi. Na hi udakena ṭhitaṭṭhāne sasambhārapathavī atthi. Aññakasiṇasambhedoti āpokasiṇādinā saṅkaro[M 2.0125]. Sabbatthāti sabbesu sesakasiṇesu. Ekadese aṭṭhatvā anavasesapharaṇaṃ pamāṇassa aggahaṇato appamāṇaṃ. Teneva hi nesaṃ kasiṇasamaññā. Tathā hi “tañhī”tiādimāha. Tattha cetasā pharantoti bhāvanācittena ārammaṇaṃ karonto. Bhāvanācittañhi kasiṇaṃ parittaṃ vā vipulaṃ vā sakalameva manasi karoti.

250. 'In the sense of entirety' (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 3.346; A. Ni. Ṭī. 3.10.25) means by way of its entire nature; the meaning is that it should be grasped completely without remainder, not by standing in one part as in the case of the signs of foulness, etc. Just as a field is the place of origin and the place of growth for crops, so too is it for the associated dhammas—hence it is called 'in the sense of a field.' 'Having delimited' should be connected with 'upwards, downwards, and sideways.' For it is only by having delimited it that the kasiṇa is to be expanded everywhere. 'By that particular cause' refers to that particular kasiṇa in the cases of 'above,' etc. How so? He says: 'like one desiring to see forms with light.'
