Just as one wishing to see a form above with the divine eye extends light upwards, or below if wishing to see a form below, or all around if desiring to see forms in all directions, so too is the meaning for all kasiṇas. 'Of one' refers to each individual one among the earth kasiṇa, etc. 'For the purpose of not assuming another nature' means for the purpose of clarifying that it does not assume the nature of another kasiṇa, or that another does not assume its kasiṇa nature. For a kasiṇa expanded by one does not assume the nature of a kasiṇa expanded by another—thus, their non-mixing with other kasiṇas should be understood. 'Not another' means earth, etc. For where water stands, there is no earth with its constituent parts. 'Mixing with other kasiṇas' means mixing with the water kasiṇa, etc. 'Everywhere' refers to all the remaining kasiṇas. Spreading without remainder after being established in one part is 'immeasurable' due to not grasping a measure. For this very reason, they have the designation 'kasiṇa.' Thus, it is said: 'That indeed,' etc. There, 'spreading with the mind' means making it the object with the mind of meditation. For the mind of meditation attends to the kasiṇa—whether limited or vast—as a whole.

Kasiṇugghāṭimākāse pavattaṃ viññāṇaṃ pharaṇaappamāṇavasena “viññāṇakasiṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ “viññāṇa”nti vuccati. Kasiṇavasenāti ugghāṭitakasiṇavasena kasiṇugghāṭimākāse uddhaṃadhotiriyatā veditabbā. Yattakañhi ṭhānaṃ kasiṇaṃ pasāritaṃ, tattakaṃ ākāsabhāvanāvasena ākāsaṃ hotīti. Evaṃ yattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ ākāsaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhitaṃ, tattakaṃ ākāsameva hutvā viññāṇassa pavattanato āgamanavasena viññāṇakasiṇepi uddhaṃadhotiriyatā [V 2.0124] vuttāti “kasiṇugghāṭimākāsavasena tattha pavattaviññāṇe uddhaṃadhotiriyatā veditabbā”ti āha.

The consciousness occurring in the space where the kasiṇa has been removed is called 'consciousness kasiṇa' by way of its immeasurable pervasion. For thus it is called 'consciousness.' 'By way of the kasiṇa' means that by way of the removed kasiṇa, 'upwards, downwards, and sideways' should be understood in the space where the kasiṇa has been removed. For to whatever extent the kasiṇa was expanded, to that extent it becomes space by way of the development of space. Thus, to whatever extent space has arisen and appeared, to that extent, because consciousness proceeds as that very space, 'upwards, downwards, and sideways' is stated even in the consciousness kasiṇa by way of derivation. Therefore, it is said: 'In the consciousness occurring there, by way of the space where the kasiṇa has been removed, "upwards, downwards, and sideways" should be understood.'

252. Vuttoyeva vammikasutte. Nissitañca chavatthunissitattā vipassanāñāṇassa. Paṭibaddhañca tena vinā appavattanato kāyasaññitānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇato ca. Suṭṭhu bhāti obhāsatīti vā subho. Kuruvindajātiādijātivisesopi maṇi ākarapārisuddhimūlako evāti āha “suparisuddhaākarasamuṭṭhito”ti. Dosanīharaṇavasena parikammanipphattīti āha “suṭṭhu kataparikammo apanītapāsāṇasakkharo”ti. Dhovanavedhanādīhīti catūsu pāsāṇesu dhovanena ceva kāḷakādiapaharaṇatthāya suttena āvunanatthāya ca vijjhanena. Tāpasaṇhakaraṇādīnaṃ saṅgaho ādi-saddena. Vaṇṇasampattinti suttassa vaṇṇasampattiṃ.

252. This is explained in the Vammika Sutta. And it is dependent, because insight knowledge is dependent on six bases. And it is bound, because without it, it does not proceed, and because it makes the material phenomena designated as 'body' its object. 'Subha' means it shines well or is radiant. Even a jewel of a special kind, such as the Kuruvinda kind, has the purity of its mine as its root—hence it is said, 'arisen from a perfectly pure mine.' Because of the accomplishment of preparatory work by way of removing defects, it is said, 'well-prepared, with stones and gravel removed.' 'By washing, piercing, etc.' refers to the four types of stones: by washing to remove blackness and other flaws, and by piercing for stringing with a thread. The word 'etc.' includes heating, polishing, and similar processes. 'The excellence of color' refers to the excellence of the thread's color.

Maṇi viya karajakāyo paccavekkhitabbato. Āvutasuttaṃ viya vipassanāñāṇaṃ anupavisitvā ṭhitattā. Cakkhumā puriso viya vipassanālābhī bhikkhu sammadeva tassa dassanato. Tadārammaṇānanti rūpadhammārammaṇānaṃ. Phassapañcamakacittacetasikaggahaṇena gahitadhammāpi vipassanācittuppādapariyāpannā evāti veditabbaṃ. Evañhi tesaṃ vipassanāñāṇagatikattā “āvutasuttaṃ viya vipassanāñāṇa”nti vacanaṃ avirodhitaṃ hoti.

The physical body is like a jewel, as it is to be reviewed. Insight knowledge is like a threaded string, as it stands having penetrated its object. A bhikkhu who has obtained insight is like a man with eyes, as he sees it rightly. 'Of their objects' means of material phenomena as objects. Even the phenomena grasped by the inclusion of consciousness and mental factors with contact as the fifth should be understood as included within the arising of insight consciousness. For thus, because they fall within the scope of insight knowledge, the statement 'insight knowledge is like a threaded string' is not contradicted.

Ñāṇassāti [M 2.0126] paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa. Yadi evaṃ ñāṇassa vasena vattabbaṃ, na puggalassāti āha “tassa panā”tiādi. Maggassa anantaraṃ, tasmā lokiyābhiññānaṃ parato chaṭṭhābhiññāya purato vattabbaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Evaṃ santepīti yadipāyaṃ ñāṇānupubbaṭṭhiti, evaṃ santepi etassa antarā vāro natthīti pañcasu lokiyābhiññāsu kathitāsu ākaṅkheyyasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 1.64 ādayo) viya chaṭṭhābhiññā kathetabbāti etassa anabhiññālakkhaṇassa vipassanāñāṇassa tāsaṃ antarā vāro na hoti, tasmā tattha avasarābhāvato idheva rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānānantarameva dassitaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Yasmā cāti ca-saddo samuccayattho. Tena na kevalaṃ tadeva, atha kho idampi kāraṇaṃ vipassanāñāṇassa idheva dassaneti imamatthaṃ dīpeti. Dibbena cakkhunā bheravarūpaṃ passatoti ettha iddhividhañāṇena bheravaṃ rūpaṃ nimminitvā cakkhunā passatoti vattabbaṃ, evampi abhiññālābhino apariññāṇavatthukassa bhayasantāso uppajjati uccavālikavāsīmahānāgattherassa viya. Idhāpīti imasmiṃ vipassanāñāṇepi, na satipaṭṭhānādīsu evāti adhippāyo.

By 'knowledge' is meant the knowledge of reviewing. If it is to be spoken of in terms of knowledge, not of a person, thus it is said: 'But in his case,' etc. Immediately after the path, therefore, insight knowledge should be spoken of after the mundane higher knowledges and before the sixth higher knowledge. Even if it is so—meaning, if this is a sequence of knowledges, even if it is so, there is no turn for it in between. Just as in the Ākaṅkheyyasutta and others (Majjhima Nikāya 1.64, etc.), where the five mundane higher knowledges are discussed, the sixth higher knowledge should be spoken of, but for this insight knowledge, which does not have the characteristic of a higher knowledge, there is no turn for it among them. Therefore, due to the lack of opportunity there, insight knowledge is shown here immediately after the fourth jhāna of the form realm. And because—the word 'ca' has the meaning of conjunction; by this, it demonstrates that not only that, but this too is a reason for insight knowledge being shown here. With the divine eye, he sees a fearful form—here, it should be said that by the knowledge of psychic powers, he creates a fearful form and sees it with the eye. Even so, for one who has attained higher knowledge but whose object is not fully understood, fear arises, as in the case of the elder Mahānāga who lived in Uccavālika. Here too—meaning in this insight knowledge, not only in the foundations of mindfulness, etc.—this is the intention.

253. Manomayiddhiyaṃ [V 2.0125] ciṇṇavasitāya abhiññā vosānapāramippattatā veditabbāti yojanā. Manena nibbattanti abhiññāmanena nibbattitaṃ. Taṃ sadisabhāvadassanatthamevāti saṇṭhānatopi vaṇṇatopi avayavavisesatopi sadisabhāvadassanatthameva. Sajātiyaṃ ṭhito, na nāgiddhiyā aññajātirūpo. Suparikammakatamattikādayo viya iddhividhañāṇaṃ vikubbanakiriyāya nissayabhāvato.

253. This is the connection: the attainment of the ultimate perfection of higher knowledges should be understood by the mastery cultivated in mind-made power. That which is produced by the mind is produced by the mind of higher knowledge. This is solely for the purpose of demonstrating similarity; that is, to show similarity in shape, color, and particular parts. Established in its own species, it is not a form transformed into another species like that produced by the power of nāgas. Just as well-prepared clay and other materials are the support for the action of transformation, so too is the knowledge of psychic powers the basis.

255. Appakasirenevāti akiccheneva.

255. By 'with little effort' is meant without difficulty.

256. Mando uttānaseyyakadārakopi “daharo”ti vuccatīti tato visesanatthaṃ “yuvā”ti vuttaṃ. Yuvāpi koci anicchanato amaṇḍanasīlo hotīti tato visesanatthaṃ “maṇḍanakajātiko”ti vuttaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “yuvāpī”tiādi. Kāḷatilappamāṇā bindavo kāḷatilakāni. Nātikammāsatilappamāṇā bindavo tilakāni. Vaṅkaṃ nāma piyaṅgaṃ. Yobbanapīḷakādayo mukhadūsipīḷakā. Mukhagato doso mukhadoso, lakkhaṇavacanañcetaṃ mukhe adosassapi pākaṭabhāvassa adhippetattā[M 2.0127]. Yathā vā mukhe doso, evaṃ mukhe adosopi mukhadoso saralopena, mukhadoso ca mukhadoso ca mukhadosoti ekasesanayenapettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Evañhi paresaṃ soḷasavidhaṃ cittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotīti vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti.

256. Even a slow infant lying on its back is called 'young,' hence the word 'youth' is used for distinction. Even a youth who is unwilling to adorn themselves or is naturally disinclined to adornment might exist, hence the term 'one by nature inclined to adornment' is used for further distinction. Therefore, it is said 'even a youth,' etc. Spots the size of black sesame seeds are black sesame marks. Spots the size of atikkamāsa sesame seeds are sesame marks. Vaṅkaṃ means piyaṅga. Youthful eruptions and the like are pimples that blemish the face. A flaw on the face is a 'facial flaw,' and this is a characteristic expression, since it implies the obvious appearance even of that which is not a flaw on the face. Or, just as a flaw on the face is a 'facial flaw,' so too that which is not a flaw on the face is also a 'facial flaw' by elision of a vowel; and 'facial flaw' and 'facial flaw' become 'facial flaw' by the principle of leaving a single remainder (ekasesa). The meaning here should be understood in this way. Thus, the statement that the sixteen kinds of states of mind of others become evident is well established.

259. Paṭipadāvasenāti yathārahaṃ samathavipassanāmaggapaṭipadāvasena. Aṭṭhasu koṭṭhāsesūti satipaṭṭhānādīsu bodhipakkhiyadhammakoṭṭhāsesu, vimokkhakoṭṭhāsesu vāti imesu aṭṭhasu koṭṭhāsesu. Sesesūti vuttāvasesesu abhibhāyatanakoṭṭhāsādīsu. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

259. By 'by way of practice' is meant by way of the path-practice of serenity and insight, as appropriate. By 'in the eight divisions' is meant in these eight divisions, namely, the divisions of the factors of enlightenment such as the foundations of mindfulness, or the divisions of liberation. By 'in the remaining' is meant in the remaining divisions such as the spheres of mastery, etc. The rest is easily understood.

Mahāsakuludāyisuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition Clarifying the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta is complete.

8. Samaṇamuṇḍikāputtasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta Sutta

260. Uggahitunti [V 2.0126] sikkhituṃ. Uggāhetunti sikkhāpetuṃ, pāṭhato attanā yathāuggahitamatthaṃ tabbibhāvanatthāya uccāraṇavasena paresaṃ gāhetunti attho. Samayanti diṭṭhiṃ. Sā hi saṃyojanabhāvato sameti sambandhā eti pavattati, daḷhaggahaṇabhāvato vā saṃyuttā ayanti pavattanti sattā yathābhinivesaṃ etenāti samayoti vuccati. Diṭṭhisaṃyojanena hi sattā ativiya bajjhantīti. Sūriyassa uggamanato atthaṅgamā ayaṃ ettako kālo rattandhakāravidhamanato divā nāma, tassa pana majjhimapahārasaññito kālo samujjalitapabhātejadahanabhāvena divā nāma. Tenāha “divasassapi divābhūte”ti. Paṭisaṃharitvāti nivattetvā. Evaṃ cittassa paṭisaṃharaṇaṃ nāma gocarakkhette ṭhapananti āha “jhānaratisevanavasena ekībhāvaṃ gato”ti. Etena kāyavivekapubbakaṃ cittavivekamāha. Sīlādiguṇavisesayogato manasā sambhāvanīyā, te pana yasmā attano sīlādiguṇehi viññūnaṃ manāpā honti (kilesaaniggahassa pañcapasādāyattattā,) tasmā āha “manavaḍḍhanakāna”ntiādi. Tattha unnamatīti udaggaṃ hoti. Vaḍḍhatīti saddhāvasena vaḍḍhati. Tenāha bhagavā – “anussaraṇampahaṃ, bhikkhave, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahūpakāraṃ vadāmī”ti (itivu. 104; saṃ. ni. 5.184).

260. 'Uggahitunti sikkhituṃ' means 'to learn'. 'Uggāhetunti sikkhāpetuṃ' means 'to teach'; that is, 'to make others learn by reciting what one has learned oneself, for the purpose of clarifying that meaning to others by uttering it'. 'Samayanti diṭṭhiṃ' means 'they bind views'. For it is called 'samaya' because it comes together, connects, and proceeds in the sense of a bond (saṃyojana). Or, it is called 'samaya' because beings, being connected, come and proceed according to their inclinations by firmly grasping it. Indeed, beings are excessively bound by the fetter of views. The time from the rising of the sun to its setting is called 'day' because it dispels the darkness of night. However, the time of that day known as the middle period is called 'day' because of its state of blazing with brilliant light and heat. Therefore, he said, 'when the day is very much day'. 'Paṭisaṃharitvāti nivattetvā' means 'having withdrawn'. The withdrawal of the mind is said to be its establishment in its object-field, as stated: 'having gone to unification through cultivating delight in jhāna'. By this, mental seclusion preceded by bodily seclusion is stated. They are to be esteemed in mind due to their possession of special qualities such as morality. And since they are pleasing to the wise by their own qualities such as morality (because the non-suppression of defilements is dependent on the five sense-faculties), therefore he said 'mind-enhancing,' etc. There, 'unnamatīti udaggaṃ hoti' means 'it is uplifted, it becomes elated'. 'Vaḍḍhatīti saddhāvasena vaḍḍhati' means 'it grows, it grows by way of faith'. Thus, the Blessed One said: 'Recollection, monks, I declare to be of great benefit to those monks.' (Itivuttaka 104; Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.184).

261. Paññapemīti [M 2.0128] pajānanabhāvena ñāpemi tathā vavatthapemi. Tenāha “dassemi ṭhapemī”ti. Paripuṇṇakusalanti sabbaso puṇṇakusaladhammaṃ, uttamakusalanti uttamabhāvaṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ pattakusaladhammaṃ. Ayojjhanti vādayuddhena ayodhanīyaṃ, vādayuddhaṃ hotu, tena parājayo na hotīti dasseti, tenāha “vādayuddhenā”tiādi. Saṃvarappahānanti pañcasu saṃvaresu yena kenaci saṃvarena saṃvaralakkhaṇaṃ pahānaṃ. Paṭisevanappahānaṃ vāti vā-saddena parivajjanappahānādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sesapadesūti “na bhāsatī”tiādīsu padesu. Eseva nayoti iminā “abhāsanamattameva vadatī”ti evamādiṃ atidisati.

261. 'Paññapemīti' means 'I make known by way of understanding, and thus I establish'. Therefore, it is said, 'I show, I establish'. 'Paripuṇṇakusalaṃ' means 'a wholesome state entirely complete'; 'uttamkusalaṃ' means 'a wholesome state that has attained the supreme state, the excellent state'. 'Ayojjhaṃ' means 'not to be fought with in a battle of arguments'. It shows that 'let there be a battle of arguments, but there is no defeat by it'. Therefore, it is said, 'by a battle of arguments,' etc. 'Saṃvarappahānaṃ' means 'the abandonment that is the characteristic of restraint, by any of the five restraints'. 'Paṭisevanappahānaṃ vā'—by the word 'vā' (or), it includes abandonment by avoiding, etc. 'Sesapadesu' refers to passages such as 'he does not speak,' etc. 'Eseva nayo'—by this, it extends the meaning to such things as 'he speaks only to the extent of not speaking,' and so on.

Nābhinandīti na sampaṭicchi. Sāsane tiṇṇaṃ duccaritānaṃ micchājīvassa vivajjanaṃ vaṇṇīyati, ayañca evaṃ katheti, tasmā sāsanassa anulomaṃ viya vadati, vadanto ca sammāsambuddhe dhamme cassa appasādaṃ na dasseti, tasmā pasannakārampi vadatīti maññamāno tassa vādaṃ na paṭisedheti.

'Nābhinandīti' means 'he did not welcome it'. In the Dispensation, the avoidance of the three kinds of misconduct and wrong livelihood is praised, and this person speaks thus. Therefore, he speaks as if in accordance with the Dispensation, and while speaking, he does not show lack of confidence in the Perfectly Enlightened One or the Dhamma. Therefore, thinking that he speaks in a way that inspires confidence, one does not refute his statement.

262. Yathā [V 2.0127] tassa vacanaṃ, evaṃ santeti yathā tassa paribbājakassa vacanaṃ, evaṃ samaṇabhāve sante labbhamāne. Mayaṃ pana evaṃ na vadāmāti etena samaṇabhāvo nāma evaṃ na hotīti dasseti. Yo hi dhammo yādiso, tatheva taṃ buddhā dīpenti. Visesañāṇaṃ na hotīti kāyavisesavisayañāṇaṃ tassa tadā natthi, yato parakāye upakkamaṃ kareyyāti dasseti, tassa pana tattha visesañāṇampi natthevāti. Yasmā kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ kāyakammaṃ, tasmā taṃ nivattento āha “aññatra phanditamattā”ti. Kilesasahagatacittenevāti dukkhasamphassassa asahananimittena domanassasahagatacitteneva. Dutiyavārepi eseva nayo. Jighacchāpipāsadukkhassa asahananimittena domanasseneva. Vikūjitamattāti ettha virūpaṃ kūjitaṃ vikūjitaṃ pubbenivāsasannissayaṃ upayaṃ, taṃ panettha rodanahasanasamuṭṭhāpakacittasahagatanti dosasahagataṃ lobhasahagatañcāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Cittanti kusalacittaṃ. Akusalacittaṃ pana atītārammaṇaṃ pavattatīti vattabbameva natthi. Saritvāti yāva na satisaṇṭhāpanā dhammā uppajjanti, tāva supinante anubhūtaṃ viya dukkhaṃ saritvā rodanti. Hasantīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ayañca nayo ye laddhasukhārammaṇā hutvā gahitapaṭisandhikā mātukucchitopi sukheneva nikkhamanti, tesaṃ vasena vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Pāyantiyāti attano janapadadesarūpena [M 2.0129] pāyantiyā. Ayampīti ājīvopi mātu aññavihitakāle ca lokassādavasena kilesasahagatacitteneva hoti.

262. 'Yathā tassa vacanaṃ, evaṃ sante' means 'just as the wanderer's statement is, so it is, the state of a recluse being attainable'. 'Mayaṃ pana evaṃ na vadāma'—by this, it shows that the state of a recluse is not like this. For whatever the nature of a phenomenon is, the Buddhas illuminate it just as it is. 'Visesañāṇaṃ na hoti' means 'at that time, he has no knowledge concerning the distinction of bodies, from which he could undertake action upon another’s body'; this shows that he has no special knowledge in that regard. Since bodily action is bound to the body, indicating its prevention, he said, 'except for mere movement.' 'Kilesasahagatacitteneva' means 'with a mind accompanied by displeasure, which is the sign of being unable to endure painful contact'. The same principle applies in the second instance: with displeasure, which is the sign of being unable to endure the suffering of hunger and thirst. 'Vikūjitamattaṃ'—here, 'distorted cooing' is 'improper cooing', a means relying on past lives. Here, it should be understood as accompanied by a mind that gives rise to weeping or laughter, and thus accompanied by aversion and greed. 'Cittaṃ' refers to a wholesome mind. As for an unwholesome mind, there is no need to say that it occurs with a past object. 'Saritvā'—until phenomena that establish mindfulness arise, they weep, remembering suffering as if experienced in a dream. Here too, the same principle applies to 'laughing'. And this principle should be understood as stated in reference to those who, having obtained a pleasant object and taken rebirth, emerge from the mother’s womb with ease. 'Pāyantiyā' means 'by nursing in the manner of one's own region'. 'Ayampi'—this livelihood also, at other times when the mother is otherwise occupied, or by way of worldly enjoyment, occurs with a mind accompanied by defilements.

263. Samadhigayhāti sammā adhigatabhāvena gahetvā abhibhavitvā visesetvā visiṭṭho hutvā. Khīṇāsavaṃ sandhāyāti byatirekavasena khīṇāsavaṃ sandhāya. Ayañhettha attho – khīṇāsavampi sotāpannakusalaṃ paññapeti sekkhabhūmiyaṃ ṭhitattā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

263. 'Samadhigayha' means 'having grasped, having overcome, having distinguished, having become distinguished, by way of having rightly attained'. 'Khīṇāsavaṃ sandhāya' means 'referring to one whose taints are destroyed, by way of contrast'. Here, the meaning is this: Even one whose taints are destroyed makes known the wholesome state of a stream-enterer, because it stands on the ground of a trainee. The same principle applies to the remaining passages.

Tīṇi padāni nissāyāti na kāyena pāpakaṃ kammaṃ karoti, na pāpakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, na pāpakaṃ ājīvaṃ ājīvatīti imāni tīṇi padāni nissāya kusalasīlamūlakā ca akusalasīlamūlakā cāti dve paṭhamacatukkā ṭhapitā. Ekaṃ padaṃ nissāyāti na pāpakaṃ saṅkappaṃ saṅkappetīti imaṃ ekapadaṃ nissāya kusalasaṅkappamūlakā akusalasaṅkappamūlakā cāti ime dve pacchimacatukkā ṭhapitā.

'Tīṇi padāni nissāya' means 'depending on these three bases: one does not commit evil deeds with the body, does not speak evil words, and does not pursue a wrong livelihood'. By depending on these, the two initial sets of four, rooted in wholesome virtue and unwholesome virtue, are established. 'Ekaṃ padaṃ nissāya' means 'depending on this single base: one does not conceive evil thoughts'. By depending on this, these two latter sets of four, rooted in wholesome thought and unwholesome thought, are established.

264. Vicikicchuddhaccasahagatacittadvayampi vaṭṭati balavatā mohena samannāgatattā. Tathā hi tāni “momūhacittānī”ti vuccanti.

264. The two types of consciousness accompanied by doubt and restlessness are also fitting, because they are possessed of strong delusion. For they are called 'utterly deluded consciousness'.

Kuhinti kiṃnimittaṃ. Kataraṃṭhānaṃ pāpuṇitvāti kiṃ kāraṇaṃ āgamma. Ettheteti etthāti kāyavacīmanosucaritabhāvanāsājīvanipphattiyaṃ[V 2.0128]. Sā pana heṭṭhimakoṭiyā sotāpattiphalena dīpetabbāti āha “sotāpattiphale bhumma”nti. Yasmā ājīvaṭṭhamakaṃ avasiṭṭhañca sīlaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlassa ca pārisuddhipātimokkhādhigamena sotāpattiphalappattiyā siddho hotīti āha – “pātimokkha…pe… nirujjhatī”ti. “Sukhasīlo dukkhasīlo”tiādīsu viya pakatiatthasīlasaddaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ “akusalasīla”ntiādi.

'Kuhin' means 'for what reason?' 'Kataraṃṭhānaṃ pāpuṇitvā' means 'resorting to what cause?' 'Ettheteti ettha' refers to 'in the accomplishment of the cultivation of good bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, and of livelihood'. But that should be shown by the fruition of stream-entry at its lowest level; therefore, it is said, 'grounded in the fruition of stream-entry'. Since the virtue with livelihood as its eighth factor and the remaining virtue are perfected with the attainment of the fruition of stream-entry through the purity of the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha and the acquisition of the Pātimokkha, therefore it is said: 'the Pātimokkha... ceases'. Just as in 'virtue of pleasure, virtue of pain,' and so on, the word 'virtue' is used in its natural sense when 'unwholesome virtue' and so on are spoken of.

265. Kāmāvacarakusalacittameva vuttaṃ sampattasamādānaviratipubbakassa sīlassa adhippetattā. Tenāha – “etena hi kusalasīlaṃ samuṭṭhātī”ti.

265. Only wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense-sphere is mentioned, because virtue preceded by abstinence on occasion and abstinence by undertaking is intended. Therefore it is said: 'For by this, wholesome virtue arises'.

Sīlavāti ettha vā-saddo pāsaṃsatthova veditabboti āha “sīlasampanno hotī”ti. Yo sīlamatte patiṭṭhito, na samādhipaññāsu, so [M 2.0130] sīlamayadhammapūritatāya sīlamayo. Tenāha “alamettāvatā”tiādi. Yatthāti yassaṃ cetovimuttiyaṃ paññāvimuttiyañca. Tadubhayañca yasmā arahattaphale saṅgahitaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “arahattaphale bhumma”nti. Asesaṃ nirujjhati sukhavipākabhāvassa sabbaso paṭippassambhanato.

'Sīlavā'—here, the particle 'vā' should be understood as having a laudatory meaning; thus it is said, 'he is endowed with virtue'. One who is established merely in virtue, not in concentration or wisdom, is 'made of virtue' because of being filled with qualities made of virtue. Hence, it is said: 'This much is enough,' and so on. 'Yattha' means 'in which liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom'. And since both are included in the fruition of arahantship, it is stated: 'grounded in the fruition of arahantship'. It ceases without remainder due to the complete calming of the state of being a pleasant resultant.

266. Kāmapaṭisaṃyuttā saññā kāmasaññā. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Itarā dveti byāpādavihiṃsāsaññā.

266. Perception connected with sensual desire is sensual perception. The same principle applies to the remaining cases. 'The other two' refers to the perception of ill will and the perception of harmfulness.

Anāgāmiphalapaṭhamajjhānanti anāgāmiphalasahagataṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ. Etthāti yathāvutte paṭhamajjhāne. Ettha ca ujuvipaccanīkena paṭipakkhappahānaṃ sātisayanti paṭhamajjhānaggahaṇaṃ. Tenāha “aparisesā nirujjhantī”ti. Nekkhammasaññānaṃ kāmāvacaracittasahagatatā tassa sīlassa samuṭṭhānatā ca sampayuttanayena veditabbā.

'Anāgāmiphalapaṭhamajjhānaṃ' means 'the first jhāna accompanied by the fruition of non-returning'. 'Ettha' means 'in the aforementioned first jhāna'. And here, the inclusion of the first jhāna is because the abandoning of the opposing factor by direct counteraction is pre-eminent. Therefore, it is said: 'they cease without remainder'. The fact that perceptions of renunciation are accompanied by consciousness pertaining to the sense-sphere, and that they are the origin of that virtue, should be understood by the method of association.

267. Kusalasaṅkappanirodhadutiyajjhānikaarahattaphalaakusalasaṅkappanirodha- paṭhamajjhānikaanāgāmiphalaggahaṇena samaṇo dassito. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

267. The recluse is shown by the inclusion of the fruition of arahantship, which pertains to the second jhāna and is the cessation of wholesome thoughts, and by the inclusion of the fruition of non-returning, which pertains to the first jhāna and is the cessation of unwholesome thoughts. The rest is easily understood.

Samaṇamuṇḍikāputtasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta Sutta is concluded.

9. Cūḷasakuludāyisuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta

271. Pañhoti [V 2.0129] ñātuṃ icchito attho, tadeva dhammadesanāya nimittabhāvato kāraṇaṃ. Upaṭṭhātūti ñāṇassa gocarabhāvaṃ upagacchatu. Yena kāraṇenāti yena tuyhaṃ upaṭṭhitena kāraṇena dhammadesanā upaṭṭhaheyya, taṃ pana paribbājakassa ajjhāsayavasena tathā vuttaṃ. Tenāha “etena hi…pe… dīpetī”ti. Ekaṅgaṇānīti pidhānābhāvena ekaṅgaṇasadisāni. Tenāha “pākaṭānī”ti.

271. 'Pañha' is the meaning one wishes to know; that itself is the cause, from being the basis for the teaching of the Dhamma. 'Upaṭṭhātu' means 'may it come into the range of knowledge'. 'Yena kāraṇena' means 'by which reason that has occurred to you the teaching of the Dhamma might be presented'; this, however, was said in accordance with the wanderer's inclination. Hence it is said, 'For by this... it is explained.' 'Ekaṅgaṇāni' means 'like a single courtyard, due to the absence of a covering'. Therefore, it is said, 'they are manifest'.

Jānantoti attano tathābhāvaṃ sayaṃ jānanto. Sakkaccaṃ sussūsatīti “tathābhūtaṃyeva maṃ tathā avocā”ti sādaraṃ sussūsati. Tasmāti dibbacakkhulābhino anāgataṃsañāṇalābhato. Evamāhāti “yo [M 2.0131] kho, udāyi, dibbena cakkhunā”ti ārabhitvā “so vā maṃ aparantaṃ ārabbha pañhaṃ puccheyyā”ti evaṃ avoca.

'Jānanto' means 'knowing oneself to be so'. 'Sakkaccaṃ sussūsati' means 'one listens respectfully, thinking, "He spoke thus to me, who am indeed so." 'Tasmā' means 'therefore, because of obtaining the divine eye and gaining knowledge of the future'. 'Evamāha' means 'he spoke thus', beginning with, 'Whoever, Udāyi, with the divine eye...' and continuing up to, 'he might ask me a question concerning the future'.

Itaranti avasiṭṭhaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne vattabbaṃ. Vuttanayamevāti “yo hi lābhī”tiādinā vuttanayameva. Atīteti pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa visayabhūte atthe. Anāgateti anāgataṃsañāṇassa visayabhūte anāgate atthe.

'Itaraṃ' means 'the remainder to be said in this place'. 'Vuttanayameva' means 'the very method that was stated', beginning with 'for one who is an obtainer'. 'Atīte' refers to a matter in the past that is the domain of the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. 'Anāgate' refers to a matter in the future that is the domain of the knowledge of the future.

Paṃsupadese nibbattanato paṃsusamokiṇṇasarīratāya paṃsupisācakaṃ. Ekaṃ mūlaṃ gahetvāti dīghaso heṭṭhimantena caturaṅgulaṃ, uparimantena vidatthikaṃ rukkhagacchalatādīsu yassa kassaci ekaṃ mūlaṃ gahetvā aññajātikānaṃ adissamānakāyo hoti. Ayaṃ kira nesaṃ jātisiddhā dhammatā. Tatrāti tassa mūlavasena adissamānakatāya. Na dissati ñāṇena na passati.

A 'dust-demon' (`paṃsupisācakaṃ`) is so called because of being born in a dusty region and because its body is strewn with dust. 'Ekaṃ mūlaṃ gahetvā' means 'taking one root of any tree, shrub, or creeper—four finger-breadths long at the lower end and a span long at the upper end—one's body becomes invisible to those of other species'. This, it is said, is their innate nature. 'Tatra' means 'therein, that is, due to being made invisible by that root'. 'Na dissati' means 'he is not seen'; 'ñāṇena na passati' means 'one does not perceive him with knowledge'.

272. Na ca atthaṃ dīpeyyāti adhippetamatthaṃ sā vācā sarūpato na ca dīpeyya, kevalaṃ vācāmattamevāti adhippāyo. Paṭiharitabbaṭṭhena parasantāne netabbaṭṭhena paṭihāriya-saddadvārena viññātabbo bhāvattho, sova pāṭihīrako niruttinayena, natthi etassa pāṭihīrakanti appāṭihīrakataṃ, ta-saddena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā tathā vuttaṃ, aniyyānaṃ. Tenāha “niratthakaṃ sampajjatī”ti. Subhakiṇhadevaloke khandhā viya jotetīti iminā – “dibbo rūpī manomayo sabbaṅgapaccaṅgī ahīnindriyo attā”ti imamatthaṃ dasseti.

272. 'It does not illuminate the meaning' means that that speech does not illuminate the intended meaning in its own nature; it is merely words—this is the intention. The state of being should be understood through the word 'paṭihāriya,' in the sense of being refutable and in the sense of being led into another's continuity. That itself is 'pāṭihīraka' according to etymology. 'For this, there is no refutation' means the state of being irrefutable (`appāṭihīrakataṃ`). It is stated thus by extending the word with the sound '-ta', meaning 'not leading out'. Therefore, it is said, 'it becomes meaningless.' 'It shines like the aggregates in the Subhakiṇha deva world'—by this, it shows this meaning: 'a divine self, possessing form, mind-made, complete in all major and minor limbs, with unimpaired faculties'.

273. Saupasaggapadassa [V 2.0130] attho upasaggena vināpi viññāyatīti āha “viddheti ubbiddhe”ti. Sā cassa ubbiddhatā upakkilesavigamena sucibhāvena upaṭṭhānanti āha “meghavigamena dūrībhūte”ti. Indanīlamaṇi viya dibbati jotetīti devo, ākāso. “Aḍḍharattasamaye”ti vattabbe bhummatthe vihitavacanānaṃ accantasaṃyogābhāvā upayogavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Puṇṇamāsiyañhi gaganamajjhassa purato vā pacchato vā ante ṭhite aḍḍharatte samayo bhinno nāma hoti, majjhe eva pana ṭhito abhinno nāma. Tenāha “abhinne aḍḍharattasamaye”ti.

273. He says, 'viddheti ubbiddhe,' meaning that the meaning of a word with a prefix can be understood even without the prefix. And that state of being prominent is its manifestation through the removal of imperfections and through purity; he says, 'when it has become distant with the departure of clouds.' It shines, it illuminates like an Indanīla gem, therefore 'deva,' the sky. Although 'at midnight' should be said, since words prescribed in the locative sense do not have an absolute connection, the word should be understood in the sense of proximity. For on the full moon, when it stands before or after the middle of the sky, at the edge, at midnight, the time is called 'divided'; but when it stands right in the middle, it is called 'undivided.' Therefore, he says, 'at the undivided midnight'.

Ye anubhontīti ye devā candimasūriyānaṃ ābhā anubhonti vinibhuñjanti vaḷañjanti ca tehi devehi bahū ceva bahutarā ca candimasūriyānaṃ ābhā [M 2.0132] ananubhonto. Tenāha – “attano sarīrobhāseneva ālokaṃ pharitvā viharantī”ti.

'Those who experience' means those devas who experience, enjoy, and make use of the radiance of the moon and sun. Many devas, and even far more than those devas, do not experience the radiance of the moon and sun. Therefore, it is said: 'They dwell, having pervaded the world with the radiance of their own bodies'.

274. Pucchāmūḷho pana jāto “ayaṃ paramo vaṇṇo”ti gahitapadassa vidhamanena. Acelakapāḷinti “acelako hoti muttācāro”tiādinayappavattaṃ (dī. ni. 1.394) acelakapaṭipattidīpakaganthaṃ, ganthasīseneva tena pakāsitavādāni vadati. Surāmerayapānamanuyuttapuggalassa surāpānato virati tassa kāyaṃ cittañca tāpentī saṃvattatīti surāpānavirati (tapo, soyeva guṇo. Tenāha “surāpānaviratīti attho”ti).

274. But he became confused in the questioning by the refutation of the phrase he had grasped, 'this is the highest beauty.' 'Acelakapāḷi' refers to the text that illuminates the practice of naked ascetics, which proceeds according to the method beginning with 'he is a naked ascetic, of loose conduct,' and he speaks the doctrines proclaimed by the very title of that text. For a person given to drinking spirits and intoxicants, abstinence from drinking spirits becomes tormenting to his body and mind; thus, abstinence from drinking spirits is austerity, and that itself is a virtue. Therefore, it is said: 'The meaning is abstinence from drinking spirits'.

275. Ekantaṃ accantameva sukhaṃ assāti ekantasukhaṃ. Pañcasu dhammesūti “pāṇātipātā paṭiviratī”tiādīsu pañcasu sīlācāradhammesu. Na jāniṃsūti sammosena anupaṭṭhahanti tadatthaṃ na bujjhanti. Buddhuppādena kira vihatatejāni mahānubhāvāni mantapadāni viya bāhirakānaṃ yogāvacaraganthena saddhiṃ yogāvacarapaṭipadā nassati. Uggaṇhiṃsūti “pañca pubbabhāgadhamme”tiādivacanamattaṃ uggaṇhiṃsu. Tatiyajjhānatoti kāraṇopacārena phalaṃ vadati, phalabhūtato tatiyajjhānato.

275. 'Ekantasukhaṃ' means that for which there is exclusively, absolutely happiness. 'In the five things' means in the five things of virtuous conduct, such as 'abstinence from taking life,' and so on. 'They did not know' means they do not attend to it through confusion; they do not understand its meaning. It is said that with the arising of a Buddha, the practice of the yogis of the outsiders, together with their texts, perishes, just like powerful mantra-verses whose power has been destroyed. 'They learned' means they learned merely the words, such as 'the five preliminary things,' and so on. 'From the third jhāna': he speaks of the result by way of a metaphor for the cause, meaning from the third jhāna which is the resultant state.

276. Ekantasukhassa lokassa paṭilābhena pattiyā tattha nibbatti paṭilābhasacchikiriyā. Ekantasukhe loke anabhinibbattitvā eva iddhiyā tattha gantvā tassa sattalokassa bhājanalokassa ca paccakkhato dassanaṃ paccakkhasacchikiriyā. Tenāha “tatthā”tiādi.

276. Rebirth there through the attainment of the world of exclusive happiness is realization by attainment. Having gone there by psychic power without being reborn in the world of exclusive happiness, the direct seeing of that world of beings and the container world is realization by direct experience. Therefore, it is said: 'there,' and so on.

277. Udañcanikoti [V 2.0131] udañcano. Viñjhupabbatapasse gāmānaṃ aniviṭṭhattā tiṃsayojanamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ aṭavī nāma, tattha senāsanaṃ, tasmiṃ aṭavisenāsane padhānakammikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahūnaṃ tattha nivāsena ekaṃ padhānagharaṃ ahosi.

277. 'Udañcaniko' means Udañcano. On the slope of the Viñjhu mountain, a place of about thirty yojanas in extent was named Aṭavī, because it was not settled with villages. There was a lodging there. In that forest lodging, due to many monks dedicated to the practice of striving residing there, there was one main hall for striving.

Cūḷasakuludāyisuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Clarification of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta is complete.

10. Vekhanasasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Vekhanasa Sutta

280. Saha [M 2.0133][V 2.0132] vatthukāmena kilesakāmo garu garukātabbo etassāti kāmagaru. Tesveva kāmesu ninnapoṇapabbhārajjhāsayoti kāmādhimutto. Pabbajjāpaṭhamajjhānādikaṃ nekkhammaṃ garu garukātabbaṃ etassāti nekkhammagaru. Tattha ninnapoṇapabbhārajjhāsayo nekkhammādhimutto svāyamattho yathā ekacce gahaṭṭhe labbhati, evaṃ ekacce anagārepīti āha “pabbajitopī”tiādi. Ayaṃ pana vekhanaso paribbājako. So hi vekhanasatāpasapabbajjaṃ upagantvā vekhanasena iminā diṭṭhimādāya samādiyitvā ṭhitattā “vekhanaso”ti vuccati. Yathā loko sayaṃ ekādasahi aggīhi ādittopi samāno paccakkhato anubhaviyamānaṃ sālākikaṃ aggisantāpaṃ viya anādikālānugatasammākavacarasantāpaṃ ādittatāya na sallakkheti, sammāsambuddhena pana mahākaruṇāsamussāhitamānasena “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, āditta”nti ādittapariyāye (saṃ. ni. 4.28; mahāva. 54) desiyamāne sallakkheti, evaṃ ayampi anādikālaparibhāvitaṃ attaajjhāsaye avaṭṭhitaṃ kāmādhimuttaṃ sarasena anupadhārento satthārā – “pañca kho ime, kaccāna, kāmaguṇā”tiādinā kāmaguṇesu kāmasukhe bhāsiyamāne “kāmādhimuttaṃ vata pabbajitassa citta”nti upadhāressatīti āha – “imāya kathāya kathiyamānāya attano kāmādhimuttataṃ sallakkhessatī”ti. Kāmaggasukhanti kāmetabbavatthūhi aggabhūtaṃ sukhaṃ. Sabbe hi tebhūmakadhammā kāmanīyaṭṭhena kāmā, te paṭicca uppajjanasukhato nibbānasukhameva aggabhūtaṃ sukhaṃ. Yathāha – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (itivu. 90; a. ni. 4.34) – “nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”nti (ma. ni. 2.215, 217; dha. pa. 203) ca. Tena vuttaṃ “nibbānaṃ adhippeta”nti.

280. One for whom sensual desire, together with its objects, is to be esteemed, is called “kāmagaru” (one who esteems sensual pleasures). One whose inclination, tendency, and resolve are deeply rooted in those very sensual pleasures is called “kāmādhimutto” (one intent on sensual pleasures). One for whom renunciation, such as going forth or the first jhāna, is to be esteemed, is called “nekkhammagaru” (one who esteems renunciation). In this context, one whose inclination, tendency, and resolve are deeply rooted in renunciation is called “nekkhammādhimutto.” This meaning applies to some householders, and similarly to some who are homeless, as stated: “even one who has gone forth,” and so on. This Vekhanasa was a wanderer. Having adopted the ascetic life of the Vekhanasa ascetics, and having embraced and adhered to this view of Vekhanasa, he is therefore called “Vekhanasa.” Just as the world, though itself burning with the eleven fires, does not notice the affliction of the round of existence that has followed since beginningless time—like the burning heat of a firebrand being directly experienced—due to the constant burning, but comes to notice it when the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, with a mind motivated by great compassion, declares in the “Discourse on Burning”: “All is burning, monks”; similarly, this person, without considering in its true nature the inclination towards sensual pleasures, which has been cultivated since beginningless time and is established in his own disposition, will come to realize his own inclination toward sensual pleasures when the Teacher speaks of sensual pleasures and sensual bliss, saying: “Kaccāna, these five strands of sensual pleasure…” Thus, it is said: “While this discourse is being spoken, he will perceive his own intent on sensual pleasures.” “The highest pleasure among desirables” means the supreme pleasure among things to be desired. For all phenomena of the three realms are “desirables” in the sense of being desirable, but of the pleasure that arises dependent on them, Nibbāna itself is the supreme pleasure. As it is said: “Whatever phenomena there are, monks, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the highest among them,” and “Nibbāna is the supreme bliss.” Therefore, it is said: “Nibbāna is what is intended.”

281. Pubbenivāsañāṇalābhino pubbantaṃ ārabbha vuccamānakathā anucchavikā tadatthassa paccakkhabhāvato, tadabhāvato vekhanasassa ananucchavikāti āha “yasmā…pe… natthī”ti. Anāgatakathāya…pe… natthīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ārakkhatthāyāti devatāhi mantapadehi saha ṭhitā [M 2.0134] tattha ārakkhatthāya. Avijjāyāti idaṃ lakkhaṇavacanaṃ, taṃmūlakattā vā sabbakilesadhammānaṃ avijjāva gahitā. Jānanaṃ pahīnakilesapaccavekkhaṇañāṇena. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

281. For those who have attained the knowledge of past lives, discussions concerning the past are appropriate because that matter is directly perceived by them. For Vekhanasa, however, such discussions are inappropriate because he lacks that knowledge—hence it is said, “Because… it is not.” The same method applies to discussions about the future… it is not. Here too, the reasoning is the same. “For the sake of protection” means that devas stood there with mantra-verses for the sake of protection. “By ignorance” is a term denoting a characteristic; or, ignorance itself is taken because it is the root of all defiling things. Knowing is by means of the knowledge that reviews abandoned defilements. The rest is easily understood.

Vekhanasasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Clarification of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Vekhanasa Sutta is complete.

Niṭṭhitā ca paribbājakavaggavaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the Chapter of the Wanderers is concluded.

4. Rājavaggo

4. The Chapter on Kings

1. Ghaṭikārasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Ghaṭikāra Sutta

282. Cariyanti [M 2.0135][V 2.0133] bodhicariyaṃ, bodhisambhārasambharaṇavasena pavattitaṃ bodhisattapaṭipattinti attho. Sukāraṇanti bodhiparipācanassa ekantikaṃ sundaraṃ kāraṇaṃ, kassapassa bhagavato payirupāsanādiṃ sandhāya vadati. Tañhi tena saddhiṃ mayā idha katanti vattabbataṃ labhati. Mandahasitanti īsakaṃ hasitaṃ. Kuhaṃ kuhanti hāsa-saddassa anukaraṇametaṃ. Haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākāramattanti haṭṭhapahaṭṭhamattaṃ. Yathā gahitasaṅketā “pahaṭṭho bhagavā”ti sañjānanti, evaṃ ākāradassanamattaṃ.

282. “Conduct” means the conduct for enlightenment, that is, the practice of a Bodhisatta undertaken by way of accumulating the requisites of enlightenment—this is the meaning. “A good reason” refers to an absolutely excellent reason for the maturation of enlightenment, spoken with reference to attending upon the Blessed One Kassapa, and so on. For that is what can be said to have been done here by me together with him. “A faint smile” means a slight smile. “Kuhuṃ kuhuṃ” is an imitation of the sound of laughter. “Merely the appearance of being delighted” means just the appearance of being delighted. It is merely the showing of an appearance, so that those who have grasped the signal recognize, “The Blessed One is delighted.”

Idāni iminā pasaṅgena tāsaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ vibhāgato dassetuṃ “hasitañca nāmeta”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ajjhupekkhanavasenapi hāso na sambhavati, pageva domanassavasenāti āha “terasahi somanassasahagatacittehī”ti. Nanu ca keci kodhavasenapi hasantīti? Na, tesampi yaṃ taṃ kodhavatthu, tassa mayaṃ dāni yathākāmakāritaṃ āpajjissāmāti duviññeyyantarena somanassacitteneva hāsassa uppajjanato. Tesūti pañcasu somanassasahagatacittesu. Balavārammaṇeti uḷāraārammaṇe yamakamahāpāṭihāriyasadise. Dubbalārammaṇeti anuḷāre ārammaṇe. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne…pe… uppādesīti idaṃ porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ tathā āgatattā vuttaṃ. Na ahetukasomanassasahagatacittena bhagavato sitaṃ hotīti dassanatthaṃ.

Now, with this connection, in order to show in detail the arising of those smiles, the section beginning “A smile, indeed…” is commenced. Here, laughter is not possible even by way of equanimity, let alone by way of sorrow—hence he said, “With thirteen joy-accompanied mind-states.” But do not some laugh even out of anger? No, for even in their case, laughter arises only with a joy-accompanied mind, through a subtle understanding of that object of anger, thinking, “Now we will subject it to our will.” “In those” refers to the five joy-accompanied mind-states. “A strong object” means a sublime object, like the Twin Miracle. “A weak object” means a non-sublime object. In this connection… “produces” is said because it is found thus in the ancient commentary. The purpose is to show that a smile does not occur for the Blessed One with a rootless joy-accompanied mind-state.

Abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ (dha. sa. mūlaṭī. 568) pana “atītaṃsādīsu appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ vatvā ‘imehi tīhi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivatta’ntiādivacanato (mahāni. 69, 156; cūḷani. māgharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5; netti. 15; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.305; vibha. mūlaṭī. suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā; dī. ni. ṭī. 3.141, 305) ‘bhagavato [V 2.0134] idaṃ cittaṃ uppajjatī’ti vuttavacanaṃ vicāretabba”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha iminā hasituppādacittena pavattiyamānampi bhagavato sitakaraṇaṃ pubbenivāsa-anāgataṃsa-sabbaññutaññāṇānaṃ anuvattakattā ñāṇānuparivattiyevāti, evaṃ pana ñāṇānuparivattibhāve sati na koci pāḷiaṭṭhakathānaṃ virodho. Tathā hi abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 568) “tesaṃ [M 2.0136] ñāṇānaṃ ciṇṇapariyante idaṃ cittaṃ uppajjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Avassañca etaṃ evaṃ icchitabbaṃ, aññathā āvajjanassapi bhagavato pavatti tathārūpe kāle na saṃyujjeyya, tassapi hi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakabhāvassa icchitattā, tathā hi vuttaṃ – “evañca katvā manodvārāvajjanassapi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakattaṃ upapannaṃ hotī”ti, na ca viññattisamuṭṭhāpakatte taṃsamuṭṭhitāya viññattiyā kāyakammādibhāvaṃ āpajjanabhāvo vibandhatīti tameva sandhāya vadati. Tenāha “evaṃ appamattakampī”ti. Sateritā vijjulatā nāma sateratāvijjulatā. Sā hi itaravijjulatā viya khaṇaṭṭhitikā sīghanirodhā ca na hoti, apica kho dandhanirodhā, tañca sabbakālaṃ catudīpikamahāmeghatova niccharati tenāha “cātuddīpikamahāmeghamukhato”ti. Ayaṃ kira tāsaṃ rasmivaṭṭīnaṃ dhammatā, yadidaṃ tikkhattuṃ siravaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dāṭhaggesuyeva antaradhānaṃ.

However, in the Abhidhamma sub-commentary (Dha. Sa. Mūlaṭī. 568), it is stated: “Having mentioned the unimpeded knowledge regarding the past, etc., and because of the statement ‘For the Blessed One, the Buddha, endowed with these three qualities, all bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and follow knowledge’ (Mahāni. 69, 156; Cūḷani. Māgharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85; Paṭi. Ma. 3.5; Netti. 15; Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.305; Vibha. Mūlaṭī. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā; Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 3.141, 305), the statement ‘This thought arises in the Blessed One,’ should be examined.” Here, even the act of smiling by the Blessed One, though impelled by the smile-producing consciousness, is indeed a consequence of knowledge, because it is a consequence of the knowledges of past lives, future destinies, and omniscience. And thus, when there is this state of following knowledge, there is no contradiction with the Pāli text and the commentaries. Indeed, in the Abhidhamma commentary (Dha. Sa. Aṭṭha. 568), it is said: “This thought arises at the culmination of those knowledges.” And this must certainly be accepted in this way; otherwise, even the advertence of the Blessed One would not be compatible at such a time, for it is accepted that even advertence produces bodily expression, as it is said: “And having done so, even the advertence at the mind-door becomes capable of producing expression.” Nor does the fact of producing expression hinder the bodily action, etc., that arises from it from coming to be. Therefore, referring to that, he says: “Even such a slight movement.” The lightning called “sateritā” is “sateratāvijjulatā.” Unlike other lightning, it does not last for a mere moment and cease quickly; rather, it ceases slowly. Moreover, it continuously emanates from the great four-continent cloud. Hence, it is said: “From the mouth of the great four-continent cloud.” This, indeed, is the nature of those streams of rays—that after circling the excellent head three times, they disappear right at the tips of the canine teeth.

283. Yadipi cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappānaṃ satasahassañca paññāpāramitā paribhāvitā, tathāpi idāni taṃ buddhantaraṃ tassā paṭipādetabbattā vuttaṃ “aparipakkañāṇattā”ti. Kāmañcassa ñāṇāya idānipi paṭipādetabbatā atthi, evaṃ santepi nanu sammāsambuddhesu pasādena sambhāvanāya bhavitabbaṃ tathā cirakālaṃ paribhāvitattā, kathaṃ tattha hīḷanāti āha “brāhmaṇakule”tiādi. Cirakālaparicitāpi hi guṇabhāvanā appakenapi akalyāṇamittasaṃsaggena viparivattati aññathattaṃ gacchati. Tena mahāsattopi jātisiddhāyaṃ laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā jātisiddhena mānena evamāha – “kiṃ pana tena muṇḍakena samaṇakena diṭṭhenā”ti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

283. Even though the perfection of wisdom was cultivated for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand kalpas, still, because that knowledge must now be brought about for him in this Buddha-interval, it is said, “due to immaturity of knowledge.” And although there is a need to bring him to knowledge now, even so, should there not be confidence and esteem for the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, given such long cultivation? How then could there be contempt in that case? He says, “in the brahmin family,” and so on. For even the cultivation of virtues, though long practiced, can be overturned and changed by association with even a few bad friends. Therefore, the great being, standing firm in the doctrine he acquired by birth, spoke thus with the pride of birth: “What is to be gained by seeing that shaven-headed ascetic?” As stated in the commentary:

“Tasmā akalyāṇajanaṃ, āsīvisamivoragaṃ,

Ārakā parivajjeyya, bhūtikāmo vicakkhaṇo”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.170-172);

“Therefore, the wise, desiring well-being, should avoid the unwholesome person from afar, like a venomous snake.”

Nhānacuṇṇena suttena katā sotti, kuruvindaguḷikā, sā eva sināyanti kāyaṃ visodhenti etāyāti sinānaṃ. Tenāha – “sotti sinānanti sinānatthāya katasotti”nti.

A sotti is made with a string and bath powder; also kuruvinda pills. That is called sināna because with it they bathe (sināyanti) and cleanse (visodhenti) the body. Therefore, he says: “A sotti is a sināna means a sotti made for the purpose of bathing.”

284. Ariyaparihārenāti [V 2.0135] ariyānaṃ parihārena, anāgāmīnaṃ nhānakāle attano kāyassa parihāraniyāmenāti attho. Attano [M 2.0137] ñāṇasampattiyā vibhavasampattiyā pasannakāraṃ kātuṃ sakkhissati. Etadatthanti “ahitanivāraṇaṃ, hite niyojanaṃ byasane parivajjana”nti yadidaṃ, etadatthaṃ mittā nāma honti. Keci “yāvettha ahupī”ti paṭhanti, tesaṃ yāva ettha kesaggagahaṇaṃ tāva ayaṃ nibandho ahupīti attho.

284. “Ariyaparihārena” means with the care of the noble ones, that is, according to the rule for non-returners regarding the care of one's own body at the time of bathing—this is the meaning. He will be able to perform acts of devotion by means of his own accomplishment in knowledge and prosperity. “Etadattham” (for this purpose) refers to this: “warding off harm, guiding toward good, not abandoning in calamity”—for this purpose friends exist. Some read “yāvettha ahupī”; for them, the meaning is that this bond existed up to the point of grasping the tip of the hair.

285. Satipaṭilābhatthāyāti bodhiyā mahābhinīhāraṃ katvā bodhisambhārapaṭipadāya pūraṇabhāve satiyā paṭilābhatthāya. Idāni tassa satuppādanīyakathāya pavattitākāraṃ saṅkhepeneva dassetuṃ “tassa hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha na lāmakaṭṭhānaṃ otiṇṇasattoti iminā mahāsattassa paṇītādhimuttataṃ dassetvā evaṃ paṇītādhimuttikassa pamādakiriyā na yuttāti dassento “tādisassa nāma pamādavihāro na yutto”ti āha. Tadā bodhisattassa nekkhammajjhāsayo telappadīpo viya visesato nibbatti, taṃ disvā bhagavā tadanurūpaṃ dhammakathaṃ karonto “tādisassa…pe… kathesī”ti. Parasamuddavāsī therā aññathā vadanti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana nāyaṃ buddhānaṃ bhāro, yadidaṃ pūritapāramīnaṃ bodhisattānaṃ tathā dhammadesanā tesaṃ mahābhinīhārasamanantarampi bodhisambhārassa sayambhuñāṇeneva paṭividitattā. Tasmā bodhisattabhāvapavedanameva tassa bhagavā akāsīti dassetuṃ “satipaṭilābhatthāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Satipaṭilābhatthāyāti sammāpaṭipattiyā ujjalane pākaṭakarasatipaṭilābhāya.

285. “For the sake of attaining mindfulness” means for the sake of attaining mindfulness upon the fulfillment of the path of the requisites of enlightenment, having made the great aspiration for enlightenment. Now, to show briefly how the discourse that brings about that mindfulness proceeds, “for him indeed” and so on is said. Herein, by “a being not descended into an inferior state,” the noble inclination of the Great Being is shown, and thus, indicating that negligence is unfitting for one so nobly inclined, he says, “for such a one, a state of heedlessness is not fitting.” At that time, the Bodhisatta's inclination toward renunciation arose with special intensity, like an oil lamp. Seeing this, the Blessed One gave a discourse in accordance with that, saying, “for such a one... he taught.” The elders who dwell on the other side of the ocean say otherwise. In the commentary, however, this is not the task of the Buddhas, namely, to give such a teaching to Bodhisattas who have fulfilled the perfections, because they have penetrated the requisites of enlightenment by their own self-born knowledge even immediately after their great aspiration. Therefore, to show that the Blessed One merely revealed his state of being a Bodhisatta, “for the sake of attaining mindfulness” and so on is said. “For the sake of attaining mindfulness” means for the attainment of mindfulness that makes manifest and illuminates right practice.

286. Ñāṇañhi kilesadhammavidālanapadālanehi siṅgaṃ viyāti siṅgaṃ. Tañhi paṭipattiyā upatthambhitaṃ ussitaṃ nāma hoti, tadabhāve patitaṃ nāma. Keci pana vīriyaṃ siṅganti vadanti. Tasmiṃ sammappadhānavasena pavatte bāhirapabbajjaṃ upagatāpi mahāsattā visuddhāsayā appicchatādiguṇasamaṅgino yathārahaṃ ganthadhuraṃ vāsadhurañca paribrūhayantā viharanti, pageva buddhasāsane appicchatādīhīti āha “catupārisuddhisīle panā”tiādi. Vipassanaṃ brūhentā sikhāppattavipassanā hontīti vuttaṃ – “yāva anulomañāṇaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhantī”ti, anulomañāṇato orameva vipassanaṃ ṭhapentīti attho. Maggaphalatthaṃ vāyāmaṃ na karonti paññāpāramitāya sabbaññutaññāṇagabbhassa aparipuṇṇattā aparipakkattā ca.

286. Knowledge, indeed, because it splits and crushes the nature of defilements, is like a horn; it is a horn. That, when supported by practice, is called "raised"; in its absence, it is called "fallen." Some, however, say that energy is the horn. When that operates by way of right efforts, even great beings who have undertaken the external going-forth, having pure intentions and endowed with qualities such as fewness of wishes, dwell developing the burden of study and the burden of residence as is fitting—how much more so in the Buddha's Dispensation with fewness of wishes and so on. Thus it is said, "but as for the fourfold purity of virtue," and so on. Developing insight, they become those whose insight has reached its peak. This is stated as: "until they stand having reached conformity knowledge," meaning they establish insight just before conformity knowledge. They do not make effort for the path and fruit due to the incompleteness and immaturity of the womb of omniscience, which is the perfection of wisdom.

287. Therehīti [M 2.0138] vuddhatarehi. Nivāse satīti yasmiṃ ṭhāne pabbajito, tattheva nivāse. Vappakālatoti sassānaṃ vappakālato. Pubbe viya tato paraṃ tikhiṇena sūriyasantāpena payojanaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ – “vappakāle vitānaṃ viya upari vatthakilañjaṃ bandhitvā”ti. Puṭaketi kalāpe.

287. "Therehi" means by the more senior ones. "Nivāse sati" means dwelling in the very place where one went forth. "Vappakālato" means from the time of sowing the crops. It is said, "there is no need for sharp sun-heat afterwards as before," meaning "at the time of sowing, having tied a cloth-mat above like a canopy." "Puṭake" means in a bundle.

288. Paccayasāmaggihetukattā [V 2.0136] dhammappattiyā padesato pariññāvatthukāpi ariyā upaṭṭhite cittavighātapaccaye yadetaṃ nātisāvajjaṃ, tadevaṃ gaṇhantīti ayamettha dhammatāti āha – “alābhaṃ ārabbha cittaññathatta”ntiādi. Soti kikī kāsirājā. Brāhmaṇabhattoti brāhmaṇesu bhatto. Deveti brāhmaṇe sandhāyāha. Bhūmidevāti tesaṃ samaññā, tadā brāhmaṇagaruko loko. Tadā hi kassapopi bhagavā brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Dhītu avaṇṇaṃ vatvāti, “mahārāja, tava dhītā brāhmaṇasamayaṃ pahāya muṇḍapāsaṇḍikasamayaṃ gaṇhī”tiādinā rājaputtiyā aguṇaṃ vatvā. Varaṃ gaṇhiṃsu ñātakā. Rajjaṃ niyyātesi “mā me vacanaṃ musā ahosi, aṭṭhame divase niggaṇhissāmī”ti.

288. Because the attainment of the Dhamma is caused by a combination of conditions, and because the object of comprehension for noble ones is only partial, when a condition for mental distress has arisen, they take only that which is not overly blameworthy. This is the nature of things here. Thus it is said: "alteration of mind on account of loss," and so on. "So" refers to Kikī, king of Kāsi. "Brāhmaṇabhatto" means devoted to brahmins. "Deve" he said, referring to the brahmins. "Bhūmidevā" was their designation, for at that time the world held brahmins in high esteem. Indeed, at that time, even the Blessed One Kassapa was born in a brahmin family. "Dhītu avaṇṇaṃ vatvā" means having spoken dispraise of the daughter, saying, "Great king, your daughter has abandoned the brahmin way and has adopted the way of the shaven-headed heretics," and so on, having spoken of the princess's fault. The relatives accepted the boon. He relinquished the kingdom, thinking, "Let my word not be false; on the eighth day, I will punish her."

Pāvanaasmanayanavasena sammā pāvīkatattā parisuddhataṇḍulāni. Pāḷiyaṃ taṇḍulapaṭibhastānīti taṇḍulakhaṇḍāni. Muggapaṭibhastakaḷāyapaṭibhastesupi eseva nayo.

The rice grains are pure because they have been well-purified by means of winnowing and removing stones. In the Pāli, "taṇḍulapaṭibhastāni" means broken rice grains. The same principle applies to broken mung beans and peas.

289. Ko nu khoti bhummatthe paccattavacananti āha – “kuhiṃ nu kho”ti pāripūriṃ yojīyanti byañjanabhojanāni etthāti pariyogo, tato pariyogā. Tenāha “sūpabhājanato”ti. Saññaṃ datvāti vuttaṃ sabbaṃ ācikkhitvā tumhākaṃ atthāya sampādetvā nikkhitto upaṭṭhākoti bhagavato ārocethāti saññaṃ datvā. Ativissatthoti ativiya vissattho. Pañcavaṇṇāti khuddikādivasena pañcappakārā.

289. "Ko nu kho" is a first-person expression in the locative sense. He says: "kuhiṃ nu kho" (where indeed?) is to be supplied for completion. "Pariyogo" is where curries and food are arranged; from that comes "pariyogā." Therefore, he said, "from the curry bowl." "Saññaṃ datvā" (having given a sign) means having given the sign to inform the Blessed One that the attendant has been appointed, after he had explained everything that was said and prepared it for your benefit. "Ativissattho" means exceedingly trusting. "Pañcavaṇṇā" refers to the five kinds, by way of the small ones, etc.

290. Kinti nissakke paccattavacanaṃ, kasmāti attho? Dhammikoti iminā āgamanasuddhiṃ dasseti[M 2.0139]. Bhikkhūnaṃ patte bhattasadisoti iminā upāsakena satthu pariccattabhāvaṃ tattha satthuno ca aparisaṅkataṃ dasseti. Sikkhāpadavelā nāma natthīti dhammassāmibhāvato sikkhāpadamariyādā nāma natthi paṇṇattivajje, pakativajje pana setughāto eva.

290. "Kinti" is a first-person expression in the sense of "without being able to"; the meaning is "why?". "Dhammiko" (righteous) shows the purity of his lineage. "The meal in the monks' bowl is similar"—by this, the lay follower shows that it was relinquished by the Teacher and the Teacher's lack of hesitation there. "There is no occasion for the training rule"—because he is the owner of the Dhamma, there is no limit of the training rule regarding offenses by formulation; but regarding natural offenses, it is indeed a breaking of the bridge.

291. Chadanaṭṭhāne yadākāsaṃ, tadeva tassa gehassa chadananti ākāsacchadanaṃ. Pakatiyā utupharaṇamevāti chādite yādisaṃ utu, chadane uttiṇabhāvepi tamhi gehe tādisameva utupharaṇaṃ ahosi. Tesaṃyevāti tesaṃ ghaṭikārassa mātāpitūnaṃ eva.

291. In place of a roof, there was the sky; that itself was the roof of that house, thus it was called "sky-roof." "By nature, it was just the pervasion of the season" means: just as the season was when it was roofed, so too, even when the roof was without thatch, the pervasion of the season in that house was just the same. "Tesaṃyeva" means just for them, that is, for the mother and father of Ghaṭikāra.

292. “Catasso [V 2.0137] muṭṭhiyo eko kuḍuvo, cattāro kuḍuvā eko pattho, cattāro patthā eko āḷhako, cattāro āḷhakā ekaṃ doṇaṃ, cattāri doṇāni ekā mānikā, catasso mānikā ekā khārī, vīsati khārikā eko vāhoti tadeva ekasakaṭa”nti suttanipātaṭṭhakathādīsu (su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.662) vuttaṃ, idha pana “dve sakaṭāni eko vāho”ti vuttaṃ. Telaphāṇitādinti ādi-saddena sappiādiṃ maricādikaṭukabhaṇḍañca saṅgaṇhāti. Nāhaṃ raññā diṭṭhapubbo, kuto paripphassoti adhippāyo. Naccitvāti naccaṃ datvā.

292. "Four fistfuls make one kuḍuva; four kuḍuvas, one pattha; four patthas, one āḷhaka; four āḷhakas, one doṇa; four doṇas, one mānikā; four mānikās, one khārī; twenty khārīs, one vāha, and that is one cartload"—this is stated in the Suttanipāta commentary and others (Su. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.662). Here, however, it is said, "Two cartloads make one vāha." "Telaphāṇitādi" (oil, molasses, etc.)—the word "etc." includes ghee and similar items, as well as pungent goods like pepper and so on. The intended meaning is: "I have not been seen by the king before; how could I have received a touch from him?" "Naccitvā" means having given a dance.

Ghaṭikārasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Ghaṭikāra Sutta is complete.

2. Raṭṭhapālasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta

293. Thūlameva [V 2.0138] thullaṃ, thullā vipulā mahantā koṭṭhā jātā imassāti thullakoṭṭhikanti odanapūpapahūtavasena laddhanāmo nigamo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana thullakoṭṭhanti attho vutto. Tena pāḷiyaṃ ika-saddena padavaḍḍhanaṃ katanti dasseti.

293. "Thulla" is indeed "thūla" (large). The market town was named "Thullakoṭṭhika" because it had large, extensive, and great granaries, on account of its abundance of rice and cakes. In the commentary, however, the meaning "Thullakoṭṭha" is given. This shows that in the Pāli, the word has been lengthened by the suffix "-ika".

294. Raṭṭhapāloti idaṃ tassa kulaputtassa nāmaṃ. Paveṇivasena āgatakulavaṃsānugatanti samudāgamato paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ “kasmā raṭṭhapālo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sandhāretunti vināsanato pubbe yādisaṃ, tatheva sammadeva dhāretuṃ samattho. Saddhāti kammaphalasaddhāya sampannā. Sāmaṇeraṃ disvāti sikkhākāmatāya etadagge ṭhapiyamānaṃ disvā.

294. "Raṭṭhapāla"—this was the name of that clansman. To show the lineage that has come down by way of tradition, starting from its origin, it is said, "Why Raṭṭhapāla?" and so on. "To sustain" means capable of maintaining it properly, just as it was before its destruction. "Faith" means endowed with faith in kamma and its results. "Having seen the novice" means seeing him being placed at the forefront because of his desire for the training.

Saha [M 2.0140] raññāti sarājikaṃ, raññā saddhiṃ rājaparisaṃ. Cātuvaṇṇanti brāhmaṇādicatuvaṇṇasamudāyaṃ. Posetunti vaddhetuṃ dānādīhi saṅgahavatthūhi saṅgaṇhituṃ. Yaṃ kulaṃ. Pahossatīti sakkhissati.

"Saha raññā" means "sarājikaṃ"; together with the king, the royal assembly. "Cātuvaṇṇaṃ" means the collection of the four castes, beginning with the brahmins. "Posetuṃ" means to foster, to support with the bases of sympathy such as giving. "Yaṃ kulaṃ." "Pahossati" means will be capable.

Tena tena me upaparikkhatoti “kāmā nāmete aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā”ti (ma. ni. 1.234; pāci. 417; mahāni. 3, 6) ca ādinā yena yena ākārena kāmesu ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, tabbipariyāyato nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ guṇaṃ pakāsentaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, tena tena pakārena upaparikkhato vīmaṃsantassa mayhaṃ evaṃ hoti evaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Sikkhattayabrahmacariyanti adhisīlādisikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ seṭṭhacariyaṃ. Akhaṇḍādibhāvāpādanena akhaṇḍaṃ lakkhaṇavacanañhetaṃ. Kañcipi sikkhekadesaṃ asesetvā ekanteneva paripūretabbatāya ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ. Cittuppādamattampi saṃkilesamalaṃ anuppādetvā accantameva visuddhaṃ katvā pariharitabbatāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ. Tato eva saṅkhaṃ viya likhitanti saṅkhalikhitaṃ. Tenāha “likhitasaṅkhasadisa”nti. Dāṭhikāpi massuggahaṇeneva gahetvā “massu”tveva vuttaṃ, uttarādharamassunti attho. Kasāyena rattāni kāsāyāni. Ananuññātaṃ puttaṃ na pabbājeti “mātāpitūnaṃ lokiyamahājanassa cittaññathattaṃ mā hotū”ti. Tathā hi suddhodanamahārājassa tathā varo dinno.

"Tena tena me upaparikkhato" means: I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, which declares the danger, degradation, and defilement in sensual pleasures in this and that way, with such statements as, "Indeed, these sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—like a skeleton" (MN 1.234; Pāc. 417; Mahāni. 3, 6), and conversely, the benefit and virtue in renunciation. For me, who examines and investigates in this and that manner, it occurs thus, it appears thus. "The holy life of the threefold training" refers to the supreme practice comprising the threefold training of higher virtue, and so on. Because it brings about the state of being unbroken, etc., "unbroken" is a term for its characteristic. Because it should be fulfilled completely, without leaving out any part of the training whatsoever, it is "entirely complete." Because it should be practiced having made it utterly pure, without producing even for a moment the stain of defilement, it is "entirely pure." Just from that, it is "polished like a conch shell" (saṅkhalikhitaṃ). Hence, it is said, "like a polished conch shell." Even the mustache, being included in the term "beard," is simply called "beard"; the meaning is the upper and lower beard. Dyed with an astringent dye, they are "saffron robes." One does not give the going-forth to a son who is not permitted, thinking, "Let there be no alteration of mind for the parents and the worldly populace." Indeed, a boon was given thus to the great king Suddhodana.

295. Piyāyitabbato [V 2.0139] piyoti āha “pītijanako”ti. Manassa appāyanato manāpoti āha “manavaḍḍhanako”ti. Sukhedhito taruṇadārakakāle. Tato parañca sappikhīrādisādurasamanuññabhojanādiāhārasampattiyā sukhaparibhato. Atha vā daḷhabhattikadhātijanādiparijanasampattiyā ceva paricchadasampattiyā ca uḷārapaṇītasukhapaccayūpahārehi ca sukhedhito, akiccheneva dukkhappaccayavinodanena sukhaparibhato. Ajjhattikaṅgasampattiyā vā sukhedhito, bāhiraṅgasampattiyā sukhaparibhato. Kassacīti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ, kiñcīti vuttaṃ hoti, ayameva vā pāṭho. Tathā hi “appamattakampi kalabhāgaṃ dukkhassa na jānāsī”ti attho vutto. Evaṃ santeti nanu mayaṃ raṭṭhapāla maraṇādīsu kenaci upāyena appatīkārena maraṇenapi tayā akāmakāpi [M 2.0141] vinā bhavissāma, evaṃ sati. Yenāti yena kāraṇena. Kiṃ panāti ettha kinti kāraṇatthe paccattavacananti dassento āha “kena pana kāraṇenā”ti.

295. He is called 'beloved' (piyo) because he should be cherished (piyāyitabbato); he said, 'because he is the generator of joy.' He is called 'pleasing' (manāpo) because he delights the mind (manassa appāyanato); he said, 'because he increases delight.' He was nurtured in happiness in his youth. And thereafter, he was bathed in happiness due to the abundance of food, such as ghee, milk, and other delicious, agreeable meals and nourishment. Alternatively, he was nurtured in happiness due to the abundance of a devoted retinue, including foster-folk, and due to abundant provisions, and by lavish and excellent requisites of comfort, he was bathed in happiness through the effortless removal of conditions for suffering. Or, he was nurtured in happiness through inner well-being and bathed in happiness through external prosperity. 'Of whom' (kassaci) is a genitive in the sense of application; it means 'anything' (kiñci) is said, or this is simply the reading. For the meaning is thus expressed: 'You do not know even the slightest fraction of suffering.' 'This being so' (evaṃ sante)—indeed, Raṭṭhapāla, even unwillingly, we will be separated from you by death or some other irremediable means; this being so. 'By which' (yena)—by which reason. 'But what' (kiṃ pana)—here, showing that 'kiṃ' is a singular term in the sense of reason, he said, 'But for what reason?'

296. Paricārehīti parito tattha tattha yathāsakaṃ visayesu cārehi. Tenāha “ito cito ca upanehī”ti. Paricārehīti vā sukhūpakaraṇehi attānaṃ paricārehi, attano paricaraṇaṃ kārehi. Tathābhūto ca yasmā laḷanto kīḷanto nāma hoti, tasmā “laḷā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Niccadānaṃ dānaṃ nāma, uposathadivasādīsu dātabbaṃ atirekadānaṃ padānaṃ nāma. Paveṇīrakkhaṇavasena vā dīyamānaṃ dānaṃ nāma, attanāva paṭṭhapetvā dīyamānaṃ padānaṃ nāma. Pacurajanasādhāraṇaṃ vā nātiuḷāraṃ dānaṃ nāma, anaññasādhāraṇaṃ atiuḷāraṃ padānaṃ nāma. Uddassetabbāti uddhaṃ dassetabbā. Kuto uddhaṃ te dassetabbā? Pabbajitato uddhaṃ attānaṃ mātāpitaro dassetabbā, tenāha “yathā”tiādi.

296. 'Serve' means to move about all around, here and there, according to one's own domain. Hence it is said, 'Bring from here and there.' Alternatively, 'serve' means to serve oneself with the instruments of comfort, to have service rendered to oneself. And because one who is so is called one who indulges and sports, therefore it is said, 'indulge,' etc. Regular giving is called 'dāna,' while extra giving on days like the Uposatha is called 'padāna.' Or, giving for the sake of protecting tradition is 'dāna,' while giving established by oneself is 'padāna.' Or, giving that is common to many people and not very lavish is 'dāna,' while giving that is exclusive and very lavish is 'padāna.' 'Should be shown upwards' means they should be shown upwards. From what should they be shown upwards? One should show oneself to one's parents as being above one who has gone forth. Hence it is said, 'as,' etc.

299. Balaṃ gahetvāti ettha balaggahaṇaṃ nāma kāyabalassa uppādanamevāti āha “kāyabalaṃ janetvā”ti. Evaṃ viharantoti yathā pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ evaṃ eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto viharanto. Tasmāti yasmā neyyo, na ugghaṭitaññū, na ca vipañcitaññū, tasmā. Cirena pabbajito dvādasame vasse arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “na cirassevā”ti, taṃ saṭṭhi vassāni tato adhikampi vipassanāparivāsaṃ vasante upādāya vuttaṃ.

299. 'Having taken strength'—here, taking strength means the very generation of bodily strength; hence it is said, 'having generated bodily strength.' 'Dwelling thus' means dwelling alone, withdrawn, and diligent, as stated in the Pāli text. 'Therefore'—because he was one to be guided, not one who understands upon a brief utterance, nor one who understands through detailed explanation, therefore... Having been ordained for a long time, he attained arahantship in the twelfth year. But what is said in the Pāli text, 'not long after,' was said with reference to those who live on probation for insight for sixty years or even more than that.

Sattadvārakoṭṭhakassāti sattagabbhantaradvārakoṭṭhakasīsena gabbhantarāni vadati. Paharāpetīti vayovuḍḍhānurūpaṃ kappāpanādinā alaṅkārāpeti. Antojātatāya ñātisadisī dāsī ñātidāsī. Pūtibhāveneva lakkhitabbo doso vā abhidoso, sova ābhidosiko, abhidosaṃ vā paccūsakālaṃ gato patto atikkantoti ābhidosiko. Tenāha “ekarattātikkantassā”tiādi[V 2.0140]. Aparibhogāraho pūtibhūtabhāvena. Ariyavohārenāti ariyasamudācārena. Ariyā hi mātugāmaṃ bhaginivādena samudācaranti. Nissaṭṭhapariggahanti pariccattālayaṃ. Vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti nirapekkhabhāvato vuttaṃ, idha pana visesato aparibhogārahattāva vatthuno. Nimīyati saññāyatīti nimittaṃ, tathāsallakkhito ākāroti āha “ākāraṃ aggahesī”ti.

'Of the seven-gated chamber'—by the heading 'seven-gated inner chamber,' he speaks of the inner chambers. 'He has it done' (paharāpeti) means he has her adorned by having her hair cut, etc., in a manner appropriate to her advanced age. A kinswoman-slave (ñātidāsī) is a slave girl like a relative because of being born within. A fault (doso) to be marked by its putrid nature is 'abhidoso,' and that itself is 'ābhidosiko.' Or, one who has gone to, reached, or passed the dawn (paccūsakālaṃ), which is 'abhidosaṃ,' is 'ābhidosiko.' Therefore he said, 'of that which has passed one night,' etc. Unfit for use because of its putrid state. 'By noble speech' means by noble conduct. For the noble ones address women with the term 'sister.' 'Relinquished possessions' means having abandoned attachment. 'It is proper to say' is said because of a state of non-concern, but here it is specifically because of the object's unfitness for use. 'A sign' (nimittaṃ) is that which is measured or perceived; a feature observed as such. Thus he said, 'he did not grasp the feature.'

300. Gharaṃ [M 2.0142] pavisitvāti gehasāminiyā nisīditabbaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ antogehaṃ pavisitvā. Ālapaneti dāsijanassa ālapane. Bahi nikkhamantāti yathāvuttaantogehato bahi nikkhamantiyo. Gharesu sālā hontīti gharesu ekamante bhojanasālā honti pākāraparikkhittā susaṃvihitadvārabandhā susammaṭṭhavālikaṅgaṇā.

300. 'Having entered the house'—having entered the inner house, which is the place where the mistress of the house sits. 'In addressing'—in addressing the servants. 'Coming out'—the women coming out from the aforementioned inner house. 'In the houses, there are halls'—in the houses, in a secluded place, there are dining halls, enclosed by a wall, with well-arranged door-frames, and with well-swept sandy courtyards.

Anokappanaṃ asaddahanaṃ. Amarisanaṃ asahanaṃ. Anāgatavacanaṃ anāgatasaddappayogo, attho pana vattamānakālikova. Tenāha “paccakkhampī”ti. Ariyiddhiyanti “paṭikūle apaṭikūlasaññī viharatī”ti (a. ni. 5.144) evaṃ vuttaariyiddhiyaṃ.

'Disapproval' is not believing. 'Not resenting' is not enduring. 'Future speech' is the use of a future word, but the meaning is in the present time. Therefore, it is said, 'even directly visible.' 'Noble psychic power'—the noble psychic power described as 'he dwells perceiving the repulsive as non-repulsive' (A. 5.144).

Pūtikummāso chaḍḍanīyadhammo tassa gehato laddhopi na dātabbayuttako dāsijanena dinnoti āha “deyyadhammavasena neva dānaṃ alatthamhā”ti. “Imehi muṇḍakehī”tiādinā nitthunanavacanena paccakkhānaṃ atthato laddhameva, tassa pana ujukaphāsusamācāravasena aladdhattā vuttaṃ “na paccakkhāna”nti. Tenāha – “paṭisanthāravasena paccakkhānampi na alatthamhā”ti. “Neva dāna”ntiādi paccāsīsāya akkhantiyā ca vuttaṃ viya pacurajano maññeyyāti tannivattanatthaṃ adhippāyamassa vivarituṃ “kasmā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Suttikāpaṭicchannanti sippikāchadāhi channaṃ.

Rotten gruel is a thing to be thrown away; even if obtained from that house, it is not suitable to be given. Because it was given by a servant, he said, 'we did not receive a gift in the sense of a proper alms-offering.' By the abusive words beginning with 'by these shavelings,' a refusal was indeed received in meaning, but because it was not received by way of straightforward and pleasant conduct, it is said, 'not a refusal.' Therefore he said, 'we did not receive even a refusal by way of a friendly welcome.' Lest many people might think that 'neither a gift...' etc., was said as if out of expectation and impatience, to avert that and to clarify his intention, 'but why...' etc., was said. 'Covered with oyster shells' means covered with coverings of oyster shells.

Ukkaṭṭhaekāsanikatāyāti idaṃ bhūtakathanamattaṃ therassa tathābhāvadīpanato. Mudukassapi hi ekāsanikassa yāya nisajjāya kiñcimattaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuttaṃ, vattasīsenapi tato vuṭṭhitassa puna bhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Tenāha tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero “āsanaṃ vā rakkheyya bhojanaṃ vā”ti. Ukkaṭṭhasapadānacārikoti purato pacchato ca āhaṭabhikkhampi aggahetvā bahidvāre ṭhatvā pattavissajjanameva karoti. Eteneva therassa ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātikabhāvo dīpito. Tenāha – “svātanāya bhikkhaṃ nāma nādhivāsetī”ti. Atha kasmā adhivāsesīti āha “mātu anuggahenā”tiādi[V 2.0141]. Paṇḍitā hi mātāpitūnaṃ ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ vā kātabbaṃ anuggahaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā dhutaṅgasuddhikā na bhavanti.

'By the strict practice of eating in one session'—this is merely a statement of fact, showing that the elder was so. For even a moderate one-sessioner, having eaten even a small amount of food at one sitting, it is not proper for one who has risen from it to eat again, even as a matter of observance. Therefore the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said, 'One should guard either the seat or the food.' 'A strict sequential alms-round walker' means that without accepting alms brought from in front or from behind, he just stands at the outer door and gives up his bowl. By this itself, the elder's state as a strict alms-food-eater is shown. Therefore it is said, 'He does not accept an invitation for alms for the next day.' Then why did he accept? It is said, 'Out of compassion for his mother,' and so forth. For the wise do not become pure in the ascetic practices by neglecting the support that should be given to mothers and fathers or to teachers and preceptors.

301. Payuttanti vaddhivasena payojitaṃ, taddhitalopaṃ katvā vuttanti veditabbaṃ yathā aññatthāpi “pitāmahaṃ dhanaṃ laddhā, sukhaṃ jīvati sañcayo”ti[M 2.0143]. Jeṭṭhakitthiyoti padhānitthiyo. Itoti imasmiṃ kule anubhavitabbavibhavasampattito. Aññatoti imassa dinnattā aññasmiṃ kule anubhavitabbasampattito.

301. 'Payuttaṃ' means employed in the sense of interest. It should be understood that this is said after eliding the taddhita suffix, just as elsewhere: 'Having received his grandfather's wealth, Sañcaya lives happily.' 'Chief women' means principal women. 'From here' means from the abundance of wealth to be experienced in this family. 'From another' means from the abundance of wealth to be experienced in another family, because of it having been given to this one.

302. Cittavicittanti kappanāya ceva araharūpena alaṅkārādinā ca cittitañceva vicittitañca. Vaṇakāyanti vaṇabhūtaṃ kāyaṃ. Samantato ussitanti heṭṭhimakāyavasena heṭṭhā upari ca sannissitaṃ. Niccāturanti abhiṇhappaṭipīḷitaṃ, sadā dukkhitaṃ vā. Bahusaṅkappanti rāgavatthubhāvena abhijanehi hāvabhāvavilāsavasena, āmisavasena ca soṇasiṅgālādīhi bahūhi saṅkappetabbaṃ. Ṭhitīti avaṭṭhānaṃ avipariṇāmo natthi. Tenāha – “bhijjanadhammatāva niyatā”ti, parissavabhāvāpatti ceva vināsapatti ca ekantikāti attho.

302. “Cittavicitta” means both designed and variegated by means of suitable decoration and ornaments. “Vaṇakāya” means a body that has become a wound. “Samantato ussita” means set up on all sides, supported both below and above in relation to the lower body. “Niccātura” means constantly afflicted, or always suffering. “Bahusaṅkappa” means it is to be conceived of in many ways: by noble persons as an object of lust through amorous gestures and charms, and by dogs, jackals, and so forth, as a source of flesh. “Ṭhiti” means stability; there is no non-transformation. Therefore, it is said: “Its nature of breaking up is certain,” meaning, it is certain to arrive at the state of oozing and the state of destruction.

Cittakatampīti gandhādīhi cittakatampi. Rūpanti sarīraṃ.

“Cittakata” means adorned even with perfumes and the like. “Rūpa” means the body.

Alattakakatāti piṇḍialattakena suvaṇṇakatā. Tenāha “alattakena rañjitā”ti. Cuṇṇakamakkhitanti dosanīharaṇehi tāpadahanādīhi katābhisaṅkhāramukhaṃ gorocanādīhi obhāsanakacuṇṇehi makkhitaṃ, tenāha “sāsapakakkenā”tiādi.

“Alattakakata” means decorated with red lac. Hence it is said, “adorned with lac.” “Cuṇṇakamakkhita” means the face is prepared with applications done to remove blemishes such as heat rash, burns, and so forth, and smeared with beautifying powders such as gorocana and the like. Hence it is said, “with mustard paste,” and so forth.

Rasodakenāti saralaniyyāsarasamissena udakena. Āvattanaparivatte katvāti āvattanaparivattanavasena nate katvā. Aṭṭhapadakaracanāyāti bhittikūṭaddhacandādivibhāgāya aṭṭhapadakaracanāya.
