By this, when it is said, 'He praises the attainment of all wholesome states,' the meaning would be stated in accordance with the question, but such an explanation would not be weighty, for even one who has not accomplished wholesome states might praise their attainment. But to show that the Blessed One, because he has rightly accomplished wholesome states, is one who acts as he speaks, he demonstrates this meaning with 'he answered thus.' The rest is easily understood.

Bāhitikasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The elucidation of the hidden meaning of the Commentary on the Bāhitika Sutta is complete.

9. Dhammacetiyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Dhammacetiya Sutta

364. Medavaṇṇā [V 2.0162][M 2.0162] uḷupavaṇṇā ca tattha tattha pāsāṇā ussannā ahesunti medāḷupanti gāmassa samaññā jātā. Uḷupavaṇṇāti candasamānavaṇṇatāya medapāsāṇā vuttāti keci. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “medavaṇṇā pāsāṇā kirettha ussannā ahesu”nti idaṃ vuttaṃ. Assāti senāpatissa. Kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthanti mallikāya sokavinodanadhammakathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ.

364. Because stones the color of fat and the color of the moon were abundant there, the designation 'Medāḷupa' arose for the village. Some say that the fat-colored stones were called 'moon-colored' because their color was similar to the moon. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Stones the color of fat, it is said, were abundant here.' 'Assā' means 'of the general.' 'For the purpose of initiating a discussion' means for the purpose of initiating a Dhamma talk to dispel Mallikā's grief.

Raññāti pasenadīkosalaraññā. Mahaccāti mahatiyā. Padavipallāsena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Pasādamarahantīti pāsādikāni. Tenāha “saha rañjanakānī”ti. Yāni pana pāsādikāni, tāni passituṃ yuttāni. Pāsādikānīti vā saddahanasahitāni. Tenāha “pasādajanakānī”ti. “Appābādha”nti ādīsu viya appasaddo abhāvatthoti āha “nissaddānī”ti. Aniyamatthavācī ya-saddo aniyamākāravācakopi hotīti “yatthā”ti padassa “yādisesū”tiādimāha. Tathā hi aṅgulimālasutte (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.347 ādayo) “yassa kho”ti padassa “yādisassa kho”ti attho vutto.

'By the king' means by King Pasenadi of Kosala. 'Mahaccā' means by a great (retinue). And this is said with a reversal of words. 'Pāsādikāni' means they are deserving of confidence. Therefore, he said, 'along with pleasing things.' For what is delightful is fit to be seen. Or, 'pāsādikāni' means accompanied by faith. Therefore, he said, 'generating confidence.' Just as in such phrases as 'appābādha' (of little illness), the word 'appa' has the meaning of absence; thus he said 'nissaddāni' (without sound). The word 'ya,' which expresses indefiniteness, can also express an indefinite mode; therefore, for the word 'yattha' (where), he gives the meaning 'in whatever sort,' and so on. For thus in the commentary on the Aṅgulimāla Sutta, the meaning of the word 'yassa kho' is given as 'of whatever sort.'

366. Paṭicchadanti paṭicchādakaṃ. Rājakakudhabhaṇḍānīti rājabhaṇḍabhūtāni. Rahāyatīti raho karoti, maṃ ajjhesatīti attho.

366. 'Paṭicchadanti' means that which conceals. 'Rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni' means things that are royal possessions. 'Rahāyati' means he takes one aside into privacy; the meaning is, 'he requests me.'

367. Yathāsabhāvato ñeyyaṃ dhāreti avadhāretīti dhammo, ñāṇanti āha “paccakkhañāṇasaṅkhātassa dhammassā”ti. Anunayoti anugacchanako. Diṭṭhena hi adiṭṭhassa anumānaṃ. Tenāha “anumānaṃ anubuddhī”ti. Āpāṇakoṭikanti yāva pāṇakoṭi, tāva jīvitapariyosānaṃ. Etanti dhammanvayasaṅkhātaṃ anumānaṃ. Evanti “idha panāha”nti vuttappakārena.

367. Dhamma is that which bears and discerns the knowable according to its true nature. It is knowledge, he says, referring to 'the Dhamma reckoned as direct knowledge.' 'Following' means going along with. For what is unseen is inferred by what is seen. Hence it is said, 'inference and subsequent understanding.' 'Until the tip of life' means as long as the tip of life, that is, until the end of life. 'This' refers to the inference called 'concordance with the teaching.' 'Thus' refers to the manner stated as 'but here I...'

369. Cakkhuṃ abandhante viyāti apāsādikatāya passantānaṃ cakkhuṃ attani abandhante viya. Kulasantānānubandho rogo kularogo. Uḷāranti sānubhāvaṃ. Yo hi ānubhāvasampanno, taṃ “mahesakkha”nti vadanti. Arahattaṃ gaṇhantoti ukkaṭṭhaniddesoyaṃ, heṭṭhimaphalāni gaṇhantopi.

369. “As if not binding the eye” means as if, due to unloveliness, not binding the eye of those who see to oneself. “The disease that follows the family line” is the family disease. “Exalted” means with great influence. For one endowed with such influence is called “of great power.” “Attaining arahantship” is a supreme designation; it also includes those attaining the lower fruits.

373. Jīvikā [V 2.0163][M 2.0163] jīvitavutti.

373. “Livelihood” means the way of maintaining life.

374. Dhammaṃ ceteti saṃvedeti etehīti dhammacetiyāni, dhammassa pūjāvacanāni. Nanu cetāni buddhasaṅghaguṇadīpanānipi santi? Kathaṃ “dhammacetiyānīti dhammassa cittīkāravacanānī”ti vuttanti āha “tīsu hī”tiādi. Tattha yasmā buddharatanamūlakāni sesaratanāni tassa vasena laddhabbato. Kosalaraññā cettha buddhagāravena dhammasaṅghagāravaṃ paveditaṃ, tasmā “bhagavati cittīkāre kate dhammopi katova hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā ca ratanattayapasādapubbikā sāsane sammāpaṭipatti, tasmā vuttaṃ – “ādibrahmacariyakānīti maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtānī”ti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

374. “That by which one reflects on and is affected by the Dhamma are called Dhamma-cetiyas, expressions of veneration for the Dhamma. But are these not also illuminations of the virtues of the Buddha and the Sangha? How then is it said, 'Dhamma-cetiyas are expressions of honouring the Dhamma'?" To this, he said, "Because in the three..." There, since the remaining jewels are rooted in the Buddha-jewel and are to be obtained dependent on him, King Kosala here made known his reverence for the Dhamma and Sangha out of reverence for the Buddha. Therefore it was said, "When honour is done to the Blessed One, honour is also done to the Dhamma." And since right practice in the Dispensation has faith in the Triple Gem as its precursor, it was said, "the beginning of the holy life," meaning those things that are the beginning of the path of the holy life. The rest is easily understood.

Dhammacetiyasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Dhammacetiya Sutta is complete.

10. Kaṇṇakatthalasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta

375. Anantarasutte [V 2.0164] vuttakaraṇīyenevāti “pāsāde vā nāṭakesu vā cittassādaṃ alabhamāno tattha tattha vicarituṃ āraddho”ti vuttakaraṇīyena. Appaduṭṭhapadosīnañhi evaṃ hotīti.

375. “By the very reason stated in the preceding sutta” means by the reason stated thus: “not obtaining satisfaction of mind in palaces or dramas, he began to wander about here and there.” For it is so for those who are not corrupt and malevolent.

376. Pucchitoti “aññaṃ dūtaṃ nālatthu”nti pucchito. Soti rājā. Tāsaṃ vandanā sace uttarakālaṃ, attano āgamanakāraṇaṃ kathessati.

376. “Asked” means he was asked, “Could you not find another messenger?” “He” refers to the king. If their homage is at a later time, he will explain the reason for his coming.

378. Ekāvajjanenāti ekavīthijavanena. Tena ekacittaṃ tāva tiṭṭhatu, ekacittavīthiyāpi sabbaṃ jānituṃ na sakkāti dasseti. “Idaṃ nāma atītaṃ jānissāmī”ti aniyametvā āvajjato yaṃ kiñci atītaṃ jānāti, niyamite pana niyamitamevāti āha – “ekena hi…pe… ekadesameva jānātī”ti. Tena cittenāti “atītaṃ sabbaṃ jānissāmī”ti evaṃ pavattacittena. Itaresūti anāgatapaccuppannesu. Kāraṇajātikanti yuttisabhāvaṃ, yuttiyā yuttanti attho. Samparāyaguṇanti samparāye katakammassa visesaṃ.

378. “With a single advertence” means with the javana of a single cognitive process. By this he shows that, let alone a single mind-moment, it is not possible to know everything even with a single cognitive process. Without predetermining, “I will know this specific past event,” one who adverts may know any past event, but when predetermining, only what is predetermined is known—hence it is said, “For with one... one knows only a portion.” “With that mind” refers to the mind operating with the thought, “I will know all the past.” “In the others” refers to the future and the present. “Of the nature of a cause” means the nature of reason, the meaning being “endowed with reason.” “The quality of the future life” refers to the distinction of actions done relating to the future life.

379. Lokuttaramissakāni kathitāni bodhirājakumārasutte viya lokiyā ceva lokuttarā ca. Yathālābhavasena cettha padhāniyaṅgānaṃ [M 2.0164] lokuttaraggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Paccekaṃ eva nesañca padhāniyaṅgatā daṭṭhabbā yathā “aṭṭhavimokkhā sandissanti lokuttaramissakā”ti. Lokuttarānevāti cettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati. Padhānanānattanti padahananānattaṃ, bhāvanānuyogavisesanti attho. Saṅkhāre parimadditvā paṭipakkhadhamme ekadesato pajahitvā ṭhitassa bhāvanānuyogo sabbena sabbaṃ aparimadditasaṅkhārassa appahīnapaṭipakkhassa bhāvanānuyogato sukhumo visadova hoti, saccābhisamayena santānassa āhitavisesattāti āha – “aññādisameva hi puthujjanassa padhānaṃ, aññādisaṃ sotāpannassā”tiādi. Ayañca viseso na kevalaṃ anariyaariyapuggalato eva, atha kho ariyesupi sekkhādivisesatopi labbhati abhisaṅkhāravisesato abhinīhārato ca ijjhanatoti dassento “aññādisaṃ sakadāgāmino”tiādimāha. Na pāpuṇātīti yasmā puthujjano sabbathāva padhānaṃ padahanto sotāpattimaggaṃ [V 2.0165] adhigacchati, sotāpanno ca sakadāgāmimagganti heṭṭhimaṃ uparimato oḷārikaṃ, uparimañca itarato sukhumaṃ tena pahātuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa pajahanato, iti adhigantabbavisesena ca adhigamapaṭipadāya saṇhasukhumatā tikkhavisadatā ca viññāyatīti āha – “puthujjanassa padhānaṃ sotāpannassa padhānaṃ na pāpuṇātī”tiādi.

379. The mixed supramundane states were explained, as in the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta, where both mundane and supramundane are present. Here, the inclusion of the supramundane among the factors of striving should be understood according to what is obtained. And their individual nature as factors of striving should be seen, as in the statement, “The eight liberations are found as mixed supramundane states.” Here, whatever is to be said about the purely supramundane will become clear later. “Diversity of striving” means diversity of exertion, meaning a distinction in the application to meditation. For one who has subdued the formations and abandoned the opposing factors to some extent, application to meditation is subtle and clear compared to one who has not subdued all formations or abandoned all opposing factors, because the continuity of consciousness has been instilled with a special quality through the penetration of the truths—hence it is said, “The striving of an ordinary person is of one kind, that of a stream-enterer is of another kind,” and so on. This distinction is not only between non-noble and noble individuals but also among noble ones themselves, such as trainees and others, and is achieved due to distinctions in volitional activities, aspiration, and accomplishment—thus it is shown: “The striving of a once-returner is of another kind,” and so on. “Does not reach” means that, since an ordinary person, striving in every way, attains the path of stream-entry, and a stream-enterer attains the path of once-returning—the lower is coarser than the higher, and the higher is subtler than the other, because of abandoning what the former is unable to abandon. Thus, through the distinction in what is to be attained and the fineness and subtlety, sharpness and clarity of the path of attainment, it is understood—hence it is said, “The striving of an ordinary person does not reach the striving of a stream-enterer,” and so on.

Akūṭakaraṇanti avañcanakiriyaṃ. Anavacchindananti atiyānaṃ. Aviñchanaṃ na ākaḍḍhanaṃ, niyuttataṃ viniveṭhetvā samantā viparivattitvā samadhārāya chaḍḍanaṃ vā. Tassa kāraṇaṃ taṃkāraṇaṃ, taṃ kāraṇanti vā taṃ kiriyaṃ taṃ adhikāraṃ. Dantehi gantabbabhūminti dantehi pattabbaṭṭhānaṃ, pattabbavatthuṃ vā. Cattāropi assaddhā nāma uparimauparimasaddhāya abhāvato. Yena hi yaṃ appattaṃ, tassa taṃ natthi. Ariyasāvakassa…pe… natthi paṭhamamaggeneva māyāsāṭheyyānaṃ pahātabbattā. Tenevāti sammadeva viruddhapakkhānaṃ saddhādīnaṃ idhādhippetattā. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ missakakathāti āha “assakhaḷuṅkasuttante panā”tiādi. Cattārova honti puthujjanādivasena.

“Not acting fraudulently” means the act of not cheating. “Not cutting off” means transgressing. “Not pulling back” means not dragging, but untwisting what is fixed, turning it all around and letting go with even bearing, or throwing. “Its cause” means that cause; or “that cause” means that action, that function. “The ground to be reached by the tamed” means the place attainable by the tamed, or the object to be attained. The four are called 'faithless' due to the absence of successively higher faith. For whatever is not attained by someone, that he does not have. For a noble disciple…there is no deceit or treachery, since these are to be abandoned by the very first path. “Therefore” means because the faith and so on of the truly opposing parties are intended here. If so, how is it a mixed discussion? It is said, “But in the Assakhaḷuṅka Sutta…” and so on. There are indeed four types, by way of ordinary people and so on.

Opammasaṃsandane adantahatthiādayo viyātiādinā kaṇhapakkhe, yathā pana dantahatthiādayotiādinā sukkapakkhe ca sādhāraṇato ekajjhaṃ [M 2.0165] katvā vuttaṃ, asādhāraṇato bhinditvā dassetuṃ “idaṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

In the comparison by way of simile, with reference to the dark side, it is said, “like the untamed elephant,” and so on; and with reference to the bright side, “just as, like the tamed elephant,” and so on. Thus, having stated them together in general, in order to show them distinctly in particular, it is said, “This is what is said,” and so on.

380. Sammappadhānā nibbisiṭṭhavīriyā. Tenāha – “na kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ vadāmi, yadidaṃ vimuttiyā vimutti”nti. Na hi sukkhavipassakatevijjachaḷabhiññānaṃ vimuttiyā nānākaraṇaṃ atthi. Tena vuttaṃ “yaṃ ekassā”tiādi. Kiṃ tvaṃ na jānāsīti sambandho. Āgacchantīti uppajjanavasena āgacchanti. Nāgacchantīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Idaṃ pucchantoti idaṃ pucchāmīti dassento. Appahīnacetasikadukkhā anadhigataanāgāmitā. Tenāha “upapattivasena āgantāro”ti. Samucchinnadukkhāti samugghāṭitacetasikadukkhā.

380. The right strivings are undifferentiated energy. Therefore it is said: “I declare no difference at all, that is, between liberation and liberation.” For there is no difference in liberation between dry-insight practitioners, those with the threefold knowledge, and those with the six higher knowledges. Hence it is said: “What is for one...” and so on. The connection is: “Do you not know?” “Coming” means coming by way of arising. “Not coming” also follows the same principle here. “Asking this” means showing “this I am asking.” “Those whose mental suffering is not abandoned” refers to those who have not yet attained non-returnership. Therefore it is said: “Those who come by way of rebirth.” “Those whose suffering is cut off” means those whose mental suffering has been eradicated.

381. Tamhā ṭhānāti tato yathādhigataissariyaṭṭhānato. Puna tamhā ṭhānāti tato duggatā. Sampannakāmaguṇanti uḷārakāmaguṇasamannāgataṃ.

381. “From that position” means from that state of sovereignty attained as it was. Again, “from that position” means from that miserable state. “Endowed with the pleasures of the senses” means possessing magnificent sensual qualities.

Tatthāti kāmadevaloke. Ṭhānabhāvatoti arahattañce adhigataṃ, tāvadeva parinibbānato. Uparideve [V 2.0166] cāti uparūpari bhūmivāse deve ca, cakkhuviññāṇadassanenapi dassanāya nappahontīti yojanā.

“There” refers to the deva world of the sensual sphere. “Because of the state of being” means that if arahantship is attained, there is final Nibbāna right then. And “among higher devas” means among devas dwelling on successively higher planes; they are not capable of seeing even with the vision of eye-consciousness—this is the construction.

382. Vuttanayenevāti devapucchāya vutteneva nayena. Sā kira kathāti “natthi so samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā, yo sakideva sabbaṃ neyya”nti kathā. Teti viṭaṭūbhasañjayā. Imasmiṃyeva ṭhāneti imasmiṃ migadāyeyeva. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

382. "In the manner stated" means in the manner stated in the deva's question. "That talk" refers to the statement: "There is no ascetic or brahmin who could know everything at once." "They" refers to Viṭaṭūbha and Sañjaya. "In this very place" refers to this very Migadāya (Deer Park). The rest is easily understood.

Kaṇṇakatthalasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of Hidden Meanings in the Commentary on the Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca rājavaggavaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the Rājavagga is concluded.

5. Brāhmaṇavaggo

5. The Brahmin Chapter

1. Brahmāyusuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Brahmāyu Sutta

383. “Mahāsatto [V 2.0167][M 2.0166] mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo”tiādīsu (mahāva. 38) uḷāratā visayo, “mahājanakāyo sannipatī”tiādīsu sambahulabhāvavisayo, idha pana tadubhayampissa atthoti “mahatāti guṇamahattenapi mahatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Appicchatādīti ādi-saddena santuṭṭhisallekhapavivekaasaṃsaggavīriyārambhādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghātasaṅkhātenāti ettha “niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo” (saṃ. ni. 2.41; 3.998, 1004) – “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropeyyāti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”tiādivacanato diṭṭhisīlānaṃ niyatasabhāvattā sotāpannāpi aññamaññaṃ diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatā, pageva sakadāgāmiādayo. “Tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharati (dī. ni. 3.324, 356; ma. ni. 1.492; 3.54; a. ni. 6.11; pari. 274) tathārūpehi sīlehi sīlasāmaññagato viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.324; ma. ni. 1.492; 3.54; a. ni. 6.12; pari. 274) vacanato puthujjanānampi diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatabhāvo labbhatiyeva.

383. In phrases like "great being, of great power, of great majesty" (Mahāva. 38), the context concerns exalted qualities; in phrases like "a great crowd gathered," the context concerns numerousness. Here, however, since both meanings are applicable, it is said: "‘Great’ means great also through greatness of qualities," and so on. "Fewness of wishes, etc."—the "etc." includes contentment, effacement, seclusion, non-association, energetic striving, and so on. "Designated as a union through sharedness of view and virtue"—here, from statements such as "he is assured, destined for enlightenment" (Saṃ. Ni. 2.41; 3.998, 1004) and "monks, this is impossible, there is no chance that a person accomplished in view would intentionally deprive a living being of life; such a thing is impossible," due to the fixed nature of view and virtue, stream-enterers are united with one another by sharedness of view and virtue, let alone once-returners and others. From statements like "he dwells having attained sharedness of view with such a view, he dwells having attained sharedness of virtue with such virtues" (Dī. Ni. 3.324, 356; Ma. Ni. 1.492; 3.54; A. Ni. 6.11; Pari. 274), it can be inferred that even ordinary people are united by sharedness of view and virtue.

Oṭṭhapahatakaraṇavasena atthavibhāgavasena. Sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānanti ettha nighaṇḍūti vacanīyavācakabhāvena atthaṃ saddañca khaṇḍati vibhajja dassetīti nikhaṇḍu. So eva idha kha-kārassa gha-kāraṃ katvā “nighaṇḍū”ti vutto. Kiṭati gameti kiriyādivibhāgaṃ, taṃ vā anavasesapariyādānato gamento pūretīti keṭubhaṃ. Vevacanappakāsakanti pariyāyasaddadīpakaṃ, ekekassa atthassa anekapariyāyavacanavibhāvakanti attho. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ anekesampi atthānaṃ ekasaddavacanīyatāvibhāvanavasenapi tassa ganthassa pavattattā. Vacībhedādilakkhaṇā kiriyā kappīyati etenāti kiriyākappo, so pana vaṇṇapadasambandhapadatthavibhāgato bahuvikappoti āha “kiriyākappavikappo”ti. Idañca mūlakiriyākappaganthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. So hi [V 2.0168] satasahassaparimāṇo nalacariyādipakaraṇaṃ. Ṭhānakaraṇādivibhāgato [M 2.0167] nibbacanavibhāgato ca akkharā pabhedīyanti etehīti akkharappabhedā, sikkhāniruttiyo. Etesanti vedānaṃ. Te eva vede padaso kāyatīti padako. Taṃ taṃ saddaṃ tadatthañca byākaroti byācikkhati etenāti byākaraṇaṃ, saddasatthaṃ. Āyatiṃ hitaṃ tena loko na yatati na īhatīti lokāyataṃ. Tañhi ganthaṃ nissāya sattā puññakiriyāya cittampi na uppādenti. Vayatīti vayo, na vayo avayo, na avayo anavayo, ādimajjhapariyosānesu katthaci aparikilanto avitthāyanto te ganthe sandhāreti pūretīti attho. Dve paṭisedhā pakatiṃ gamentīti dassento “avayo na hotī”ti vatvā tattha avayaṃ dassetuṃ “avayo…pe… na sakkotī”ti vuttaṃ.

By means of articulation involving the striking of the lips and by means of the division of meaning. Regarding `sanighaṇḍukeṭubhāni`, herein `nighaṇḍu` is so called from `nikhaṇḍu`, because through the relationship between what is expressed and the expression, it splits and displays by dividing both the meaning and the word. It is called `nighaṇḍu` by changing the letter `kha` to `gha`. `Keṭubha` is so called because it `kiṭati`, that is, it comprehends the division of actions and so on; or because it fulfills that, encompassing it by taking it up completely without remainder. `Vevacanappakāsaka` means an illuminator of synonyms; the meaning is that it reveals the various synonymous expressions for each single meaning. And this is merely an example, since that text proceeds also by way of revealing that many meanings can be expressed by a single word. `Kiriyākappo` is so called because action, characterized by variations in speech and so on, is arranged by it. But since it has many varieties due to the division of letters, words, connections, and word-meanings, it is called `kiriyākappavikappo`. And this is said with reference to the root text of `Kiriyākappo`. For that text, the `Nalacariyādipakaraṇa`, has a hundred thousand verses. `Akkharappabhedā` are so called because letters are distinguished by them through the division of place of articulation, articulator, effort, and so on; these are phonetics (`sikkhā`) and etymology (`nirutti`). `Etesaṃ` means 'of the Vedas'. `Padako` is so called because he recites those very Vedas word by word. `Byākaraṇaṃ` is so called because one analyzes and explains each word and its meaning by means of it; it is the science of words. `Lokāyataṃ` is so called because by means of it, the world does not strive or exert itself for future welfare. For, relying on that text, beings do not even give rise to a thought of meritorious action. `Vayo` means decay; `na vayo` is `avayo` (non-decay); `na avayo` is `anavayo` (not non-decay). The meaning is that he sustains and fulfills those texts without becoming weary or distorting them anywhere in the beginning, middle, or end. To show that 'two negations establish the original meaning', it is said, 'it is not non-decay,' and then to show 'non-decay,' it is stated, 'non-decay... cannot...'

384. Garūti bhāriyaṃ attānaṃ tato mocetvā gamanaṃ dukkaraṃ hoti. Anatthopi uppajjati nindābyārosaupārambhādi. Abbhuggatoti ettha abhisaddayogena itthambhūtākhyānatthe upayogavacanaṃ.

384. `Garu` (teacher; lit. heavy): It is difficult to depart, having freed oneself from such a weighty person. Disadvantage also arises, such as blame, harsh words, and reproach. Regarding `abbhuggato`, here, through its connection with the prefix `abhi-`, the word is used in the sense of describing a specific state.

Lakkhaṇānīti lakkhaṇadīpanāni mantapadāni. Antaradhāyantīti na kevalaṃ lakkhaṇamantāniyeva, aññānipi brāhmaṇānaṃ ñāṇabalābhāvena anukkamena antaradhāyanti. Tathā hi vadanti “ekasataṃ addhariyaṃ dipaññāsamattato sāmā”tiādi. Paṇidhimahato samādānamahatotiādinā paccekaṃ maha-saddo yojetabbo. Paṇidhimahantatādi cassa buddhavaṃsacariyāpiṭakavaṇṇanādivaseneva veditabbo. Niṭṭhāti nipphattiyo. Jātisāmaññatoti lakkhaṇajātiyā lakkhaṇabhāvena samānabhāvato. Yathā hi buddhānaṃ lakkhaṇāni suvisuddhāni suparibyattāni paripuṇṇāni ca honti, na evaṃ cakkavattīnaṃ. Tenāha “na teheva buddho hotī”ti.

`The marks` means the mantra-verses that illuminate the marks. `They disappear` means not only the mantras about the marks, but other things also, gradually disappear for the brahmins due to their lack of the power of knowledge. For instance, they say, "One hundred and one Addhariyas, from fifty-two Sāmas," and so on. The word `mahā` (great) should be connected individually with each term, as in `paṇidhimahato` (of great aspiration), `samādānamahato` (of great undertaking), and so forth. And the greatness of his aspiration, etc., should be understood by way of the commentaries on the Buddhavaṃsa, Cariyāpiṭaka, and so on. `Niṭṭhā` means `nipphatti` (accomplishment, perfection). `Jātisāmaññato` (by commonality of kind) means due to the sameness of the marks with respect to their kind and their nature as marks. For while the marks of the Buddhas are perfectly pure, very distinct, and complete, they are not so for wheel-turning monarchs. Therefore, it is said, "One does not become a Buddha merely by them."

Abhirūpatā dīghāyukatā, appātaṅkatā brāhmaṇādīnaṃ piyamanāpatāti catūhi acchariyadhammehi. Dānaṃ piyavacanaṃ atthacariyā samānattatāti imehi catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi. Rañjanatoti pītijananato. Cakkaṃ cakkaratanaṃ vatteti pavattetīti cakkavattī, sampatticakkehi sayaṃ vatteti, tehi ca paraṃ sattanikāyaṃ vatteti pavattetīti cakkavattī, parahitāvaho iriyāpathacakkānaṃ vatto vattanaṃ etassa atthīti cakkavattī, appaṭihataṃ vā [M 2.0168] āṇāsaṅkhātaṃ cakkaṃ vattetīti cakkavatī, appaṭihataṃ vā āṇāsaṅkhātaṃ cakkaṃ vattetīti cakkavattī, khattiyamaṇḍalādisaññitaṃ cakkaṃ samūhaṃ attano vase vattetīti cakkavattī. Dhammaṃ caratīti dhammiko. Dhammato anapetattā dhammo rañjanatthena rājāti dhammarājā. Kopādīti ādi-saddena kāmalobhamānamadādike [V 2.0169] saṅgaṇhāti. Vijitāvīti vijitavā. Kenaci akampiyaṭṭhena janapadatthāvariyappatto. Daḷhabhattibhāvato vā janapado thāvariyaṃ patto etthāti janapadatthāvariyappatto. Cittīkatabhāvādināpi (khu. pā. aṭṭha. 6.3; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.33; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.223; su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.226; mahāni. aṭṭha. 50) cakkassa ratanaṭṭho veditabbo. Esa nayo sesesupi. Ratinimittatāya vā cittīkatādibhāvassa ratijananaṭṭhena ekasaṅgahatāya visuṃ aggahaṇaṃ.

By the four wonderful qualities: beauty, longevity, freedom from illness, and being dear and agreeable to brahmins and others. By the four bases of sympathy: giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. `Rañjanato` (by delighting) means by generating joy. He is a `cakkavattī` (wheel-turner) because he turns (`vatteti`) the wheel (`cakkaṃ`), the wheel-treasure. He is a `cakkavattī` because he himself turns the wheels of prosperity, and with them he turns the multitude of beings. He is a `cakkavattī` because he brings benefit to others and possesses the turning (`vatto, vattanaṃ`) of the wheels of deportment. Or, he is a `cakkavattī` because he turns the unstoppable wheel known as his command. Or, he is a `cakkavattī` because he turns the unstoppable wheel known as his command. He is a `cakkavattī` because he brings the wheel—the assembly of nobles and others—under his control. He is `dhammiko` (righteous) because he practices the Dhamma. He is a `dhammarājā` (righteous king) because he is not devoid of Dhamma, and because the Dhamma itself is a king in the sense that it delights. `Kopādi` (anger, etc.)—the word `ādi` (etc.) includes sensual desire, greed, pride, conceit, and so on. `Vijitāvī` (conqueror) means one who has conquered. He has `janapadatthāvariyappatto` (attained stability in the country) because he is unshakable by anyone. Or, he has `janapadatthāvariyappatto` because the country has attained stability in him due to its firm devotion. The nature of the wheel as a treasure (`ratana`) should also be understood through its being esteemed (`cittīkata`), and so on (Khp-a 6.3; DN-a 2.33; SN-a 3.5.223; Su-a 1.226; Mahāni-a 50). This same method applies to the other treasures as well. Or, since being esteemed and so on is a cause of delight (`rati`), it is not mentioned separately, as it is included under the single meaning of 'producing delight'.

Imehi pana ratanehi rājā cakkavattī yaṃ yamatthaṃ paccanubhoti, taṃ taṃ dassetuṃ “imesu panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ajitaṃ jināti mahesakkhatāsaṃvattaniyakammanissandabhāvato. Vijite yathāsukhaṃ anuvicarati hatthiratanaṃ assaratanañca abhiruhitvā tesaṃ ānubhāvena antopātarāseyeva sakalaṃ pathaviṃ anusaṃyāyitvā rājadhāniyaṃ paccāgamanato. Pariṇāyakaratanena vijitamanurakkhati tena tattha tattha kattabbakiccassa saṃvidhānato. Sesehīti maṇiratanaitthiratanagahapatiratanehi. Tattha maṇiratanena yojanappamāṇe dese andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ālokadassanādinā sukhamanubhavati, itthiratanena atikkantamānusarūpasampattidassanādivasena, gahapatiratanena icchiticchitamaṇikanakarajatādidhanappaṭilābhavasena. Ussāhasattiyogo yena kenaci appaṭihatāṇācakkabhāvasiddhito. Hatthiassaratanādīnaṃ mahānubhāvattā kosasampattiyāpi pabhāvasampattisiddhito “hatthi…pe… yogo”ti vuttaṃ. Koso hi nāma sati ussāhasampattiyaṃ (uggatejassa sukumāraparakkamassa pasannamukhassa sammukhe pāpuṇāti). Pacchimenāti pariṇāyakaratanena. Tañhi sabbarājakiccesu kusalaṃ avirajjhanapayogaṃ. Tenāha “mantasattiyogo”ti. Tividhasattiyogaphalaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hotīti sambandho. Sesehīti sesehi pañcahi ratanehi. Adosakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvenāti adosasaṅkhātena kusalamūlena sahajātādipaccayavasena uppāditakammassa [M 2.0169] ānubhāvena sampajjanti sommatararatanajātikattā. Majjhimāni maṇiitthigahapatiratanāni. Alobha…pe… kammānubhāvena sampajjanti uḷāradhanassa uḷāradhanapaṭilābhakāraṇassa ca pariccāgasampadāhetukattā. Pacchimanti pariṇāyakaratanaṃ. Tañhi amoha…pe… kammānubhāvena sampajjati mahāpaññeneva cakkavattirājakiccassa pariṇetabbattā.

To show what benefits the universal monarch experiences by means of these treasures, it is said, 'among these...' and so forth. He conquers the unconquered due to the powerful result of kamma conducive to great might. In his dominion, he roams at will, mounted on the elephant and horse treasures, and by their power, he travels around the entire earth and returns to his capital city before the morning meal. The advisor treasure protects his conquests by arranging the necessary duties here and there. By the remaining treasures, that is, the gem treasure, the queen treasure, and the householder treasure: with the gem treasure, he dispels darkness over an area of a yojana, experiencing comfort by seeing light and so forth; with the queen treasure, by seeing her surpassing human beauty and so forth; with the householder treasure, by gaining desired wealth such as gems, gold, and silver. His application of the power of energy is due to the accomplishment of his wheel of command being unopposed by anyone. Because of the great power of the elephant and horse treasures, and also because the accomplishment of power is established through the accomplishment of the treasury, it is said, 'the elephant... and so forth... application of power.' For a treasury, when there is accomplishment of energy, is attained in the presence of one of fierce energy, of delicate exertion, of serene countenance. By the last, that is, by the advisor treasure. For it is skilled in all royal duties, its application never failing. Therefore, it is said, 'the application of the power of counsel.' The fruit of the threefold application of power is fulfilled—this is the connection. By the remaining, that is, by the remaining five treasures: they arise through the power of kamma generated by the wholesome root called non-hatred, by way of conditions such as co-nascence, due to their nature as treasures of a most excellent kind. The middle ones are the gem, queen, and householder treasures. They arise through the power of kamma rooted in non-greed... due to the perfection of giving, which is the cause of great wealth and the attainment of great wealth. The last is the advisor treasure. It arises through the power of kamma rooted in non-delusion... since the duties of a universal monarch must be managed by one of great wisdom.

Saraṇato paṭipakkhavidhamanato sūrā. Tenāha “abhīrukajātikā”ti. Asure vijinitvā ṭhitattā vīro, sakko devānamindo, tassa aṅgaṃ devaputto senaṅgabhāvatoti vuttaṃ “vīraṅgarūpāti devaputtasadisakāyā”ti. Sabhāvoti sabhāvabhūto attho. Vīrakāraṇanti vīrabhāvakāraṇaṃ. Vīriyamayasarīrā viyāti saviggahavīriyasadisā saviggahañce vīriyaṃ siyā, taṃsadisāti attho. [V 2.0170] Nanu rañño cakkavattissa paṭisenā nāma natthi, yamassa puttā pamaddeyyuṃ, atha kasmā “parasenapamaddanā”ti vuttanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “sace”tiādi. Tena parasenā hotu vā mā vā, te pana evaṃ mahānubhāvāti dasseti. Dhammenāti katūpacitena attano puññadhammena. Tena hi sañcoditā pathaviyaṃ sabbarājāno paccuggantvā “svāgataṃ te mahārājā”tiādiṃ vatvā attano rajjaṃ rañño cakkavattissa niyyādenti. Tena vuttaṃ “so imaṃ…pe… ajjhāvasatī”ti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana tassa yathāvuttadhammassa cirataraṃ vipaccituṃ paccayabhūtaṃ cakkavattivattasamudāgataṃ payogasampattisaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ dassetuṃ “pāṇo na hantabbotiādinā pañcasīladhammenā”ti vuttaṃ. Evañhi “adaṇḍena asatthenā”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ samatthitaṃ hoti, yasmā rāgādayo pāpadhammā uppajjamānā sattasantānaṃ chādetvā pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhanti, kusalapavattiṃ nivārenti, tasmā te “chadanā, chadā”ti ca vuttā.

From crushing and dispelling opponents, they are brave. Hence it is said, 'born fearless.' Because he stood victorious over the asuras, he is a hero—Sakka, the lord of devas. A deva prince is a component of his army; thus it is said, 'having the form of a hero's limb,' meaning a body like that of a deva prince. 'Natural' means the natural state. 'The cause of heroism' means the reason for being a hero. They are as if bodies made of energy, meaning they are like energy with a body; if energy were to have a body, they would be like that. Now, a universal monarch has no opposing army for his sons to crush. So why is it said, 'crushing foreign armies'? Addressing this objection, it is said, 'if,' and so forth. This shows that whether there are foreign armies or not, they are of such great power. 'By righteousness' means by his own accumulated meritorious principle. Urged on by this, all the kings on earth come forth to meet him, saying, 'Welcome, great king,' and so on, and they relinquish their kingdoms to the universal monarch. Hence it is said, 'he dwells... having conquered this earth.' In the commentary, however, to show the Dhamma that is the condition for the aforementioned meritorious principle to ripen over a long time—the Dhamma known as the perfection of application, which comes from the practice of a universal monarch—it is said, 'by the Dhamma of the five precepts, beginning with "one should not kill living beings."' In this way, the statement 'without rod or sword' is very well supported. Because unwholesome states like greed arise, concealing and enveloping the mental continuum of beings, they obstruct the occurrence of the wholesome; therefore, they are called 'coverings' or 'concealments.'

Vivaṭṭetvā parivattetvā. Pūjārahatā vuttā “arahatīti araha”nti. Tassāti pūjārahatāya. Yasmā sammāsambuddho, tasmā arahanti. Buddhattahetubhūtā vivaṭṭacchadatā vuttā savāsanasabbakilesappahānapubbakattā buddhabhāvasiddhiyā. Arahaṃ vaṭṭābhāvenāti phalena hetuanumānadassanaṃ. Sammāsambuddho chadanābhāvenāti hetunā phalānumānadassanaṃ. Hetudvayaṃ vuttaṃ “vivaṭṭo vicchado cā”ti. Dutiyavesārajjenāti “khīṇāsavassa te paṭijānato”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.150) āgatena vesārajjena. Purimasiddhīti [M 2.0170] purimassa padassa atthasiddhi. Paṭhamenāti “sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.150) āgatena vesārajjena. Dutiyasiddhīti buddhattasiddhi. Tatiyacatutthehīti “ye kho pana te antarāyikā dhammā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.150), “yassa kho pana te atthāyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.150) ca āgatehi tatiyacatutthehi vesārajjehi. Tatiyasiddhīti vivaṭṭacchadanatā siddhi. Yāthāvato antarāyikaniyyānikadhammāpadesena hi satthu vivaṭṭacchadabhāvo loke pākaṭo ahosi. Purimaṃ dhammacakkhunti purimapadaṃ bhagavato dhammacakkhuṃ sādheti kilesārīnaṃ saṃsāracakkassa ca arānaṃ hatabhāvadīpanato. Dutiyaṃ padaṃ buddhacakkhuṃ sādheti sammāsambuddhasseva taṃ sambhavato. Tatiyaṃ padaṃ samantacakkhuṃ sādheti savāsanasabbakilesappahānadīpanato. “Sammāsambuddho”ti hi vatvā “vivaṭṭacchado”ti vacanaṃ buddhabhāvāvahameva sabbakilesappahānaṃ vibhāvetīti. Sūrabhāvanti lakkhaṇavibhāvanena visadañāṇataṃ.

Having unfolded, having turned around. Worthiness of offerings is stated: 'He is worthy, thus an Arahant.' 'Of that' means 'of being worthy of offerings.' Because he is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, therefore he is an Arahant. The state of having unfolded the covering is stated as the cause of Buddhahood, because the attainment of Buddhahood is preceded by the abandonment of all defilements together with their latent tendencies. 'Arahant' is explained by the absence of the round of rebirth; this shows the inference of the cause from the result. 'Perfectly Self-Enlightened One' is explained by the absence of covering; this shows the inference of the result from the cause. Two causes are stated: 'unfolded and uncovered.' By the second ground of confidence—that which comes from the text beginning, 'for you who claim to have destroyed the taints' (MN 1.71), with the confidence thus derived. The accomplishment of the first is the accomplishment of the meaning of the first term. By the first ground of confidence—that which comes from the text beginning, 'for you who claim to be a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One' (MN 1.71), with the confidence thus derived. The accomplishment of the second is the accomplishment of Buddhahood. By the third and fourth grounds of confidence—those which come from the texts beginning, 'those things which you have declared to be obstructive' (MN 1.71), and 'the Dhamma taught by you for a purpose' (MN 1.71), with the third and fourth grounds of confidence thus derived. The accomplishment of the third is the accomplishment of the state of having the covering unfolded. For by teaching the obstructive and liberating states as they really are, the Teacher’s state of having the covering unfolded became manifest in the world. The first term establishes the Dhamma-eye of the Blessed One by showing that the enemies, the defilements, and the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have been destroyed. The second term establishes the Buddha-eye, since that is possible only for a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The third term establishes the all-around eye by showing the abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies. For having said 'Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,' the statement 'having unfolded the covering' reveals that the abandonment of all defilements is what brings about Buddhahood. 'Heroism' means clarity of knowledge through the elucidation of characteristics.

385. Gavesīti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.287) ñāṇena pariyesanaṃ akāsi. Samānayīti ñāṇena saṅkalento samānaṃ ānayi samāhari. Na sakkoti saṃkucite iriyāpathe yebhuyyena [V 2.0171] tesaṃ dubbibhāvanato. Kaṅkhatīti padassa ākaṅkhatīti ayamatthoti āha – “aho vata passeyyanti patthanaṃ uppādetī”ti. Kicchatīti kilamati. “Kaṅkhatī”ti padassa pubbe āsīsanatthataṃ vatvā idāni tassa saṃsayatthattameva vikappantaravasena dassento “kaṅkhāya vā dubbalā vimati vuttā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tīhi dhammehi tippakārehi saṃsayadhammehi. Kālussiyabhāvoti appasannatāya hetubhūto āvilabhāvo. Yasmā bhagavato kosohitaṃ sabbabuddhāveṇikaṃ vatthaguyhaṃ suvisuddhakañcanamaṇḍalasannikāsaṃ attano saṇṭhānasannivesasundaratāya ājāneyyagandhahatthino varaṅgacārubhāvaṃ vikasamānatapaniyāravindasamujjalakesarāvattavilāsaṃ sañjhāpabhānurañjitajalavanantarābhilakkhita-sampuṇṇacandamaṇḍalasobhañca attano siriyā abhibhuyya virājati, yaṃ bāhirabbhantaramalehi anupakkiliṭṭhatāya cirakālaṃ suparicitabrahmacariyādhikāratāya susaṇṭhitasaṇṭhānasampattiyā ca kopīnampi santaṃ akopīnameva, tasmā vuttaṃ “bhagavato hī”tiādi. Pahūtabhāvanti [M 2.0171] puthulabhāvaṃ. Ettheva hi tassa saṃsayo, tanumudusukumāratādīsu panassa guṇesu tassa vicāraṇā eva nāhosi.

385. 'Gavesī' means he searched with knowledge. 'Samānayī' means he, contemplating with knowledge, brought together, collected. He could not, in a constricted posture, mostly because of their difficulty in being discerned. 'Kaṅkhatī' means he desires; the meaning of this word is, as it is said, 'Oh, if only I could see!', he produces the wish. 'Kicchatī' means he labors. Having previously stated the meaning of 'kaṅkhatī' as wishing, now, by way of an alternative explanation showing its meaning as doubt, it is said, 'or by doubt, weak uncertainty is meant,' and so forth. By three phenomena, that is, by three kinds of phenomena of doubt. 'Kālussiyabhāvo' refers to the state of turbidity which is the cause of disquiet. Because the Blessed One’s sheathed private member—unique to all Buddhas—is perfectly pure, like a golden disk; due to the beauty of its natural form and arrangement, it shines forth, surpassing with its own splendor the excellence and grace of a noble, scented elephant, the splendor of a blooming gold-colored lotus with radiant filaments and whorls, and the flawless beauty of the full moon’s orb, distinguished amid water and forest tinged with the light of twilight. Due to its being untainted by external and internal impurities, and due to the accomplishment of its well-established form through long-practiced pure conduct, even when it is covered by a loincloth, it is as if uncovered. Therefore, it is said, 'of the Blessed One,' and so forth. 'Pahūtabhāva' means being large. Here indeed was his doubt, but regarding qualities such as its fineness, softness, and delicacy, there was no consideration of these on his part.

Hirikaraṇokāsanti hiriyitabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Chāyanti paṭibimbaṃ. Kīdisanti āha “iddhiyā”tiādi. Chāyārūpanti bhagavato paṭibimbarūpaṃ. Tañca kho buddhasantānato vinimuttaṃ rūpakamattaṃ bhagavato sarīravaṇṇasaṇṭhānāvayavaṃ iddhimayaṃ bimbakamattaṃ, taṃ pana dassento bhagavā yathā attano buddharūpaṃ na dissati, tathā katvā dasseti. Nīharitvāti pharitvā.

'Hirikaraṇokāsa' means the ground for feeling shame. 'Chāyā' means a reflection. 'What kind?' he said, 'by psychic power,' and so forth. 'Chāyārūpa' refers to the reflected form of the Blessed One. And that is merely a form, a replica, detached from the Buddha's continuum, an image made of psychic power, having the color, shape, and limbs of the Blessed One's body. But when showing that, the Blessed One makes it so that his own Buddha-form is not seen, and then displays it. 'Nīharitvā' means having pervaded.

Kaṇṇasotānaṃ upacitatanutambalomatāya dhotarajatapanāḷikāsadisatā vuttā. Mukhapariyanteti kesante.

The ear-orifices, due to the fine, coppery hair grown within, are described as resembling a polished silver tube. 'Mukhapariyanta' means the hairline at the edge of the face.

Kiriyākaraṇanti kiriyāya kāyikassa vācasikassa paṭipatti. Tatthāti tesu kiccesu. Dhammakathikānaṃ vattaṃ dassetuṃ bījaniggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Na hi aññathā sabbassapi lokassa alaṅkārabhūtaṃ paramukkaṃsagataṃ sikkhāsaṃyamānaṃ buddhānaṃ mukhacandamaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādetabbaṃ hoti.

The performance of action means the practice of action, whether bodily or verbal. Therein, in those duties, a summary of principles is made to show the conduct for the Dhamma-preachers. For otherwise, it would not be fitting to obscure the moon-like face of the Buddhas, which is the ornament of the entire world and which has attained the highest excellence in training and restraint.

Pattharitavitānaolambitagandhadāmakusumadāmake gandhamaṇḍalamāḷe. Pubbabhāgena paricchinditvāti “ettakaṃ velaṃ samāpattiyā vītināmessāmī”ti evaṃ pavattena pubbabhāgena kālaṃ paricchinditvā. Paccayadāyakesu anurodhavasena parisaṃ ussādento vā paggaṇhanto, adāyakesu virodhavasena parisaṃ apasādento vā.

In a fragrant pavilion with a spread canopy and hanging garlands of fragrant flowers. 'Having determined the time beforehand' means having determined the time by means of a prior intention that has arisen, thinking, 'I will spend this much time in meditative attainment.' Either encouraging or uplifting the assembly out of favor towards the donors, or disparaging the assembly out of opposition towards the non-donors.

Yogakkhemaṃ [V 2.0172] antarāyābhāvaṃ. Sabhāvaguṇenevāti yathāvuttaguṇeneva. Bhoto gotamassa guṇaṃ saviggahaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ atisambādhaṃ vitthārena sandhāretuṃ appahontato. Bhavaggaṃ atinīcaṃ uparūpari sandhāretuṃ appahontato.

'Yogakkhema' means security from bondage. 'By its inherent quality' means by the quality already stated. Because the universe, even if greatly compressed, is unable to contain the virtues of the venerable Gotama along with his physical form in full extent. Because the highest existence is too low, and it is unable to contain them even higher and higher.

386. Ṭhānagamanādīsu (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.35) bhūmiyaṃ suṭṭhu samaṃpatiṭṭhitā pādā etassāti suppatiṭṭhitapādo. Taṃ pana bhagavato suppatiṭṭhitapādataṃ byatirekamukhena vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha aggatalanti aggapādatalaṃ. Paṇhīti paṇhitalaṃ. Passanti pādatalassa dvīsu passesu ekekaṃ, ubhayameva vā pariyantaṃ passaṃ. Suvaṇṇapādukatalaṃ viya ujukaṃ nikkhipiyamānaṃ. Ekappahārenevāti ekakkhaṇeyeva. Sakalaṃ pādatalaṃ bhūmiṃ phusati nikkhipane. Ekappahāreneva sakalaṃ pādatalaṃ bhūmito uṭṭhahatīti yojanā.

386. In standing, walking, and so on, 'well-planted feet' means that one's feet are very well and evenly placed on the ground. To distinguish this quality of the Blessed One's well-planted feet by way of contrast, 'just as' and so on was said. There, 'aggatala' means the forepart of the sole. 'Paṇhī' means the heel surface. 'Passa' means one side of each of the two sides of the sole, or the entire edge of both. It is placed straight, like the sole of a golden sandal. 'Ekappahārena' means in a single instant. At placement, the entire sole touches the ground. The explanation is: In a single instant, the entire sole rises from the ground.

Tatrāti [M 2.0172] tāya suppatiṭṭhitapādatāya anupubbaninnāva acchariyabbhutaṃ idaṃ vuccamānaṃ nissandaphalaṃ. Vuttamevatthaṃ satthu tidivagamanena supākaṭaṃ kātuṃ “tathā hī”tiādiṃ vatvā “na hī”tiādinā taṃ samattheti. Tena paṭhamalakkhaṇatopi dutiyalakkhaṇaṃ mahānubhāvanti dasseti. Tathā hi vakkhati “antamaso cakkavattirañño parisaṃ upādāya sabbopi cakkalakkhaṇasseva parivāro”ti. Yugandharapabbatassa tāvatiṃsabhavanassa ca pakatipadanikkhepaṭṭhānupasaṅkamane neva buddhānaṃ, na devatānaṃ ānubhāvo, atha kho buddhānaṃ lakkhaṇānubhāvoti imamatthaṃ nidassitaṃ. Sīlatejena…pe… dasannaṃ pāramīnaṃ ānubhāvenāti idampi lakkhaṇanibbattakammavisesakittanamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbāvantehīti sabbapadesavantehi.

Therein, this marvelous and astonishing result which is being spoken of, the gradual slope, is the consequence of that quality of having well-planted feet. To make the meaning already stated perfectly clear through the Teacher's journey to the threefold heaven, he says, 'Thus indeed,' and so on, and then establishes it by 'Not so,' and so on. Thus he shows that the second characteristic is of greater power than the first characteristic. For he will say, 'Even taking the assembly of a wheel-turning monarch as far as it goes, all are merely the retinue of the wheel-mark.' In the matter of the natural placement of the footing and the approach to Mount Yugandhara and the Tāvatiṃsa realm, it is not the power of the Buddhas, nor of the deities, but rather the power of the marks of the Buddhas—this meaning is indicated. 'By the splendor of virtue...by the power of the ten perfections'—this too should be seen as praise for the distinctive kamma that brings about the marks. 'Sabbāvantehi' means with all regions.

Nābhiparicchinnāti nābhiyaṃ paricchinnā paricchedavasena ṭhitā. Nābhimukhaparikkhepapaṭṭoti pakaticakkassa akkhabbhāhatapariharaṇatthaṃ nābhimukhe ṭhapetabbaparikkhepapaṭṭo. Nemimaṇikāti nemiyaṃ āvaḷibhāvena ṭhitamaṇikālekhā.

'Nābhiparicchinna' means distinctly defined at the navel, remaining in a defined state by way of definition. 'Nābhimukhaparikkhepapaṭṭa' means a covering plate to be placed facing the navel to prevent damage to the natural wheel's axle. 'Nemimaṇika' means jewel-like lines that appear as a band along the rim.

Sambahulavāroti bahuvidhalekhaṅgavibhāvanavāro. Sattīti āvudhasatti. Sirivacchoti sirimukhaṃ. Nandīti dakkhiṇāvaṭṭaṃ. Sovattikoti sovattiaṅko. Vaṭaṃsakoti āveḷaṃ. Vaḍḍhamānakanti purisahāri purisaṅgaṃ. Morahatthakoti morapiñchakalāpo, morapiñcha parisibbito vā bījaniviseso. Vālabījanīti cāmarivālaṃ. Siddhatthādi puṇṇaghaṭapuṇṇapātiyo. “Cakkavāḷo”ti vatvā tassa padhānāvayave dassetuṃ “himavā sineru…pe… sahassānī”ti vuttaṃ.

'Sambahulavāra' means the section elaborating on diverse characteristics. 'Satti' means a weapon-spear. 'Sirivaccha' means a fortunate face. 'Nandī' means a rightward-whirling mark. 'Sovattika' means the sovattika mark. 'Vaṭaṃsaka' means a coil or wreath. 'Vaḍḍhamānaka' means a man-shaped offering stand. 'Morahattha' means a bunch of peacock feathers, or a special kind of fan woven with peacock feathers. 'Vālabījanī' means a yak-tail whisk. 'Siddhattha' and so on refer to white mustard seeds, full pots, and full bowls. Having said 'the universe,' to indicate its principal parts, it is stated: 'Himavā, Sineru... up to thousands.'

Āyatapaṇhīti [V 2.0173] idaṃ aññesaṃ paṇhito dīghataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pana atidīghatanti āha “paripuṇṇapaṇhī”ti. Yathā pana paṇhilakkhaṇaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ nāma hoti, taṃ byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Āraggenāti maṇḍalāya sikhāya. Vaṭṭetvāti yathā suvaṭṭaṃ hoti, evaṃ vaṭṭetvā. Rattakambalageṇḍukasadisāti rattakambalamayageṇḍukasadisā.

'Āyatapaṇhī' (long-heeled) means this was said with reference to the length of the heel compared to others, but not excessively long, hence it is called 'paripuṇṇapaṇhī' (fully-rounded heel). To show how the characteristic of the heel is 'complete', this is shown by way of contrast, saying 'just as' and so on. 'Āraggena' means with a rounded point. 'Vaṭṭetvā' means rounding it, so that it is well-rounded. 'Rattakambalageṇḍukasadisā' means resembling a ball made of red wool.

Makkaṭassevāti vānarassa viya. Dīghabhāvena samataṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Niyyāsatelenāti chadikaniyyāsādiniyyāsasammissena telena.

'Like a monkey' means like a monkey. This is said with reference to its equality in length. 'With resin oil' means with oil mixed with resin from the chadikā tree and other resins.

Talunāti [M 2.0173] sukumārā.

'Talunā' means tender and delicate.

Cammenāti aṅgulantaraveṭhitacammena. Paṭibaddhaaṅgulantaroti ekato sambaddhaaṅgulantaro. Ekappamāṇāti dīghato samānappamāṇā. Yavalakkhaṇanti abbhantarato aṅgulipabbeṭhitaṃ yavalakkhaṇaṃ. Paṭivijjhitvāti taṃtaṃpabbānaṃ samānadesatāya aṅgulīnaṃ pasāritakāle aññamaññaṃ vijjhitāni viya phusitvā tiṭṭhanti.

'Cammena' means with skin wrapped around the spaces between the fingers. 'Paṭibaddhaaṅgulantaro' means the spaces between the fingers are connected together. 'Ekappamāṇā' means equal in length. 'Yavalakkhaṇaṃ' means the barley-grain mark wrapped around the finger joints on the inside. 'Paṭivijjhitvā' means that when the fingers are spread out, they stand touching each other as if pierced through, due to the identical position of their respective joints.

Saṅkhā vuccanti gopphakā, uddhaṃ saṅkhā etesanti ussaṅkhā, pādā. Piṭṭhipādeti piṭṭhipādasamīpe. Sukhena pādā parivattanti pādanāmanādīsu, teneva gacchantānaṃ tesaṃ heṭṭhā pādatalāni dissanti. Tenāti gopphakānaṃ piṭṭhipādato uddhaṃ patiṭṭhitattā. Caturaṅgulamattañhi tāni uddhaṃ ārohitvā patiṭṭhahanti, niguḷhāni ca honti, na aññesaṃ viya paññāyamānāni. Satipi desantarappavattiyaṃ niccaloti dassanatthaṃ nābhiggahaṇaṃ.

'Saṅkhā' refers to the ankles. 'Ussaṅkhā' means 'with prominent ankles,' referring to the feet, because their ankles are raised. 'Piṭṭhipāde' means near the back of the foot. The feet turn comfortably when bending them and so on, and for that reason, as they walk, the soles of their feet are seen below. Thus, because the ankles are fixed above the back of the foot, they rise about four fingerbreadths and are established there; they are also hidden, not appearing like those of others. The mention of the navel is for the purpose of showing that it is motionless even when travelling to another country.

Yasmā eṇīmigassa samantato ekasadisamaṃsā anukkamena uddhaṃ thūlā jaṅghā honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “eṇīmigasadisajaṅghā”ti. Paripuṇṇajaṅghoti samantato maṃsūpacayena paripuṇṇajaṅgho. Tenāha “na ekato”tiādi.

Because the shanks of the eṇī deer are uniformly fleshed on all sides, gradually becoming thicker upwards, it is said, 'with shanks like those of an eṇī deer.' 'Paripuṇṇajaṅgho' means one whose shanks are completely full of flesh all around due to the accumulation of flesh. Hence it is said, 'not from one side only,' and so on.

Etenāti “anonamanto”tiādivacanena, jāṇuphāsubhāvadīpanenāti attho. Avasesajanāti iminā lakkhaṇena rahitā janā. Khujjā vā honti heṭṭhimakāyato uparimakāyassa rassatāya. Vāmanā vā uparimakāyato heṭṭhimakāyassa rassatāya. Etena ṭhapetvā sammāsambuddhaṃ cakkavattinañca itare sattā khujjā vāmanā cāti dasseti.

'By this' means by the saying 'not bending down,' and so on, which means by indicating the excellence of the knees. 'Other people' refers to people lacking this characteristic. They may be hunchbacked, due to the shortness of the upper body compared to the lower body, or dwarfed, due to the shortness of the lower body compared to the upper body. By this, it is shown that, excluding the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha and the Wheel-Turning Monarch, other beings are either hunchbacked or dwarfed.

Ohitanti [V 2.0174] samohitaṃ antogadhaṃ. Tathābhūtaṃ pana taṃ tena channaṃ hotīti āha “paṭicchanna”nti.

'Ohita' means well-placed, gone inside. Being in such a state, it is covered by that; hence it is said 'paṭicchanna' (concealed).

Suvaṇṇavaṇṇoti suvaṇṇavaṇṇavaṇṇoti ayamettha atthoti āha “jātihiṅgulakenā”tiādi. Svāyamattho āvuttiñāyena ca veditabbo. Sarīrapariyāyo idha vaṇṇasaddoti adhippāyena paṭhamavikappaṃ vatvā tathārūpāya pana ruḷhiyā abhāvaṃ manasi katvā vaṇṇadhātupariyāyameva vaṇṇasaddaṃ gahetvā dutiyavikappo vutto.

'Suvaṇṇavaṇṇa' (golden-colored) means having the color of gold; this is the meaning here, as stated: 'like natural vermilion,' and so on. This meaning should also be understood by way of recurrence. Having stated the first alternative with the intention that the word 'vaṇṇa' here is a synonym for 'body,' but bearing in mind the absence of such a conventional usage, the second alternative is stated by taking the word 'vaṇṇa' as a synonym for the color element itself.

Rajoti [M 2.0174] sukhumarajo. Jallanti malīnabhāvāvaho reṇusañcayo. Tenāha “malaṃ vā”ti. Yadi vivaṭṭati, kathaṃ nhānādīti āha “hatthadhovanā”tiādi.

'Rajo' means fine dust. 'Jalla' means an accumulation of dust that brings about a soiled condition. Therefore, he says, 'or impurity.' If it rolls off, why is there bathing and so on? He says, 'for washing the hands,' and so on.

Āvaṭṭapariyosāneti padakkhiṇāvaṭṭāya ante.

'Āvaṭṭapariyosāne' means at the end of a clockwise turning.

Brahmuno sarīraṃ purato vā pacchato vā anonamitvā ujukameva uggatanti āha “brahmā viya ujugatto”ti. Passavaṅkāti dakkhiṇapassena vā vāmapassena vā vaṅkā.

Because the body of Brahmā rises straight up without bending forward or backward, he says, 'straight-bodied like Brahmā.' 'Passavaṅkā' means bent to the right side or the left side.

Hatthapiṭṭhiādivasena satta ussadā etassāti sattussado.

'Sattussado' means one who has seven elevations, in places such as the backs of the hands.

Sīhassa pubbaddhaṃ sīhapubbaddhaṃ, paripuṇṇāvayavatāya sīhapubbaddhaṃ viya sakalo kāyo assāti sīhapubbaddhakāyo. Sīhassevāti sīhassa viya. Saṇṭhantīti saṇṭhahanti. Nānācittenāti vividhacittena. Puññacittenāti pāramitāpuññacittarūpena. Cittitoti sañjātacittabhāvo.

The front part of a lion is 'sīhapubbaddhaṃ.' 'Sīhapubbaddhakāyo' means one whose entire body is like the front part of a lion, due to having complete limbs. 'Sīhasseva' means like a lion's. 'Saṇṭhanti' means they stand firm. 'Nānācittena' means with a varied mind. 'Puññacittena' means in the form of a mind of the merit of the perfections. 'Cittito' means the state of a mind having arisen.

Dvinnaṃ koṭṭānamantaranti dvinnaṃ piṭṭhibāhānaṃ vemajjhaṃ, piṭṭhimajjhassa uparibhāgo. Citaṃ paripuṇṇanti aninnabhāvena citaṃ, dvīhi koṭṭehi samatalatāya paripuṇṇaṃ. Uggammāti uggantvā.

'Between two protuberances' means the space between the two shoulder blades, the upper part of the middle of the back. 'Citaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ' (filled and complete) means filled so as to be without any depression, complete by being level with the two shoulder blades. 'Uggamma' means having risen.

Nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo viya parimaṇḍalo nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo ekassa parimaṇḍalasaddassa lopaṃ katvā. Na hi sabbo nigrodho maṇḍalo. Tenāha “samakkhandhasākho nigrodho”ti. Parimaṇḍalasaddasannidhānena vā parimaṇḍalova nigrodho gayhatīti parimaṇḍalasaddassa lopena vināpi [V 2.0175] ayamattho labbhatīti āha “nigrodho viya parimaṇḍalo”ti. Yāvatakvassāti o-kārassa va-kārādesaṃ katvā vuttaṃ.

'Nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo' means round like a banyan tree, by eliding one instance of the word 'parimaṇḍala.' For not every banyan is round. Hence it is said, 'a banyan with even trunk and branches.' Alternatively, because of the proximity of the word 'parimaṇḍala,' a round banyan itself is understood, so this meaning is obtained even without eliding the word 'parimaṇḍala.' Hence it is said, 'round like a banyan.' 'Yāvatakvassā' is stated by substituting the letter 'va' for the letter 'o'.

Samavaṭṭitakkhandhoti samaṃ suvaṭṭitakkhandho. Koñcā viya dīghagalā, bakā viya vaṅkagalā, varāhā viya puthulagalāti yojanā. Suvaṇṇāliṅgasadisoti suvaṇṇamayakhuddakamudiṅgasadiso.

'Samavaṭṭitakkhandho' means having an evenly and well-rounded neck. Like curlews with long necks, like cranes with crooked necks, like boars with thick necks—this is the application. 'Resembling a golden āliṅga' means like a small golden drum.

Rasaggasaggīti madhurādibhedaṃ rasaṃ gasanti anto pavesantīti rasaggasā, rasaggasānaṃ aggā rasaggasaggā, tā etassa santīti rasaggasaggī. Tenāti ojāya apharaṇena, hīnadhātukattā te bahvābādhā honti.

'Rasaggasaggī' means that because they consume, that is, cause sweet and other kinds of flavors to enter within, they are called 'rasaggasā' (taste-conveyors); the best of these 'rasaggasā' are 'rasaggasaggā'; and because these are present in him, he is called 'rasaggasaggī'. 'Tena' (by that) means by the non-diffusion of nutritive essence; due to being of inferior elements, they are subject to many diseases.

“Hanū”ti [M 2.0175] sannissayadantādhārassa samaññā, taṃ bhagavato sīhahanusadisaṃ, tasmā bhagavā sīhahanu. Tattha yasmā buddhānaṃ rūpakāyassa dhammakāyassa ca upamā nāma nihīnupamāva, natthi samānupamā, kuto adhikūpamā, tasmā ayampi nihīnupamāti dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tibhāgavasena maṇḍalatāya dvādasiyaṃ pakkhassa candasadisāni.

'Hanu' is the designation for the support of the teeth upon which they depend. That jaw of the Blessed One resembles a lion’s jaw; therefore, the Blessed One is called Sīhahanu (Lion-jawed). In this regard, since any simile for the physical body and the Dhamma body of the Buddhas is only an inferior simile—there is no equal simile, let alone a superior one—therefore, to indicate that this too is an inferior simile, it is said, ‘Therein,’ and so forth. Due to its roundness in three parts, it is like the moon on the twelfth day of the fortnight.

Dantānaṃ uccanīcatā abbhantarabāhirapassavasenapi veditabbā, na aggavaseneva. Tenāha “ayapaṭṭachinnasaṅkhapaṭalaṃ viyā”ti. Ayapaṭṭanti ca kakacaṃ adhippetaṃ. Visamāti visamasaṇṭhānā.

The highness and lowness of the teeth should be understood with respect to their inner and outer sides, not just with respect to their tips. Therefore, it is said, ‘like a layer of conch shell cut by an iron plate.’ And by ‘ayapaṭṭa’ (iron plate), a saw is intended. ‘Visamā’ means of uneven shape.

Vicchinditvā vicchinditvā pavattasaratāya chinnassarāpi. Anekākāratāya bhinnassarāpi. Kākassa viya amanuññasaratāya kākassarāpi. Apalibuddhattāti anupaddutavatthukattā. Vatthunti ca akkharuppattiṭṭhānamāha. Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatoti ettha aṭṭhaṅgāni parato āgamissanti. Mañjughosoti madhurassaro.

They also have a broken voice, due to the voice proceeding with repeated interruptions. They also have a split voice, due to its manifold nature. They also have a crow-like voice, due to the voice being disagreeable like a crow's. ‘Apalibuddhattā’ means because of having an unhindered basis. And ‘vatthu’ (basis) refers to the place where syllables arise. ‘Endowed with eight factors’—here the eight factors will be mentioned later. ‘Mañjughosa’ means sweet-voiced.

Karavīkasaddo yesaṃ sattānaṃ sotapathaṃ upagacchati, te attano sarasampattiyā pakatiṃ jahāpetvā avase karonto attano vase vatteti, evaṃ madhuroti dassento “tatrida”ntiādimāha. Taṃ pītinti taṃ buddhagataṃ pītiṃ. Teneva nīhārena punappunaṃ pavattantaṃ avijahitvā vikkhambhitakilesā therānaṃ santike laddhadhammassavanasappāyā upanissayasampattiyā paripakkañāṇatāya [V 2.0176] “sattahi…pe… patiṭṭhāsī”ti. Sattasatamattena orodhajanena saddhiṃ padasāva therānaṃ santikaṃ upagatattā “sattahi jaṅghāsatehi saddhi”nti vuttaṃ.

When the sound of the karavīka bird reaches the ears of beings, by the richness of its sound it makes them abandon their natural state, and bringing them under its sway, it makes them act according to its will. To show how sweet it is, he said, ‘Therein,’ and so forth. ‘That joy’ means that joy directed towards the Buddha. Not abandoning that joy, which arose again and again in the same way, and because his defilements were suppressed, because of the suitability for hearing the Dhamma obtained in the presence of the elders, because of the accomplishment of supporting conditions, and because of the maturity of his wisdom, it is said, ‘by seven… he was established.’ Because he approached the elders on foot, accompanied by about seven hundred members of the harem, it is said, ‘with seven hundred shanks.’

Abhinīlanettoti adhikanīlanetto. Adhikanīlatā ca sātisayaṃ nīlabhāvena veditabbā, na nette nīlavaṇṇasseva adhikabhāvatoti āha “na sakalanīlanettovā”tiādi. Pītalohitavaṇṇā setamaṇḍalagatarājivasena, nīlasetakāḷavaṇṇā pana taṃtaṃmaṇḍalavaseneva veditabbā.

‘Abhinīlanetto’ means having intensely blue eyes. And the intense blueness should be understood as an excellent degree of blueness, not merely as an excess of blue color in the eye itself. Therefore, it is said, ‘not with the whole eye blue,’ and so forth. The yellow and red colors are to be understood as being present by way of streaks located in the white circle, while the blue, white, and black colors are to be understood as being present by way of their respective circles.

Cakkhubhaṇḍanti akkhidalanti keci, akkhidalapattanti aññe. Akkhidalehi pana saddhiṃ akkhibimbanti veditabbaṃ. Evañhi viniggatagambhīrajotanāpi yuttā hoti.

Some say ‘cakkhubhaṇḍa’ means ‘akkhidala’ (eyelid); others say ‘akkhidalapatta’ (eyelash). However, it should be understood as ‘akkhibimba’ (the orb of the eye) together with the ‘akkhidala’ (eyelids). For in this way, the profound radiance that has issued forth is also fitting.

Uṇṇāsaddo [M 2.0176] loke avisesato lomapariyāyo, idha pana lomavisesavācakoti āha “uṇṇaloma”nti. Nalāṭamajjhajātāti nalāṭamajjhagatā. Odātatāya upamā, na mudutāya. Rajatapubbuḷakāti rajatamayatārakā.

The word ‘uṇṇā’ in the world generally refers to hair, but here it denotes a particular kind of hair. Therefore, it is said, ‘uṇṇaloma.’ ‘Nalāṭamajjhajātā’ means situated in the middle of the forehead. The comparison is to whiteness, not softness. ‘Rajatapubbuḷakā’ means a silver star.

Dve atthavase paṭicca vuttanti yasmā buddhā cakkavattino ca paripuṇṇanalāṭatāya paripuṇṇasīsabimbatāya ca “uṇhīsasīsā”ti vuccanti, tasmā te dve atthavase paṭicca “uṇhīsasīso”ti idaṃ vuttaṃ. Idāni taṃ atthadvayaṃ bhagavati suppatiṭṭhitanti dassetuṃ “tathāgatassahī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Saṇhatamatāya suvaṇṇavaṇṇatāya ca rañño baddhauṇhīsapaṭṭo viya virocati. Kappasīsāti dvidhābhūtasīsā. Phalasīsāti phalasadisasīsā. Aṭṭhisīsāti maṃsassa abhāvato tacopariyonaddhaaṭṭhimattasīsā. Tumbasīsāti lābusadisasīsā. Pabbhārasīsāti piṭṭhibhāgena olambamānasīsā. Purimanayenāti paripuṇṇanalāṭatāpakkhena. Uṇhīsaveṭhitasīso viyāti uṇhīsapaṭṭena veṭhitasīsapadeso viya. Uṇhīsaṃ viyāti chekena sippinā viracitauṇhīsamaṇḍalaṃ viya.

It is said with reference to two meanings: because Buddhas and wheel-turning monarchs are called ‘uṇhīsasīsā’ due to their perfectly rounded foreheads and fully formed cranial protuberances, therefore, this term ‘uṇhīsasīso’ is stated with reference to those two meanings. Now, to show that these two meanings are firmly established in the Blessed One, it is said, ‘tathāgatassa hi,’ and so forth. It shines like a turban-band bound around a king’s head due to its extreme smoothness and golden hue. ‘Kappasīsā’ means a head divided into two parts. ‘Phalasīsā’ means a head resembling a fruit. ‘Aṭṭhisīsā’ means a head covered only by skin over bone, due to the absence of flesh. ‘Tumbasīsā’ means a head like a gourd. ‘Pabbhārasīsā’ means a head that hangs down at the back. ‘Purimanayena’ means by the aspect of a perfectly rounded forehead. ‘Uṇhīsaveṭhitasīso viya’ means like the part of the head wrapped with a turban-band. ‘Uṇhīsaṃ viya’ means like a circular turban crafted by a skilled artisan.

Kammanti yena yena kammena yaṃ yaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ nibbattaṃ, taṃ taṃ kammaṃ. Kammasarikkhakanti tassa tassa lakkhaṇassa taṃkammānurūpatā. Lakkhaṇanti tassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇassa aviparītasabhāvo. Lakkhaṇānisaṃsanti taṃ lakkhaṇapaṭilābhena laddhabbaguṇo. Imāni kammādīnīti imāni anantaraṃ vuttāni kammakammasarikkhakādīni dassetvā taṃ sarūpato vibhāvetvā kathetabbāni saṃvaṇṇakena.

‘Kamma’ means that kamma by which each mark is produced. ‘Kammasarikkhaka’ means the conformity of that mark to that kamma. ‘Lakkhaṇa’ means the unfailing nature of that great man’s mark. ‘Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa’ means the quality to be attained by the acquisition of that mark. These terms—‘kamma,’ ‘kammasarikkhaka,’ and so on—should be explained and elaborated in detail by the commentator after showing their nature and distinguishing them appropriately.

Ratanavicittasuvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ [V 2.0177] tasmiṃ kāle manussaloke natthīti vuttaṃ “devanagare”ti. Sabbaso supupphitasālarukkho asādhāraṇasobho manussūpacāre na labbhatīti āha “selantaramhī”ti. Kiriyācāranti kāyikavācasikakiriyāpavattiṃ.

It is said, ‘in the city of the gods,’ because at that time there was no golden archway adorned with jewels in the human world. It is said, ‘in a mountain cleft,’ because a fully blossomed sāla tree of extraordinary beauty is not found in the world of humans. ‘Kiriyācāra’ means the proceeding of bodily and verbal actions.

387. Satatapāṭihāriyanti satataṃ carimabhave sabbakālaṃ lakkhaṇanibbattakakammānubhāvahetukaṃ buddhāveṇikaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ. Buddhānaṃ atidūre pādaṃ nikkhipitukāmānampi nātidūre eva nikkhipanaṃ hotīti “na atidūre ṭhapessāmīti [M 2.0177] uddharatī”ti vuttaṃ. Pakatisañcaraṇavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ, tādisena pādena anekayojane ṭhapessāmīti uddharaṇampi hotiyeva. Atidūraṃ hītiādi pamāṇātikkame dosadassanaṃ. Evaṃ satīti evaṃ dakkhiṇapādavāmapādānaṃ yathādhippetapatiṭṭhitaṭṭhāne sati. Padavicchedoti padavāravicchedo. Yādisaṃ pasārento vāmapādassa uddharaṇaṃ patiṭṭhānañca, dakkhiṇapādassa tādisameva, iti nesaṃ uddharaṇapatiṭṭhānānaṃ samānato aññamaññabhāvena anūnānadhikatāya vuttaṃ “dakkhiṇapādakiccaṃ vāmapādena niyamitaṃ, vāmapādakiccaṃ dakkhiṇapādena niyamita”nti.

387. ‘Satatapāṭihāriya’ means the constant miracle, unique to Buddhas, which is caused by the power of kamma producing the distinctive marks, throughout his final existence and at all times. Even when Buddhas wish to place their feet at an extreme distance, the placing occurs not too far away. Thus it is said, ‘He lifts it with the intention, “I will not place it too far away.”’ This is stated in terms of natural movement, yet with such a foot, the lifting with the intention to place it many yojanas away also occurs. ‘Too far,’ and so forth, indicates the fault in exceeding the proper measure. ‘Thus being’ means that when the right foot and left foot are in their intended positions, that is the case. ‘Padaviccheda’ means the division of the succession of steps. Just as the extending, lifting, and placing of the left foot is done in a certain manner, so too is that of the right foot. Thus, because their lifting and placing are equal, without deficiency or excess relative to each other, it is stated: ‘The function of the right foot is regulated by the left foot, and the function of the left foot is regulated by the right foot.’

Divāti upakaṭṭhāya velāya. Vihārabhattatthāyāti vihāre yathāvuddhaṃ gahetabbabhattatthāya. Pacchato āgacchantoti pakatigamanena pacchato āgacchanto. Okāsaṃ na labhatīti padanikkhepaṭṭhānaṃ na labhati. Ūrupariyāyo idha satthi-saddoti āha “na ūruṃ unnāmetī”ti. Daṇḍaṅkusaṃ vuccati dīghadaṇḍo aṅkuso, tena rukkhasākhaṃ chindato purisassa yathā pacchābhāgena pādānaṃ osakkanaṃ hoti, evaṃ bhagavato pādā na osakkantīti āha “rukkhasākhāchedana…pe… osakkāpetī”ti. Obaddhānābaddhaṭṭhānehi pādaṃ koṭṭento viyāti ābaddhaṭṭhānena anābaddhaṭṭhānena ca pādakhaṇḍaṃ koṭṭetvā thaddhaṃ karonto viya. Na ito cito ca cāletīti aparāparaṃ na cāleti. Ussaṅkhapādatāya sukheneva pādānaṃ parivattanato nābhito paṭṭhāya uparimakāyo na iñjatīti heṭṭhimakāyova iñjati. Tenāha “uparima…pe… niccalo hotī”ti. Na jānāti aniñjanato. Kāyabalenāti gamanapayogasaṅkhātena kāyagatena visesabalena. Javagamanahetubhūtena vā kāyabalena. Tenāha “bāhā khipanto”tiādi. Javena gacchanto hi bāhā khipati, sarīrato sedā muccanti. Nāgāpalokitavasenāti nāgassa apalokanamiva sakalakāyeneva parivattetvā apalokanavasena.

‘Diva’ means at the approaching time of midday. ‘For the meal at the monastery’ means for the meal to be taken at the monastery according to seniority. ‘Coming from behind’ means coming from behind in the normal way of walking. ‘He does not get an opportunity’ means he does not get a place to put his foot down. The word ‘satthi’ here is a synonym for ‘ūru’ (thigh); thus it says: ‘He does not raise his thigh.’ A ‘daṇḍaṅkusa’ is called a long stick with a hook; just as when a man cuts a tree branch with that, his feet might slip backwards, in the same way the Blessed One’s feet do not slip. Thus it is said, ‘As when cutting a tree branch…he does not cause them to slip.’ ‘As if striking the foot between bound and unbound places’ means as if making the foot firm by striking the foot-part between a bound place and an unbound place. ‘He does not move it from here to there’ means he does not move it back and forth. Because of his arched feet, and because his feet turn smoothly, his upper body does not shake from the navel upwards; only the lower body shakes. Therefore, it is said, ‘The upper…remains still.’ He is unaware of shaking because he does not shake. ‘By bodily strength’ means by the special physical strength consisting of the effort of walking, or by the bodily strength that is the cause of rapid walking. Therefore it is said, ‘Swinging his arms,’ and so on. For someone walking rapidly swings his arms, and sweat is released from the body. ‘In the manner of an elephant’s glance’ means in the manner of glancing by turning the whole body, like an elephant does.

Anāvaraṇañāṇassāti anāvaraṇañāṇabalena dassanassa. Anāvaraṇavāro pana kāye patiṭṭhitarūpadassanampi anāvaraṇamevāti dassanatthaṃ vutto. Indakhīlato paṭṭhāyāti nagaradvāre indakhīlato [V 2.0178] paṭṭhāya. Pakatiiriyāpathenevāti [M 2.0178] onamanādiṃ akatvā ujukagamanādinā eva. Yadi evaṃ koṭṭhakadvāragehappavese kathanti āha “daliddamanussāna”ntiādi. Parivattentenāti nipajjanatthaṃ kāyaṃ parivattentena.

‘Anāvaraṇañāṇassa’ means of the seeing through the power of unobstructed knowledge. However, the section on unobstructedness is stated to show that even seeing forms established in the body is unobstructed. ‘Starting from the Indakhīla pillar’ means starting from the Indakhīla pillar at the city gate. ‘By the natural posture’ means simply by walking straight and so on, without bending or the like. If so, how is the entrance through a gatehouse or into a house explained? He says, ‘Of poor people,’ and so forth. ‘By turning’ means by turning the body for the purpose of lying down.

Hatthehi gahetvāti ubhohi hatthehi ubhosu kaṭippadesesu pariggahetvā. Patati nisīdanaṭṭhāne nipajjanavasena patati. Orimaṃ aṅgaṃ nissāya nisinnoti pallaṅkamābhujitvā ukkuṭikanisajjāya uparimakāyaṃ heṭṭhimakāye patiṭṭhapentoyeva bhārīkaraṇavasena orimaṅgaṃ nissāya nisinno. Ghaṃsantoti ānisadadesena āsanaṭṭhānaṃ ghaṃsanto. Pārimaṅganti satthibhāgasammaddaṃ ānisadapadesaṃ. Tathevāti ghaṃsanto eva. Olambakaṃ dhārento viyāti olambakasuttaṃ otārento viya. Tena ujukameva nisīdanamāha. Sarīrassa garukabhāvahetūnaṃ dūrato samupāyitabhāvena sallahukabhāvato tūlapicuṃ ṭhapento viya.

‘Hatthehi gahetvā’ means grasping with both hands at both hip regions. ‘Patati’ means he falls, falling in the manner of lying down in the place for sitting. ‘Orimaṃ aṅgaṃ nissāya nisinno’ means sitting supported by the lower part of the body; having bent the legs crosswise or in the squatting posture, establishing the upper part of the body upon the lower part, he is sitting supported by the lower limbs in the manner of making them heavy. ‘Ghaṃsanto’ means rubbing the sitting place with the part of the robe one sits on. ‘Pārimaṅgaṃ’ means the part of the robe one sits on, which is pressed by the thigh. ‘Tatheva’ means just rubbing. ‘Olambakaṃ dhārento viya’ means as if holding a plumb-line, as if lowering a plumb-line thread. By this, he indicates sitting straight. Because the causes of the body’s heaviness have been kept at a distance, due to its lightness, it is as if placing a tuft of cotton.

Appesakkhānaṃ mahānubhāvagehappavese siyā chambhitattaṃ, cittakkhobho, darathavasena nānappakārakappanaṃ, bhayavasena taṇhāvasena paritassanaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato natthīti dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “na chambhatī”tiādi (ma. ni. 2.387) vuttanti āha “na chambhatī”tiādi.

For those of little power, upon entering the house of a great being, there might be stupefaction, mental agitation, various kinds of speculation due to anxiety, and trembling due to fear and craving. To show that none of this exists in the Blessed One, it is said in the Pāli, ‘He is not stupefied,’ etc. (MN 2.387). Thus he says, ‘He is not stupefied,’ etc.

Udakaṃ dīyati etenāti udakadānaṃ, bhiṅkārādi udakabhājanaṃ. Baddhaṃ katvāti hatthagatamattikaṃ viya attano vase avattantaṃ katvā. Parivattetvāti kujjitvā. Vichaḍḍayamāno udakassa vikkhipanavasena chaḍḍayamāno.

An ‘udakadāna’ is so called because water is given with it; it is a water vessel, such as a `bhiṅkāra`. ‘Baddhaṃ katvā’ means having made it not proceed according to one’s own will, like clay that has come into one’s hand. ‘Parivattetvā’ means having become angry. ‘Vichaḍḍayamāno’ means discarding by way of scattering the water.

Tathā na gaṇhāti, byañjanamattāya eva gaṇhanto. Bhattaṃ vā amanāpanti ānetvā yojanā. Byañjanena ālopaatināmanaṃ, ālopena byañjanaatināmananti imesu pana dvīsu paṭhamameva asāruppatāya aniṭṭhaṃ vajjetabbanti pāḷiyaṃ paṭikkhittanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbatthevāti sabbasmiṃ āharitabbavatthusmiṃ supaṇītabhāvena raso pākaṭo hoti ñāṇena pariññātattā. Rasagedho pana natthi setughātattā.

He does not grasp it thus, grasping only the mere seasoning. The phrase 'or the food is disagreeable' is a connection made by bringing it forward. Overpowering the morsel with the seasoning, and overpowering the seasoning with the morsel—among these two, the first, being unsuitable and undesirable, should be avoided; it should be understood that this is rejected in the Pāli text. 'In every case' means in every object to be consumed, the taste becomes evident through its excellence, because it is fully understood with knowledge. But there is no greed for taste, because the causeway has been destroyed.

Assāti “neva davāyā”tiādipadassa. Vuttametanti “visuddhimagge vinicchayo āgato”ti sabbāsavasutte (ma. ni. 1.23) saṃvaṇṇayantena vuttametaṃ, tasmā [M 2.0179] na ettha taṃ vattabbanti adhippāyo, tasmā yo tasmiṃ tasmiṃ vinicchaye visesavādo icchitabbo. So paramatthamañjūsāya visuddhimaggavaṇṇanāya vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Pattassa gahaṇaṭṭhānanti hatthena pattassa [V 2.0179] gahaṇapadesaṃ. Vinivattitvāti patte sabbaṃ āmisagataṃ saddhiṃ bhattena vinivattitvā gacchati. Pamāṇātikkantanti kelāyanavasena atikkantapamāṇaṃ ārakkhaṃ ṭhapeti. Cīvarabhogantaranti cīvarapaṭalantaraṃ. Udarena akkamitvāti udareneva sannirumbhitvā.

The word 'assa' refers to the phrase beginning with 'neva davāya'. 'This has been stated' means this has been stated by the one commenting on the Sabbāsava Sutta (MN 2), saying, 'the analysis has come in the Visuddhimagga.' Therefore, the intention is that it should not be stated here; thus, the specific explanation in each analysis should be sought. That should be understood according to the method stated in the Paramatthamañjūsā, the commentary on the Visuddhimagga. 'The place for taking the bowl' means the spot on the bowl taken by the hand. 'Having turned back' means having withdrawn all the food together with the cooked rice in the bowl, he goes. 'Exceeding the measure' means he sets a guard beyond the limit by way of playfulness. 'Between the folds of the robe' means between the layers of the robe. 'Having pressed with the belly' means having completely pressed down with the belly itself.

Appattakālaṃ abhimukhaṃ nāmeti upanāmetīti atināmeti, pattakālaṃ atikkāmento nāmeti apanetīti atināmeti. Ubhayampi ekajjhaṃ gahetvā pāḷiyaṃ “na ca anumodanassa kālamatināmetī”ti vuttanti dassento “yo hī”tiādimāha.

When the time has not yet arrived, he brings it forward, he presents it; this is 'to extend beyond'. When the time has arrived, he passes it by, he removes it; this is 'to extend beyond'. Taking both together, to show what is stated in the Pāli, 'And he does not extend beyond the time for the giving of thanks,' he said, 'For one who...' and so on.

Vegagamanena paṭisaṃmuñcitvā dhāvitvā gacchati. Accukkaṭṭhanti ativiya uddhaṃ katvā kaḍḍhitapārutaṃ. Tenāha “yo hi yāva hanukaṭṭhito…pe… hotī”ti. Accokkaṭṭhanti ativiya heṭṭhā katvā kaḍḍhitapārutaṃ. Tenāha “yāva gopphakā otāretvā”ti. Ubhato ukkhipitvāti dakkhiṇato vāmatoti ubhosu passesu uttarāsaṅgaṃ ukkhipitvā. Thananti dakkhiṇathanaṃ.

Having wrapped himself with a swift movement, he goes running. 'Pulled up too high' means a robe pulled and worn excessively high. Therefore, it is said, 'For one who... up to the jawbone... is.' 'Pulled down too low' means a robe pulled and worn excessively low. Therefore, it is said, 'having lowered it down to the ankles.' 'Having lifted it on both sides' means having lifted the upper robe on both sides, that is, on the right and on the left. 'Breast' means the right breast.

Vissaṭṭhoti vimutto. Tenāha “vissaṭṭhattāyeva cesa viññeyyo”ti. Yasmā amuttavādino vacanaṃ avissaṭṭhatāya na siniyhati, na evaṃ muttavādinoti āha “siniddho”ti. Viññeyyoti suparibyattatāya akkharato ca byañjanato ca viññātuṃ sakkuṇeyyo. Tenāha “pākaṭo”ti. Viññāpaniyoti vijānitabbo. Byañjanavaseneva cettha viññeyyatā veditabbā ghosassa adhippetattā. Madhuroti piyo pemanīyo apalibuddho. Savanamarahati, savanassa sotassa hitoti vā savanīyo. Sampiṇḍitoti sahito. Bhagavato hi saddo uppattiṭṭhānakatāsañcitattā sahitākāreneva āpāthamāgacchati, na ayosalākāya pahaṭakaṃsathālaṃ viya vippakiṇṇo. Tenāha “avisārī”ti. Gambhīroti yathā gambhīravatthuparicchindanena ñāṇassa gambhīrasamaññā, evaṃ gambhīraṭṭhānasambhavato saddassa gambhīrasamaññāti āha “gambhīroti gambhīrasamuṭṭhito”ti[M 2.0180]. Ninnādavāti savisesaṃ ninnādavā. Svāyaṃ viseso gambhīrabhāvasiddhoti āha “gambhīrattāyeva cesa ninnādī”ti. Evamettha cattāri aṅgāni caturaṅganipphādīni veditabbāni.
