Akāraṇā mā nassīti buddhānubhāvena viya sarassa parisapariyantatā vuttā, dhammatāvaseneva pana sā veditabbā tassa mūlakāraṇassa tathā avaṭṭhitattā.

‘Released’ means liberated. Therefore, it is said, ‘And this is to be understood as due to its being released.’ Because the speech of one who is not liberated is not smooth due to not being released, it is not so for one who is liberated; thus, it is said to be ‘smooth.’ ‘Intelligible’ means it can be understood in its letters and syllables due to being well-articulated. Therefore, it is said to be ‘clear.’ ‘Instructive’ means it should be known. Here, intelligibility should be understood by way of the syllables, as the sound is what is intended. ‘Sweet’ means pleasing, endearing, and unobstructed. ‘Audible’ means it is worthy of hearing, or it is beneficial to the hearing, to the ear. ‘Cohesive’ means unified. For the Blessed One’s voice, being concentrated at its place of origin, comes into range in a unified manner, not scattered like a bronze bowl struck by an iron rod. Therefore, it is said to be ‘non-dispersed.’ ‘Deep’: just as wisdom is designated as deep because it delimits profound subjects, so the voice is designated as deep because it arises from a profound place; thus, it is said, ‘“Deep” means arisen from depth.’ ‘Resonant’ means possessing a special resonance. This special quality is established by its state of depth; thus, it is said, ‘And it is resonant precisely because of its depth.’ In this way, four qualities should be understood here as producing four qualities. The phrase ‘May it not perish without reason’ is stated as if due to the Buddha’s power, regarding the voice reaching the limits of the assembly. But this should be understood as being due to the natural order of things, because its root cause is established in that way.

Paccosakkitvāti paṭinivattitvā. Samussitakañcanapabbataṃ viya upari indanīlaratanavitatasikhaṃ [V 2.0180] vijjullatābhūsitaṃ. Mahāpathavīādayo satthuguṇapaṭibhāgatāya nidassanaṃ, kevalaṃ mahantatāmattaṃ upādāya nidassitā.

‘Having drawn back’ means having turned back. Like a lofty golden mountain, its peak on high spread with sapphire gems and adorned with lightning-creepers. The great earth and so on are examples on account of their resemblance to the Teacher's virtues, shown merely by taking into account their great size.

390. Appaṭisaṃviditoti anārocito. Āgamanavasena cettha paṭisaṃveditanti āha “aviññātaāgamano”ti. Uggatabhāvanti kulabhogavijjādīhi uḷārabhāvaṃ. Anuddayasampannāti kāruṇikā.

390. ‘Unannounced’ means not informed of. Here, it is with respect to his arrival that he is unannounced; thus he says, ‘of unknown arrival.’ ‘Eminence’ means a noble state on account of family, wealth, knowledge, and so on. ‘Endowed with compassion’ means compassionate ones.

391. Sahasāva okāsakaraṇena uccakulīnatā dīpitā hotīti āha “vegena uṭṭhāya dvidhā bhijjitvā”tiādi.

391. By suddenly making space, high birth is demonstrated; thus he says, ‘rising up with speed, splitting in two,’ and so on.

Nārisamānanāmanti itthiatthajotakanāmaṃ. Tenāha “itthiliṅga”nti. Avhātabbāti kathetabbā.

‘A name common to women’ means a name that indicates the meaning of ‘woman.’ Therefore, he says, ‘the feminine gender.’ ‘To be addressed’ means to be spoken to.

394. Ekanīhāreneva aṭṭha pañhe byākaronto. “Pubbenivāsaṃ…pe… pavuccatī”ti iminā pubbenivāsassa viditakāraṇaṃ vuttanti āha “tassa pubbenivāso pākaṭo”ti. Dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ kathitaṃ tassa paribhaṇḍañāṇabhāvato yathākammūpagañāṇassa. “Jātikkhayaṃ patto, abhiññā vosito”ti ca vuttattā munīti asekkhamuni idhādhippetoti āha “arahattañāṇamoneyyena samannāgato”ti.

394. Answering eight questions with a single method. By the phrase, 'Past lives... is said,' the reason for past lives being known is stated; thus he says, 'his past lives are manifest.' The knowledge of the divine eye is mentioned because it is an accessory knowledge to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma. And because it is said, 'He has attained the destruction of birth, he has reached the culmination of direct knowledge,' the sage meant here is the adept-sage; thus he says, 'endowed with the sagehood of the knowledge of arahantship.'

Kilesarāgehi kilesavivaṇṇatāhi. Jātikkhayappattattā “atho jātikkhayaṃ patto”ti vuttattā. Abhijānitvāti abhivisiṭṭhatāya aggamaggapaññāya ñatvā. Idāni paṭisambhidāyaṃ āgatanayena pariññāpahānabhāvanāsacchikiriyāsamāpattīnaṃ pāragamanena pāragūti ayamettha atthoti dassetuṃ “pāragūti vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Abhiññeyyadhammānaṃ jānanavasena abhiññāpāragū. Tādisoti yādiso “pāragū sabbadhammāna”nti padadvayena [M 2.0181] vutto, tādiso. Chahi ākārehīti pajānanādīhi yathāvuttehi chahi ākārehi.

By the passions that are defilements, by the discolorations that are defilements. Because he has reached the destruction of birth, as it is said, 'Moreover, he has reached the destruction of birth.' 'Having directly known' means having known with the superior wisdom of the highest path. Now, to show that the meaning here is 'one who has gone beyond' by having gone to the far shore of full understanding, abandoning, development, realization, and attainment, according to the method that comes in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is said, 'Or, one who has gone beyond,' and so on. He is one who has gone beyond in direct knowledge by way of knowing things to be directly known. 'Such a one' means such as is described by the two words, 'one who has gone beyond all things.' 'By six modes' means by the six modes beginning with full understanding, as stated.

Kāmañcettha dve eva pucchāgāthā dve ca vissajjanāgāthā, pucchāpaṭipāṭiyā pana asaṅkarato ca vissajjanaṃ pavattati, taṃ niddhāretuṃ kiṃ panātiādi vuttaṃ. Vedehi gatattāti vedehi maggañāṇehi pāraṅgatattā. Pubbenivāsantiādīhi vijjānaṃ atthitāya bodhitattā. Pāpadhammānanti chattiṃsapāpadhammānaṃ sotthānaṃ maggaṃ pāpanena nissesato sodhitattā.

Although there are here only two stanzas of questions and two of answers, the answering proceeds according to the sequence of the questions and without confusion; to determine this, 'What then?' and so on was said. 'Because of having gone by the knowledges' means because of having gone to the far shore by the knowledges, that is, the path-knowledges. 'Past lives,' and so on: because he is awakened through the existence of the true knowledges. 'Of evil qualities' means because he is completely purified by attaining the path to safety from the thirty-six evil qualities.

395. Dhammo [V 2.0181] nāma arahattamaggo kusaladhammesu ukkaṃsapāramippattiyā ukkaṭṭhaniddesena. Tassa anurūpadhammabhāvato anudhammo nāma heṭṭhimamaggaphaladhammā. Yo satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ na paṭipajjati, so tathāgataṃ dhammādhikaraṇaṃ viheṭheti nāma. Yo pana paṭipajjanto ca dandhābhiññatāya kammaṭṭhānasodhanatthaṃ antarantarā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā anekavāraṃ kathāpeti, so ettāvatā dhammādhikaraṇaṃ tathāgataṃ viheṭhetīti na vattabbo. Na hi bhagavato dhammadesanāya parissamo atthi, ayañca attho mahāsudassanasuttādīhi (dī. ni. 2.241 ādayo) dīpetabbo, tasmā – “saccadhammassa anudhamma”nti vattabbe vuttameva byatirekamukhena vibhāvetuṃ “na ca maṃ dhammādhikaraṇaṃ vihesesī”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha parinibbāyīti parakāle cettha parinibbānampi saṅgayhati, taṃ pana imasmiṃ gahitameva hotīti āha “desanāya arahatteneva kūṭaṃ gahita”nti.

395. The term 'Dhamma,' by way of an eminent designation, refers to the path to arahantship, due to its attainment of the highest excellence among wholesome states. Because they are dhammas corresponding to that, the lower path-and-fruition dhammas are called 'anudhamma.' Whoever, having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, does not practice as instructed, is said to trouble the Tathāgata in matters of the Dhamma. But one who, while practicing, is slow to attain higher knowledge and from time to time repeatedly approaches the Blessed One to have the meditation subject clarified, cannot on that account be said to trouble the Tathāgata in matters of the Dhamma. For the Blessed One experiences no fatigue in teaching the Dhamma, and this point should be illustrated by the Mahāsudassana Sutta and others. Therefore, it should be understood that when 'the anudhamma of the true Dhamma' should be said, the phrase 'nor would he trouble me in matters of the Dhamma' was said to elucidate this very thing by way of contrast. Herein, 'one who attains parinibbāna' also includes the final parinibbāna at a later time, but since that is already included in this, it is said, 'in the teaching, the culmination is taken as arahantship itself'.

Brahmāyusuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The clarification of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Brahmāyu Sutta is concluded.

2. Selasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Sela Sutta

396. Keṇiyoti [V 2.0182] tassa nāmaṃ, pubbe keṇiyā jīvikākappanatoti vadanti. Jaṭiloti jaṭādharo. Brāhmaṇajātikattā koṭisāratāya ca brāhmaṇamahāsālo. Payojetvā nissayo hutvā vasati, rattiṃ kāmasampattiṃ anubhavatīti vā yojanā. Susaṅkhatanti sappimadhusakkarādīhi ceva maricasiṅgīverādīhi ca suṭṭhu abhisaṅkhataṃ.

396. 'Keṇiya' is his name; they say it is because he formerly made his living as a ferryman. 'Jaṭila' means a wearer of matted hair. Because he was of brahmin birth and possessed immense wealth, he was a brahmin of great wealth. The explanation is either: having become a patron, he lives there; or, he enjoys the fulfillment of sensual pleasures at night. 'Well-prepared' means thoroughly prepared with ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, and with pepper, ginger, and so forth.

Paṭikkhepapasannatāyāti [M 2.0182] ahovatāyaṃ appiccho, yo nimantiyamānopi na sādiyatīti upanimantiyamānassa paṭikkhepe titthiyānaṃ pasannabhāvatoti. Taṃ kathaṃ? Viruddhametanti “akāraṇameta”nti paṭikkhipati.

'Because of being pleased by the rejection' means: because the heretics were pleased at his refusal when he was repeatedly invited, thinking, 'Oh, this one is of few desires, who does not accept even when invited.' How so? He rejects it, saying, 'This is contradictory,' that is, 'This is without reason.'

398. Kappasahassehipi…pe… ahosīti idaṃ nānussavasiddhaṃ anumānaggahaṇaṃ sandhāyāha. Padeti uttarapadalopena niddesoti āha “padappamāṇe”ti. Pajjati nikkhipati etthāti vā padaṃ pakatiyā pādanikkhipaṭṭhānaṃ, tasmiṃ pade. Kīḷāpasutatādinā pamādaṃ āpajjati. Bodhisattacārikanti dukkaracariyaṃ sandhāya vadati.

398. 'Even for a thousand eons... he was not'—this is said referring to an inference, not to something established by oral tradition. Regarding `pade`, it is said 'of foot-measure' because it is a designation with the elision of the latter word. Or, `padaṃ` is where one places (`pajjati`) or sets down the foot; it is the natural place for setting down the foot; in that place. He falls into heedlessness through being devoted to play and so forth. 'The Bodhisatta's conduct' is said referring to the practice of austerities.

399. Paripuṇṇatāyāti anūnatāya. Ahīnaṅgatāyāti avekallabhāvato. Rocatīti ruci, dehappabhā, sobhaṇā ruci etassāti suruci. Ārohasampatti kāyassa pamāṇayuttauccatā. Pariṇāhasampatti kisathūlabhāvavajjitapariṇāhatā. Saṇṭhānasampatti avayavānaṃ susaṇṭhitatā. Cārudassanoti piyadassano tenāha “sucirampī”tiādi. Suvaṇṇasadisavaṇṇoti jātihiṅgulakena madditvā silānighaṃseneva parikammaṃ katvā ṭhapitaghanasuvaṇṇarūpavaṇṇo. Mahāpurisabhāvaṃ byañjenti pakāsentīti byañjanāni, mahāpurisalakkhaṇānīti āha “paṭhamaṃ vuttabyañjanānevā”ti.

399. 'Completeness' means without deficiency. 'Not having deficient limbs' means the state of not being incomplete. 'It shines' (`rocati`), hence 'radiance' (`ruci`), the body's radiance; 'he has a beautiful radiance,' hence `suruci`. 'Perfection of stature' is the body's proper height. 'Perfection of girth' is a girth that is devoid of being thin or stout. 'Perfection of form' is the well-formedness of the limbs. 'Of charming appearance' means pleasing to see; therefore it is said, 'even for a long time...' and so on. 'Having a complexion like gold' means having a complexion like the color of a solid gold image that has been prepared by being smeared with pure cinnabar and polished as if by rubbing on a stone. 'They indicate, they make manifest the state of a great man,' thus they are 'indications' (`byañjanāni`), that is, the marks of a great man; therefore it is said, 'the very secondary marks mentioned before'.

Pubbe vuttanti “surucī”ti pubbe vuttaṃ, “ādiccova virocasī”ti puna vuttaṃ. “Cārudassano suvaṇṇavaṇṇosī”ti pubbe vuttaṃ, “kalyāṇadassano bhikkhu kañcanābhattaco”ti puna vuttanti imamatthaṃ sandhāyāha “uttaragāthāyapi eseva nayo”ti. Sātisayaṃ uttamavaṇṇe vaṇṇetvā uttamavaṇṇinoti padena santaṃ pakāsetīti āha “uttamavaṇṇasampannassā”ti. Uttamasārathīti [V 2.0183] seṭṭhapurisasārathi. Tattha tattha jambuvanasaṇḍamaṇḍitatāya jambudīpo “jambusaṇḍo”ti vuccati. Issariyanti cakkavattissariyaṃ.

As to 'previously stated': 'of beautiful radiance' was stated before, and 'you shine like the sun' was stated again. 'Of charming appearance, of golden complexion' was stated before, and 'the monk of lovely appearance, with skin like gold' was stated again. Referring to this meaning, he says, 'this same method applies also in the subsequent verse.' Having described the supreme complexion with exaggeration, with the word `uttamavaṇṇino` he reveals what is real; therefore he says 'of one endowed with supreme complexion.' 'Supreme charioteer' means charioteer of noble men. Because it is adorned here and there with groves of rose-apple trees, Jambudīpa is called 'Jambusaṇḍa.' 'Sovereignty' means the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch.

Jātikhattiyāti jātimanto khattiyā. Rājābhirājāti ettha abhi-saddo pūjatthoti āha “rājūnaṃ pūjanīyo”ti.

'Khattiyas by birth' means khattiyas of high birth. Regarding 'king over kings,' here the prefix 'abhi' is in the sense of veneration; therefore it is said, 'venerable to kings.'

Appamāṇāti aparimāṇā lokadhātuyo. “Yāvatā pana ākaṅkheyyā”ti (a. ni. 3.81) hi vuttaṃ. Dhammarājā anuttaroti ettha vuttaanuttarabhāvaṃ “yāvatā [M 2.0183] hī”tiādinā pākaṭataraṃ katvā dhammarājabhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “svāha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Dhammenāti paṭivedhadhammena. Tenāha “anuttarenevā”ti. Anuttarenāti visiṭṭhena uttamena. Imasmiṃ pakkhe dhammenāti paṭipattidhammenātipi saṅgayhati. Pariyattidhammenāti desanādhammena āṇācakkaṃ pavattemīti yojanā. Desanāñāṇapaṭivedhañāṇavibhāgaṃ dhammacakkameva vā. Appaṭivattiyanti paṭivattituṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ.

'Immeasurable' means limitless world-systems. For it is said, 'As far as one might wish' (AN 3.81). Regarding 'the Dhamma King, the unsurpassed,' here 'I...' and so on is said to elucidate the state of being the Dhamma King, after making clearer the state of being unsurpassed mentioned here by means of 'as far as...' and so on. 'By the Dhamma' means by the Dhamma of penetration. Therefore he says, 'by the unsurpassed indeed.' 'By the unsurpassed' means by the distinguished, the supreme. In this alternative, 'by the Dhamma' also includes 'by the Dhamma of practice.' 'By the Dhamma of learning' means by the Dhamma of teaching; the construction is: 'I set the wheel of authority in motion.' Or, the Wheel of Dhamma itself, which is divided into the knowledge of teaching and the knowledge of penetration. 'Irreversible' means that which cannot be turned back.

Tathāgatena jātoti tathāgatena hetunā ariyāya jātiyā jāto. Hetuatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Anujātoti ca vutte anu-saddassa vasena tathāgatanti ca upayogavacanameva hoti, so ca anu-saddo hetuatthajotakoti āha “tathāgataṃ hetuṃ anujāto”ti. Avaññātabbabhāvena jātoti avajāto duppaṭipannattā. Tenāha “dussīlo”ti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ kokālikaṃ ārabbha “purisantakali avajāto”ti. Putto nāma na hoti tassa ovādānusāsaniyaṃ aṭṭhitattā. Evamāhāti “anujāto tathāgata”nti evamāha.

'Born by the Tathāgata' means born with the noble birth through the Tathāgata as cause. The instrumental case is in the sense of cause. And when 'born after' is said, by means of the prefix 'anu-,' 'Tathāgata' is just a term of connection, and that prefix 'anu-' illuminates the sense of cause; therefore he says, 'born after, with the Tathāgata as cause.' 'Born lowly' means born in a way to be despised, because of wrong practice. Therefore he says, 'immoral.' For thus it was said concerning Kokālika: 'a base man, born lowly.' He is not a 'son' because of not being established in his advice and instruction. Thus he says: 'born after the Tathāgata'.

Vijjāti maggavijjā. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesena vimuttīti phalavimutti. Nanu ca maggo bhāvetabbena gahitoti? Saccaṃ gahito, sabbe ca pana satta dhammā abhiññeyyāti vijjāya abhiññeyyabhāvo vutto. Iminā vā nayena sabbesampi abhiññeyyabhāvo vutto evāti veditabbo. Phalena vinā hetubhāvasseva abhāvato hetuvacanena phalasiddhi, nirodhassa ca sampāpanena maggassa hetubhāvo. Dukkhassa nibbattanena taṇhāya samudayabhāvoti imamatthaṃ saṅgahitameva atthato āpannattā. Yuttahetunāti yuttiyuttena hetunā buddhabhāvaṃ sādheti saccavinimuttassa bujjhitabbassa abhāvato saccasambodhaneneva ca tassa anavasesato buddhattā. Atthavacanañcetaṃ, payogavacanāni pana – brāhmaṇa, ahaṃ sammāsambuddho sabbathā aviparītadhammadesano, sammāsambuddhattā sabbattha aviparītamācikkhati yathāhaṃ sabbamaggadesakoti[V 2.0184]. Kiṃ pana bhagavā sayameva attano sammāsambuddhabhāvaṃ ārocetīti? Mahākaruṇāya aññesaṃ mahāvisayato. Tattha “ekomhi sammāsambuddho, sabbābhibhū sabbavidūhamasmī”tiādīni (mahāva. 11; ma. ni. 1.285; 2.341; kathā. 405) suttapadāni idameva ca suttapadaṃ etassa atthassa sādhakaṃ.

'Knowledge' is the knowledge of the path. 'Liberation,' by way of an eminent designation, is the liberation of the fruit. But is not the path taken as something to be developed? True, it is so taken; however, all seven dhammas are to be directly known, so the state of being directly knowable is stated for knowledge. Or, it should be understood that by this method the state of being directly knowable is stated for all of them. The fruit is established by the mention of the cause, because without the fruit the state of being a cause does not exist; and the path's state as a cause is by its bringing about cessation. Craving's state as an origin is by its producing suffering—this meaning is included because it is implied by the sense. 'With a suitable cause' means he establishes Buddhahood through a cause connected with reason, because for one liberated from the truths there is nothing left to be awakened to, and because he is a Buddha through having completely awakened to the truths without remainder. This is a term of meaning, but the terms of application are: 'Brahmin, I am a Perfectly Awakened One, a teacher of the unerring Dhamma in every way; being perfectly awakened, I declare what is unerring in every respect, as I am the teacher of the entire path.' But does the Blessed One himself declare his own state of perfect awakening? He does so out of great compassion, because of the vast range of other beings. Herein, sutta passages such as, 'I am the one Perfectly Awakened One, the all-conqueror, the all-knower,' and this very sutta passage, serve to establish this meaning.

Sallakantanoti [M 2.0184] sallānaṃ samucchinnattā. Rogassāti kilesarogassa. Tasmāti apunapavattipādanena tikicchanato. Brahmaṃ vā seṭṭhaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ pattoti brahmabhūto. Evaṃ āgatāyāti iminā –

"Extractor of the dart" means because the darts are completely uprooted. "Of disease" refers to the disease of defilements. "Therefore" means because he cures by preventing recurrence. "He has become Brahma" means he has attained the supreme, perfect awakening. "Thus come" means by this:

“Kāmā te paṭhamā senā, dutiyā arati vuccati;

Tatiyā khuppipāsā te, catutthī taṇhā pavuccati.

“Sensual pleasures are your first army, the second is called discontent; your third is hunger and thirst, the fourth is called craving.

Thinamiddhaṃ tepañcamaṃ thinamiddhaṃ te, chaṭṭhā bhīrū pavuccati;

Sattamī vicikicchā te, makkho thambho te aṭṭhamo.

Your fifth is sloth and torpor, the sixth is called fear; your seventh is doubt, your eighth is disdain and obstinacy.

Lābho siloko sakkāro, micchāladdho ca yo yaso;

Yo cattānaṃ samukkaṃse, pare ca avajānati;

Esā namuci te senā, kaṇhassābhippahārinī”ti. (su. ni. 438-441);

Gain, renown, honor, and whatever fame is wrongly obtained; and whoever exalts himself and disparages others—this, Namuci, is your army, the Dark One's assaulting host.”

Evaṃ vuttaṃ navavidhaṃ senaṃ saṅgayhati. Vase vattetvāti samucchindanena anuppādatāpādanena vase vattetvā. Kutoci abhayo nibbhayo.

Thus, the ninefold army spoken of is comprised. 'Having brought under control' means having brought them under his power by utterly eradicating them and preventing their future arising. He is fearless, free from terror from any quarter.

Sayameva daṭṭhabbanti yena yena adhigato, tena tena parasaddhāya gantabbaṃ hitvā asammohato paccavekkhaṇāñāṇeneva sāmaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “paccakkha”nti. Pasaṭṭhā diṭṭhi sandiṭṭhi. Yathā rathena jayatīti rathiko, evaṃ idaṃ maggabrahmacariyaṃ sandiṭṭhiyā jayatīti sandiṭṭhikaṃ. Atha vā diṭṭhanti dassanaṃ vuccati, diṭṭhameva sandiṭṭhaṃ, sandassananti attho. Sandiṭṭhaṃ arahatīti sandiṭṭhiko yathā vatthayugaṃ arahatīti vatthayugiko. Sandiṭṭhikaṃ phaladānaṃ sandhāya nāssa kāloti akālaṃ, akālameva akālikaṃ, na kālantaraṃ khepetvā phalaṃ deti, attano pana pavattisamanantarameva phalaṃ detīti attho. Atha vā attano phalappadāne pakaṭṭho kālo patto assāti kāliko, lokiyo kusaladhammo, idaṃ pana samanantaraphalattā na kālikaṃ.

'It should be seen by oneself' means: in whatever way it has been attained, it should be seen by oneself with the knowledge of reviewing, having abandoned proceeding by faith in others, and without delusion. Therefore it is said, 'directly visible.' An excellent view is a direct view (sandiṭṭhi). Just as one who conquers with a chariot is called a charioteer, so this holy life of the path conquers through direct vision; hence it is called 'directly visible' (sandiṭṭhikaṃ). Alternatively, 'seen' (diṭṭhaṃ) is called vision; what is itself seen is a direct view (sandiṭṭhaṃ), meaning it is a clear seeing. One is 'a possessor of direct vision' (sandiṭṭhiko) because one is worthy of what is directly seen, just as one is 'a possessor of a pair of garments' because one is worthy of a pair of garments. With reference to the giving of its fruit being directly visible, there is no time for it, hence it is 'timeless' (akālaṃ). 'Timeless' itself is 'immediate' (akālikaṃ); it does not give its fruit after a lapse of time, but gives its fruit immediately after its own occurrence. This is the meaning. Alternatively, a worldly wholesome state is 'timely' (kālika) because its proper time for giving its own fruit has arrived; but this, because its fruit is immediate, is not 'timely'.

400. “Mahāyaññaṃ [V 2.0185] pavattayī”tiādīsu kevalaṃ dānadhammādīsu yaññapariyāyasambhavato “brāhmaṇānaṃ yaññābhāvato”ti vuttaṃ. Brāhmaṇā hi “aggimukhā devā”ti aggijuhanapubbakaṃ yaññaṃ vidahanti. Tenāha “aggijuhanappadhānāti attho”ti “bhūrbhuva? Sva?” Iti sāvittī pubbakattā mukhaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ[M 2.0185]. “Mukhamiva mukha”ntiādīsu viya idhāpi padhānapariyāyo mukhasaddoti dassento “manussānaṃ seṭṭhato rājā ‘mukha’nti vutto”ti āha. Ādhāratoti ogāhantīnaṃ nadīnaṃ ādhārabhāvato paṭisaraṇato gantabbaṭṭhānabhāvato. Saññāṇatoti candayogavasena ajja asukanakkhattanti paññāyanato. Ālokakaraṇatoti nakkhattāni abhibhavitvā ālokakaraṇato. Sommabhāvatoti sītahimavāsītavātūpakkharabhāvato. Tapantānanti dīpasikhā aggijālā asanivicakkanti evamādīnaṃ vijjalantānaṃ. Āyamukhaṃ aggadakkhiṇeyyabhāvena.

400. In phrases such as 'He performed the great sacrifice,' the statement 'because brahmins have no sacrifice' is made because the term 'sacrifice' can refer simply to practices such as giving. For brahmins, indeed, perform sacrifices preceded by fire-offerings, believing 'the gods are fire-mouthed.' Therefore it is said, 'the meaning is "that which has fire-offering as primary".' Because the Sāvitrī verse begins with 'Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ,' the beginning (mukhaṃ) is the leader. Showing that here too, as in phrases like 'the mouth is like the mouth,' the word 'mouth' is a term for 'primary,' he said, 'the king is called "mouth" among men because he is the foremost.' 'Because it is a support' means because it is the support for rivers that flow into it, a refuge, and a destination. 'Because it is a sign' means because it is known through conjunction with the moon, as in 'today is such-and-such a constellation.' 'Because it makes light' means because it gives light, overpowering the stars. 'Because of its gentle nature' means because of its coolness, its dwelling in snow, and its nature as a cool wind and shade. 'Of those that burn' refers to blazing things such as lamp flames, fire-brands, and lightning flashes. 'Source of income' (Āyamukhaṃ) means because of being the foremost recipient of offerings.

Dibbacakkhu dhammacakkhu paññācakkhu buddhacakkhu samantacakkhūti imehi pañcahi cakkhūhi. Te saraṇassāti te saraṇassa ca, te saraṇabhāvamūlakattā itaradvayassa ca, yathāvutta te-padena vuttatthato parassa cāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “te tuyhaṃ, itarassa ca saraṇassa aho ānubhāvo”ti. Āvuttivasena vā te saraṇassāti ettha attho vibhāvetabbo – tuyhaṃ saraṇabhūtassa ca itarasaraṇassa ca ānubhāvoti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

By these five eyes: the divine eye, the Dhamma eye, the wisdom eye, the Buddha eye, and the all-seeing eye. 'Of the refuge' (Te saraṇassa) means: of your refuge, and of the other two because they are rooted in the state of being a refuge, and of another from the meaning stated by the aforesaid word 'te'. This is the meaning. This is what is said: 'Oh, the power of your refuge and of the other refuge!' Alternatively, the meaning of 'of the refuge' should be explained here by way of repetition: 'the power of you who have become a refuge, and of the other refuge.' The rest is easily understood.

Selasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The elucidation of the hidden meanings in the commentary on the Sela Sutta is concluded.

3. Assalāyanasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Assalāyana Sutta

401. Aññamaññavisiṭṭhattā [V 2.0186] visadisaṃ rajjaṃ virajjaṃ, virajjato āgatā, tattha jātāti vā verajjakā, evaṃ jātā kho pana te, yasmā vatthābharaṇādivibhāgena nānappakārā honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “nānāverajjakāna”nti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana verajjasseva vasena nānappakāratā vuttā. Yaññupāsanādināti yaññānubhavanamantajjhenadakkhiṇapariyesanādinā. Catuvaṇṇasādhāraṇanti khattiyādīnaṃ catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ saṃsārasuddhipāpatassanaṃ. Nhānasuddhiyāti titthasamuddakhātesu mantajappanapubbakaṃ sāyaṃtatiyaudakorohanādinhānasuddhiyā. Bhāvanāsuddhiyāti paramajotibhūtāya purisabhāvanāsaṅkhātāya suddhiyā. Vāpitasiroti oropitakeso. Tameva hi siro vāpitanti vuccati.

401. Because they are distinct from one another, a dissimilar kingdom is a 'virajja'; those who have come from a 'virajja', or were born there, are 'verajjakā'. Since they, being thus born, are of various kinds due to distinctions in clothing, ornaments, and so on, it is therefore said 'of various verajjakas'. In the commentary, however, the diversity is explained by way of the 'verajja' itself. 'Through sacrifices, worship, and so on' means through the performance of sacrifices, the recitation of mantras, study, the seeking of offerings, and so on. 'Common to the four castes' means the purification from saṃsāra and the expiation of evil, which is common to the four castes—khattiyas and so on. 'Purification by bathing' means purification by bathing in sacred fords, seas, or excavated pools, preceded by the muttering of mantras, such as descending into the water for the third time in the evening. 'Purification by meditation' means purification through what is termed the development of the person, which is a supreme light. 'Shaven-headed' means one whose hair has been cut off. Indeed, such a head is called 'shaven'.

Sabhāvavādīti [M 2.0186] yathābhūtavādī. Pabbajantāti brāhmaṇapabbajjaṃ upagacchantā, tasmā brāhmaṇānaṃ pabbajjāvidhānaṃ sikkhantena bhotā “brāhmaṇāva sujjhanti, no abrāhmaṇā”ti ayaṃ vidhi sahetuko saupādāno sakkaccaṃ uggahito, tasmā tuyhaṃ parājayo natthi…pe… evamāhaṃsu.

'A speaker of the nature of things' means one who speaks according to reality. 'Going forth' means those undertaking the going forth of a brahmin. Therefore, since you, venerable sir, while learning the rule of the brahmins' going forth, have carefully and attentively learned this rule—'Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins'—with its reason and its basis, there is no defeat for you… thus they said.

402. Laddhibhindanatthanti “brāhmaṇāva brahmuno puttā orasā mukhato jātā brahmajā”ti evaṃ pavattaladdhiyā viniveṭhanatthaṃ. Puttapaṭilābhatthāyāti “evaṃ mayaṃ pettikaṃ iṇadhāraṃ sodheyyāmā”ti laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā puttapaṭilābhatthāya. Ayañhettha adhammikānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ ajjhāsayo. Nesanti brāhmaṇānaṃ. Saccavacanaṃ siyāti “brahmuno puttā”tiādivacanaṃ saccaṃ yadi siyā brāhmaṇīnaṃ…pe… bhaveyya, na cetaṃ atthi. Mahābrahmuno mukhato jātoti vādacchedakavādo mukhatojātacchekavādo. Assalāyanoviññū jātiko “nirakkhepaṃ samaṇena gotamena vutta”nti jānantopi sahagatānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ cittānurakkhaṇatthaṃ “kiñcāpi bhavaṃ gotamo”tiādimāha.

402. 'For the purpose of breaking the belief' means for the purpose of dispelling the prevailing belief that 'brahmins alone are Brahmā's sons, his own offspring, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā.' 'For the sake of obtaining a son' means for the purpose of gaining a son, while holding to the belief, 'Thus we may clear our paternal debt.' This, here, is the intention of the unrighteous brahmins. 'Of them' (Nesaṃ) means 'of the brahmins.' 'If it were a true statement' means: if the statement 'sons of Brahmā,' and so on, were true, then for brahmin women... it would be so, but this is not the case. 'Born from the mouth of Mahābrahmā' is a debate-ending statement, a statement that cuts off the 'born from the mouth' argument. Although Assalāyana, being intelligent by birth, knew that 'the ascetic Gotama has spoken irrefutably,' yet in order to protect the minds of the brahmins who accompanied him, he said, 'Although the venerable Gotama...' and so on.

403. Idāni brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇoti vādaṃ bhindituṃ “sutaṃ te yonakakambojesū”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Yadi brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, sabbattha brāhmaṇova seṭṭho bhaveyya, atha kasmā yonakakambojādijanapadesu brāhmaṇānaṃ seṭṭhabhāvo natthi? Evañhi tattha vaṇṇā[V 2.0187], tasmā “brāhmaṇova seṭṭho”ti laddhimattametaṃ. Tesu hi janapadesu janā ekajjhaṃ sannipatitvā sammantayitvā katikaṃ akaṃsu, dāsaṃ sāmikaṃ katvā itare sabbe taṃ pūjetvā tassa vase vattanti, yo tesaṃ ayyo hoti itare sabbe tassa dāsā honti, te katipayasaṃvaccharātikkamena tassa kiñci dosaṃ disvā taṃ tato ṭhānato apanetvā aññaṃ ṭhapenti, iti so ayyo hutvā dāso hoti, itaro dāso hutvā ayyo hoti, evaṃ tāva keci “ayyo hutvā dāso hoti, dāso hutvā ayyo hotī”ti ettha atthaṃ vadanti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana purimavaseneva tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “brāhmaṇo sabhariyo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vayappatte putte asatīti idaṃ vakkhamānassa dārakassa dāyajjasāmikabhāvassa tāva dassanaṃ. Mātito suddhoti ettha [M 2.0187] yo mātito suddhattā ayyo, pitito asuddhattā dāso hoti, so eva pitito asuddhattā dāso hutvā mātito ayyo hotīti jātiṃ sambhedeti. Sova sabbena sabbaṃ hotīti na sakkā vattunti apare. Ko thāmoti mahante lokasannivāse anamatagge atīte kāle itthīnaṃ vā citte anavaṭṭhite dāsā dāsā eva honti, ayyā ayyā eva hontīti ettha ko ekantiko sahetuko avassayo, tassa sādhako siddhanto, kiṃ nidassananti attho.

403. Now, to refute the claim that 'brahmins alone are the highest caste,' the passage beginning 'Have you heard of the Yonas and Kambojas?' is introduced. If brahmins alone were the highest caste, then brahmins alone would be supreme everywhere. But why is there no supremacy of brahmins in the lands of the Yonas, Kambojas, and so on? For such are the castes there; therefore, the belief that 'brahmins alone are supreme' is merely a belief. In those lands, people gathered together, deliberated, and made an agreement, making a slave a master, while all the others, honoring him, lived subject to him. Whoever was the lord among them, all the others became his slaves. After some years had passed, seeing some fault in him, they removed him from that position and appointed another. Thus, one who was a lord became a slave, and another who was a slave became a lord. So indeed, some explain the meaning of 'a lord becomes a slave, a slave becomes a lord' in this way. In the commentary, however, 'a brahmin with his wife,' and so on, is stated to show that meaning according to the earlier account. 'When there is no son who has reached maturity'—this is a demonstration of the boy's claim to ownership of the inheritance, which will be spoken of. 'Pure from the mother's side' means that here, he who, being pure from the mother's side, is a lord, but, being impure from the father's side, is a slave, he himself, being impure from the father's side, becomes a slave, but, being pure from the mother's side, becomes a lord—thus he mixes the lineage. 'He becomes everything in every way'—this cannot be said, say others. 'What power?' means what is the conclusive, reasoned, certain basis, what is the supporting principle, what is the demonstration, for the statement that in the great assembly of the world, in the past that is without beginning, or when women's minds are unstable, slaves remain slaves, and lords remain lords? This is the meaning.

404. Sukkacchedakavādo nāmāti “brāhmaṇova sukko vaṇṇo”ti evaṃ vutto sukkacchedakavāro nāma.

404. The discourse is called 'The Cutting of the White' because it is said, 'The brahmin caste alone is white.' This is the section named 'The Cutting of the White'.

408. Sabbasmiṃ aggikiccaṃ karonteti etena yathā yato kutoci nissayato uppanno aggiupādānasampanno aggikiccaṃ karoti, evaṃ yasmiṃ kasmiñci dāsakule jāto upanissayasampanno sammāpaṭipajjamāno saṃsārato sujjhati evāti dasseti.

408. 'Performing all fire duties' means that just as fire, arising from any source whatsoever and endowed with fuel, performs fire duties, so too does one born in any slave family whatsoever, endowed with proper support and practicing rightly, become purified from the cycle of existence. This is what is shown.

409. Pādasikavaṇṇoti antarāḷavaṇṇo. Etesanti khattiyakumārena brāhmaṇakaññāya uppannaputto, brāhmaṇakumārena khattiyakaññāya uppannaputtoti etesaṃ dvinnaṃ māṇavakānaṃ. Matakabhatteti mate uddissa katabhatte. Thālipāketi katamaṅgalabhatte.

409. 'Foot-caste' means intermediate caste. 'Etesaṃ' refers to these two youths, namely, a son born of a khattiya prince and a brahmin maiden, and a son born of a brahmin youth and a khattiya maiden. 'Meal for the dead' means a meal made in dedication to the dead. 'Thālipāka' means a meal prepared for an auspicious ceremony.

410. Tumheti jātisāmaññato māṇavaṃ brāhmaṇehi saddhiṃ ekajjhaṃ saṅgaṇhanto āha. Ko nu khoti avaṃsiro isivādo, tesaṃ brāhmaṇīsīnaṃ asāmatthiyadassanena jātiyā appamāṇataṃ vibhāvetuṃ gāmadārakavesena upagacchi. Tena vuttaṃ “gāmaṇḍalarūpo viyā”ti. Koṇḍadamakoti adantadamako.

410. 'You' refers to his addressing the young brahmin, including him together with the other brahmins due to their common birth. 'Who now' is the speech of the sage Avaṃsira, who, seeing the incompetence of those brahmin seers, approached in the guise of a village boy to reveal that birth is not the measure. Therefore it is said, 'like the form of a village boy'. 'Koṇḍadamaka' means a tamer of the untamed.

411. Janetīti [V 2.0188] janikā janetti. Janako pitāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Gandhabbapañhanti gandhabbassa mātukucchiyaṃ uppajjanakasattassa khattiyabhāvādipucchaṃ. Dabbigahaṇasippampi ekā vijjā veditabbā. Tattha kira kusalo yaṃ kiñci āhārūpagapaṇṇapupphaphalabījaṃ antamaso elālukampi gahetvā bhesajjehi yojetvā pacanto sappimadhuphāṇitehi samānarasaṃ katvā sampādetuṃ [M 2.0188] sakkoti, puṇṇopi tādiso, tena ñātaṃ tvaṃ dabbigahaṇasippamattampi na jānāsīti sambandho. Saddhoti kammaphalasaddhāya saddho, pothujjanikeneva ratanattayapasādena pasanno. Tenevāha – “upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ…pe… saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

411. "She who gives birth" is the mother, the birth-giver. "The father" also follows the same principle. The question about the gandhabba pertains to the questioning of the khattiya nature, etc., of the being that is to arise in the mother's womb. The skill of handling a ladle should also be understood as a single science. There, it is said that one skilled in it can take any item suitable as food—leaf, flower, fruit, seed, even a cucumber—and combining it with medicines and cooking it, can make it of equal taste with ghee, honey, and molasses. Puṇṇa was such a one. Hence the connection is: "You do not know even the mere skill of handling a ladle." "Faithful" means faithful in the fruit of kamma, devoted with the ordinary person's faith in the Triple Gem. Therefore, he said: "May the Venerable One consider me a lay follower... gone for refuge."

Assalāyanasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Assalāyana Sutta is complete.

4. Ghoṭamukhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Ghoṭamukha Sutta.

412. Khemiyā [V 2.0189] nāma rañño deviyā ropitattā taṃ ambavanaṃ khemiyambavananti vuccatīti vadanti. Dhammikoti dhammayutto sabbasova adhammaṃ pahāya dhamme ṭhito. Paribbajati pabbajati etenāti paribbajo, gharāvāsato nikkhamanapubbakaṃ liṅgaggahaṇavasena sīlasamādānaṃ. Etthāti etasmiṃ paribbaje. Sabhāvoti taṃ paribbājaniyaṃ, tehi tehi paribbājakehi anuṭṭhātabbo paṭipattidhammasaṅkhāto sabhāvo. Dhammova pamāṇanti etena mayaṃ ahirimanā cittassa yathāupaṭṭhitaṃ kathema, tasmā taṃ appamāṇaṃ, yo panettha avitatho dhammo, tadeva pamāṇaṃ. Adhigatapaṭipattisaṅkhāto sabhāvo atthi, tassa tumhehi tumhehi bahunā nānāsandassanādi kammena idha bhavitabbaṃ, bahudevettha vattabbanti adhippāyo.

412. They say that because it was planted by Queen Khemī, that mango grove is called Khemī's Mango Grove. 'Dhammika' means one endowed with Dhamma, having entirely abandoned what is not Dhamma and being established in the Dhamma. 'Paribbajo' means that by which one goes forth, that by which one wanders; it is the going forth, the undertaking of precepts by way of adopting the outward signs, preceded by leaving the household life. 'Here' means in this going forth. 'Sabhāva' means that which pertains to going forth, the nature which is the practice, to be undertaken by those various wanderers. 'The Dhamma alone is the measure'—by this, we speak with an unashamed mind as it arises, therefore that mind is immeasurable. But here, whatever Dhamma is not false, that indeed is the measure. There is a nature consisting of the attainment of the practice; you all must develop it here through much action such as diverse views and so on; much indeed should be practiced here—this is the meaning.

414. Sārattarattāti sārajjanavasena rattā, bahularāgavasena abhirattāti attho. Attanā ñāpetabbamatthaṃ anuggahāpeti bodhetīti anuggaho, ñāpitakāraṇaṃ, saha anuggahenāti sānuggahā. Tenāha “sakāraṇā”ti. Kiṃ pana taṃ kāraṇaṃ? Imassādhippāyo “natthi dhammiko paribbajo”ti mayā vutto, addhā panāyasmā udeno yāthāvato dhammikaṃ paribbajaṃ me ācikkhatīti. Tenāha “vuttañheta”ntiādi.

414. 'Sārattarattā' means impassioned, or exceedingly impassioned through strong lust—this is the meaning. 'Anuggaha' is that which causes one to understand the meaning to be known by oneself, that which enlightens; it is the reason for making something known. 'Sānuggahā' means together with a reason. Therefore, it is said, 'with a reason.' But what is that reason? The intention here is: 'There is no righteous wanderer,' as I said. 'Surely, however, venerable Udena will declare to me a righteous wanderer as he actually is.' Therefore, it is said, 'this was said,' and so on.

421. Sabbamidaṃ thāvarajaṅgamaṃ purisakataṃ, tasmā yaṃ kiñci katvā attā posetabbo rakkhitabboti lokāyatanissito nītimaggo ghoṭamukhakanto, tasmā āha “etassa kira jānanasippe”tiādi. Sagge [M 2.0189] nibbatto nāma natthi akattabbameva karaṇato. Devalokapariyāpannadhanaṃ manussānaṃ upakappapuññābhāvato pubbe attanā nihitadhanaṃ “asuke cā”ti ācikkhitvā gato. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

421. All this, whether stationary or moving, is made by a person. Therefore, having done anything whatsoever, one must nourish and protect oneself—this is a path of conduct relying on materialism, pleasing to Ghoṭamukha. Therefore, he said, 'indeed in the art of knowing this,' and so on. There is indeed no one born in heaven from doing what should not be done. Wealth included in the realm of the gods is of no use to humans due to a lack of merit conducive to it. Previously, having declared, 'in such and such a place,' one has departed, having deposited wealth oneself. The rest is easily understood.

Ghoṭamukhasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Ghoṭamukha Sutta is complete.

5. Caṅkīsuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Caṅkī Sutta.

422. Tasminti [V 2.0190] sālavane. Uttarena opāsādanti opāsādagāmassa uttaradisāyaṃ. Uttarenāti ena-saddayogena hi opāsādanti upayogavacanaṃ. Ajjhāvasatīti ettha adhi-ā-saddānaṃ anatthantarataṃ hadaye katvā āha “vasatī”ti. Idāni tesaṃ atthavisesabhāvitaṃ dassento “abhibhavitvā vā āvasatī”tiādimāha. Etthāti opāsādapade. Sattussadantiādīsu pana kathanti āha – “tassa anuppayogattāva sesapadesū”ti. Upa-anu-adhi-iti-evaṃ-pubbake vasanakiriyayāṭṭhāne upayogavacanameva pāpuṇātīti saddavidū icchantīti āha “lakkhaṇaṃ saddasatthato pariyesitabba”nti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “upasaggavasena panettha bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ veditabba”nti. Ussadatā nāmettha bahulatāti taṃ bahulataṃ dassetuṃ “bahujana”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Āvajjitvāti parikkhipitvā.

422. In that sāl grove. 'To the north of Opāsāda' means in the northern direction of the village of Opāsāda. In 'to the north' (`uttarena`), the `ena` suffix governs 'Opāsāda' in a locative sense. Regarding 'He dwells' (`ajjhāvasati`), having considered that the prefixes 'adhi' and 'ā' are essentially synonymous, it is simply said 'he dwells' (`vasati`). Now, to show their distinct meanings, it is said 'having mastered, he dwells,' and so on. 'Here' means in the word 'Opāsāda.' But how is it in cases like 'sattussada' and so on? It is said: 'Because that locative sense does not apply to it, and likewise in the remaining words.' Because grammarians wish that prefixes such as 'upa,' 'anu,' and 'adhi,' when preceding a verb of dwelling, should govern a word in the locative sense, it is said 'the rule must be sought from the science of grammar.' For it is said: 'Here, by the force of the prefix, the locative sense should be understood.' 'Abundance' (`ussadatā`) here means multitude; to indicate that multitude, 'many people,' and so on, is said. 'Having adverted' (`āvajjitvā`) means having surrounded (`parikkhipitvā`).

Raññā viya bhuñjitabbanti vā rājabhoggaṃ. Rañño dāyabhūtanti kulaparamparāya bhoggabhāvena raññā laddhadāyabhūtaṃ. Tenāha “dāyajjanti attho”ti. Rājanīhārena paribhuñjitabbato uddhaṃ paribhogalābhassa seṭṭhadeyyatā nāma natthīti āha – “chattaṃ ussāpetvā rājasaṅkhepena paribhuñjitabba”nti. Titthapabbatādīsūti nadītitthapabbatapādagāmadvāraaṭavīmukhādīsu. Nissaṭṭhapariccattanti muttacāgavasena pariccattaṃ katvā. Etesaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ.

'To be enjoyed like a king' or 'royal enjoyment.' 'Belonging to the king as an inheritance' means obtained by the king as an ancestral possession through family succession. Hence it is said, 'The meaning is inheritance.' Because there is no superior bestowal of enjoyment beyond that to be enjoyed by royal custom, it is said: 'Having raised the parasol, it should be enjoyed with royal ceremony.' 'At fords, mountains, etc.' means at river fords, mountain foothills, village gates, forest edges, and so on. 'Given up, abandoned' means having abandoned by way of unconditional relinquishment. Of these brahmins and householders.

423. Ti sannipatitā. Yo koci viññūnaṃ icchito pañho, tassa pucchitassa yāthāvato kathanasamattho pucchitapañhabyākaraṇasamattho.Kulāpadesādinā mahatī mattā etassāti mahāmatto.

423. They are assembled. Any question desired by the wise, when asked, he is capable of explaining it truthfully, capable of answering the question asked. One of great measure due to designation of lineage, etc., is a great minister.

424. Teti [M 2.0190] “nānāverajjakā”ti vuttabrāhmaṇā. “Ubhato sujāto”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.303; a. ni. ṭī. 3.5.134) ettake vutte yehi kehici dvīhi bhāgehi sujātatā viññāyeyya, sujātasaddo ca “sujāto cārudassano”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 553; theragā. 818) ārohapariṇāhasampattipariyāyoti jātivaseneva sujātataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “mātito ca pitito cā”ti vuttaṃ. Anorasaputtavasenapi loke mātupitusamaññā dissati, idha panassa orasaputtavaseneva icchīyatīti dassetuṃ “saṃsuddhagahaṇīko”ti [V 2.0191] vuttaṃ. Pitā ca mātā ca pitaro, pitūnaṃ pitaro pitāmahā, tesaṃ yugo pitāmahayugo, tasmā yāva sattamā pitāmahayugāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yugasaddo cettha ekasesanayena daṭṭhabbo “yugo ca yugo ca yugā”ti. Evañhi tattha tattha dvinnaṃ gahitameva hoti. Tenāha – “tato uddhaṃ sabbepi pubbapurisā pitāmahaggahaṇeneva gahitā”ti. Purisaggahaṇañcettha ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañhi “mātito”ti pāḷivacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Akkhittoti appattakhepo. Anavakkhittoti saddhathālipākādīsu na avakkhitto. Jātivādenāti hetumhi karaṇavacananti dassetuṃ “kena kāraṇenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ca ubhato…pe… pitāmahayugāti etena brāhmaṇassa yonidosābhāvo dassito saṃsuddhagahaṇikabhāvakittanato. Akkhittoti iminā kiriyāparādhābhāvo. Kiriyāparādhena hi sattā khepaṃ pāpuṇanti. Anupakuṭṭhoti iminā ayuttasaṃsaggābhāvo. Ayuttasaṃsaggampi hi paṭicca sattā akkosaṃ labhanti.

424. These are the brahmins spoken of as 'from various kingdoms.' Regarding 'well-born on both sides,' when this much is said, being well-born might be understood by any two aspects whatsoever; and the word 'well-born,' in contexts such as 'well-born and handsome,' is a synonym for accomplishment in height and girth. Thus, to clarify that being well-born is by way of birth alone, it is said, 'from the mother’s side and from the father’s side.' In the world, the designation of 'mother' and 'father' is seen even in the case of those who are not legitimate children, but to show that here it is desired only in the case of a legitimate child, it is said, 'of pure conception.' Father and mother are 'parents' (pitaro); the parents of parents are 'grandparents' (pitāmahā); their pair is a 'grandparental pair' (pitāmahayugo). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as 'up to the seventh grandparental pair.' The word 'pair' (yuga) here should be understood by the principle of ellipsis (ekasesa), as in 'a pair and a pair become pairs (yugā).' For in that way, in each case, two are included. Therefore, it is said, 'Beyond that, all forefathers are included by the term 'grandparent.'' The inclusion of 'men' (purisa) here should be understood as made by way of an eminent designation. In this way, the Pāli phrase 'from the mother’s side' is supported. 'Uncensured' (akkhitto) means one who has not received blame. 'Not disparaged' (anavakkhitto) means not disparaged in matters of offerings for the deceased, food cooked in a pot, and so on. Regarding 'by reason of birth' (jātivādena), to show that the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause, it is said, 'for what reason,' and so on. Here, by the phrase 'on both sides... up to the seventh grandparental pair,' the brahmin’s freedom from defects of birth is shown by the declaration of his being of pure conception. By 'uncensured,' the absence of faults in action is shown, for beings incur blame due to faults in action. By 'unblemished' (anupakuṭṭho), the absence of improper association is shown, for beings receive abuse on account of improper association.

Issaroti adhipateyyasaṃvattaniyakammaphalena īsanasīlo. Sā panassa issaratā vibhavasampattipaccayā pākaṭā jātāti aḍḍhatāpariyāyabhāvena vadanto “aḍḍhoti issaro”ti āha. Mahantaṃ dhanamassa bhūmigatañceva vehāsaṭṭhañcāti mahaddhano. Tassāti tassa tassa. Vadanti “anvayato byatirekato ca anupasaṅkamanakāraṇaṃ kittemā”ti.

'Lord' (issaro) means one whose nature is to rule, due to the result of kamma that leads to sovereignty. But since his lordship becomes manifest on account of the accomplishment of prosperity, speaking by way of a synonym for wealthiness, he said, '“Wealthy” (aḍḍho) means “lord” (issaro).' 'He has great wealth' (mahaddhano) means great is his wealth, both that which is on the ground and that which is in the air. 'Of him' (tassa) means of each one. They say, 'Let us declare the reason for not approaching, both positively and negatively.'

Adhikarūpoti visiṭṭharūpo uttamasarīro. Dassanaṃ arahatīti dassanīyo. Tenāha “dassanayoggo”ti. Pasādaṃ āvahatīti pāsādiko. Tenāha “cittapasādajananato”ti. Vaṇṇassāti vaṇṇadhātuyā[M 2.0191]. Sarīranti sannivesavisiṭṭho karacaraṇagīvāsīsādi avayavasamudāyo, so ca saṇṭhānamukhena gayhatīti “paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti paramāya…pe… sampattiyā cā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbavaṇṇesu suvaṇṇavaṇṇova uttamoti vuttaṃ “seṭṭhena suvaṇṇavaṇṇena samannāgato”ti. Tathā hi buddhā cakkavattino ca suvaṇṇavaṇṇāva honti. Brahmavacchasīti uttamasarīrābho suvaṇṇābhoti attho. Imameva hi atthaṃ sandhāyāha “mahābrahmuno sarīrasadisena sarīrena samannāgato”ti. Na brahmujugattataṃ. Akhuddāvakāso dassanāyāti ārohapariṇāhasampattiyā avayavapāripūriyā ca dassanāya okāso na khuddako. Tenāha “sabbānevā”tiādi.

'Of superior form' (adhikarūpo) means of distinguished form, of excellent body. 'Handsome' (dassanīyo) means he is worthy of being seen. Hence it is said, 'fit to be seen.' 'Inspiring' (pāsādiko) means he inspires confidence. Hence it is said, 'because he generates mental confidence.' 'Of complexion' (vaṇṇassa) means of the element of color. 'Body' (sarīraṃ) means the collection of limbs—such as hands, feet, neck, and head—distinguished by its arrangement, and this is understood by way of its form. Thus it is said, 'by the supreme beauty of his complexion... and by the perfection...' Among all complexions, the golden complexion is the highest. Thus it is said, 'endowed with the finest golden complexion.' For indeed, Buddhas and wheel-turning monarchs are of golden complexion. 'With the splendor of Brahmā' (brahmavacchasī) means with the radiance of a supreme body, with a golden radiance. With this very meaning in mind, it is said, 'endowed with a body similar to the body of the great Brahmā,' not with the uprightness of Brahmā. 'Not a small opportunity for seeing him' (akhuddāvakāso dassanāya) means that due to the perfection of his height and girth and the fullness of his limbs, the opportunity for seeing him is not small. Hence it is said, 'all...' and so on.

Yamaniyamalakkhaṇaṃ sīlamassa atthīti sīlavā, taṃ panassa rattaññutāya vuddhaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ sīlaṃ assa atthīti vuddhasīlī, tena ca sabbadā samāyogato vuḍḍhasīlena samannāgato. Pañcasīlamattameva sandhāya vadanti tato paraṃ sīlassa tattha abhāvato tesañca ajānanato.

He is 'virtuous' (sīlavā) because he possesses virtue (sīla), which is characterized by restraint and observance. He is 'of mature virtue' (vuddhasīlī) because he possesses that virtue of his which is mature and developed due to his long experience, and he is endowed with that mature virtue because of his constant association with it. They speak with reference only to the five precepts, because of the absence of any virtue beyond that there, and because of their ignorance.

Ṭhānakaraṇasampattiyā [V 2.0192] sikkhāsampattiyā ca katthacipi anūnatāya parimaṇḍalapadāni byañjanāni akkharāni etissāti parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā. Atha vā pajjati attho etenāti padaṃ, nāmādi, yathādhippetamatthaṃ byañjetīti byañjanaṃ vākyaṃ, tesaṃ paripuṇṇatāya parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā. Atthañāpanasādhanatāya vācāva karaṇanti vākkaraṇaṃ, udāharaṇaghoso. Guṇaparipuṇṇabhāvena tassa brāhmaṇassa, tena vā bhāsitabbaatthassa. Pūre puṇṇabhāve. Pūreti ca purimasmiṃ atthe ādhāre bhummaṃ, dutiyasmiṃ visaye. Sukhumālattanenāti iminā tassā vācāya mudusaṇhabhāvamāha. Apalibuddhāya pittasemhādīhi. Sandiṭṭhaṃ sabbaṃ dassetvā viya ekadesakathanaṃ. Vilambitaṃ saṇikaṃ cirāyitvā kathanaṃ. “Sandiddhavilambitādī”ti vā pāṭho. Tattha sandiddhaṃ sandehajanakaṃ. Ādi-saddena khalitānukaḍḍhitādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvāti iminā cassa vācāya atthapāripūriṃ vadanti.

Her words (padāni), syllables (byañjanāni), and letters (akkharāni) are 'well-rounded' (parimaṇḍala) due to the perfection of the places and means of articulation and the perfection of training, being deficient in no respect; thus she is one of 'well-rounded words and syllables' (parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā). Alternatively, a 'word' (padaṃ) is that by which meaning is attained, such as a noun; a 'syllable' (byañjanaṃ) is that which clarifies the intended meaning, a sentence. Due to their completeness, she is one of 'well-rounded words and syllables.' Because speech is the instrument for making meaning known, it is 'articulation' (vākkaraṇaṃ), the sound of an utterance. Due to the perfection of qualities of that brahmin, or of the meaning to be expressed by him. 'Full' (pūre) means in a state of fullness. And 'fills' (pūreti) is in the locative case in the first sense, that of a basis, and in the second, that of a sphere. By 'tenderness' (sukhumālattanena), he speaks of the soft and gentle nature of that speech. Unobstructed by bile, phlegm, and the like. 'Clipped' (sandiṭṭhaṃ) is speaking of a part as if showing the whole. 'Delayed' (vilambitaṃ) is speaking slowly, after a long pause. Or the reading is 'doubtful, delayed, etc.' (sandiddhavilambitādi). Therein, 'doubtful' (sandiddhaṃ) means causing doubt. By the word 'etc.' (ādi), he includes faltering, drawing out, and so on. By 'making the beginning, middle, and end clear,' they speak of the complete fulfillment of meaning in his speech.

425. Sadisāti ekadesena sadisā. Na hi buddhānaṃ guṇehi sabbathā sadisā kecipi guṇā aññesu labbhanti. Itareti attano guṇehi asadisaguṇe. Idanti idaṃ atthajātaṃ. Gopadakanti gāviyā pade ṭhitaudakaṃ. Kulapariyāyenāti kulānukkamena.

425. 'Similar' (sadisā) means similar in one aspect. For no qualities whatsoever found in others are in every way similar to the qualities of the Buddhas. 'Others' (itare) refers to those with qualities dissimilar to his own qualities. 'This' (idaṃ) means this collection of matters. 'A cow's footprint' (gopadakaṃ) means water standing in a cow's footprint. 'By family succession' (kulapariyāyena) means by the order of the lineage.

Tatthāti [M 2.0192] mañcake. Sīhaseyyaṃ kappesīti yathā rāhu asurindo āyāmato vitthārato ubbedhato ca bhagavato rūpakāyassa paricchedaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharonto sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi.

'There' (tattha) means on the couch. 'He assumed a lion's posture' (sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi) means that, just as Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, is unable to grasp the measure of the Blessed One's physical form in length, breadth, or height, so too did he, creating a corresponding formation of psychic power, assume the lion's posture.

Parisuddhaṭṭhena ariyanti āha “ariyaṃ uttamaṃ parisuddha”nti. Anavajjaṭṭhena kusalaṃ, na sukhavipākaṭṭhena. Katthaci caturāsīti pāṇasahassāni katthaci aparimāṇāpi devamanussā yasmā catuvīsatiyā ṭhānesu asaṅkhyeyyā aparimeyyā maggaphalāmataṃ pivanti. Koṭisatasahassādiparimāṇenapi bahū eva. Tasmā anuttarācārasikkhāpanavaseneva bhagavā bahūnaṃ ācariyo. Teti kāmarāgato aññe bhagavatā pahīnakilese.

'Noble' (ariya) is said in the sense of purity: 'noble, supreme, pure.' 'Wholesome' (kusala) means faultless, not in the sense of having a happy result. In some places, eighty-four thousand beings are mentioned; in other places, countless devas and humans, because in twenty-four locations, innumerable and immeasurable beings drink the deathless nectar of the path and fruit. Even by a measure of a hundred thousand crores, there are indeed many. Therefore, by the power of teaching the unsurpassed training in conduct, the Blessed One is the teacher of many. 'They' (te) refers to those defilements other than sensual desire, which were abandoned by the Blessed One.

Apāpapurekkhāroti apāpehi purakkharīyati, na vā pāpaṃ purato karotītipi apāpapurekkhāroti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “apāpe nava lokuttaradhamme”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha apāpeti pāpapapaṭipakkhe pāparahite ca. Brahmani bhavā, brahmuno vā hitā garukaraṇādinā, brahmānaṃ vā maggaṃ jānātīti brahmaññā, tassā brahmaññāya pajāya.

'Foremost in non-evil' (apāpapurekkhāro) means he is honored by those without evil, or that he does not place evil before himself. To explain this meaning, it is said: 'in the nine supramundane states, which are without evil,' and so on. There, 'without evil' (apāpe) refers to what is the opposite of evil and is devoid of evil. It arises in Brahmā, or is beneficial to Brahmā through honoring and so on, or it knows the path of Brahmā—thus 'brahmaññā'. 'For his brahmaññā people' refers to the populace with that quality of brahmaññā.

Tiroraṭṭhā [V 2.0193] tirojanapadāti ettha rajjaṃ raṭṭhaṃ rājanti rājāno etenāti katvā. Tadekadesabhūtā padesā pana janapado janā pajjanti ettha sukhajīvikaṃ pāpuṇantīti katvā. Pucchāya dosaṃ sallakkhetvāti sambandho. Bhagavā vissajjeti tesaṃ upanissayasampattiṃ cintetvāti adhippāyo. Navakāti āgantukabhāvena amhākaṃ abhinavā.

'Beyond kingdoms, beyond territories' (tiroraṭṭhā tirojanapadā). Here, a kingdom (rajjaṃ) is a `raṭṭha`; it is so called because kings (rājāno) rule (rājanti) by means of it. A 'territory' (janapada), however, is a region that is a portion of that, so called because people (janā) go there (pajjanti), attaining a comfortable living. 'Having discerned the fault in the question' (pucchāya dosaṃ sallakkhetvā)—this is the connection. The Blessed One answers, considering their accomplishment of supporting conditions—this is the meaning. 'Newcomers' (navakā) means they are new to us on account of being visitors.

426. Opāteti nippātetīti attho. Tathābhūto ca tattha pesitā hotīti vuttaṃ “pavesetī”ti. Saṃpurakkharontīti sakkaccaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ karonti. Tenāha “purato katvā vicarantī”ti.

426. 'Opāteti' means 'to strike down' or 'to destroy.' And being of such a nature, he is sent there—thus it is said 'he causes to enter' (paveseti). 'Saṃpurakkharonti' means they respectfully make him foremost. Hence it is said: 'they live, having made him foremost' (purato katvā vicaranti).

427. Sudde bahi katvā raho sāsitabbaṭṭhena mantā eva taṃtaṃatthapaṭipattihetutāya padanti mantapadaṃ vedaṃ. Tenāha “vedo”ti. Evaṃ kirāti paramparabhāvena ābhatanti ācariyaparamparāya ābhataṃ. Pāvacanasaṅkhātasampattiyāti [M 2.0193] pamukhavacanamhi udattādisampattiyā. Sāvittiādīhi chandabandhehi vaggabandhehi cāti gāyattīādīhi ajjhāyānuvākādīhi chandabandhehi ca vaggabandhehi ca. Sampādetvāti padasampattiṃ ahāpetvā. Pavattāroti vā pāvacanavasena vattāro. Sajjhāyitanti gāyanavasena sajjhāyitaṃ, taṃ pana padeneva icchitanti āha “padasampattivasenā”ti. Aññesaṃ vuttanti pāvacanavasena aññesaṃ vuttaṃ. Rāsikatanti iruvedayajuvedasāmavedādivasena, tatthāpi paccekaṃ mantabrahmādivasena ajjhāyānuvākādivasena rāsikataṃ. Dibbena cakkhunā oloketvāti dibbacakkhuparibhaṇḍena yathākammūpagañāṇena sattānaṃ kammassakataṃ, paccakkhato dassanaṭṭhena dibbacakkhusadisena pubbenivāsañāṇena atītakappe brāhmaṇānaṃ mantajjhenavidhiñca oloketvā. Pāvacanena saha saṃsandetvāti kassapasammāsambuddhassa yaṃ vacanaṃ vaṭṭasannissitaṃ, tena saha aviruddhaṃ katvā. Na hi tesaṃ vivaṭṭasannissito attho paccakkho hoti. Aparāpareti aṭṭhakādīhi aparāpare, pacchimā okkākarājakālādīsu uppannā. Pakkhipitvāti aṭṭhakādīhi ganthitamantapadesu kilesasannissitapadānaṃ tattha tattha pade pakkhipanaṃ katvā. Viruddhe akaṃsūti brāhmaṇadhammikasuttādīsu (khu. ni. brāhmaṇadhammikasuttaṃ) āgatanayeneva saṃkilesikatthadīpanato paccanīkabhūte akaṃsu.

427. Having excluded the common people, the mantras should be taught in private; hence, they are called 'mantra-words' (mantapadaṃ) because they are counsels (`mantā`) and the means (`pada`) for attaining their respective meanings, which is the Veda. Therefore, it is said, 'the Veda' (vedo). 'Thus it is said' (evaṃ kira) means it is traditionally handed down through the lineage of teachers. By the excellence known as 'recitation' (pāvacana), it means the excellence of intonation, etc., in the foremost utterance. With the meters like Sāvittī and so on, and the groupings—that is, by the meters like Gāyattī and so on, the chapters, the sections, and so on, and by the metrical and group arrangements. 'Sampādetvā' means having perfected the excellence of the words without losing it. 'Pavattāro' means those who recite through the method of recitation. 'Sajjhāyitaṃ' means studied through chanting, but it is desired that it be done word by word; hence it is said, 'by the excellence of the words' (padasampattivasena). 'Others have spoken' (aññesaṃ vuttaṃ) means through the method of recitation, others have spoken. 'Arranged in groups' (rāsikataṃ) means arranged in groups like the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and so on; and there too, individually, by the mantras, the Brāhmaṇas, and so on, the chapters, the sections, and so on, arranged in groups. Having surveyed with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā oloketvā)—that is, with the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings according to their karma (the instrument of the divine eye), having surveyed the ownership of karma of beings; and with the knowledge of past lives (which is like the divine eye in its direct seeing), having surveyed the method of mantra study of the brahmins in past eons. Having harmonized with the recitation (pāvacanena saha saṃsandetvā)—the words of the Buddha Kassapa, which are connected with the round of existence, are made non-contradictory with it. For their meaning connected with liberation is not directly evident. 'Aparāpare' means the later ones like the Aṭṭhakas and so on, those who arose in the later times like the Okkākarāja period. 'Pakkhipitvā' means having inserted the words connected with defilements here and there into the compiled mantra passages by the Aṭṭhakas and so on. 'They did what was contradictory' (viruddhe akaṃsu)—as in the Brāhmaṇadhammikasutta and so on, they did what was contradictory by explaining the defiled meaning, in a manner that became hostile.

428. Paṭipāṭiyā ghaṭitāti paṭipāṭiyā sambaddhā. Paramparasaṃsattāti ādāniyāya yaṭṭhiyā saṃsattā. Tenāha “yaṭṭhiggāhakena cakkhumatā”ti. Purimassāti maṇḍalākārena ṭhitāya andhaveṇiyā sabbapurimassa hatthena sabbapacchimassa kacchaṃ gaṇhāpetvā. Divasampīti anekadivasampi[V 2.0194]. Cakkhussa anāgatabhavaṃ ñatvā yathāakkantaṭṭhāneyeva anupatitvā akkamanaṃva sallakkhetvā “kahaṃ cakkhumā kahaṃ maggo”ti pariveditvā.

428. 'Connected in sequence' (paṭipāṭiyā ghaṭitā) means connected in sequence. 'Linked in succession' (paramparasaṃsattā) means linked like those clinging to a relay stick. Hence it is said, 'by the one with vision holding the stick' (yaṭṭhiggāhakena cakkhumatā). 'Of the foremost one' (purimassa) means having caused the foremost one in the line of blind people (andhaveṇī), standing in the form of a circle, to grasp the armpit of the hindmost one with his hand. 'Even for a day' (divasampi) means even for many days. Knowing the future state of the one with vision, stepping exactly where one had stepped before, observing the stepping as if one knew, and lamenting, 'Where is the one with vision? Where is the path?'

Pāḷiāgatesu dvīsūti saddhā anussavoti imesu dvīsu. Evarūpeti yathā saddhānussavā, evarūpe eva paccakkhagāhinoti attho. Tayoti ruciākāraparivitakkadiṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyo. Bhūtavipākāti bhūtatthaniṭṭhāyakā adhippetatthasādhakā, vuttavipariyāyena abhūtatthavipākā veditabbā[M 2.0194]. Etthāti etesu saddhāyitādivatthūsu. Ekaṃseneva niṭṭhaṃ gantuṃ nālaṃ anekantikattā saddhādiggāhassa. Upari pucchāya maggaṃ vivaritvā ṭhapesi saccānurakkhāya ñātukāmatāya uppāditattā. Passati hi bhagavā – mayā “saccamanurakkhatā…pe… niṭṭhaṃ gantu”nti vutte saccānurakkhaṇaṃ ñātukāmo māṇavo “kittāvatā”tiādinā pucchissati, tassa taṃ vissajjetvā saccānubodhe pucchāya avasaraṃ datvā tassa upanissaye upakāradhamme kathessāmīti. Tena vuttaṃ – “upari pucchāya maggaṃ vivaritvā ṭhapesī”ti.

In the two [terms] found in the Pāli, that is, in these two: 'faith' (saddhā) and 'hearsay' (anussava). 'Of such a kind' (evarūpe) means that just as there is faith and hearsay, so too are those who grasp what is directly perceived—this is the meaning. 'Three' (tayo) refers to inclination, reasoning about appearances, and acceptance through reflecting on views. 'Having true results' (bhūtavipākā) means those that establish the true meaning, accomplishing the intended purpose. Conversely, those that have untrue results (abhūtavipākā) should be understood. 'Here' (ettha) refers to these matters involving faith and the like. One cannot decisively reach a conclusion due to the inconclusive nature of grasping at faith and the like. Further on, in response to a question, he opened up and established the path for the sake of protecting the truth, because the question was prompted by a desire to know. For the Blessed One sees: 'When I have said, “By protecting the truth... one reaches a conclusion,” the young man, desiring to understand the protection of the truth, will ask, “To what extent...?” and so on. Having answered him, and giving an opportunity for a question regarding the realization of truth, I will explain the supporting and beneficial teachings relevant to his potential.' Therefore, it is said: 'Further on, in response to a question, he opened up and established the path'.

430. Attānaññeva sandhāya vadati, yato vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ – “yaṃ kho panāyamāyasmā dhammaṃ deseti, gambhīro so dhammo duddaso duranubodho”tiādi. Lubbhantīti lobhanīyā yathā “apāyagamanīyā”ti āha “lobhanīyesu dhammesūti lobhadhammesū”ti. Yathā vā rūpādidhammā lobhanīyā, evaṃ lobhoti āha “lobhanīyesu dhammesūti lobhadhammesū”ti. Tenevāha – “yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.133; vibha. 203). Ese nayo sesapadadvayepi.

430. He speaks referring to himself, as stated in the Pāli: 'The Dhamma that this venerable one teaches is deep, hard to see, hard to understand,' and so on. 'Lubbanti' is explained as 'enticing' (lobhanīyā), a term formed like 'leading to the plane of misery' (apāyagamanīyā). Hence it is said, 'in enticing things' (lobhanīyesu dhammesu), that is, 'in things pertaining to greed' (lobhadhammesu). Or, just as things like form are enticing, so too is greed itself. Hence it is said, 'in enticing things' (lobhanīyesu dhammesu), that is, 'in things pertaining to greed' (lobhadhammesu). Therefore, it is said: 'Whatever in the world is agreeable and pleasurable, there this craving, when arising, arises; there, when settling, it settles.' This is the method for the remaining two terms as well.

432. Nivesetīti ṭhapeti paṭṭhapeti. Payirupāsatīti upaṭṭhānavasena upagantvā nisīdati. Suyyati etenāti sotanti āha “pasādasota”nti. Tañhi savanāya odahitabbanti. Dhāreti sandhāreti tattheva manaṃ ṭhapeti. Atthatoti yathāvuttassa dhammassa atthato. Kāraṇatoti yuttito hetudāharaṇehi upapattito. Olokananti evametanti yathāsabhāvato paññācakkhunā daṭṭhabbataṃ khamanti, tañca mahantassa maṇino pajjalantassa viya āvikatvā atthassa citte upaṭṭhānanti āha “idhā”tiādi. Kattukamyatāchandoti kattukāmatāsaṅkhāto kusalacchando. Vāyamatītiādito catunnampi vīriyānaṃ vasena vāyāmaṃ parakkamaṃ karoti. Maggapadhānaṃ padahatīti maggāvahaṃ maggapariyāpannañca sammappadhānaṃ padahati, padahanavasena taṃ paripūreti. Paramasaccanti amoghadhammattā paramatthasaccaṃ. Sahajātanāmakāyenāti maggapaññāsahajātanāmakāyena[V 2.0195]. Tadevāti tadeva paramasaccaṃ nibbānaṃ. Tenevāha – “sacchikiriyābhisamayena vibhūtaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto passatī”ti.

432. ‘Niveseti’ means ‘establishes, sets up’. ‘Payirupāsati’ means ‘approaches and sits near in order to attend’. ‘Suyyati etenāti sota’ means ‘that by which one hears, thus it is called ‘ear’ (sota)’, and he says, ‘the ear of confidence (pasādasota)’. For that should be directed towards hearing. ‘Dhāreti’ means ‘sustains, holds firmly, fixes the mind there’. ‘Atthato’ means ‘in terms of the meaning of the Dhamma as stated’. ‘Kāraṇato’ means ‘in terms of the reason, the justification, the logical basis, through cause, example, and reason’. ‘Olokana’ means the fitness to be seen with the eye of wisdom according to its intrinsic nature as ‘it is so’; and that, like a great, blazing jewel, is the arising of the meaning in the mind, having been revealed, as he says, ‘here’ and so on. ‘Kattukamyatāchanda’ is the wholesome desire to act, known as the desire to do good. ‘Vāyamati’ and so on refers to the exertion and striving through the four efforts. ‘Maggapadhānaṃ padahati’ means ‘strives with the right effort that leads to the path and is included in the path, fulfilling it through exertion’. ‘Paramasacca’ is the ultimate truth because it is the non-deceptive Dhamma. ‘Sahajātanāmakāyena’ refers to the mental body born together with path-wisdom. ‘Tadeva’ is that very ultimate truth, Nibbāna. Therefore, he says: ‘By realizing and directly experiencing, he makes it clear and evident, he sees it’.

433-4. Maggānubodhoti [M 2.0195] maggapaṭipāṭiyā bodho bujjhanaṃ, yesaṃ kilesānaṃ samucchindanavasena maggappaṭivedho, tesaṃ paṭipassambhanavasena pavattamānaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ, maggena paṭividdhāni saccāni, paramatthasaccameva vā anurūpabujjhananti adhippāyo. “Saccānuppattīti phalasacchikiriyā”ti vuttaṃ. Evañhi sati heṭṭhā vuttā saddhāpaṭilābhādayo dvādasa dhammā saccānuppattiyā upakārā honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “tesaṃyevāti heṭṭhā vuttānaṃ dvādasanna”nti. Nāyaṃ “tesaṃyevā”ti padassa attho. Satipi kusalavipākādibhāvena nānatte vatthārammaṇabhūmikiccādivasena pana sadisāti upāyatova maggadhammā āsevitā bahulīkatā phalabhūtāti vattabbataṃ arahatīti taṃsadise tabbohāraṃ katvā “tesaṃ maggasampayuttadhammāna”nti vuttaṃ. Evañhi āsevanāgahaṇaṃ samatthitaṃ, na aññathā. Na hi ekacittakkhaṇikānaṃ maggadhammānaṃ āsevanā, bahulīkammaṃ vā atthīti. Tulanāti vipassanā. Sā hi vuṭṭhānagāminibhūtā maggappadhānassa bahukārā tassa abhāve maggappadhānasseva abhāvato, evaṃ ussāho tulanāya chando ussāhassa bahukārotiādinā heṭṭhimassa uparimūpakārataṃ suviññeyyamevāti āha – “iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo”ti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

433-4. ‘Maggānubodha’ means ‘awakening or understanding in the sequence of the path’; the penetration of the path by way of uprooting defilements; the fruit of recluseship that arises by way of pacifying them; the truths penetrated by the path; or the appropriate understanding of the ultimate truth itself—this is the intention. It is said: ‘Realization of the truth (saccānuppatti) means direct experience of the fruit’. Thus, when the twelve qualities previously mentioned, such as the acquisition of faith, are present, they assist in the realization of the truth. Therefore, it is said, ‘of those very ones (tesaṃyeva)’, meaning ‘of the twelve previously mentioned’. This is not the meaning of the word ‘tesaṃyeva’ itself. Even though there is diversity in terms of wholesome results and so on, in terms of basis, object, plane, function, and so forth, they are similar. Thus, the path factors, when cultivated and frequently practiced, are worthy of being called ‘the fruit’ by way of being a means. By considering them as similar and applying this usage, it is said, ‘of those path-associated states’. In this way, the understanding of cultivation is established, not otherwise. For the path factors, being momentary, do not have cultivation or frequent practice. ‘Tulanā’ refers to insight (vipassanā). For insight, being conducive to emergence, greatly aids the striving for the path. In its absence, the striving for the path itself is absent. Thus, effort aids insight, zeal aids effort, and so on. The supporting role of the lower for the upper is easily understood. Therefore, he says, ‘In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances’. The rest is easily understood.

Caṅkīsuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Caṅkī Sutta is complete.

6. Esukārīsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Esukārī Sutta

437. Koṭṭhāsanti [V 2.0196] maṃsabhāgaṃ. Laggāpeyyunti nhārunā vā vākena vā bandhitvā purisassa hatthe vā vasanagehe vā olambanavasena bandheyyuṃ. Satthadhammanti satthikesu satthavāhena paṇetabbaṃ āṇādhammaṃ. Tassa nikkhamanatthanti taṃ mūlaṃ satthikehi nittharaṇatthaṃ. Pāpaṃ assāti paricarantassa pāricariyāya ahitaṃva assa. Tenāha “na seyyo”ti. Uccakulīnādayo dutiyavārādīhi vuccanti, idha upadhivipattisampattiyo pāpiyādipadehi vuttāti adhippāyo. Tenāha – “pāpiyoti pāpako lāmako attabhāvo assā”ti. Seyyaṃsoti hitakoṭṭhāso, hitasabhāvoti attho. Uccakulīnatāti karaṇatthe paccattavacananti āha “uccākulīnattenā”ti. “Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”tiādīsu [M 2.0196] (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.305; 3.141; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.425; udā. 53; apa. aṭṭha. 2.7.20; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 4.4; cariyā. aṭṭha. 1.nidānakathā; 2.pakiṇṇakakathā; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.2.1; a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.1; vajira. ṭī. ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā; sārattha. ṭī. 1.ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā; netti. ṭī. ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā; ma. ni. ṭī. 1.1) viya vaṇṇasaddo idha pasaṃsāpariyāyoti āha “vessopi hi uḷāravaṇṇo hotī”ti.

437. ‘Koṭṭhāsa’ means ‘a portion of meat’. ‘Laggāpeyyuṃ’ means ‘they should tie it with sinews or bark and suspend it from a man’s hand or in a dwelling’. ‘Satthadhamma’ means ‘the law of the caravan, the rule to be enacted by the caravan leader among the caravan members’. ‘Tassa nikkhamanatthaṃ’ means ‘for the purpose of the caravan members getting free from that debt’. ‘Pāpaṃ assa’ means ‘it would be harmful to one who attends to such service’. Therefore, he says, ‘it would not be better’. ‘High-born’ and so on are explained by way of the second round and so on; here, the intention is that the misfortunes and fortunes of attachment are described with words like ‘worse’ and so forth. Therefore, he says: ‘‘Pāpiyo’ means ‘his state of being would be bad and inferior’’. ‘Seyyaṃso’ refers to ‘the beneficial share’, meaning ‘a nature that is beneficial’. ‘Uccakulīnatā’ is in the instrumental case, therefore he says, ‘by high birth’. Like in passages such as ‘The Tathāgata’s complexion would not decline’ (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.305; 3.141; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.425; Udā. 53; Apa. Aṭṭha. 2.7.20; Bu. Vaṃ. Aṭṭha. 4.4; Cariyā. Aṭṭha. 1.nidānakathā; 2.pakiṇṇakakathā; Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā; Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 1.2.1; A. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1.1; Vajira. Ṭī. ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā; Sārattha. Ṭī. 1.ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā; Netti. Ṭī. ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā; Ma. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1), the word ‘vaṇṇa’ here is a synonym for praise. Therefore, he says, ‘Even a Vessa may possess excellent praise’.

440. “Niravo padasaddo soḷāragottassa akiṇṇamattikāpatto tiṭṭheyya asaṅgacārī”ti vuttattā bhikkhā caritabbāva, ayaṃ tesaṃ kuladhammoti adhippāyo. Haritvāti apanetvā. Sattajīvo sattavāṇijako. Gopeti rakkhatīti gopo, ārakkhādhikāre niyutto. Asanti lūnanti tenāti asitaṃ, lavittaṃ. Vividhaṃ bhāraṃ ābhañjanti olambanti etthāti byābhaṅgī, kājaṃ.

440. Since it is said, ‘The footstep of the one of the Soḷāra clan is silent; with an unsoiled clay bowl, he should stand, wandering unattached’, therefore alms should be sought. This is their family custom—such is the meaning. ‘Haritvā’ means ‘having taken away’, that is, ‘having removed’. ‘Sattajīvo’ means ‘a trader in living beings’. ‘Gopeti’ means ‘he protects, he guards’, thus ‘gopa’ (cowherd), appointed to the duty of protection. ‘Asitaṃ’ means ‘that by which one cuts’, thus ‘asitaṃ’, the sickle. ‘Byābhaṅgī’ means ‘that on which various loads are brought and hung’, thus ‘byābhaṅgī’, the carrying pole.

441. Anussaratoti anussaraṇahetu kulavaṃsānussaraṇakkhaṇe khattiyotiādinā saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tenāha “porāṇe…pe… anussariyamāne”ti. Uccanīcattajānanatthañca kulavavatthānaṃ kataṃ hotīti khattiyādikulakammunā tesaṃ catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ sandhanaṃ jīvikaṃ paññapenti brāhmaṇā, tathāgato pana lokuttaradhammameva purisassa sandhanaṃ paññapeti tena sattassa lokaggabhāvasiddhito. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

441. ‘Anussarato’ means ‘because of recollecting’. At the moment of recollecting the family lineage, one is designated as ‘khattiya’, and so on. Therefore, he says, ‘ancient… and so forth… when recollected’. The determination of high and low birth is also established so as to know the difference. Thus, the brahmins teach the connection and livelihood of those four castes—khattiya and so on—through their caste duties. However, the Tathāgata teaches only the supramundane Dhamma as the connection for a person, by which the highest state of that being is achieved. The rest is easily understood.

Esukārīsuttavaṇṇanā līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Esukārī Sutta is complete.

7. Dhanañjānisuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Dhanañjāni Sutta

445. Rājagahaṃ [V 2.0197] parikkhipitvā ṭhitapabbatassāti paṇḍavapabbataṃ sandhāyāha. Rājagahanagarassa dakkhiṇadisābhāge pabbatassa samīpe ṭhito janapado dakkhiṇāgiri. Taṇḍulapuṭakānaṃ pāli etthāti taṇḍulapāli. Tassa [M 2.0197] kira dvārasamīpe taṇḍulavāṇijā taṇḍulapasibbake vivaritvā paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapetvā nisīdanti, tenassa “taṇḍulapālidvāra”nti samaññā ahosi. Sabbameva sassaṃ gaṇhātīti daliddakassakānaṃ divasaparibbayamattameva vissajjetvā sabbameva āyato nipphannaṃ dhaññaṃ gaṇhāti. Mandasassānīti mandanipphattikāni sassāni.

445. ‘Of the mountain that stands surrounding Rājagaha’—this refers to the Paṇḍava mountain. Dakkhiṇāgiri is a district in the southern part of the city of Rājagaha, located near a mountain. The line of rice bundles is here, hence Taṇḍulapāli. It is said that rice merchants, opening their rice sacks, would sit in order near its gate, arranging them in rows; hence, it became known as 'Taṇḍulapālidvāra.' He takes all the grain—meaning he releases only enough for the daily expenses of the impoverished farmers, taking for himself all the grain produced from his resources. 'Poor crops' means crops with low production.

446. Iminā nayenāti dāsakammakarassa nivāsanabhattavettanānuppadānena maṅgaladivasesu dhanavatthālaṅkārānuppadānādinā ca posetabbo. Mittāmaccānaṃ piyavacanaatthacariyāsamānattatādi mittāmaccakaraṇīyaṃ kattabbaṃ, tathā ñātisālohitānaṃ. Tattha āvāhavivāhasambaddhena “amhākaṃ ime”ti ñāyantīti ñātī, mātāpitādisambaddhatāya samānalohitāti sālohitā. Sammā dadantesupi asajjanato natthi etesaṃ tithīti atithi, tesaṃ attanā samānaparibhogavasena atithikaraṇīyaṃ kātabbaṃ, atithibalīti attho. Ñātakabhūtapubbā pettivisayaṃ upagatā pubbapetā, dakkhiṇeyyesu kālena kālaṃ dānaṃ datvā tesaṃ uddisanaṃ pubbapetakaraṇīyaṃ, petabalīti attho. Gandhapupphavilepanajālābhattehi kālena kālaṃ devatānaṃ pūjā devatākaraṇīyaṃ, devatābalīti attho, rājakiccakaraṇaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ rājakaraṇīyaṃ. Ayampi kāyoti attano kāyaṃ sandhāya vadati. Imamatthaṃ sandhāyāha “iminā nayena attho veditabbo”ti.

446. In this manner—one should support servants and laborers by providing clothing, food, and wages, and by offering wealth, garments, ornaments, and so on, on auspicious occasions. For friends and advisors, one should perform the duties of a friend and advisor by speaking kind words, acting for their welfare, treating them as equals, and so on; and likewise for relatives and kin. Herein, 'relatives' are those known as 'these are ours' through connection by marriage; 'kin' are those of the same blood through connection to one's mother, father, and so on. Since there is no fixed date for them, they are called 'atithi' (without a date); one should perform the duty to guests by sharing one's own provisions with them—this is the meaning of 'guest offering.'
